Quantum Mechanics — Contents Appendix A

Appendix ASolutions to the Exercises

This appendix collects the complete solutions to the exercises at the end of each chapter. Before reading a solution, please be sure to work through the problem yourself at least once. If you get stuck along the way, go back to the hints at the end of the chapter and to the worked examples in the text, and then read the solution here. From the end of each solution, you can return to the corresponding chapter.

Chapter 1: Why Is Quantum Mechanics Hard? — A World Where the Common Sense of Classical Physics Does Not Apply

Exercise 1.1: Calculating the de Broglie wavelength

Solution

The momentum of a particle with kinetic energy $E$ is $p=\sqrt{2mE}$, and its de Broglie wavelength is $\lambda=h/p=h/\sqrt{2mE}$.

(a) Thermal neutron: $m_{\mathrm n}=1.6749\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $E=25.3\ \mathrm{meV}=25.3\times10^{-3}\times1.6022\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}=4.053\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{J}$, so $p=\sqrt{2\times1.6749\times10^{-27}\times4.053\times10^{-21}}=\sqrt{1.3577\times10^{-47}}=3.685\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, and therefore $$ \lambda=\frac{6.626\times10^{-34}}{3.685\times10^{-24}}\ \mathrm{m}=1.798\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}=0.180\ \mathrm{nm} $$ Checking with the formula in the hint, $0.0286/\sqrt{0.0253}=0.0286/0.1591=0.180\ \mathrm{nm}$, which agrees.

(b) Proton ($m_{\mathrm p}=1.6726\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$): for $E=1\ \mathrm{eV}$, $\lambda=0.0286\ \mathrm{nm}/\sqrt{1}=0.0286\ \mathrm{nm}=28.6\ \mathrm{pm}$ (more precisely, $28.62\ \mathrm{pm}$).

(c) Electron with speed $v=c/100=2.998\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m/s}$: $\lambda=\dfrac{h}{m_{\mathrm e}v}=\dfrac{6.626\times10^{-34}}{9.109\times10^{-31}\times2.998\times10^{6}}\ \mathrm{m}=2.426\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}=0.243\ \mathrm{nm}$. This wavelength is exactly 100 times the Compton wavelength of the electron, $h/(m_{\mathrm e}c)=2.426\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}$. The kinetic energy is $\tfrac12m_{\mathrm e}v^2=25.5\ \mathrm{eV}$, and since the speed is $1/100$ of the speed of light, the nonrelativistic formula is adequate.

Compared with the interatomic spacing of a crystal, $0.25\ \mathrm{nm}$, the values (a) $0.180\ \mathrm{nm}$ and (c) $0.243\ \mathrm{nm}$ are of the same order and are well suited to observing diffraction by a crystal. The value $0.0286\ \mathrm{nm}$ in (b) is short, about $1/9$ of the interatomic spacing, so by the Bragg condition the diffraction angle is small (for planes with a spacing of $0.25\ \mathrm{nm}$, $\sin\theta=\lambda/2d=0.057$ and $\theta\approx3^\circ$), and diffraction is hard to observe. A proton carries charge and interacts strongly with matter, so it cannot penetrate into a crystal.

Exercise 1.2: An electron confined to $1\ \mathrm{nm}$

Solution

From $\Delta p=m_{\mathrm e}\Delta v$ and $\Delta x\,\Delta p\ge\hbar/2$, we obtain $$ \Delta v_{\min}=\frac{\hbar}{2m_{\mathrm e}\Delta x}=\frac{1.0546\times10^{-34}}{2\times9.109\times10^{-31}\times1\times10^{-9}}\ \mathrm{m/s}=5.79\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m/s} $$ which is $1/10$ of the value for $\Delta x=0.1\ \mathrm{nm}$ in Example 1.2.

(a) Letting $p\sim\hbar/\Delta x$, we get $$ E\sim\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_{\mathrm e}\Delta x^2}=\frac{(1.0546\times10^{-34})^2}{2\times9.109\times10^{-31}\times(10^{-9})^2}\ \mathrm{J}=\frac{1.112\times10^{-68}}{1.822\times10^{-48}}\ \mathrm{J}=6.10\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{J}=0.0381\ \mathrm{eV}=38.1\ \mathrm{meV} $$ (we divided by $1.602\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J/eV}$).

(b) Using the lower bound $\Delta p=\hbar/(2\Delta x)=5.27\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$ set by the uncertainty principle, we find $E=(\Delta p)^2/(2m_{\mathrm e})=(5.27\times10^{-26})^2/(1.822\times10^{-30})\ \mathrm{J}=1.53\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{J}=9.52\ \mathrm{meV}$. The value in (a) is exactly four times this, and (b) is the minimum value that follows from the uncertainty principle.

Both are of the same order as the thermal energy at room temperature, $k_{\mathrm B}T=25.9\ \mathrm{meV}$. If an electron is confined to a region smaller than $1\ \mathrm{nm}$, the kinetic energy due to the confinement exceeds the thermal energy at room temperature. This is why quantum effects become important in nanometer-scale structures.

Exercise 1.3: Unit conversion for infrared absorption

Solution

The wavelength is $\lambda=1/\tilde\nu=1/(1000\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}})=10^{-3}\ \mathrm{cm}=10\ \mathrm{\mu m}$. Since $1\ \mathrm{eV}=8065.54\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, the energy is $E=1000/8065.54\ \mathrm{eV}=0.12398\ \mathrm{eV}=124.0\ \mathrm{meV}$. The frequency is $\nu=c\tilde\nu=2.998\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s}\times1000\times10^{2}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}=2.998\times10^{13}\ \mathrm{Hz}=29.98\ \mathrm{THz}$ (using $1\ \mathrm{eV}\leftrightarrow241.799\ \mathrm{THz}$ gives the same result, $0.12398\times241.799=29.98$). Converted to a temperature, $E/k_{\mathrm B}=0.12398\times11604.5\ \mathrm{K}=1438.8\ \mathrm{K}$.

The thermal energy at room temperature, $300\ \mathrm{K}$, is $k_{\mathrm B}T=25.85\ \mathrm{meV}$, so the ratio is $E/k_{\mathrm B}T=124.0/25.85=4.80$ (one may equally write $=1438.8/300$). The occupation of the excited state is $e^{-4.80}=8.3\times10^{-3}$ times that of the ground state, only about $0.8\ \%$. That is, the vibration of such a molecule is mostly in the ground state at room temperature, and a vibrationally excited state is produced only when infrared light is absorbed (in other words, when the molecule is excited).

Exercise 1.4: Designing the band gap of a light-emitting diode

Solution

From $E_{\mathrm g}=hc/\lambda=1239.84\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}/\lambda$, we obtain $$ 650\ \mathrm{nm}:\ \frac{1239.84}{650}=1.907\ \mathrm{eV},\qquad 530\ \mathrm{nm}:\ \frac{1239.84}{530}=2.339\ \mathrm{eV},\qquad 1.55\ \mathrm{\mu m}=1550\ \mathrm{nm}:\ \frac{1239.84}{1550}=0.800\ \mathrm{eV} $$ AlGaInP-based semiconductors are used for red light ($E_{\mathrm g}\approx1.9\ \mathrm{eV}$), InGaN-based ones for green light ($E_{\mathrm g}\approx2.3\ \mathrm{eV}$), and InGaAsP-based ones for optical communication at $1.55\ \mathrm{\mu m}$ ($E_{\mathrm g}\approx0.80\ \mathrm{eV}$, smaller than the $1.12\ \mathrm{eV}$ of Si). With the band gap of Si, $1.12\ \mathrm{eV}$ ($1107\ \mathrm{nm}$), light of the optical-communication wavelength $1.55\ \mathrm{\mu m}$ can be neither absorbed nor emitted.

Exercise 1.5: Resolution of the STM

Solution

For $W=5.0\ \mathrm{eV}$, $\kappa=\dfrac{\sqrt{2m_{\mathrm e}W}}{\hbar}=\dfrac{\sqrt{2\times9.109\times10^{-31}\times5.0\times1.602\times10^{-19}}}{1.0546\times10^{-34}}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}=1.1456\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}=11.46\ \mathrm{nm^{-1}}$. When the separation shrinks by $0.05\ \mathrm{nm}$, the current increases by a factor of $e^{2\kappa\times0.05\ \mathrm{nm}}=e^{2\times11.456\times0.05}=e^{1.1456}=3.14$.

The change in separation $\Delta d$ for which the current increases by $10\ \%$ (becomes $1.1$ times as large) satisfies $e^{2\kappa\Delta d}=1.1$, so $$ \Delta d=\frac{\ln1.1}{2\kappa}=\frac{0.09531}{2\times1.1456\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}}=4.16\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}=4.2\ \mathrm{pm} $$ In other words, an STM that can read the current to an accuracy of $10\ \%$ can detect a change in separation with an accuracy of about $4\ \mathrm{pm}$ ($0.004\ \mathrm{nm}$). This is about $1/50$ of the size of an atom (about $0.2\ \mathrm{nm}$), so it can fully resolve the corrugation of an atomic surface.

Exercise 1.6: Spreading of an electron wave packet

Solution

The time for the width to double is $t_2=\dfrac{2\sqrt3\,m_{\mathrm e}\Delta x_0^{2}}{\hbar}$. With $\Delta x_0=10\ \mathrm{nm}=10^{-8}\ \mathrm{m}$, we have $$ t_2=\frac{3.464\times9.109\times10^{-31}\times(10^{-8})^2}{1.0546\times10^{-34}}\ \mathrm{s}=\frac{3.155\times10^{-46}}{1.0546\times10^{-34}}\ \mathrm{s}=2.99\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{s}\approx3.0\ \mathrm{ps} $$ The speed of an electron with kinetic energy $1\ \mathrm{eV}$ is $v=\sqrt{2E/m_{\mathrm e}}=\sqrt{2\times1.602\times10^{-19}/9.109\times10^{-31}}\ \mathrm{m/s}=5.93\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{m/s}$, so the distance traveled during this time is $vt_2=5.93\times10^{5}\times2.99\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}=1.77\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}\approx1.8\ \mathrm{\mu m}$. By the time the wave packet spreads from $10\ \mathrm{nm}$ to $20\ \mathrm{nm}$, the electron travels as far as $1.8\ \mathrm{\mu m}$ (about 100 times the width of the wave packet).

Exercise 1.7: Classical common sense and quantum theory (descriptive question)

Solution (sample answer)

In classical theory, position and momentum are determined simultaneously, the trajectory is fixed as a single line by the equation of motion, a physical quantity takes a definite value when it is measured, and a wave is represented by a real $\cos(kx-\omega t)$. In quantum theory, position and momentum cannot be determined simultaneously because $\Delta x\,\Delta p\ge\hbar/2$, and the trajectory is blurred into a band of the probability density $|\Psi|^2$ determined by the wave function $\Psi(x,t)$. A physical quantity is described by a probability distribution and is known only through its expectation value (except in an eigenstate). A wave is represented by the complex $e^{i(kx-\omega t)}$, with the traveling wave being $e^{ikx}$ and the standing wave $\cos kx$. However, since $\hbar$ is extremely small, classical theory holds for macroscopic objects. (About 200 characters, counting each formula as one character.)

Chapter 2: Naive Questions about Quantum Mechanics — Wavelength, Probability, Particles and Waves, and Temperature

Exercise 2.1: An electron in a box

Solution

The wavelength is $\lambda_n=2L/n$, the magnitude of the momentum is $p_n=h/\lambda_n=hn/(2L)$, and the energy is $E_n=p_n^2/2m_{\mathrm e}=n^2h^2/(8m_{\mathrm e}L^2)=n^2E_1$. Since $h^2/(8m_{\mathrm e})=0.3760\ \mathrm{eV\,nm^2}$, for $L=2.0\ \mathrm{nm}$ ($L^2=4.0\ \mathrm{nm^2}$) we have $E_1=0.3760/4.0=0.0940\ \mathrm{eV}$.

$n$$\lambda_n=2L/n$$p_n=h/\lambda_n$$E_n=n^2E_1$
1$4.0\ \mathrm{nm}$$\dfrac{6.626\times10^{-34}}{4.0\times10^{-9}}=1.66\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$$0.0940\ \mathrm{eV}$
2$2.0\ \mathrm{nm}$$3.31\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$$4E_1=0.376\ \mathrm{eV}$
3$1.33\ \mathrm{nm}$$4.97\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$$9E_1=0.846\ \mathrm{eV}$

The energy of the photon emitted in the $n=2\to1$ transition is $\Delta E=E_2-E_1=3E_1=0.282\ \mathrm{eV}$, and its wavelength is $$ \lambda_{\mathrm{ph}}=\frac{hc}{\Delta E}=\frac{1239.84\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}}{0.282\ \mathrm{eV}}=4.40\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{nm}=4.40\ \mathrm{\mu m} $$ This is infrared radiation (mid-infrared). If the box is made $4$ times as long ($L=0.5\ \mathrm{nm}\to2.0\ \mathrm{nm}$), the level spacing becomes $1/16$, and the energy of the $n=2\to1$ transition drops from $4.51\ \mathrm{eV}$ (ultraviolet light of wavelength $275\ \mathrm{nm}$) to $0.282\ \mathrm{eV}$ (infrared).

Exercise 2.2: Fringe spacing of a double slit

Solution

(1) The wavelength of an electron with $E=100\ \mathrm{eV}$ is $\lambda=1.226\ \mathrm{nm}/\sqrt{100}=0.1226\ \mathrm{nm}$. The fringe spacing is $\Delta x=\dfrac{\lambda L}{d}=\dfrac{0.1226\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m}\times0.5\ \mathrm{m}}{0.5\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}}=1.23\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m}=123\ \mathrm{\mu m}$.

(2) The mass of C60 is $m=720\times1.6605\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}=1.196\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{kg}$, and its momentum is $mv=1.196\times10^{-24}\times200=2.39\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$. The wavelength is $$ \lambda=\frac{h}{mv}=\frac{6.626\times10^{-34}}{2.39\times10^{-22}}\ \mathrm{m}=2.77\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}=2.77\ \mathrm{pm} $$ The fringe spacing is $\Delta x=\dfrac{2.77\times10^{-12}\times1.25}{100\times10^{-9}}\ \mathrm{m}=3.46\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m}=34.6\ \mathrm{\mu m}$.

(3) The main conditions for the fringes to be observable are the following. (i) The spatial resolution of the detector must be sufficiently smaller than the fringe spacing ($34.6\ \mathrm{\mu m}$ in (2)), that is, a few $\mathrm{\mu m}$ or less. (ii) The wavelength of the incident beam must be uniform. Since the fringe spacing is proportional to $\lambda$, if there is a spread in the speed (and hence in the wavelength), the fringes formed by the components of different wavelengths are shifted in position and overlap, and the pattern is blurred. For $k$ fringes to be visible, the spread in wavelength must satisfy roughly $\Delta\lambda/\lambda\lesssim1/k$. (iii) The incident wave must be in phase across the two slits (the transverse coherence length must be at least $d$). (iv) The width of each slit must be narrower than the spacing, so that the waves diffract sufficiently at the slits and the two waves overlap.

Exercise 2.3: Spreading of a Gaussian wave packet

Solution

By Theorem 2.1, for $\sigma=1\ \mathrm{nm}$ we have $$ \Delta x=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{2}}=0.707\ \mathrm{nm},\qquad \Delta p=\frac{\hbar}{\sqrt{2}\,\sigma}=\frac{1.0546\times10^{-34}}{1.4142\times10^{-9}}=7.46\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s} $$ $$ \Delta v=\frac{\Delta p}{m_{\mathrm e}}=\frac{7.46\times10^{-26}}{9.109\times10^{-31}}=8.19\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m/s} $$ The product $\Delta x\,\Delta p=0.707\times10^{-9}\times7.46\times10^{-26}=5.27\times10^{-35}\ \mathrm{J\,s}=\hbar/2$ agrees with $\hbar/2=5.273\times10^{-35}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$. If $\sigma$ is made $10$ times as large ($10\ \mathrm{nm}$), then, since $\Delta p\propto1/\sigma$, the spread in momentum becomes $\Delta p=7.46\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, which is $1/10$ of the former value ($\Delta v=8.19\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{m/s}$), and the spread in position becomes $\Delta x=7.07\ \mathrm{nm}$, which is $10$ times the former value. The product remains $\hbar/2$. Comparing with the case $\sigma=0.1\ \mathrm{nm}$ in Example 2.7 ($\Delta p=7.46\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$), we confirm that the more the confinement is relaxed, the smaller the spread in momentum becomes. The estimate of the kinetic energy, $(\Delta p)^2/2m_{\mathrm e}$, is $0.019\ \mathrm{eV}$ for $\sigma=1\ \mathrm{nm}$ and $1.90\ \mathrm{eV}$ for $0.1\ \mathrm{nm}$; that is, it becomes $1/100$.

Exercise 2.4: Probability of finding the electron in hydrogen 1s

Solution

The radial distribution is $4\pi r^2\abs{\psi_{1s}}^2=\dfrac{4r^2}{a_0^3}e^{-2r/a_0}$. Letting $x=r/a_0$, the probability is $4x^2e^{-2x}\dd x$, and using the indefinite integral in the hint, we obtain $$ P(r\lt r_0)=4\int_0^{x_0}x^2e^{-2x}\dd x=4\left[-e^{-2x}\Bigl(\frac{x^2}{2}+\frac{x}{2}+\frac14\Bigr)\right]_0^{x_0} =1-e^{-2x_0}\bigl(2x_0^2+2x_0+1\bigr) $$ (the term at $x=0$ is $-4\cdot\dfrac14\cdot(-1)=1$). Writing $x$ for $x_0=r_0/a_0$, we obtain the desired expression $P=1-e^{-2x}(1+2x+2x^2)$.

We find the $x$ for which $P=1/2$. At $x=1.3$, $e^{-2.6}=0.07427$ and $1+2.6+2\times1.69=6.98$, so $P=1-0.5184=0.4816$. At $x=1.4$, $e^{-2.8}=0.06081$ and $1+2.8+2\times1.96=7.72$, so $P=1-0.4695=0.5305$. The value $1/2$ lies between these, and interpolation gives $x\approx1.3+0.1\times\dfrac{0.5-0.4816}{0.5305-0.4816}=1.338$. As a check, at $x=1.34$ we have $e^{-2.68}=0.06856$ and $1+2.68+2\times1.7956=7.2712$, so $P=1-0.4985=0.5015$. Also, at $x=1.33$, $P=0.4965$, so $1/2$ is indeed bracketed. Hence $r_0/a_0\approx1.34$ ($r_0=1.34\,a_0=0.0709\ \mathrm{nm}$). (Solving more precisely gives $r_0=1.337\,a_0=0.0707\ \mathrm{nm}$.)

By comparison, the most probable radius $a_0$ (the peak of the radial distribution), the median $r_0=1.34\,a_0$ (the radius at which the probabilities of finding the electron inside and outside are equal), and the average $\expval{r}=1.5\,a_0$ increase in this order. Because the radial distribution has a long tail extending outward from $r=a_0$, the average, the median, and the most probable value line up in this order (the distribution is skewed to the right).

Exercise 2.5: Position spread of a harmonic oscillator and temperature

Solution

(1) Letting $y=\hbar\omega/2k_{\mathrm B}T$, we have $\expval{x^2}_T=\dfrac{\hbar}{2m\omega}\coth y$. For $y\to0$ (high temperature), $\coth y=\dfrac{1}{y}+\dfrac{y}{3}-\dfrac{y^3}{45}+\cdots$, so $$ \expval{x^2}_T\to\frac{\hbar}{2m\omega}\cdot\frac{1}{y}=\frac{\hbar}{2m\omega}\cdot\frac{2k_{\mathrm B}T}{\hbar\omega}=\frac{k_{\mathrm B}T}{m\omega^2} $$ which agrees with the classical-mechanical value (from the equipartition law $\tfrac12m\omega^2\expval{x^2}=\tfrac12k_{\mathrm B}T$). The first correction is $\dfrac{k_{\mathrm B}T}{m\omega^2}\Bigl(1+\dfrac{y^2}{3}+\cdots\Bigr)$.

(2) The ratio of the quantum-mechanical value to the classical-mechanical value is $\dfrac{(\hbar/2m\omega)\coth y}{k_{\mathrm B}T/m\omega^2}=\dfrac{(\hbar\omega/2k_{\mathrm B}T)\coth y}{1}=y\coth y$. For $T=2\Theta$ ($\Theta=\hbar\omega/k_{\mathrm B}$), $y=\dfrac{\Theta}{2T}=\dfrac14$, and since $\coth0.25=1/\tanh0.25=1/0.24492=4.0830$, we have $$ y\coth y=0.25\times4.0830=1.0208 $$ The ratio of the spreads ($\sqrt{\expval{x^2}}$) is $\sqrt{1.0208}=1.0103$, so the quantum-mechanical value is larger by about $1\ \%$. (For $T=\Theta$, $y=0.5$ and the ratio is $1.082$, a $4\ \%$ difference in the spread. For $T=\Theta/2$, $y=1$ and the ratio is $1.313$, a $15\ \%$ difference in the spread.) We see that for $T\gtrsim2\Theta$ the classical treatment holds to an accuracy of $1\ \%$.

Exercise 2.6: Replicating the Davisson–Germer experiment

Solution

(1) The wavelength of an electron accelerated through $100\ \mathrm{V}$ is $\lambda=1.226\ \mathrm{nm}/\sqrt{100}=0.1226\ \mathrm{nm}$. From $D\sin\theta=\lambda$, $\sin\theta=\lambda/D=0.1226/0.215=0.5703$, so $\theta=\arcsin0.5703=34.8^\circ$.

(2) At $54\ \mathrm{V}$, $\lambda=0.1669\ \mathrm{nm}$ (Example 2.11), and $\sin\theta=0.1669/0.215=0.7763$, so $\theta=50.9^\circ$. The measured value is $50^\circ$, which differs by about $0.9^\circ$. When the accelerating voltage is raised, the wavelength becomes shorter as $\lambda\propto V^{-1/2}$, and the peak angle decreases from $50.9^\circ$ ($54\ \mathrm{V}$) to $34.8^\circ$ ($100\ \mathrm{V}$). Thus the fact that the peak angle moves according to $\sin\theta\propto V^{-1/2}$ when the voltage is varied is evidence for the wave nature of the electron.

(3) The second-order diffraction satisfies $\sin\theta=2\lambda/D$, and at $100\ \mathrm{V}$ we get $2\times0.1226/0.215=1.14\gt1$; there is no angle satisfying $\sin\theta\le1$, so it is not observed. (At $54\ \mathrm{V}$ as well, $2\lambda/D=1.55\gt1$ and it is not observed.) The second order appears when $2\lambda\le D$, that is, $\lambda\le0.1075\ \mathrm{nm}$, which holds for $V\ge(1.226/0.1075)^2=130\ \mathrm{V}$ and above.

Exercise 2.7: Descriptive question on electrons sent one at a time and the fringes

Solution

Let $\psi_1(x)$ and $\psi_2(x)$ denote the wave functions (probability amplitudes) of the electron on the detection plane when only one slit is open. The probability density of finding the electron near $x$ is given by $\abs{\psi}^2$. When both slits are open, the electron does not “pass through one or the other”; rather, the amplitudes of the two possible paths are added, giving $\psi=\psi_1+\psi_2$, so that $$ P(x)=\abs{\psi_1+\psi_2}^2=\abs{\psi_1}^2+\abs{\psi_2}^2+2\,\Real(\psi_1^*\psi_2) $$ The third term is the interference term. It oscillates between positive and negative values depending on the position $x$: at positions where the phase difference between $\psi_1$ and $\psi_2$ is an integer multiple of $2\pi$ the two waves reinforce each other (bright fringes), and at odd multiples of $\pi$ they cancel each other (dark fringes). Even if the electrons are sent one at a time, each one is detected at a single point according to the same probability distribution $P(x)$, so when many electrons are accumulated on the detection plane, the shape of $P(x)$—the fringes—appears.

If a detector is placed immediately behind one of the slits so that a record of “the electron passed through” remains, the state of the electron becomes a state that contains the information about “which slit it passed through,” and the path through $\psi_1$ and the path through $\psi_2$ become separate, distinguishable situations. For distinguishable situations, we add not the amplitudes of the two paths but the probabilities. That is, the interference term vanishes, $P=\abs{\psi_1}^2+\abs{\psi_2}^2$, and the fringes disappear. (In the view of quantum mechanics, the interference term disappears not so much because we “touch” and disturb the electron in order to obtain the information about its path, but because the mere fact that “the information exists in principle” eliminates it. The theory of measurement will be studied in Chapter 8.)

Exercise 2.8: Size of a muonic atom

Solution

Replacing the electron mass $m_{\mathrm e}$ by $m_\mu=206.77\,m_{\mathrm e}$, we carry out the same procedure as for $E(a)=\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2m_{\mathrm e}a^2}-\dfrac{e_0^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0a}$ in the main text (minimization of the sum of the kinetic energy $\hbar^2/2m_\mu a^2$ and the Coulomb energy $-e_0^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0a$). The derivation is the same as in the main text, and gives $$ a_\mu=\frac{4\pi\varepsilon_0\hbar^2}{m_\mu e_0^2}=\frac{a_0}{206.77}=\frac{0.0529\ \mathrm{nm}}{206.77}=2.56\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{nm}=0.256\ \mathrm{pm} $$ $$ E_\mu=-\frac{e_0^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0a_\mu}=206.77\times(-13.606\ \mathrm{eV})=-2813\ \mathrm{eV}\approx-2.8\ \mathrm{keV} $$ Compared with the hydrogen atom, the size is $1/206.77$ (about $1/200$) and the magnitude of the binding energy is $206.77$ times as large (about $200$ times). The lighter the particle, the smaller its kinetic energy $\hbar^2/2ma^2$ when confined to the same size, so it spreads over a wider region. The heavier the particle, the smaller the gain in kinetic energy, and the more narrowly it is confined. Even so, $a_\mu=2.56\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{nm}$ is still about $256$ times larger than the size of the proton ($\sim10^{-6}\ \mathrm{nm}=1\ \mathrm{fm}$). (In actual muonic hydrogen, the reduced mass $185.84\,m_{\mathrm e}$, which arises from the finite mass of the proton, is used, so the binding energy is about $2.5\ \mathrm{keV}$.)

Chapter 3: Blackbody Radiation and the Discovery of the Quantum — Wien, Rayleigh–Jeans, and Planck

Exercise 3.1: The color of stars

Solution

Substitute into Wien's displacement law $\lambda_m=b/T$, $b=2.898\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m\,K}$.

$$ \text{Betelgeuse:}\ \lambda_m=\frac{2.898\times10^{-3}}{3600}=8.05\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}=805\ \mathrm{nm} $$ $$ \text{Sirius:}\ \lambda_m=\frac{2.898\times10^{-3}}{9940}=2.92\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}=292\ \mathrm{nm} $$

The visible region is $380$–$780\ \mathrm{nm}$. The peak of Betelgeuse at $805\ \mathrm{nm}$ lies in the near-infrared, just outside the long-wavelength edge of the visible region (red). Since the peak lies on the infrared side, within the visible region the spectrum is stronger toward the longer-wavelength side (red), and the star looks reddish (orange-red). The peak of Sirius at $292\ \mathrm{nm}$ lies in the ultraviolet, outside the short-wavelength edge of the visible region (violet). Within the visible region the spectrum is stronger toward the shorter-wavelength side (blue), and the star looks bluish white (see the slopes, within the visible region, of the $2800\ \mathrm{K}$ and $10000\ \mathrm{K}$ curves in Figure 3.8). The peak of Sirius itself is ultraviolet light, which is invisible to the eye, but it raises the intensity on the blue side of the visible region.

Numerical check. Planck's formula on a wavelength basis is $U_\lambda\propto\dfrac{\lambda^{-5}}{e^{c_2/\lambda T}-1}$ ($c_2=hc/k_{\mathrm{B}}=1.4388\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m\,K}$), so the ratio of the values at $450\ \mathrm{nm}$ and $650\ \mathrm{nm}$ is

$$ \frac{U_\lambda(450\ \mathrm{nm})}{U_\lambda(650\ \mathrm{nm})}=\left(\frac{650}{450}\right)^5\frac{e^{c_2/(650\ \mathrm{nm}\,T)}-1}{e^{c_2/(450\ \mathrm{nm}\,T)}-1} $$

We have $(650/450)^5=6.288$. For Betelgeuse ($T=3600\ \mathrm{K}$), $c_2/(450\ \mathrm{nm}\,T)=8.881$ and $c_2/(650\ \mathrm{nm}\,T)=6.149$, and since $e^{8.881}-1=7195$ and $e^{6.149}-1=467.1$, the ratio is $6.288\times\dfrac{467.1}{7195}=0.408$. Blue ($450\ \mathrm{nm}$) is only about $0.41$ times red ($650\ \mathrm{nm}$), so the red side is stronger. For Sirius ($T=9940\ \mathrm{K}$), $c_2/(450\ \mathrm{nm}\,T)=3.217$ and $c_2/(650\ \mathrm{nm}\,T)=2.227$, and since $e^{3.217}-1=23.94$ and $e^{2.227}-1=8.271$, the ratio is $6.288\times\dfrac{8.271}{23.94}=2.17$. Blue is about $2.2$ times stronger than red, so the star looks bluish white. Whether the ratio is smaller or larger than $1$ corresponds to the difference between red stars and bluish-white stars.

Exercise 3.2: Dependence of the mode density on the dimension of space

Solution

One dimension (a string of length $L$, one polarization): the wavenumber of a standing wave is $k=n\pi/L$ ($n=1,2,\dots$), and from $k=2\pi\nu/c$ we get $\nu=cn/2L$, that is, $n=2L\nu/c$. The number of modes with frequency at most $\nu$ equals the number of integers $n$, so $N(\nu)=n=\dfrac{2L\nu}{c}$. The mode density per unit length is

$$ g_1(\nu)=\frac1L\frac{\dd N}{\dd\nu}=\frac{2}{c} $$

(a constant independent of the frequency). Two dimensions (a square membrane of area $L^2$): among the lattice sites $(n_x,n_y)$ ($n_x,n_y\ge1$), those at or inside $n=\sqrt{n_x^2+n_y^2}=\dfrac{2L\nu}{c}$ are counted by the area of a quarter circle of radius $n$, giving $N(\nu)=\dfrac14\pi n^2=\dfrac{\pi L^2\nu^2}{c^2}$. Per unit area,

$$ g_2(\nu)=\frac1{L^2}\frac{\dd N}{\dd\nu}=\frac{2\pi\nu}{c^2} $$

Three dimensions: for one polarization, $g_3=4\pi\nu^2/c^3$ (differentiate the volume of an eighth of a sphere, $\dfrac18\cdot\dfrac{4\pi}{3}n^3$, and divide by $L^3$), and for two polarizations it is $8\pi\nu^2/c^3$. In summary, $g_d(\nu)\propto\nu^{d-1}$ ($d$ is the dimension of space), and the higher the dimension, the more modes there are on the high-frequency side.

Total energy. In classical theory each mode has the energy $k_{\mathrm{B}}T$, so $U_d=g_d\,k_{\mathrm{B}}T\propto\nu^{d-1}$. In every dimension $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty U_d\,\dd\nu$ diverges (even in one dimension, integrating the constant $U_1=2k_{\mathrm{B}}T/c$ over $\nu$ diverges). In Planck's quantum hypothesis each mode has the energy $\dfrac{h\nu}{e^{h\nu/k_{\mathrm{B}}T}-1}$, so, letting $x=h\nu/k_{\mathrm{B}}T$, in one dimension we have

$$ u_1=\int_0^\infty\frac2c\cdot\frac{h\nu}{e^{h\nu/k_{\mathrm{B}}T}-1}\dd\nu=\frac{2}{c}\frac{(k_{\mathrm{B}}T)^2}{h}\int_0^\infty\frac{x}{e^x-1}\dd x=\frac{2(k_{\mathrm{B}}T)^2}{hc}\cdot\frac{\pi^2}{6}=\frac{\pi^2(k_{\mathrm{B}}T)^2}{3hc} $$

(using $\int_0^\infty x/(e^x-1)\dd x=\Gamma(2)\zeta(2)=\pi^2/6$). In two dimensions,

$$ u_2=\int_0^\infty\frac{2\pi\nu}{c^2}\cdot\frac{h\nu}{e^{h\nu/k_{\mathrm{B}}T}-1}\dd\nu=\frac{2\pi(k_{\mathrm{B}}T)^3}{h^2c^2}\int_0^\infty\frac{x^2}{e^x-1}\dd x=\frac{4\pi\zeta(3)(k_{\mathrm{B}}T)^3}{h^2c^2} $$

(using $\int_0^\infty x^2/(e^x-1)\dd x=\Gamma(3)\zeta(3)=2\zeta(3)$). In three dimensions it is the $u\propto T^4$ of the main text. In every dimension the result is finite, and the temperature dependence is $T^{d+1}$ ($T^2$ in one dimension, $T^3$ in two dimensions, $T^4$ in three dimensions). This is because $\nu^{d-1}\dd\nu$ gives $(k_{\mathrm{B}}T/h)^d$, and the $k_{\mathrm{B}}T$ per mode contributes one more factor of $T$.

Exercise 3.3: Expansion of the average energy

Solution

From $e^x=1+x+\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{x^3}{6}+\dots$ we have $e^x-1=x\left(1+\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{x^2}{6}+\dots\right)$. Letting $\epsilon=\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{x^2}{6}+\dots$, we obtain

$$ \frac{x}{e^x-1}=\frac{1}{1+\epsilon}=1-\epsilon+\epsilon^2-\dots $$

Taking terms up to $x^2$, we have $\epsilon=\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{x^2}{6}$ and $\epsilon^2=\dfrac{x^2}{4}+O(x^3)$, so

$$ \frac{x}{e^x-1}=1-\frac{x}{2}-\frac{x^2}{6}+\frac{x^2}{4}+O(x^3)=1-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{x^2}{12}+O(x^3) $$

(the $x^3$ terms cancel to give $0$, and the next term is $-x^4/720$). Therefore

$$ \langle E\rangle=k_{\mathrm{B}}T\left(1-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{x^2}{12}-\cdots\right)=k_{\mathrm{B}}T-\frac{h\nu}{2}+\frac{(h\nu)^2}{12k_{\mathrm{B}}T}-\cdots $$

and, since $x=h\nu/k_{\mathrm{B}}T$ gives $k_{\mathrm{B}}T\cdot\dfrac{x}{2}=\dfrac{h\nu}{2}$, the first correction term is $-\dfrac{h\nu}{2}$. The effect of quantization appears as the subtraction of a half quantum $h\nu/2$ from the classical value $k_{\mathrm{B}}T$. (For $\tfrac12h\nu+\dfrac{h\nu}{e^x-1}$, which includes the zero-point energy $\tfrac12h\nu$, this $-h\nu/2$ is canceled.)

Exercise 3.4: Radiation from the filament of an incandescent light bulb

Solution

(a) The lateral surface area of the cylinder, with diameter $d=0.050\ \mathrm{mm}=5.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m}$ and length $L=0.50\ \mathrm{m}$, is

$$ S=\pi dL=\pi\times5.0\times10^{-5}\times0.50=7.854\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^2} $$

At $T=2800\ \mathrm{K}$ we have $T^4=(2800)^4=6.147\times10^{13}\ \mathrm{K^4}$, so the radiant exitance as a blackbody is $\sigma_{\mathrm{SB}}T^4=5.670\times10^{-8}\times6.147\times10^{13}=3.485\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$. The radiated power as a gray body (emissivity $\varepsilon=0.30$) is

$$ P=\varepsilon\sigma_{\mathrm{SB}}S\,T^4=0.30\times3.485\times10^{6}\times7.854\times10^{-5}=82.1\ \mathrm{W} $$

(b) If the surroundings are at $T_0=300\ \mathrm{K}$ (regarded as a blackbody), the power of the radiation absorbed is $\varepsilon\sigma_{\mathrm{SB}}S\,T_0^4$, and since $T_0^4=8.1\times10^9\ \mathrm{K^4}$ and $\sigma_{\mathrm{SB}}T_0^4=459.3\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$, it is only $0.30\times459.3\times7.854\times10^{-5}=1.08\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{W}$. The net power is $82.1-0.011=82.11\ \mathrm{W}$, which differs from the value in (a) by $0.013\ \%$. Because of the proportionality to $T^4$, the radiation from the room-temperature surroundings is negligible compared with that of the $2800\ \mathrm{K}$ filament.

(c) From Table 3.4 of Example 3.12, the fraction of the blackbody radiation at $2800\ \mathrm{K}$ that falls in visible light ($380$–$780\ \mathrm{nm}$) is $0.0973$. For a gray body the emissivity does not depend on the wavelength, so the fraction is the same. The power emitted as visible light is $0.0973\times82.1=7.99\ \mathrm{W}\approx8.0\ \mathrm{W}$. In the steady state, the electrical power consumption equals the power lost by radiation ($82\ \mathrm{W}$), so the efficiency of converting electricity into visible light is about $9.7\ \%$ (roughly $10\ \%$), and the remaining approximately $90\ \%$ is emitted as infrared radiation (heat). (Real tungsten has a somewhat higher emissivity in the visible region than in the infrared region, so the actual efficiency is slightly better than this estimate.)

Exercise 3.5: Radiation from the human body

Solution

(a) Substitute into $P=\varepsilon\sigma_{\mathrm{SB}}A_{\mathrm{body}}T^4$. Since $310^4=9.235\times10^9\ \mathrm{K^4}$, we have $\sigma_{\mathrm{SB}}T^4=5.670\times10^{-8}\times9.235\times10^9=523.7\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$, and

$$ P=0.97\times523.7\times1.7=863.5\ \mathrm{W}\approx864\ \mathrm{W} $$

(b) For a wall temperature of $293\ \mathrm{K}$, $293^4=7.370\times10^9\ \mathrm{K^4}$ and $\sigma_{\mathrm{SB}}T^4=417.9\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$, so the radiation received from the wall is $0.97\times417.9\times1.7=689.1\ \mathrm{W}$. The net power lost is

$$ P_{\mathrm{net}}=\varepsilon\sigma_{\mathrm{SB}}A_{\mathrm{body}}\left(T_{\mathrm{body}}^4-T_{\mathrm{wall}}^4\right)=863.5-689.1=174.4\ \mathrm{W}\approx174\ \mathrm{W} $$

This is of the same order of magnitude as the heat generated by the human body (about $100\ \mathrm{W}$ at rest), so the exchange of heat by radiation plays a major role in maintaining body temperature. (In reality the skin temperature is somewhat lower than $310\ \mathrm{K}$, and the effects of clothing, convection, and evaporation are also present.)

Exercise 3.6: Planck's formula on a wavelength basis

Solution

From $U_\lambda(\lambda)\,\dd\lambda=U(\nu)\,\abs{\dd\nu}$, $\nu=c/\lambda$, and $\abs{\dd\nu}=\dfrac{c}{\lambda^2}\dd\lambda$, we get $U_\lambda(\lambda)=\dfrac{c}{\lambda^2}\,U\!\left(\dfrac{c}{\lambda}\right)$. Substituting $\nu=c/\lambda$ into Planck's formula gives

$$ U\!\left(\frac{c}{\lambda}\right)=\frac{8\pi h}{c^3}\cdot\frac{(c/\lambda)^3}{e^{hc/\lambda k_{\mathrm{B}}T}-1}=\frac{8\pi h}{\lambda^3}\cdot\frac{1}{e^{hc/\lambda k_{\mathrm{B}}T}-1} $$

($c^3/c^3=1$ was canceled). Multiplying this by $c/\lambda^2$, we have

$$ U_\lambda(\lambda)=\frac{c}{\lambda^2}\cdot\frac{8\pi h}{\lambda^3}\cdot\frac{1}{e^{hc/\lambda k_{\mathrm{B}}T}-1}=\frac{8\pi hc}{\lambda^5}\cdot\frac{1}{e^{hc/\lambda k_{\mathrm{B}}T}-1} $$

As $\lambda\to\infty$, we have $z=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda k_{\mathrm{B}}T}\to0$ and $e^z-1\approx z$, so

$$ U_\lambda\to\frac{8\pi hc}{\lambda^5}\cdot\frac{\lambda k_{\mathrm{B}}T}{hc}=\frac{8\pi k_{\mathrm{B}}T}{\lambda^4} $$

This agrees with $\dfrac{c}{\lambda^2}\cdot\dfrac{8\pi(c/\lambda)^2}{c^3}k_{\mathrm{B}}T=\dfrac{8\pi k_{\mathrm{B}}T}{\lambda^4}$, which is obtained by applying the same transformation to the Rayleigh–Jeans formula $U=\dfrac{8\pi\nu^2}{c^3}k_{\mathrm{B}}T$.

Exercise 3.7: Number density of a photon gas

Solution

The number of photons per unit volume and unit frequency is $U(\nu)/h\nu$, so

$$ n=\int_0^\infty\frac{U(\nu)}{h\nu}\dd\nu=\frac{8\pi}{c^3}\int_0^\infty\frac{\nu^2}{e^{h\nu/k_{\mathrm{B}}T}-1}\dd\nu=\frac{8\pi}{c^3}\left(\frac{k_{\mathrm{B}}T}{h}\right)^3\int_0^\infty\frac{x^2}{e^x-1}\dd x=\frac{8\pi}{c^3}\left(\frac{k_{\mathrm{B}}T}{h}\right)^3\cdot2\zeta(3) $$

(where $\nu^2\dd\nu=(k_{\mathrm{B}}T/h)^3x^2\dd x$). Since $h=2\pi\hbar$, we have $h^3=8\pi^3\hbar^3$, so $\dfrac{8\pi}{c^3h^3}=\dfrac{8\pi}{8\pi^3\hbar^3c^3}=\dfrac{1}{\pi^2\hbar^3c^3}$, and

$$ n=\frac{2\zeta(3)}{\pi^2}\left(\frac{k_{\mathrm{B}}T}{\hbar c}\right)^3 $$

For $T=2.725\ \mathrm{K}$, $k_{\mathrm{B}}T=1.380649\times10^{-23}\times2.725=3.762\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J}$ and $\hbar c=1.0546\times10^{-34}\times2.9979\times10^8=3.1615\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{J\,m}$, so $\dfrac{k_{\mathrm{B}}T}{\hbar c}=1190\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$ and $(1190)^3=1.686\times10^9\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$. Multiplying by $\dfrac{2\zeta(3)}{\pi^2}=\dfrac{2.404}{9.870}=0.2436$, we obtain

$$ n=0.2436\times1.686\times10^9=4.11\times10^8\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}=411\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}} $$

In the universe, about $410$ photons of the background radiation are flying through every $1\ \mathrm{cm^3}$.

Exercise 3.8: Descriptive question: the role of the quantum hypothesis

Solution

(a) If the energy may take continuous values, the result of classical statistical mechanics applies, and the average energy of every mode is $\langle E\rangle=k_{\mathrm{B}}T$ (the equipartition law). Since the number of modes is proportional to $8\pi\nu^2/c^3$, the spectrum becomes the Rayleigh–Jeans formula $U=8\pi\nu^2k_{\mathrm{B}}T/c^3$. This agrees with experiment on the low-frequency side, but on the high-frequency side it keeps increasing in proportion to $\nu^2$, and the total energy $\int U\,\dd\nu$ diverges (the ultraviolet catastrophe).

(b) If the energy takes only the values $E_n=nh\nu$, the probability that a mode is in the $n$th state is proportional to the Boltzmann factor $e^{-nh\nu/k_{\mathrm{B}}T}$. The ratio of the probabilities of the first excited state ($n=1$) and the ground state ($n=0$) is $e^{-h\nu/k_{\mathrm{B}}T}$. For $h\nu\gg k_{\mathrm{B}}T$ this ratio is very small. For example, if $h\nu=10k_{\mathrm{B}}T$, then $e^{-10}=4.5\times10^{-5}$, and the mode can be raised to $n=1$ only with a probability of about one in 20,000. Because the energy quantum $h\nu$ is much larger than the thermal energy $k_{\mathrm{B}}T$, the mode can hardly ever receive energy of that size from the heat bath. Therefore, the mode remains almost always at $n=0$ (energy $0$), and the average energy becomes exponentially small, $\langle E\rangle\approx h\nu\,e^{-h\nu/k_{\mathrm{B}}T}$; at $x=10$ we have $\langle E\rangle=4.5\times10^{-4}k_{\mathrm{B}}T$. This effect cancels the increase in proportion to $\nu^2$ on the high-frequency side and resolves the ultraviolet catastrophe.

Chapter 4: The Particle Nature of Light — The Photoelectric Effect and the Photon

Exercise 4.1: The photoelectric effect of Cu

Solution

(a) The threshold wavelength is $\lambda_0=\dfrac{hc}{W_0}=\dfrac{1239.84\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}}{4.65\ \mathrm{eV}}=266.6\ \mathrm{nm}$ (the threshold frequency is $\nu_0=W_0/h=\dfrac{4.65\times1.602\times10^{-19}}{6.626\times10^{-34}}=1.124\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{Hz}$).

(b) Since $254\ \mathrm{nm}$ is shorter than $\lambda_0=266.6\ \mathrm{nm}$, photoelectrons are emitted. The energy of a single photon is $h\nu=\dfrac{1239.84}{254}\ \mathrm{eV}=4.881\ \mathrm{eV}$. From Einstein's photoelectric equation $K_{\max}=h\nu-W_0$,

$$ K_{\max}=4.881-4.65=0.231\ \mathrm{eV}\approx0.23\ \mathrm{eV}\quad(=0.231\times1.602\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}=3.7\times10^{-20}\ \mathrm{J}) $$

The stopping potential is $V_0=K_{\max}/e_0=0.23\ \mathrm{V}$.

(c) If the intensity of the light is tripled, the number of photons triples. Since the energy of a single photon $h\nu$ does not change, $K_{\max}=h\nu-W_0=0.23\ \mathrm{eV}$ (and hence the stopping potential of $0.23\ \mathrm{V}$) is unchanged. Since the probability that a single photon ejects an electron does not change, the number of ejected electrons triples, and the photocurrent also becomes three times as large. (In classical wave theory, the energy of the electrons is predicted to increase as the intensity increases.)

Exercise 4.2: Determining $h$ and $W_0$ from stopping-potential data

Solution

We find the frequencies from $\nu=c/\lambda$. For $435.8,\ 404.7,\ 365.0,\ 334.1,\ 313.2\ \mathrm{nm}$ we get $\nu=6.879,\ 7.408,\ 8.213,\ 8.973,\ 9.572\ (\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz})$ (for example, $2.998\times10^{8}/(435.8\times10^{-9})=6.879\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$). Let $x=\nu/(10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz})$ and $y=V_0/\mathrm{V}$. The averages are $\bar x=(6.879+7.408+8.213+8.973+9.572)/5=8.209$ and $\bar y=(0.54+0.76+1.10+1.41+1.66)/5=1.094$. The deviations, the products of the deviations, and the squares of the deviations are as follows.

$$ \begin{array}{c|ccccc|c} i & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & \text{sum}\\ \hline x_i & 6.879 & 7.408 & 8.213 & 8.973 & 9.572 & \\ y_i & 0.54 & 0.76 & 1.10 & 1.41 & 1.66 & \\ x_i-\bar x & -1.330 & -0.801 & 0.004 & 0.764 & 1.363 & 0 \\ y_i-\bar y & -0.554 & -0.334 & 0.006 & 0.316 & 0.566 & 0 \\ (x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y) & 0.7368 & 0.2675 & 0.0000 & 0.2414 & 0.7715 & 2.0173 \\ (x_i-\bar x)^2 & 1.7689 & 0.6416 & 0.0000 & 0.5837 & 1.8578 & 4.8520 \end{array} $$

Therefore $S_{xy}=\sum(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)=2.0173$ and $S_{xx}=\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2=4.8520$. The slope and intercept of the least-squares line are

$$ a=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}=0.4158,\qquad b=\bar y-a\bar x=1.094-0.4158\times8.209=-2.319 $$

Comparing the line $V_0=a\nu+b$ with Einstein's equation $V_0=\dfrac{h}{e_0}\nu-\dfrac{W_0}{e_0}$, the slope is $a=0.4158\ \mathrm{V}/(10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz})=4.158\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{V\,s}$, and so

$$ h=e_0a=(1.602\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C})(4.158\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{V\,s})=6.66\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s} $$

From the intercept $-2.319\ \mathrm{V}$ we obtain $W_0=2.32\ \mathrm{eV}$. The threshold frequency, from $V_0=0$, is $\nu_0=-b/a=2.319/0.4158\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}=5.58\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$, and the threshold wavelength is $\lambda_0=c/\nu_0=2.998\times10^8/(5.58\times10^{14})\ \mathrm{m}=537\ \mathrm{nm}$ (green). These agree with the true values ($h=6.626\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$, $W_0=2.30\ \mathrm{eV}$, $\lambda_0=539\ \mathrm{nm}$), with a difference of $0.5\ \%$ for $h$ and $0.8\ \%$ for $W_0$.

Why the slope does not depend on the material. In the equation $V_0=\dfrac{h}{e_0}\nu-\dfrac{W_0}{e_0}$, the coefficient of $\nu$, $h/e_0$, is a ratio of universal constants, fixed by the fact that the energy of a single photon is $h\nu$ and that it is converted into electron volts (divided by the elementary charge $e_0$). The properties of the material enter only through the energy $W_0$ subtracted from the photon (the “admission fee” an electron must pay to leave the metal), which merely shifts the line up or down (changes the intercept). For this reason, the lines for different materials are parallel (Figure 4.6 in Chapter 4).

Exercise 4.3: The number of photons in sunlight

Solution

(a) The energy of a single photon is $E=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}=\dfrac{(6.626\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s})(2.998\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s})}{550\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m}}=3.61\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\ (=2.25\ \mathrm{eV})$. Since the intensity is $I=\Phi E$, the photon flux is

$$ \Phi=\frac{I}{E}=\frac{1000\ \mathrm{W/m^2}}{3.61\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}}=2.77\times10^{21}\ \mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}} $$

(b) Since $1\ \mathrm{cm^2}=10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}$, $2.77\times10^{21}\times10^{-4}=2.77\times10^{17}$ photons strike it every second. With so many photons, light looks like a continuous wave, and the effect of each individual photon ordinarily does not show up in observations.

Exercise 4.4: Light pressure on a mirror

Solution

(a) In perfect reflection, the momentum of a photon changes from $+p$ to $-p$, so the momentum received by the mirror is $2p$ per photon. Since $N=P/(h\nu)$ photons are reflected per second, the force is $F=N\cdot2p=\dfrac{P}{h\nu}\cdot\dfrac{2h\nu}{c}=\dfrac{2P}{c}$, and so

$$ F=\frac{2\times1.0\ \mathrm{W}}{2.998\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s}}=6.67\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{N}=6.7\ \mathrm{nN} $$

(b) Since the mass is $m=1.0\ \mathrm{mg}=1.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{kg}$, the acceleration is $a=F/m=6.67\times10^{-9}/(1.0\times10^{-6})=6.7\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. The speed after one second is $v=at=6.7\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m/s}=6.7\ \mathrm{mm/s}$. Note that the weight of the mirror is $mg=1.0\times10^{-6}\times9.8=9.8\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{N}$, and the light pressure of $6.7\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{N}$ is only about $7\times10^{-4}$ times as large. Even a $1\ \mathrm{W}$ laser does not provide a force that can move everyday objects. (For a minute object with a mass of the order of $1\ \mu\mathrm g$, or in outer space where gravity does not act, the light pressure becomes large enough to matter, comparable to the weight or greater.)

Exercise 4.5: Comparing the predictions of classical wave theory and the photon hypothesis

Solution

AspectPrediction of classical wave theoryPrediction of the photon hypothesisExperiment
(i) Raising the intensity of lightSince the intensity of the wave $I\propto E_0^2$ increases, the kinetic energy of the electrons increasesThe number of photons increases. The number of electrons (the photocurrent) increases, but the energy of a single photon $h\nu$ is the same, so $K_{\max}=h\nu-W_0$ does not changeOnly the number of electrons increases, and $K_{\max}$ does not change → photon hypothesis
(ii) Lowering the frequencyWith intense light, enough energy gathers at any frequency, and electrons are emittedFor $h\nu\lt W_0$ ($\nu\lt\nu_0$), a single photon cannot make an electron escape. The energies of different photons are not added together, so no electrons are emitted no matter how intense the light isNo electrons are emitted for $\nu\lt\nu_0$ → photon hypothesis
(iii) Time until the electrons are emittedWith weak light, accumulating the energy takes time (about $10^{3}\ \mathrm{s}$, as in Example 4.2 of Chapter 4)A single photon hands the whole of its energy to a single electron in an instant. Even if the light is weak, an electron is emitted immediately when a photon strikesShorter than $10^{-9}\ \mathrm{s}$ → photon hypothesis
(iv) (Added) Raising the frequencyThe energy of the electrons is determined by the intensity (amplitude). There is no reason for the energy of the electrons to increase when the frequency is raised$K_{\max}=h\nu-W_0$ increases in proportion to $\nu$The straight line $V_0\propto\nu$ (Figure 4.6 in Chapter 4) → photon hypothesis

In all four aspects, the photon hypothesis agrees with experiment. The reason classical wave theory breaks down lies in the premise that “an electron can accumulate the energy of a wave continuously, as much as it likes.” In the photon hypothesis, energy is handed over in units of $h\nu$, from one photon to one electron, all at once.

Exercise 4.6: X-rays from a W tube

Solution

(a) From the Duane–Hunt law, $\lambda_{\min}=\dfrac{hc}{e_0V}=\dfrac{1239.84\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}}{100\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{eV}}=1.240\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{nm}=12.4\ \mathrm{pm}$.

(b) To produce the characteristic X-rays of the K series, an accelerated electron must knock an electron of the K shell of W out of the atom and create a vacancy. For this, the kinetic energy of the electron $e_0V$ must be at least the binding energy of the K shell, $69.5\ \mathrm{keV}$: $e_0V\ge69.5\ \mathrm{keV}$, that is, the tube voltage must satisfy $V\ge69.5\ \mathrm{kV}$. Since $100\ \mathrm{kV}$ satisfies this condition, the K series is emitted. At $60\ \mathrm{kV}$, $e_0V=60\ \mathrm{keV}\lt69.5\ \mathrm{keV}$, so the K shell cannot be ionized and the K series is not emitted (in this case the shortest wavelength of the continuous X-rays is $\lambda_{\min}=\dfrac{1239.84}{60\times10^{3}}\ \mathrm{nm}=2.07\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{nm}=20.7\ \mathrm{pm}$). Caution: To emit the K$\alpha$ line, one must first drive an electron of the K shell out of the atom. The minimum energy required is the binding energy of the K shell, $69.5\ \mathrm{keV}$, and not the photon energy of the K$\alpha$ line (about $59.3\ \mathrm{keV}$). A $60\ \mathrm{keV}$ electron does not reach $69.5\ \mathrm{keV}$, so the K$\alpha$ line is not emitted either. Note also that the binding energy of the L shell of W is small, about $10$–$12\ \mathrm{keV}$, so X-rays of the L series are emitted even at $60\ \mathrm{kV}$.

Exercise 4.7: The chemical states of carbon seen by XPS

Solution

(a) $E_{\mathrm{kin}}=h\nu-E_{\mathrm B}-\phi_{\mathrm{sp}}=1253.6-284.8-4.5=964.3\ \mathrm{eV}$.

(b) The binding energy of carbon in a C–O bond is $284.8+1.5=286.3\ \mathrm{eV}$, so the kinetic energy is $E_{\mathrm{kin}}=1253.6-286.3-4.5=962.8\ \mathrm{eV}$. The two peaks are $1.5\ \mathrm{eV}$ apart. If only the spectroscope resolution of $0.5\ \mathrm{eV}$ is considered, the separation is three times the peak width, and the peaks can be resolved sufficiently well. Taking into account the linewidth of the Mg K$\alpha$ line itself, $0.7\ \mathrm{eV}$, the independent spreads combine as the square root of the sum of squares, giving $\sqrt{0.5^2+0.7^2}\ \mathrm{eV}=0.86\ \mathrm{eV}$. Since the peak separation of $1.5\ \mathrm{eV}$ is larger than this combined width of $0.86\ \mathrm{eV}$, the two peaks appear separated (however, the margin is not large, and the peaks are often separated by analyzing the overlap of the peak shapes). If monochromatized Al K$\alpha$ X-rays (linewidth of about $0.25\ \mathrm{eV}$) are used, the peaks can be separated even more clearly.

Exercise 4.8: Rethinking the meaning of “threshold”: the multiphoton photoelectric effect

Solution

(a) The energy of a single photon is $h\nu=\dfrac{1239.84}{800}\ \mathrm{eV}=1.55\ \mathrm{eV}$. We look for the smallest $n$ for which the energy $nh\nu$ obtained by absorbing $n$ photons simultaneously is at least $W_0=5.1\ \mathrm{eV}$. For $n=3$, $3\times1.55=4.65\ \mathrm{eV}\lt5.1\ \mathrm{eV}$; for $n=4$, $4\times1.55=6.20\ \mathrm{eV}\ge5.1\ \mathrm{eV}$. Therefore four photons must be absorbed simultaneously.

(b) $K_{\max}=nh\nu-W_0=6.20-5.1=1.10\ \mathrm{eV}$ (this is the one-photon formula $K_{\max}=h\nu-W_0$ with $h\nu$ replaced by $nh\nu$; in a very strong field, processes that absorb more photons than necessary also come into play).

(c) The probability that $n$ photons arrive near an electron at the same time is proportional to the $n$th power of the photon density. Since the photon density is proportional to the intensity of the light $I$, the photocurrent is proportional to $I^n$. Here $n=4$, so it is $I^4$. If the intensity is doubled, the photocurrent becomes $2^4=16$ times as large. (A hallmark of a multiphoton process is that on a log–log plot ($\log$ of the photocurrent against $\log I$) the data fall on a straight line of slope $n$.)

(d) Fact 1 is revised from “no electrons are emitted if $h\nu\lt W_0$” to “when the energy of a single photon is smaller than $W_0$, no electrons are emitted as long as the light is within the range of ordinary intensities.” More precisely, the threshold condition is “$n$ photons with $nh\nu\ge W_0$ are absorbed simultaneously,” and the threshold frequency becomes $\nu_0^{(n)}=\dfrac{W_0}{nh}$ (in terms of the threshold wavelength, $\lambda_0^{(n)}=\dfrac{nhc}{W_0}$). For Au ($W_0=5.1\ \mathrm{eV}$) with $n=4$, $\lambda_0^{(4)}=4\times\dfrac{1239.84\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}}{5.1\ \mathrm{eV}}=4\times243.1\ \mathrm{nm}=972\ \mathrm{nm}$, and since $800\ \mathrm{nm}$ is shorter than this, four-photon absorption occurs (for $n=3$, $\lambda_0^{(3)}=729\ \mathrm{nm}$, and since $800\ \mathrm{nm}$ is longer than this, it does not occur). However, the probability of simultaneous absorption of $n$ photons is proportional to $I^n$ and becomes drastically small, so it is not observed unless the light is a very intense pulsed laser beam. This is why a “threshold” seems to exist with ordinary light. On the other hand, the point that energy is handed over in integer multiples of the unit $h\nu$ does not change (the photons are absorbed as quanta). Fact 2 is revised from “proportional to $I$” to “proportional to $I^n$,” and Fact 4 (no delay) is unchanged.

Chapter 5: Atomic Structure and the Old Quantum Theory — Atomic Spectra and the Bohr Model

Exercise 5.1: Rutherford scattering

Solution

(a) For a head-on collision, the distance of closest approach is the distance at which all of the kinetic energy $K$ has been converted into the Coulomb potential energy $\dfrac{2Ze_0^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0d}$, so $d=\dfrac{2Ze_0^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0K}$. Using $\dfrac{e_0^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}=1.44\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}$, for copper ($Z=29$) this gives

$$ d=\frac{2\times29\times1.44\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}}{5.5\ \mathrm{MeV}}=\frac{83.5}{5.5}\ \mathrm{fm}=15.2\ \mathrm{fm} $$

The radius of a copper nucleus is $1.2\times63^{1/3}\ \mathrm{fm}=4.8\ \mathrm{fm}$ and the radius of the $\alpha$ particle is $1.9\ \mathrm{fm}$, so their sum, $6.7\ \mathrm{fm}$, is smaller than $15.2\ \mathrm{fm}$. Hence the $\alpha$ particle turns back before it touches the nucleus, and Rutherford's formula can be used.

(b) For gold ($Z=79$), $d=\dfrac{2\times79\times1.44}{5.5}\ \mathrm{fm}=41.4\ \mathrm{fm}$. In the relation between the scattering angle and the impact parameter, $\tan\dfrac\theta2=\dfrac d{2b}$, that is, $b=\dfrac d2\cot\dfrac\theta2$, we set $\theta=90^\circ$; since $\cot45^\circ=1$,

$$ b=\frac d2=20.68\ \mathrm{fm}\approx20.7\ \mathrm{fm} $$

(c) For $\theta=10^\circ$, $\cot5^\circ=\dfrac1{\tan5^\circ}=\dfrac{1}{0.08749}=11.43$, so

$$ b=20.68\ \mathrm{fm}\times11.43\approx236\ \mathrm{fm} $$

Thus even a particle passing at a distance of $236\ \mathrm{fm}$ ($=2.4\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{m}$) from the nucleus is deflected by $10^\circ$. This distance is about $1/400$ of the atomic radius, $10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$, and yet it is still more than 30 times the nuclear radius ($7\ \mathrm{fm}$). The smaller the scattering angle, the farther from the nucleus the particle passes; to produce scattering through a large angle ($90^\circ$ or more), a particle must pass through the very narrow range $b\le20.7\ \mathrm{fm}$. This is why large-angle scattering is extremely rare.

Exercise 5.2: The Paschen and Brackett series

Solution

The first line of the Paschen series has $m=3$, $n=4$:

$$ \frac1\lambda=R_{\mathrm H}\left(\frac1{3^2}-\frac1{4^2}\right)=R_{\mathrm H}\cdot\frac{7}{144}=1.096\,776\times10^7\times0.048\,611\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}=5.3316\times10^5\ \mathrm{m^{-1}} $$

Hence $\lambda=1.8756\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}=1875.6\ \mathrm{nm}$. The photon energy is $E=\dfrac{1239.84\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}}{1875.6\ \mathrm{nm}}=0.661\ \mathrm{eV}$. The first line of the Brackett series has $m=4$, $n=5$:

$$ \frac1\lambda=R_{\mathrm H}\left(\frac1{4^2}-\frac1{5^2}\right)=R_{\mathrm H}\cdot\frac{9}{400}=1.096\,776\times10^7\times0.0225\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}=2.4677\times10^5\ \mathrm{m^{-1}} $$

Hence $\lambda=4.0523\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}=4052.3\ \mathrm{nm}$, and the photon energy is $\dfrac{1239.84}{4052.3}=0.306\ \mathrm{eV}$. Both are infrared radiation, with wavelengths longer than that of visible light ($380\sim780\ \mathrm{nm}$); the Paschen series lies in the near-infrared ($1.9\ \mu\mathrm{m}$) and the Brackett series in the mid-infrared ($4.1\ \mu\mathrm{m}$). Neither is visible to the human eye.

Exercise 5.3: The Bohr model of $\mathrm{Li^{2+}}$

Solution

For a hydrogen-like ion we replace $e_0^2\to Ze_0^2$, which gives $E_n=-Z^2\dfrac{13.606\ \mathrm{eV}}{n^2}$ and $r_n=\dfrac{n^2a_0}{Z}$. For $Z=3$, $n=1$,

$$ E_1=-9\times13.606\ \mathrm{eV}=-122.45\ \mathrm{eV},\qquad r_1=\frac{0.0529\ \mathrm{nm}}{3}=0.0176\ \mathrm{nm} $$

The wavenumber of the $n=3\to2$ transition is obtained by multiplying the Rydberg formula by $Z^2$ (we take the mass of the nucleus to be infinite and use $R_\infty$):

$$ \frac1\lambda=Z^2R_\infty\left(\frac1{2^2}-\frac1{3^2}\right)=9\times1.097\,373\times10^7\times\frac{5}{36}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}=1.3717\times10^7\ \mathrm{m^{-1}} $$

Hence $\lambda=7.290\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{m}=72.9\ \mathrm{nm}$. Compared with the H$\alpha$ line of hydrogen ($656.47\ \mathrm{nm}$), the hydrogen wavelength is $656.47/72.9=9.0$ times longer; that is, the wavelength is $1/Z^2=1/9$ of it (apart from the $0.05\ \%$ difference between $R_\infty$ and $R_{\mathrm H}$). The wavelength $72.9\ \mathrm{nm}$ lies in the extreme-ultraviolet (vacuum-ultraviolet) region and is absorbed even by air. (The reduced-mass correction, which takes the finite mass of the nucleus into account, is of order $10^{-4}$ and gives $72.91\ \mathrm{nm}$.)

Exercise 5.4: Ionization of hydrogen and the photoelectric effect

Solution

(a) From the photon energy $E=hc/\lambda$, $\lambda=\dfrac{1239.84\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}}{13.6\ \mathrm{eV}}=91.2\ \mathrm{nm}$. This is the series limit of the Lyman series ($91.18\ \mathrm{nm}$), in the vacuum ultraviolet.

(b) The binding energy of an electron in the $n=2$ state is $\dfrac{13.6\ \mathrm{eV}}{2^2}=3.40\ \mathrm{eV}$. From the photoelectric equation $h\nu=E_{\mathrm{bind}}+K_{\max}$ (Chapter 4),

$$ K_{\max}=13.6\ \mathrm{eV}-3.40\ \mathrm{eV}=10.2\ \mathrm{eV} $$

Most of the photon energy becomes the kinetic energy of the electron. (c) A hydrogen atom in the $n=2$ state can be ionized when the photon energy is at least the binding energy, $3.40\ \mathrm{eV}$, and the longest wavelength is $\lambda_{\max}=\dfrac{1239.84}{3.40}\ \mathrm{nm}=365\ \mathrm{nm}$. This agrees with the series limit of the Balmer series ($364.7\ \mathrm{nm}$) and lies in the near-ultraviolet, shorter than the shortest wavelength of visible light (about $380\ \mathrm{nm}$). Therefore, with visible light, a hydrogen atom in the $n=2$ state cannot be ionized.

Exercise 5.5: A Rydberg atom ($n=50$)

Solution

The orbit radius is $r_{50}=50^2a_0=2500\times0.0529\ \mathrm{nm}=132\ \mathrm{nm}$ (2500 times that of the ground state), and the binding energy is $\dfrac{13.606\ \mathrm{eV}}{2500}=5.44\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV}=5.44\ \mathrm{meV}$. Using $R_\infty c=3.2898\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, the frequency of the $50\to49$ transition is

$$ \nu=R_\infty c\left(\frac1{49^2}-\frac1{50^2}\right)=3.2898\times10^{15}\times(4.1649\times10^{-4}-4.0000\times10^{-4})\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}=5.426\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{Hz}=54.3\ \mathrm{GHz} $$

The classical orbital frequency is $f_{50}=\dfrac{2R_\infty c}{50^3}=\dfrac{2\times3.2898\times10^{15}}{125\,000}=5.264\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{Hz}=52.6\ \mathrm{GHz}$. The relative difference is $\dfrac{54.26-52.64}{52.64}=3.1\ \%$, in good agreement with the approximate formula $\dfrac{3}{2n}=\dfrac{3}{100}=3\ \%$. For $n=100$ (Example 5.10) it was $1.5\ \%$, so we also confirm that the relative difference decreases in proportion to $1/n$ (the correspondence principle).

Exercise 5.6: The Lyman $\alpha$ line of muonic hydrogen

Solution

In the Bohr model, replacing $m_{\mathrm e}\to\mu$, the level energies are proportional to $\mu$, so $E_n=-13.606\ \mathrm{eV}\times\dfrac{\mu}{m_{\mathrm e}}\dfrac1{n^2}$. The photon energy of the $2\to1$ transition is

$$ h\nu=E_2-E_1=13.606\ \mathrm{eV}\times185.84\times\left(1-\frac14\right)=13.606\times185.84\times0.75\ \mathrm{eV}=1896\ \mathrm{eV}=1.896\ \mathrm{keV} $$

The wavelength is $\lambda=\dfrac{1239.84\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}}{1896\ \mathrm{eV}}=0.654\ \mathrm{nm}$, which lies in the X-ray (soft X-ray) region. This is $1896/10.20\approx186$ times the $10.20\ \mathrm{eV}$ of the Ly$\alpha$ line of ordinary hydrogen, approximately $\mu/m_{\mathrm e}=185.84$ times ($185.94$ times if the correction $0.99946$ to the $\mu$ of hydrogen is included).

Exercise 5.7: Solving the harmonic oscillator with the quantization condition

Solution

(a) The trajectory in phase space is the ellipse $\dfrac{p^2}{2mE}+\dfrac{x^2}{2E/(m\omega^2)}=1$, whose semi-axis in the $p$ direction is $\sqrt{2mE}$ and whose semi-axis in the $x$ direction is $\sqrt{2E/m\omega^2}$, so its area is

$$ \oint p\,\dd x=\pi\sqrt{2mE}\sqrt{\frac{2E}{m\omega^2}}=\pi\cdot\frac{2E}{\omega}=\frac{2\pi E}{\omega} $$

From the quantum condition $\dfrac{2\pi E}{\omega}=nh$ we obtain $E_n=\dfrac{nh\omega}{2\pi}=n\hbar\omega=nh\nu$ ($n=0,1,2,\dots$). This is the oscillator energy that Planck assumed in his treatment of blackbody radiation (Chapter 3).

(b) In exact quantum mechanics (Chapter 13), the levels are $E_n=(n+\tfrac12)\hbar\omega$, and the lowest energy (the zero-point energy) is $\tfrac12\hbar\omega$. In the result obtained from the quantum condition, the zero-point energy is $0$, and the energy of the $n=0$ state is 0. This means that the oscillator is at rest at the origin, so that position and momentum would be determined simultaneously, which contradicts the uncertainty principle (Chapter 8). On the other hand, the spacing between adjacent levels, $E_{n+1}-E_n=\hbar\omega$, is the same in both treatments, so the frequencies of the light emitted in transitions (the positions of the spectral lines) agree. With the quantum condition modified to $\oint p\,\dd x=(n+\tfrac12)h$, the semiclassical approximation (WKB approximation) gives the exact result for the harmonic oscillator.

(c) The level spacing is $h\nu=\dfrac{6.626\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}\times1.0\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}}{1.602\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J/eV}}=0.4136\ \mathrm{eV}$, and the zero-point energy is $\tfrac12h\nu=0.207\ \mathrm{eV}$ ($\nu=1.0\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ is infrared radiation with wavelength $c/\nu=3\ \mu\mathrm{m}$, a rough guide to the stretching vibration of an O–H bond).

Exercise 5.8: What the old quantum theory could and could not explain

Solution

ItemClassificationExplanationChapter where resolved
(1) Wavelengths of the Balmer series of hydrogen(a)From $E_n=-13.606\ \mathrm{eV}/n^2$ and the frequency condition, the result agrees even down to the value of the Rydberg constant (the reduced-mass correction is included).— (also derived from the Schrödinger equation in Chapter 15)
(2) Line spectrum of $\mathrm{He^+}$(a)Treating it as a hydrogen-like ion with $Z=2$, the wavelengths can be calculated with $Z^2R_{\mathrm{He}}$ (Example 5.6).—
(3) Ground-state energy of the helium atom(b)The repulsion between electrons cannot be treated, and $-108.8\ \mathrm{eV}$ disagrees with the measured value $-79.0\ \mathrm{eV}$ (Example 5.12).Chapter 29 (perturbation theory), Chapter 31 (variational method), Chapters 33–37 (many-electron systems)
(4) Moseley's law(a)For the $2\to1$ transition of a hydrogen-like atom, taking the shielding as $Z-1$ reproduces it to an accuracy of $0.4\sim2\ \%$ (Example 5.11). The detailed treatment of shielding is a problem of many-electron atoms.Chapter 18, Chapter 33 onward
(5) Intensities of spectral lines(b)The probabilities, intensities, and selection rules of the jumps cannot be calculated (the correspondence principle gives only a rough estimate).Chapter 51 (time-dependent perturbation theory), Chapter 52 (absorption and emission of light)
(6) Angular momentum of the 1s state of hydrogen(b)The Bohr model gives $L=\hbar$, whereas quantum mechanics gives $L=0$ ($l=0$). The picture of orbits in the Bohr model is not literally correct.Chapters 15–17, Chapter 22
(7) Fine structure of hydrogen for $n=2$(a)/(b)With Sommerfeld's elliptical orbits and relativistic corrections, the numerical value ($0.365\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$) could be reproduced (a). However, the physical origin (a relativistic effect due to the electron spin) was not correctly understood, and the correspondence between $k$ and $l$ also differs from that in quantum mechanics (b).Chapter 23 (spin), Chapter 26 (spin–orbit interaction), Chapters 62 and 63 (the Dirac equation and its nonrelativistic limit)
(8) Reconciling the interference and diffraction of light with the photon(b)There was no framework that explains the wave nature of light and the light-quantum hypothesis in a single theory.Chapter 7 (electrons passing through slits), Chapter 8 (probability interpretation)

To summarize: what the old quantum theory could explain concerned the energy levels of systems with a single electron (or systems that can be regarded as having a single electron), as in (1), (2), and (4). What it could not explain were systems with interactions between electrons, as in (3); matters such as the intensities of transitions and the properties of light, as in (5) and (8); and matters in which the classical concept of an orbit itself is called into question, as in (6).
