Chapter 6: Compton Scattering and Matter Waves — From the Photon's Momentum to de Broglie's Hypothesis and Electron Diffraction

Exercise 6.1: Numerical values for Compton scattering

Solution

Substituting $\theta=45^\circ$ and $\cos45^\circ=1/\sqrt{2}=0.70711$ into Compton's formula $\Delta\lambda=\lambda_{\mathrm C}(1-\cos\theta)$ ($\lambda_{\mathrm C}=h/(m_{\mathrm e}c)=2.4263\ \mathrm{pm}$), we obtain

$$ \Delta\lambda=2.4263\ \mathrm{pm}\times(1-0.70711)=2.4263\times0.29289\ \mathrm{pm}=0.7106\ \mathrm{pm}\approx0.711\ \mathrm{pm} $$

The wavelength of the scattered X-ray is $\lambda'=\lambda+\Delta\lambda=70.9\ \mathrm{pm}+0.711\ \mathrm{pm}=71.61\ \mathrm{pm}$. The kinetic energy of the recoil electron is equal to the energy lost by the photon; expressing all lengths in nm, we obtain

$$ T=\frac{hc}{\lambda}-\frac{hc}{\lambda'}=\frac{hc\,\Delta\lambda}{\lambda\lambda'} =\frac{1239.84\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}\times7.106\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{nm}}{0.0709\ \mathrm{nm}\times0.07161\ \mathrm{nm}} =\frac{0.8811\ \mathrm{eV\,nm^2}}{5.077\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{nm^2}}=173.5\ \mathrm{eV}\approx174\ \mathrm{eV} $$

About $1\ \%$ of the energy of the incident photon, $hc/\lambda=1239.84/0.0709\ \mathrm{eV}=17.49\ \mathrm{keV}$, is transferred to the electron.

Exercise 6.2: The accelerating voltage that produces electrons of wavelength $0.05\ \mathrm{nm}$

Solution

Solving $\lambda\,[\mathrm{nm}]=1.2264/\sqrt{V\,[\mathrm{V}]}$ for $V$ gives $V=(1.2264/\lambda)^2$. Substituting $\lambda=0.05\ \mathrm{nm}$, we obtain

$$ V=\left(\frac{1.2264}{0.05}\right)^2=24.528^2=601.6\ \mathrm{V}\approx602\ \mathrm{V} $$

The kinetic energy of the electron is $T=602\ \mathrm{eV}$, which is extremely small compared with $2m_{\mathrm e}c^2=1.022\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{eV}$: $T/(2m_{\mathrm e}c^2)=5.9\times10^{-4}$. The relativistic correction factor $\sqrt{1+T/(2m_{\mathrm e}c^2)}$ is $1.0003$, so its effect on the wavelength is only $0.03\ \%$. Therefore, we may use the nonrelativistic formula (the speed of the electron here is $v=\sqrt{2T/m_{\mathrm e}}=0.049c$).

The wavelength of a $100\ \mathrm{V}$ electron is $0.1226\ \mathrm{nm}$, which is $2.45$ times the target value $0.05\ \mathrm{nm}$. Since $V\propto1/\lambda^2$, the voltage must be $(0.1226/0.05)^2=6.01$ times larger; that is, we need $100\ \mathrm{V}\to602\ \mathrm{V}$. The relation that the voltage must be multiplied by four to halve the wavelength can be used.

Exercise 6.3: Electrons and neutrons of the same energy

Solution

$E=25\ \mathrm{meV}=0.025\times1.602\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}=4.005\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{J}$. For the electron, the practical formula gives $\lambda_{\mathrm e}=1.2264/\sqrt{0.025}\ \mathrm{nm}=1.2264/0.15811\ \mathrm{nm}=7.756\ \mathrm{nm}$. For the neutron, $\lambda_{\mathrm n}=h/\sqrt{2m_{\mathrm n}E}$, where $2m_{\mathrm n}E=2\times1.6749\times10^{-27}\times4.005\times10^{-21}=1.3416\times10^{-47}$ and its square root is $3.663\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, so that

$$ \lambda_{\mathrm n}=\frac{6.626\times10^{-34}}{3.663\times10^{-24}}\ \mathrm{m}=1.809\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}=0.181\ \mathrm{nm} $$

For the same energy $E$, $\lambda=h/\sqrt{2mE}$, so $\lambda_{\mathrm e}/\lambda_{\mathrm n}=\sqrt{m_{\mathrm n}/m_{\mathrm e}}=\sqrt{1838.7}=42.9$, and indeed $7.756/0.181=42.9$ (the wavelength is inversely proportional to the square root of the mass).

The interatomic spacing in a crystal is about $0.2\ \mathrm{nm}$, so for diffraction to occur the wavelength must be of the same order as the spacing. The wavelength $0.181\ \mathrm{nm}$ of a $25\ \mathrm{meV}$ neutron is just about this size, and thermal neutrons are diffracted by crystals. The wavelength $7.76\ \mathrm{nm}$ of an electron of the same energy is nearly 40 times the interatomic spacing, so it cannot be used for diffraction at the atomic scale (for electrons, several tens to a hundred-odd eV are needed).

Exercise 6.4: The thermal de Broglie wavelength

Solution

(1) He atom ($4\ \mathrm{K}$): $2\pi mk_{\mathrm B}T=2\pi\times6.646\times10^{-27}\times1.3806\times10^{-23}\times4=2.306\times10^{-48}\ \mathrm{kg^2\,m^2/s^2}$, its square root is $1.519\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, and $\lambda_T=6.626\times10^{-34}/1.519\times10^{-24}=4.36\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}=0.436\ \mathrm{nm}$. Electron ($300\ \mathrm{K}$): $2\pi\times9.109\times10^{-31}\times1.3806\times10^{-23}\times300=2.371\times10^{-50}$, its square root is $1.540\times10^{-25}$, and $\lambda_T=6.626\times10^{-34}/1.540\times10^{-25}=4.30\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m}=4.30\ \mathrm{nm}$.

(2) The average spacing in liquid helium is $n^{-1/3}=(2\times10^{28})^{-1/3}\ \mathrm{m}=3.7\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}=0.37\ \mathrm{nm}$, and $\lambda_T=0.44\ \mathrm{nm}$ is larger ($n\lambda_T^3=2\times10^{28}\times(4.36\times10^{-10})^3=1.7$). That is, the waves of the atoms overlap one another, and quantum-mechanical effects (Bose condensation, superfluidity) become pronounced. The average spacing of the conduction electrons in copper is $n^{-1/3}=(8.5\times10^{28})^{-1/3}\ \mathrm{m}=0.227\ \mathrm{nm}$, and even at $300\ \mathrm{K}$, $\lambda_T=4.30\ \mathrm{nm}$ is about 19 times the spacing ($n\lambda_T^3=6.8\times10^{3}\gg1$). Therefore, even at room temperature the waves of the electrons overlap strongly, and the electrons must be treated not as a classical gas but as a degenerate Fermi gas obeying the Pauli exclusion principle. On the other hand, for the molecules of air at room temperature ($\mathrm{N_2}$, $\lambda_T\approx0.019\ \mathrm{nm}$, intermolecular spacing about $3.5\ \mathrm{nm}$), $\lambda_T\ll n^{-1/3}$, and the air may be treated as a classical gas.

Exercise 6.5: Electrons at $300\ \mathrm{kV}$

Solution

From $T=300\ \mathrm{keV}$ and $m_{\mathrm e}c^2=511.0\ \mathrm{keV}$ we get $\gamma=1+T/(m_{\mathrm e}c^2)=1+0.5871=1.5871$, and the speed is $\beta=\sqrt{1-1/\gamma^2}=\sqrt{1-0.3970}=0.7765$, that is, $v=0.777c=2.33\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s}$. The momentum is $pc=\sqrt{T(T+2m_{\mathrm e}c^2)}=\sqrt{300\times1322.0}=\sqrt{396\,600}=629.8\ \mathrm{keV}$, and $p=629.8\ \mathrm{keV}/c=629.8\times10^{3}\times1.602\times10^{-19}/(2.998\times10^{8})=3.37\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$. The wavelength is

$$ \lambda=\frac{hc}{pc}=\frac{1239.84\ \mathrm{keV\,pm}}{629.8\ \mathrm{keV}}=1.97\ \mathrm{pm} $$

With the nonrelativistic formula, $\lambda_{\mathrm{nr}}=1226.4/\sqrt{3\times10^{5}}\ \mathrm{pm}=2.239\ \mathrm{pm}$, which is larger than the relativistic value by $(2.239-1.969)/1.969=13.7\ \%$ (this corresponds to the factor $\sqrt{1+T/(2m_{\mathrm e}c^2)}=\sqrt{1+0.2935}=1.137$).

Exercise 6.6: Finding the phase velocity and group velocity from the dispersion relation

Solution

Using the de Broglie relations $\omega=E/\hbar$, $k=p/\hbar$, that is, $E=\hbar\omega$, $p=\hbar k$, and substituting them into $E^2=(pc)^2+(m_{\mathrm e}c^2)^2$, we get $\hbar^2\omega^2=\hbar^2k^2c^2+m_{\mathrm e}^2c^4$. Dividing both sides by $\hbar^2$ and taking the square root, we obtain

$$ \omega(k)=c\sqrt{k^2+k_{\mathrm c}^2},\qquad k_{\mathrm c}=\frac{m_{\mathrm e}c}{\hbar} $$

Since the derivative of $\sqrt{k^2+k_{\mathrm c}^2}$ is $k/\sqrt{k^2+k_{\mathrm c}^2}$, the group velocity is

$$ v_{\mathrm g}=\frac{\dd\omega}{\dd k}=\frac{ck}{\sqrt{k^2+k_{\mathrm c}^2}}=\frac{c^2k}{\omega} $$

The phase velocity is $v_{\mathrm{ph}}=\omega/k$, so the product is $v_{\mathrm g}v_{\mathrm{ph}}=c^2$. Substituting here $k=p/\hbar=\gamma m_{\mathrm e}v/\hbar$ and $\omega=E/\hbar=\gamma m_{\mathrm e}c^2/\hbar$, we find

$$ v_{\mathrm g}=\frac{c^2k}{\omega}=c^2\cdot\frac{\gamma m_{\mathrm e}v}{\gamma m_{\mathrm e}c^2}=v,\qquad v_{\mathrm{ph}}=\frac{\omega}{k}=\frac{\gamma m_{\mathrm e}c^2}{\gamma m_{\mathrm e}v}=\frac{c^2}{v} $$

Hence we can confirm that $v_{\mathrm g}v_{\mathrm{ph}}=v\cdot c^2/v=c^2$. For a photon, whose mass is $0$, $k_{\mathrm c}=0$, so $\omega=ck$ and $v_{\mathrm g}=v_{\mathrm{ph}}=c$, and $v_{\mathrm g}v_{\mathrm{ph}}=c^2$ also holds (a photon has $v=c$). Note also that for $k\ll k_{\mathrm c}$ (low speed) we can expand $\omega\approx ck_{\mathrm c}+ck^2/(2k_{\mathrm c})=m_{\mathrm e}c^2/\hbar+\hbar k^2/(2m_{\mathrm e})$, and $v_{\mathrm g}=\hbar k/m_{\mathrm e}=v$ agrees with the nonrelativistic result.

Exercise 6.7: Why is the Bragg angle of an electron beam small?

Solution

From the Bragg condition $2d\sin\theta=\lambda$ ($n=1$), $\sin\theta=\lambda/(2d)$. For electrons ($100\ \mathrm{keV}$, $\lambda=3.70\ \mathrm{pm}$, $d=0.2\ \mathrm{nm}=200\ \mathrm{pm}$), $\sin\theta=3.70/400=9.25\times10^{-3}$ and $\theta=0.530^\circ$ ($=9.25\ \mathrm{mrad}$). For Cu $\mathrm{K}\alpha$ X-rays ($\lambda=0.15406\ \mathrm{nm}$), $\sin\theta=0.15406/0.4=0.3852$ and $\theta=22.7^\circ$.

The wavelength of the electron beam, $3.70\ \mathrm{pm}$, is extremely short, about $1/54$ of the plane spacing $200\ \mathrm{pm}$, and with $\theta\approx\lambda/(2d)$ the angle becomes small. The wavelength of X-rays is of the same order as the interatomic spacing, so the diffraction angle is large. With an electron beam, because the diffraction angles are small, many planes that are nearly parallel to the crystal plane come close to the Bragg condition simultaneously, many spots appear in a single diffraction pattern, and the diffraction pattern effectively shows a single cross section of the crystal (a single plane of the reciprocal lattice; the reciprocal lattice is a lattice that expresses the periodicity of the crystal in wavenumber space, and the arrangement of the diffraction spots corresponds to the arrangement of the reciprocals of the periods of the crystal).

Exercise 6.8: Why a component with the incident wavelength remains in Compton scattering

Solution

If an electron is strongly bound to an atom, a collision with an X-ray photon cannot knock out the electron alone, and the whole atom recoils. The mass of the collision partner is then not the electron mass $m_{\mathrm e}$ but the mass $M$ of the atom. The derivation from conservation of momentum and conservation of energy is the same, merely with $m_{\mathrm e}$ replaced by $M$, so the shift in wavelength becomes $\Delta\lambda=\dfrac{h}{Mc}(1-\cos\theta)$, and for $M\gg m_{\mathrm e}$ the shift $\Delta\lambda$ becomes extremely small and the wavelength is practically unchanged.

The mass of a carbon atom is $M=12\ \mathrm{u}=1.99\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{kg}=2.19\times10^{4}\,m_{\mathrm e}$. We have $h/(Mc)=\lambda_{\mathrm C}\times m_{\mathrm e}/M=2.426\ \mathrm{pm}/(2.19\times10^{4})=1.11\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{pm}$, and the maximum shift in wavelength ($\theta=180^\circ$) is only $2\times1.11\times10^{-4}=2.2\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{pm}$, about $3\times10^{-6}$ times the wavelength $71.1\ \mathrm{pm}$, which is too small to be observed. In this way, a component with the same wavelength as the incident one remains.

← Back to Chapter 6, “Compton Scattering and Matter Waves — From the Photon's Momentum to de Broglie's Hypothesis and Electron Diffraction”

Chapter 7: Electrons Passing through Slits — Wave Nature and Probability

Exercise 7.1: A single slit for 100 eV electrons

Solution

Since the width is $2a=1.0\ \mathrm{\mu m}$, the half-width is $a=0.50\ \mathrm{\mu m}$. The wavelength is $\lambda=0.1226\ \mathrm{nm}=1.226\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$, and $L=0.10\ \mathrm{m}$.

(1) The first zero of the single slit is given by $u=\dfrac{pax}{\hbar L}=\dfrac{2\pi a}{\lambda L}x=\pi$, so $x_1=\dfrac{\lambda L}{2a}$. $$ x_1=\frac{1.226\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}\times0.10\ \mathrm{m}}{1.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}}=1.226\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m}=12.3\ \mathrm{\mu m} $$ The principal maximum extends from $-x_1$ to $x_1$, so its full width is $2x_1=24.5\ \mathrm{\mu m}$. (The diffraction angle is $\theta_1\approx\lambda/(2a)=1.2\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{rad}$.)

(2) The Fresnel number is $$ N_{\mathrm F}=\frac{a^2}{\lambda L}=\frac{(0.50\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m})^2}{1.226\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}\times0.10\ \mathrm{m}}=\frac{2.5\times10^{-13}}{1.226\times10^{-11}}=0.020 $$ We have $N_{\mathrm F}\ll1$, and the phase at the edge of the slit, $\pi N_{\mathrm F}=0.064\ \mathrm{rad}$, is also small, so the Fraunhofer approximation holds.

(3) The width of the geometric shadow equals the slit width $2a=1.0\ \mathrm{\mu m}$, so the full width of the principal maximum is $24.5\ \mathrm{\mu m}/1.0\ \mathrm{\mu m}\approx25$ times the width of the shadow. Even an electron with a wavelength of $0.12\ \mathrm{nm}$, when it passes through a narrow slit of the order of $\mu\mathrm{m}$, spreads to 25 times the width of the shadow while traveling $10\ \mathrm{cm}$.

Exercise 7.2: The secondary maxima of $(\sin u/u)^2$

Solution

The condition for a maximum of $f(u)=\sin^2u/u^2$ is the solution with $\sin u\ne0$ of $f'(u)=\dfrac{2\sin u\,(u\cos u-\sin u)}{u^3}=0$, that is, $\tan u=u$. In this case $\sin u=u\cos u$, so $\sin^2u=u^2\cos^2u$, and $f=\cos^2u=\dfrac{1}{1+\tan^2u}=\dfrac{1}{1+u^2}$.

We find the solutions of $\tan u=u$ numerically. The function $g(u)=\tan u-u$ takes the value $g=-n\pi\lt0$ at $u=n\pi$ and tends to $+\infty$ as $u\to(n+\tfrac12)\pi$; since its derivative is $g'(u)=\tan^2u\ge0$, it increases monotonically on the interval $(n\pi,\,(n+\tfrac12)\pi)$. Therefore this interval contains exactly one point where the sign changes, which is the solution (for $n=1$, $g(\pi)=-\pi$ and $g\to+\infty$, so there is one solution in the interval $(\pi,\,1.5\pi)$). Solving by bisection or a similar method, we obtain $$ u_1=4.4934,\qquad u_2=7.7253,\qquad(u_3=10.9041) $$ (where $u_1=1.430\pi$ and $u_2=2.459\pi$). The heights are $$ f(u_1)=\frac{1}{1+4.4934^2}=\frac{1}{21.19}=0.0472,\qquad f(u_2)=\frac{1}{1+7.7253^2}=\frac{1}{60.68}=0.0165 $$ so the first secondary maximum is $4.72\ \%$ of the principal maximum, and the second secondary maximum is $1.65\ \%$.

Approximation for large $n$: let $u=(n+\tfrac12)\pi-\varepsilon$. Then $\tan u=\cot\varepsilon\approx1/\varepsilon$ (for small $\varepsilon$), and from $\tan u=u$ we get $\varepsilon\approx\dfrac{1}{u}\approx\dfrac{1}{(n+\frac12)\pi}$. Therefore $$ u_n\approx\left(n+\tfrac12\right)\pi-\frac{1}{(n+\frac12)\pi} $$ Comparing numerical values, for $n=1$ we have $4.7124-0.2122=4.5002$ (exact solution $4.4934$, difference $0.15\ \%$); for $n=2$, $7.8540-0.1273=7.7267$ (exact solution $7.7253$); and for $n=3$, $10.9956-0.0909=10.9047$ (exact solution $10.9041$). The larger $n$ is, the better the agreement. Even the crudest approximation $u_n\approx(n+\tfrac12)\pi$ gives $4.712$ for $n=1$ (error $4.9\ \%$) and $7.854$ for $n=2$ (error $1.7\ \%$), and the height can be estimated as $f\approx\dfrac{1}{(n+\frac12)^2\pi^2}$ ($0.0450$ for $n=1$ and $0.0162$ for $n=2$).

Exercise 7.3: The sum-to-product formula and fringes × envelope

Solution

(1) Let $\alpha=\dfrac{A+B}{2}$ and $\beta=\dfrac{B-A}{2}$; then $A=\alpha-\beta$ and $B=\alpha+\beta$. By the addition theorem for the sine, $\sin(\alpha\pm\beta)=\sin\alpha\cos\beta\pm\cos\alpha\sin\beta$, we have $$ \sin B-\sin A=\bigl(\sin\alpha\cos\beta+\cos\alpha\sin\beta\bigr)-\bigl(\sin\alpha\cos\beta-\cos\alpha\sin\beta\bigr)=2\cos\alpha\,\sin\beta $$ and so we obtain $2\cos\dfrac{A+B}{2}\sin\dfrac{B-A}{2}$.

(2) With $q=\dfrac{px}{\hbar L}$, the probability amplitude of the double slit, apart from the phase factor, is $\dfrac{2}{q}\bigl(\sin q(a+b)-\sin qa\bigr)$. Setting $A=qa$ and $B=q(a+b)$, we have $\dfrac{A+B}{2}=\dfrac{q(2a+b)}{2}=\dfrac{qd}{2}$ and $\dfrac{B-A}{2}=\dfrac{qb}{2}$, so $$ \frac{2}{q}\bigl(\sin q(a+b)-\sin qa\bigr)=\frac{4}{q}\cos\frac{qd}{2}\sin\frac{qb}{2}=2b\,\cos\frac{qd}{2}\;\frac{\sin(qb/2)}{qb/2} $$ Squaring, we obtain $\abs{\psi}^2=4b^2A_0^{\,2}\cos^2\dfrac{qd}{2}\left(\dfrac{\sin(qb/2)}{qb/2}\right)^2$. Since $q=\dfrac{2\pi x}{\lambda L}$, we have $\dfrac{qd}{2}=\dfrac{\pi d\,x}{\lambda L}$, and the factor $\cos^2$ has its maxima at $\dfrac{\pi dx}{\lambda L}=m\pi$, that is, at $x_m=m\dfrac{\lambda L}{d}$. The spacing between adjacent bright fringes is $\dfrac{\lambda L}{d}$.

(3) For $d=3b$ and $x=\lambda L/d$ ($m=1$), we have $\cos^2\dfrac{qd}{2}=\cos^2\pi=1$ and $\dfrac{qb}{2}=\dfrac{\pi bx}{\lambda L}=\dfrac{\pi b}{d}=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$. At the center ($x=0$), $\cos^2=1$ and $\dfrac{\sin(qb/2)}{qb/2}\to1$, so the intensity ratio is $$ \frac{\abs{\psi(\lambda L/d)}^2}{\abs{\psi(0)}^2}=\left(\frac{\sin(\pi/3)}{\pi/3}\right)^2=\left(\frac{0.8660}{1.0472}\right)^2=0.684 $$ The first-order fringe has $68\ \%$ of the intensity of the central fringe.

Exercise 7.4: The ratio of the slit width $b$ to the center-to-center spacing $d$

Solution

The bright fringes are at $x_m=m\lambda L/d$, and the zeros of the envelope are at $x=n\lambda L/b$ ($n=\pm1,\pm2,\dots$). The condition that the two coincide, $\dfrac{m}{d}=\dfrac{n}{b}$, gives $m=n\,\dfrac{d}{b}$.

(1) For $d/b=2$, $m=2n$: the fringes of order 2, 4, … are missing. For $d/b=3$, $m=3n$: the fringes of order 3, 6, … are missing. For $d/b=5$, $m=5n$: the fringes of order 5, 10, … are missing.

(2) The bright fringes that fall within the central peak of the envelope, $\abs{x}\lt\lambda L/b$, are those with an integer $m$ satisfying $m\lambda L/d\lt\lambda L/b$, that is, $\abs{m}\lt d/b$. For $d/b=2$ there are three bright fringes, $m=0,\pm1$; for $d/b=3$ there are five, $m=0,\pm1,\pm2$; and for $d/b=5$ there are nine, $m=0,\pm1,\dots,\pm4$ (the position $\abs{m}=d/b$ coincides with a zero of the envelope and vanishes). In general, if $d/b=N$ (an integer), there are $2N-1$ bright fringes.

(3) For $d/b=2.5$, the smallest pair of integers $(m,n)$ satisfying $m=2.5\,n$ is $n=2$, $m=5$. The first missing fringe is the fifth-order fringe, and the first through fourth orders are visible. Inside the central peak, $\abs{m}\lt2.5$, that is, $m=0,\pm1,\pm2$, there are five bright fringes.

Exercise 7.5: The diffraction grating ($N$ slits)

Solution

(1) Let the center of slit $j$ ($j=0,1,\dots,N-1$) be $y_j=\bigl(j-\tfrac{N-1}{2}\bigr)d$. The integral over a slit of width $b$, taken about its center, is $$ \int_{y_j-b/2}^{y_j+b/2}e^{-iqy}\dd y=e^{-iqy_j}\int_{-b/2}^{b/2}e^{-iqs}\dd s=e^{-iqy_j}\,b\,\frac{\sin(qb/2)}{qb/2} $$ (where $y=y_j+s$ and $q=px/\hbar L$; the common phase factor that comes out in front has been omitted). The sum over the $N$ slits has the form of the common factor $b\,\dfrac{\sin(qb/2)}{qb/2}$ multiplied by $\displaystyle\sum_je^{-iqy_j}$. Setting $\delta=qd$, we have $e^{-iqy_j}=e^{iq(N-1)d/2}e^{-ij\delta}$, and by the formula for the sum of a geometric series, $$ \sum_{j=0}^{N-1}e^{-ij\delta}=\frac{1-e^{-iN\delta}}{1-e^{-i\delta}}=e^{-i(N-1)\delta/2}\,\frac{\sin(N\delta/2)}{\sin(\delta/2)} $$ (we factored $e^{-iN\delta/2}$ out of the numerator and $e^{-i\delta/2}$ out of the denominator, and used $e^{i\theta}-e^{-i\theta}=2i\sin\theta$). The phase factors $e^{iq(N-1)d/2}$ and $e^{-i(N-1)\delta/2}=e^{-iq(N-1)d/2}$ cancel each other, so $\displaystyle\sum_je^{-iqy_j}=\frac{\sin(N\delta/2)}{\sin(\delta/2)}$ (a real number). Therefore $$ \abs{\psi}^2=A_0^{\,2}b^2\left(\frac{\sin(qb/2)}{qb/2}\right)^2\left(\frac{\sin(N\delta/2)}{\sin(\delta/2)}\right)^2 $$

(2) For $N=2$, $\dfrac{\sin\delta}{\sin(\delta/2)}=\dfrac{2\sin(\delta/2)\cos(\delta/2)}{\sin(\delta/2)}=2\cos\dfrac{\delta}{2}$, so $\abs{\psi}^2=4A_0^{\,2}b^2\cos^2\dfrac{qd}{2}\left(\dfrac{\sin(qb/2)}{qb/2}\right)^2$, which agrees with the double-slit formula of Chapter 7 (fringes × envelope).

(3) Principal maxima: when $\delta\to2\pi m$, the numerator and the denominator both become 0. Setting $\delta=2\pi m+\epsilon$, we have $\sin(N\delta/2)=\sin(N\pi m+N\epsilon/2)=(-1)^{Nm}\sin(N\epsilon/2)\approx(-1)^{Nm}N\epsilon/2$ and $\sin(\delta/2)\approx(-1)^m\epsilon/2$, so the ratio is $\pm N$, and squaring it, the height is $N^2$ (for $N=2$ this agrees with $4\cos^2(m\pi)=4$).

Zeros: $\sin(N\delta/2)=0$ and $\sin(\delta/2)\ne0$ hold when $\delta=2\pi n/N$ ($n$ is an integer that is not a multiple of $N$). Between the adjacent principal maxima $\delta=0$ and $\delta=2\pi$ there are $N-1$ zeros, $n=1,2,\dots,N-1$, and since there is one peak between each pair of adjacent zeros, the number of peaks (secondary maxima) is $N-2$. For example, for $N=5$ there are four zeros and three secondary maxima, and the heights of the secondary maxima are $0.0625,\ 0.040,\ 0.0625$ (relative to the principal maximum). For large $N$, the first secondary maximum approaches about $4.7\ \%$ of the principal maximum (the same as for single-slit diffraction).

Width of the principal maximum: the first zeros on either side of the principal maximum $\delta=0$ are at $\delta=\pm2\pi/N$, so the width of the principal maximum (the full width measured in $\delta$, $4\pi/N$) is inversely proportional to $N$. As the number of slits increases, the principal maximum becomes sharper, and the positions of the fringes can be measured with high precision. This is the origin of the resolution of a diffraction grating.

Exercise 7.6: Placing a detector at only one of the slits

Solution

Let the amplitudes for passing through the two slits both have magnitude $1$ and let the phase difference be $\delta$, and write $\psi_1=1$ and $\psi_2=e^{i\delta}$. (We ignore the overall normalization of the electrons and look only at the relative intensities.)

(1) Electrons that triggered the detector: it is established that they passed through slit 1. The amplitude is the product of “the amplitude $\psi_1$ for passing through slit 1” and “the amplitude $\sqrt{\eta}$ for the detector to respond”, and the distribution is $\eta\,\abs{\psi_1}^2=\eta$. Since it does not depend on $\delta$, there are no fringes (visibility $0$). The probability that the detector responds is $\eta/2=0.25$, which is the probability $\tfrac12$ that the electron passes through slit 1 multiplied by $\eta$.

(2) Electrons that did not trigger the detector: whether (i) the electron passed through slit 2, or (ii) it passed through slit 1 but the detector did not respond (the amplitude is multiplied by $\sqrt{1-\eta}$), the record is the same, “did not respond”, and the two cases cannot be distinguished. Therefore we add the amplitudes. $$ I_{\text{no}}(\delta)=\abs{\psi_2+\sqrt{1-\eta}\,\psi_1}^2=1+(1-\eta)+2\sqrt{1-\eta}\cos\delta $$ (we used $\abs{e^{i\delta}+\sqrt{1-\eta}}^2=1+(1-\eta)+2\sqrt{1-\eta}\cos\delta$). For $\eta=0.5$, $I_{\text{no}}=1.5+1.414\cos\delta$, so $I_{\max}=2.914$ and $I_{\min}=0.0858$, and the visibility is $$ V_{\text{no}}=\frac{2\sqrt{1-\eta}}{2-\eta}=\frac{1.414}{1.5}=0.943 $$ The fraction of electrons that did not trigger the detector is $1-\eta/2=0.75$.

(3) The overall distribution is the sum of the distributions of the electrons that triggered the detector and those that did not, $\eta+I_{\text{no}}$: $$ I(\delta)=\eta+\bigl[2-\eta+2\sqrt{1-\eta}\cos\delta\bigr]=2+2\sqrt{1-\eta}\cos\delta $$ Therefore the overall visibility is $$ V=\frac{2\sqrt{1-\eta}}{2}=\sqrt{1-\eta}=\sqrt{0.5}=0.707 $$ Even if the efficiency of the detector is 50%, the fringes remain with a visibility of about 71%. This value differs from that of the case in Example 7.11, in which “the two slits are illuminated with the same intensity and the path is recorded” ($V=1-p$), because the recording mechanism is different. When a detector is placed at only one of the slits, the fact that it “did not respond” itself becomes the information that “the electron seems to have passed through slit 2”, and the fringes fade as $\sqrt{1-\eta}$.

(Using the distinguishability of the path provided by the detector, $D=\sqrt{\eta}=0.707$, we get $V^2+D^2=(1-\eta)+\eta=1$, so equality holds in the inequality $V^2+D^2\le1$ between the fringe visibility and the path distinguishability.)

Exercise 7.7: Mass and the spread of diffraction

Solution

We have $a=1\ \mathrm{mm}$, $L=1\ \mathrm{m}$, and $v=1\ \mathrm{m/s}$. (1) Using $\alpha=\dfrac{mva}{\hbar L}=\dfrac{m\times1\times10^{-3}}{1.0546\times10^{-34}}$, we find $x_1=\pi/\alpha$ to be $$ m=10^{-30}\ \mathrm{kg}:\ \alpha=9.48\ \mathrm{m^{-1}},\ x_1=0.331\ \mathrm{m};\qquad m=10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}:\ \alpha=9.48\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}},\ x_1=0.331\ \mathrm{mm}; $$ $$ m=10^{-24}\ \mathrm{kg}:\ \alpha=9.48\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}},\ x_1=0.331\ \mathrm{\mu m} $$ (each time the mass increases by three orders of magnitude, the position of the first zero becomes smaller by three orders of magnitude).

(2) The Fresnel number $N_{\mathrm F}=\dfrac{a^2mv}{hL}=\dfrac{10^{-6}\,m}{6.626\times10^{-34}}$ is $1.5\times10^{-3}$ for $m=10^{-30}\ \mathrm{kg}$, $1.5$ for $10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$, and $1.5\times10^{3}$ for $10^{-24}\ \mathrm{kg}$. For the first mass, $N_{\mathrm F}\ll1$, and the result of (1) is valid. For the second, $N_{\mathrm F}\sim1$, which is at the limit of the Fraunhofer approximation; $x_1=0.33\ \mathrm{mm}$ is smaller than the half-width of the slit, $a=1\ \mathrm{mm}$, so the spread due to diffraction is smaller than the width of the shadow, that is, we have entered the regime in which the approximation does not hold. For the third, $N_{\mathrm F}\gg1$, and $x_1=0.331\ \mathrm{\mu m}$ in (1) has no meaning.

(3) For $m=10^{-24}\ \mathrm{kg}$, the wavelength is $\lambda=h/(mv)=6.6\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$, and the distribution from wave optics (the Fresnel integral) is spread almost uniformly over the geometric shadow of the slit, that is, over the range $\abs{x}\lt a=1\ \mathrm{mm}$. The blurring of the edge of the shadow is about $\sqrt{\lambda L}=2.6\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m}=26\ \mathrm{\mu m}$. The probability of reaching $\abs{x}\lt1\ \mathrm{\mu m}$ is given by the ratio to the width of the uniform shadow, $1\ \mathrm{\mu m}/1\ \mathrm{mm}=10^{-3}$, which is completely different from the $0.966$ given by the Fraunhofer formula. The $\delta$ function for a heavy particle means “zero spread due to diffraction”.

Exercise 7.8: Descriptive question: electrons arriving one at a time and “passing through both slits”

Solution

(1) Each electron is detected at a single point on the screen, one at a time (it is not divided, and the arrival point of an individual electron cannot be predicted). However, the probability density of arriving near the position $x$ is given by the square of the absolute value of the probability amplitude $\psi(x)=\psi_1(x)+\psi_2(x)$, that is, $\abs{\psi_1+\psi_2}^2$. Here $\psi_1$ and $\psi_2$ are the probability amplitudes of arriving at the point $x$ through the upper and the lower slit, respectively. At positions where the phase difference is an integer multiple of $2\pi$, the amplitudes reinforce each other and electrons arrive often; at positions where it is an odd multiple of $\pi$, they cancel each other and electrons do not arrive. Since the electrons fly one at a time, independently of one another, when many of them are collected each electron appears at one point according to the same probability distribution, and that distribution forms the fringes (the product of $\cos^2$ and an envelope).

(2) The statement “one electron passes through both slits at the same time” is wrong if it means that the electron splits in two and passes through both slits. As an observed fact, an electron is detected as a single particle at a single point; it has never been detected split in two. The correct meaning is: “the probability of arriving at the point $x$ is determined by the sum of two probability amplitudes, one for the process of passing through slit 1 and one for the process of passing through slit 2 (it cannot be distinguished which of the two slits the electron went through).” “Which slit the electron passed through” has no definite value unless it is examined by a measurement.

(3) If we place a device that records the electrons passing through, it becomes possible (in principle) to distinguish which slit the electron went through, so we are in case 2 of Law 7.1, and the fringes (the interference term) disappear. The distribution becomes the sum of the probabilities of the diffraction patterns of the individual slits (a plain peak with no interference term). If the probability that the device responds is $p$, the fringe visibility is $1-p$; if the efficiency of a detector at only one of the slits is $\eta$, it is $\sqrt{1-\eta}$ (Example 7.11, Exercise 7.6). The fringes disappear not only because the device disturbs the electron, but also because the information about the path remains (if the information is erased, the fringes return).

← Back to Chapter 7, “Electrons Passing through Slits — Wave Nature and Probability”

Chapter 8: The Axioms of Quantum Mechanics — The Born Interpretation, Commutation Relations, and the Uncertainty Principle

Exercise 8.1: Normalization and expectation values

Solution

(1) The probability density is $\abs{\psi}^2=A^2x^2e^{-2x/\ell}$ ($x\ge0$). Using the formula $\int_0^{\infty}x^ne^{-x/a}\dd x=n!\,a^{n+1}$ with $a=\ell/2$, we obtain

$$ \int_0^{\infty}A^2x^2e^{-2x/\ell}\dd x=A^2\cdot2!\left(\frac{\ell}{2}\right)^3=\frac{A^2\ell^3}{4}=1\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad A=\frac{2}{\ell^{3/2}} $$

The unit of the constant is $\mathrm{m^{-3/2}}$, which agrees with the fact that the unit of $\psi$, $\mathrm{m^{-1/2}}$, is obtained from $A\,x$.

(2) We use $A^2=4/\ell^3$. We compute the integrals for $n=3$ and $n=4$ with the same formula.

$$ \langle x\rangle=A^2\int_0^{\infty}x^3e^{-2x/\ell}\dd x=\frac{4}{\ell^3}\cdot3!\left(\frac{\ell}{2}\right)^4=\frac{4}{\ell^3}\cdot\frac{6\ell^4}{16}=\frac{3}{2}\ell $$ $$ \langle x^2\rangle=A^2\int_0^{\infty}x^4e^{-2x/\ell}\dd x=\frac{4}{\ell^3}\cdot4!\left(\frac{\ell}{2}\right)^5=\frac{4}{\ell^3}\cdot\frac{24\ell^5}{32}=3\ell^2 $$

The variance is $(\Delta x)^2=\langle x^2\rangle-\langle x\rangle^2=3\ell^2-\dfrac{9}{4}\ell^2=\dfrac{3}{4}\ell^2$, and $\Delta x=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\ell=0.866\,\ell$.

(3) Differentiating $\rho(x)=A^2x^2e^{-2x/\ell}$ gives $\rho'(x)=A^2\left(2x-\dfrac{2x^2}{\ell}\right)e^{-2x/\ell}=2A^2x\left(1-\dfrac{x}{\ell}\right)e^{-2x/\ell}$, and for $x\gt0$ we have $\rho'=0$ only at $x=\ell$. Since $\rho'\gt0$ for $0\lt x\lt\ell$ and $\rho'\lt0$ for $x\gt\ell$, the maximum (the mode) is at $x=\ell$. The expectation value $\langle x\rangle=\frac{3}{2}\ell$ is larger than the mode $\ell$. This is because the distribution has a long tail on the right.

(4) For $\ell=0.1\ \mathrm{nm}$, $A=\dfrac{2}{(0.1\ \mathrm{nm})^{3/2}}=63.2\ \mathrm{nm^{-3/2}}$, $\langle x\rangle=0.15\ \mathrm{nm}$, $\Delta x=0.0866\ \mathrm{nm}$, and the mode is $0.10\ \mathrm{nm}$.

Exercise 8.2: A uniform probability density and the Riemann-sum method

Solution

(1) $\displaystyle\int_0^L\frac{1}{L}\dd x=\frac{L}{L}=1$.

(2) The term at $x=kL/n$ is $\dfrac{kL}{n}\cdot\dfrac{1}{L}\cdot\dfrac{L}{n}=\dfrac{kL}{n^2}$, so using $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}k=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ we obtain

$$ E_n=\frac{L}{n^2}\cdot\frac{n(n+1)}{2}=\frac{L}{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right) $$

For $n=10$ this is $0.55\,L$, and for $n=100$ it is $0.505\,L$; as $n\to\infty$, $E_n\to L/2$. On the other hand, the exact expectation value is $\displaystyle\int_0^Lx\cdot\frac{1}{L}\dd x=\frac{1}{L}\cdot\frac{L^2}{2}=\frac{L}{2}$, which agrees.

(3) From $\langle x^2\rangle=\displaystyle\int_0^L\frac{x^2}{L}\dd x=\frac{L^2}{3}$ we get $(\Delta x)^2=\dfrac{L^2}{3}-\dfrac{L^2}{4}=\dfrac{L^2}{12}$, so $\Delta x=\dfrac{L}{\sqrt{12}}=0.2887\,L$. For $L=2\ \mathrm{nm}$, $\Delta x=0.577\ \mathrm{nm}$ and $\langle x\rangle=1.0\ \mathrm{nm}$.

Exercise 8.3: Probabilities of measurement outcomes

Solution

(1) Using the orthonormality of $\psi_n$, $\int\psi_m\psi_n\dd x=\delta_{mn}$, we get $\int\abs{\psi}^2\dd x=\dfrac{1}{9}\left(1^2+2^2+2^2\right)=\dfrac{9}{9}=1$ (the cross terms are 0). Thus the state is normalized.

(2) The expansion coefficients are $c_1=\dfrac{1}{3}$ and $c_2=c_3=\dfrac{2}{3}$ ($c_n=\int\psi_n\psi\dd x$). The probability of obtaining the energy $E_n=n^2E_1$ is $\abs{c_n}^2$, so $P(E_1)=\dfrac{1}{9}=0.111$, $P(E_2)=\dfrac{4}{9}=0.444$, and $P(E_3)=\dfrac{4}{9}=0.444$ (the sum is 1). The measured values are $E_1=0.376\ \mathrm{eV}$, $E_2=1.504\ \mathrm{eV}$, and $E_3=3.384\ \mathrm{eV}$, respectively.

(3) The expectation value is $\langle E\rangle=\dfrac{1}{9}\cdot1\cdot E_1+\dfrac{4}{9}\cdot4E_1+\dfrac{4}{9}\cdot9E_1=\dfrac{1+16+36}{9}E_1=\dfrac{53}{9}E_1=5.889\,E_1=2.214\ \mathrm{eV}$. The expectation value of the square is $\langle E^2\rangle=\dfrac{1}{9}E_1^2+\dfrac{4}{9}\cdot16E_1^2+\dfrac{4}{9}\cdot81E_1^2=\dfrac{1+64+324}{9}E_1^2=\dfrac{389}{9}E_1^2=43.22\,E_1^2$. The variance is $(\Delta E)^2=43.22\,E_1^2-\left(\dfrac{53}{9}\right)^2E_1^2=(43.22-34.68)E_1^2=8.543\,E_1^2$, and $\Delta E=2.923\,E_1=1.099\ \mathrm{eV}$. The expectation value $2.21\ \mathrm{eV}$ lies between $E_2$ and $E_3$, and it is not a value obtained in a single measurement.

(4) Immediately after $E_3$ is obtained, the state has collapsed to $\psi_3$. Since $\psi_3$ is an eigenfunction of $\hat{H}$, if we measure the energy once more, $E_3$ is obtained with probability $1$ ($c_3=\int\psi_3\psi_3\dd x=1$).

Exercise 8.4: Computing commutators

Solution

In what follows, $\comm{\hat{x}}{\hat{p}}=i\hbar$ is a number, so it commutes with every operator. We use the formulas $\comm{\hat{A}}{\hat{B}\hat{C}}=\comm{\hat{A}}{\hat{B}}\hat{C}+\hat{B}\comm{\hat{A}}{\hat{C}}$ and $\comm{\hat{A}\hat{B}}{\hat{C}}=\hat{A}\comm{\hat{B}}{\hat{C}}+\comm{\hat{A}}{\hat{C}}\hat{B}$.

(1) First, $\comm{\hat{x}}{\hat{p}^2}=\comm{\hat{x}}{\hat{p}}\hat{p}+\hat{p}\comm{\hat{x}}{\hat{p}}=i\hbar\hat{p}+i\hbar\hat{p}=2i\hbar\hat{p}$. Next, writing $\hat{p}^3=\hat{p}\cdot\hat{p}^2$, we have

$$ \comm{\hat{x}}{\hat{p}^3}=\comm{\hat{x}}{\hat{p}}\hat{p}^2+\hat{p}\comm{\hat{x}}{\hat{p}^2}=i\hbar\hat{p}^2+\hat{p}\cdot2i\hbar\hat{p}=3i\hbar\hat{p}^2 $$

(In general, $\comm{\hat{x}}{\hat{p}^n}=i\hbar n\hat{p}^{n-1}$.)

(2) Writing $\hat{x}^2=\hat{x}\cdot\hat{x}$, we use the second formula: $\comm{\hat{x}^2}{\hat{p}^2}=\hat{x}\comm{\hat{x}}{\hat{p}^2}+\comm{\hat{x}}{\hat{p}^2}\hat{x}=\hat{x}\cdot2i\hbar\hat{p}+2i\hbar\hat{p}\cdot\hat{x}=2i\hbar\left(\hat{x}\hat{p}+\hat{p}\hat{x}\right)$. Using $\hat{p}\hat{x}=\hat{x}\hat{p}-i\hbar$, this can also be written as $=2i\hbar\left(2\hat{x}\hat{p}-i\hbar\right)=4i\hbar\,\hat{x}\hat{p}+2\hbar^2$.

(3) By the axiom, $\hat{x}\hat{p}=\hat{p}\hat{x}+i\hbar$. Using this, $\comm{\hat{x}\hat{p}}{\hat{p}\hat{x}}=\comm{\hat{p}\hat{x}+i\hbar}{\hat{p}\hat{x}}=\comm{\hat{p}\hat{x}}{\hat{p}\hat{x}}+\comm{i\hbar}{\hat{p}\hat{x}}=0+0=0$ (the commutator of an operator with itself is 0, and the commutator with a number is 0). Therefore $\hat{x}\hat{p}$ and $\hat{p}\hat{x}$ commute. (Check: for any function $f$, $\hat{x}\hat{p}f=-i\hbar xf'$ and $\hat{p}\hat{x}f=-i\hbar(f+xf')$; the two differ only by the constant $i\hbar$, so the commutator is 0.)

Exercise 8.5: An alternative proof of the Schwarz inequality

Solution

Let $\int f^*g\dd\tau=\abs{\int f^*g\dd\tau}\,e^{i\alpha}$ and $g'=e^{-i\alpha}g$. Then $\int f^*g'\dd\tau=e^{-i\alpha}\int f^*g\dd\tau=\abs{\int f^*g\dd\tau}$ is a nonnegative real number. Also $\int g'^*f\dd\tau=\left(\int f^*g'\dd\tau\right)^*=\abs{\int f^*g\dd\tau}$ and $\abs{g'}^2=\abs{g}^2$. For a real number $t$,

$$ 0\le\int\abs{f+tg'}^2\dd\tau=\int\abs{f}^2\dd\tau+t\int f^*g'\dd\tau+t\int g'^*f\dd\tau+t^2\int\abs{g'}^2\dd\tau =\int\abs{f}^2\dd\tau+2t\,\abs{\int f^*g\dd\tau}+t^2\int\abs{g}^2\dd\tau $$

The right-hand side is the quadratic $at^2+bt+c$ in $t$ ($a=\int\abs{g}^2\dd\tau\gt0$, $b=2\abs{\int f^*g\dd\tau}$, $c=\int\abs{f}^2\dd\tau$). The condition for it to be $0$ or greater for all real numbers $t$ is that the discriminant be $0$ or less: $b^2-4ac\le0$, that is,

$$ 4\left|\int f^*g\dd\tau\right|^2-4\int\abs{g}^2\dd\tau\int\abs{f}^2\dd\tau\le0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad\int\abs{f}^2\dd\tau\int\abs{g}^2\dd\tau\ge\left|\int f^*g\dd\tau\right|^2 $$

(In the case $a=0$, that is, $g\equiv0$, both sides are $0$ and the inequality holds.) Equality holds when the discriminant is 0, that is, when the quadratic has a double root at the real number $t_0=-b/2a$; then $\int\abs{f+t_0g'}^2\dd\tau=0$, that is, $f=-t_0g'=-t_0e^{-i\alpha}g$. Therefore equality holds only when $f$ and $g$ are related by a constant multiple ($g=cf$ or $f=cg$, where $c$ is a complex number).

Exercise 8.6: Lifetime and natural linewidth

Solution

The natural linewidth is $\Delta E=\hbar/\tau$ (full width at half maximum) and $\Delta\nu=1/(2\pi\tau)$.

(1) $\tau=1\ \mathrm{ps}=10^{-12}\ \mathrm{s}$: $\Delta E=\dfrac{6.582\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{eV\,s}}{10^{-12}\ \mathrm{s}}=6.582\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV}=0.658\ \mathrm{meV}$, $\Delta\nu=\dfrac{1}{2\pi\times10^{-12}}=1.59\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{Hz}=0.159\ \mathrm{THz}$. Relative to the room-temperature thermal energy $k_{\mathrm{B}}T\approx25.9\ \mathrm{meV}$, the ratio is $\dfrac{0.658}{25.9}=0.0254$, that is, about $\dfrac{1}{39}$. The spectral line of a state with a lifetime of about $1\ \mathrm{ps}$ has a width of a few $\%$ of the thermal energy.

(2) $\tau=1\ \mathrm{ms}=10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s}$: $\Delta E=\dfrac{6.582\times10^{-16}}{10^{-3}}=6.58\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{eV}$, $\Delta\nu=\dfrac{1}{2\pi\times10^{-3}}=159\ \mathrm{Hz}$. This is a very narrow line; the linewidths of actual solids and gases are determined by other broadening mechanisms (thermal motion and strain of the crystal).

Exercise 8.7: Estimating the kinetic energy of a quantum dot

Solution

The uncertainty principle $\Delta x\,\Delta p\ge\hbar/2$ gives $\Delta p\ge\dfrac{\hbar}{2\Delta x}=\dfrac{1.0546\times10^{-34}}{2\times1.0\times10^{-9}}=5.27\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$. The estimate of the kinetic energy is

$$ \frac{(\Delta p)^2}{2m_{\mathrm{e}}}\ge\frac{(5.27\times10^{-26})^2}{2\times9.109\times10^{-31}}=1.53\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{J}=\frac{1.53\times10^{-21}}{1.602\times10^{-19}}\ \mathrm{eV}=9.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV}=9.5\ \mathrm{meV} $$

In comparison with this, $E_1=0.376\ \mathrm{eV}$ of an infinite well of width $L=1\ \mathrm{nm}$ is about $39$ times larger. The reason is that $\Delta x=1.0\ \mathrm{nm}$ and $L=1\ \mathrm{nm}$ are different quantities. The spread of the position (the standard deviation) in the ground state of the infinite well is $\Delta x=0.181\,L=0.181\ \mathrm{nm}$, which is much smaller than $1.0\ \mathrm{nm}$. If we therefore redo the estimate of the lower bound using $\Delta x=0.181\ \mathrm{nm}$, we obtain $\Delta p\ge\hbar/(2\times0.181\ \mathrm{nm})$ and $\dfrac{(\Delta p)^2}{2m_{\mathrm{e}}}\ge9.525\ \mathrm{meV}\times\dfrac{1}{0.1808^2}=0.29\ \mathrm{eV}$, which comes close to $E_1=0.376\ \mathrm{eV}$. The remaining difference arises because $\Delta x\,\Delta p=0.568\,\hbar$ for the ground state of the box slightly exceeds the lower bound $\hbar/2$ (by a factor of $0.568/0.5=1.136$); in energy this becomes a factor of $1.136^2=1.29$ ($0.29\times1.29=0.376\ \mathrm{eV}$). Note also that for a state with $\langle p\rangle=0$ we have $\langle p^2\rangle=(\Delta p)^2$, so $(\Delta p)^2/2m_{\mathrm{e}}$ is itself the expectation value of the kinetic energy.

Exercise 8.8: Correcting misconceptions

Solution

(1) The uncertainty principle as a spread of the state. In the inequality $\Delta x\,\Delta p\ge\hbar/2$, $\Delta x$ and $\Delta p$ are, for a large number of particles prepared in the state represented by the same wave function $\psi$, the scatter of the values obtained when the position is measured (the standard deviation) and the scatter of the values obtained when the momentum is measured. The group of particles whose position is measured and the group whose momentum is measured may be different. Therefore, the idea that one measurement disturbs the other does not appear here. Moreover, however precise the measuring instrument with which the position is measured (even if the measurement error is zero), the values obtained scatter according to $\psi$, and their spread $\Delta x$ does not disappear. This inequality is derived mathematically from a property of the Fourier transform of the wave function (a function that is narrow in the position representation is broad in the momentum representation) and the commutation relation $\comm{\hat{x}}{\hat{p}}=i\hbar$; it is unrelated to the performance of the measuring instrument.

(2) The uncertainty relation as measurement error and disturbance. What the performance of the measuring instrument is relevant to is the “error $\varepsilon(x)$ of the apparatus that measures the position” and the “disturbance $\eta(p)$ that this measurement gives to the momentum.” In Heisenberg's $\gamma$-ray microscope, if the wavelength is shortened to make $\varepsilon(x)$ small, the momentum of the photon becomes large and $\eta(p)$ becomes large. However, a relation in this sense does not hold in general in the form $\varepsilon(x)\,\eta(p)\ge\hbar/2$ that Heisenberg first wrote down. Ozawa's relation is $\varepsilon(A)\eta(B)+\varepsilon(A)\sigma(B)+\sigma(A)\eta(B)\ge\frac{1}{2}\abs{\langle\comm{\hat{A}}{\hat{B}}\rangle}$, in which the first term is the product of the error and the disturbance, and the second and third terms contain the scatter of the state before the measurement, $\sigma(A)=\Delta A$ and $\sigma(B)=\Delta B$. Because there are terms for the scatter of the state itself, the product $\varepsilon\,\eta$ can be made smaller than $\hbar/2$ by a clever design of the measuring instrument. The explanation “because the performance is poor” concerns only the part corresponding to the error $\varepsilon$, and overlooks the lower bound that comes from the scatter $\sigma$ of the state (the lower bound in the sense of (1)).

To sum up, $\Delta x\,\Delta p\ge\hbar/2$ is an essential property of the quantum state that cannot be removed by improving the measuring instrument. For the error and the disturbance of a measurement, a different relation holds.
