Chapter 9: The Schrödinger Equation — Wave Functions and Operators

Exercise 9.1: Wavelengths of electrons and neutrons, and particles suited to crystal diffraction

Solution

The kinetic energy is $E=25.3\ \mathrm{meV}=25.3\times10^{-3}\times1.602\,177\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}=4.0535\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{J}$. The wavelength is $\lambda=h/p=h/\sqrt{2mE}$ (with $h=6.626\,070\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$).

(a) Electron: $2m_{\mathrm e}E=2\times9.109\,384\times10^{-31}\times4.0535\times10^{-21}=7.385\times10^{-51}\ \mathrm{kg^2\,m^2/s^2}$, $p=\sqrt{7.385\times10^{-51}}=8.594\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, $\lambda=\dfrac{6.626\,070\times10^{-34}}{8.594\times10^{-26}}=7.71\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m}=7.71\ \mathrm{nm}$.

(b) Neutron: $2m_{\mathrm n}E=2\times1.674\,927\times10^{-27}\times4.0535\times10^{-21}=1.3579\times10^{-47}$, $p=3.685\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, $\lambda=\dfrac{6.626\,070\times10^{-34}}{3.685\times10^{-24}}=1.798\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}=0.180\ \mathrm{nm}$ (the speed is $p/m_{\mathrm n}=2.20\times10^3\ \mathrm{m/s}$).

(c) Proton: Its mass is almost the same as that of the neutron ($m_{\mathrm p}/m_{\mathrm n}=0.9986$), so from $\lambda\propto m^{-1/2}$ we get $\lambda=0.180\ \mathrm{nm}\times\sqrt{m_{\mathrm n}/m_{\mathrm p}}=0.180\ \mathrm{nm}$ (the numerical value is $1.799\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$).

The particles with a wavelength of the same order as the interatomic spacing of a crystal ($0.1\sim0.3\ \mathrm{nm}$) are (b) the neutron and (c) the proton; the electron's wavelength of $7.7\ \mathrm{nm}$ is far too long (at the same energy, the electron's mass is about $1/1839$ of the neutron's, so its wavelength is $\sqrt{1839}=42.9$ times longer). However, because the proton is charged and loses energy rapidly in matter, thermal neutrons, which carry no charge, are used for diffraction that probes the interior of a crystal (Chapter 6). (d) The same wavelength means the same momentum $p$, so the kinetic energy of the electron is $E_{\mathrm e}=\dfrac{p^2}{2m_{\mathrm e}}=E_{\mathrm n}\dfrac{m_{\mathrm n}}{m_{\mathrm e}}=25.3\ \mathrm{meV}\times\dfrac{1.674\,927\times10^{-27}}{9.109\,384\times10^{-31}}=25.3\ \mathrm{meV}\times1838.7=46.5\ \mathrm{eV}$. This is the reason why electrons of several tens to several hundred $\mathrm{eV}$ are used in electron diffraction.

Exercise 9.2: Phase and group velocities of a free particle, and the envelope of the beats

Solution

(a) Substitute $\Psi=e^{i(kx-\omega t)}$ into $i\hbar\,\partial_t\Psi=-\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2m}\partial_x^2\Psi$. The left-hand side is $i\hbar(-i\omega)\Psi=\hbar\omega\Psi$ and the right-hand side is $-\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2m}(ik)^2\Psi=\dfrac{\hbar^2k^2}{2m}\Psi$, so $\omega(k)=\dfrac{\hbar k^2}{2m}$. The phase velocity is $v_{\mathrm p}=\dfrac{\omega}{k}=\dfrac{\hbar k}{2m}$, and the group velocity is $v_{\mathrm g}=\dfrac{\dd\omega}{\dd k}=\dfrac{\hbar k}{m}$. Compared with the speed of the particle, $v=p/m=\hbar k/m$, we have $v_{\mathrm p}=v/2$ and $v_{\mathrm g}=v$.

(b) From $p=\sqrt{2m_{\mathrm n}E}=3.685\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$ (Exercise 9.1), $k=\dfrac{p}{\hbar}=\dfrac{3.685\times10^{-24}}{1.054\,572\times10^{-34}}=3.494\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$ ($\lambda=2\pi/k=0.180\ \mathrm{nm}$), and $\omega=\dfrac{E}{\hbar}=\dfrac{4.0535\times10^{-21}}{1.054\,572\times10^{-34}}=3.844\times10^{13}\ \mathrm{rad/s}$. The group velocity is $v_{\mathrm g}=\dfrac{\hbar k}{m_{\mathrm n}}=\dfrac{3.685\times10^{-24}}{1.674\,927\times10^{-27}}=2.200\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{m/s}$, and the phase velocity is $v_{\mathrm p}=\dfrac{\omega}{k}=\dfrac{3.844\times10^{13}}{3.494\times10^{10}}=1.100\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{m/s}$ ($=v_{\mathrm g}/2$).

(c) The expansion in the hint is exact (since $\omega$ is a quadratic function of $k$, the expansion terminates at the second-order term): $\omega(k\pm\delta)=\dfrac{\hbar(k\pm\delta)^2}{2m}=\omega\pm\dfrac{\hbar k}{m}\delta+\dfrac{\hbar\delta^2}{2m}$. Using $v_{\mathrm g}=\hbar k/m$, we get

$$ \Psi=e^{i\left[(k+\delta)x-\omega t-v_{\mathrm g}\delta t-\frac{\hbar\delta^2}{2m}t\right]}+e^{i\left[(k-\delta)x-\omega t+v_{\mathrm g}\delta t-\frac{\hbar\delta^2}{2m}t\right]} =e^{i\left(kx-\omega t-\frac{\hbar\delta^2}{2m}t\right)}\left[e^{i\delta(x-v_{\mathrm g}t)}+e^{-i\delta(x-v_{\mathrm g}t)}\right] $$

Here we factored out the common factor $e^{i(kx-\omega t-\hbar\delta^2t/2m)}$ and used $(k\pm\delta)x\mp v_{\mathrm g}\delta t=kx\pm\delta(x-v_{\mathrm g}t)$. From Euler's formula $e^{i\theta}+e^{-i\theta}=2\cos\theta$ we obtain

$$ \Psi=2\cos\left[\delta(x-v_{\mathrm g}t)\right]\,e^{i\left(kx-\omega t-\frac{\hbar\delta^2}{2m}t\right)} $$

Since $2\cos[\delta(x-v_{\mathrm g}t)]$ is a function of $x-v_{\mathrm g}t$, it travels to the right at speed $v_{\mathrm g}$ without changing its shape (the envelope, the beats). The remaining factor is a phase factor of absolute value $1$, and $\abs{\Psi}^2=4\cos^2[\delta(x-v_{\mathrm g}t)]$ is determined by the envelope alone. That is, the speed at which the wave packet (the peaks of the beats) travels is the group velocity $v_{\mathrm g}=\hbar k/m=v$.

Exercise 9.3: Calculating commutators, and $\langle T\rangle=\langle V\rangle$ for the harmonic oscillator

Solution

(a) Setting $\hat{A}=\hat{B}=\hat{x}$ and $\hat{C}=\hat{p}^2$ in the formula $\comm{\hat{A}\hat{B}}{\hat{C}}=\hat{A}\comm{\hat{B}}{\hat{C}}+\comm{\hat{A}}{\hat{C}}\hat{B}$, we get $\comm{\hat{x}^2}{\hat{p}^2}=\hat{x}\comm{\hat{x}}{\hat{p}^2}+\comm{\hat{x}}{\hat{p}^2}\hat{x}$. Since $\comm{\hat{x}}{\hat{p}^2}=\comm{\hat{x}}{\hat{p}}\hat{p}+\hat{p}\comm{\hat{x}}{\hat{p}}=2i\hbar\hat{p}$, we have $\comm{\hat{x}^2}{\hat{p}^2}=\hat{x}\,2i\hbar\hat{p}+2i\hbar\hat{p}\,\hat{x}=2i\hbar\left(\hat{x}\hat{p}+\hat{p}\hat{x}\right)=2i\hbar\hat{D}$.

(b) We compute $\comm{\hat{H}}{\hat{D}}=\dfrac{1}{2m}\comm{\hat{p}^2}{\hat{D}}+\dfrac{m\omega^2}{2}\comm{\hat{x}^2}{\hat{D}}$ by splitting it into the two terms. We have $\comm{\hat{p}^2}{\hat{x}}=-\comm{\hat{x}}{\hat{p}^2}=-2i\hbar\hat{p}$. Because $\hat{p}^2$ commutes with $\hat{p}$, $\comm{\hat{p}^2}{\hat{x}\hat{p}}=\comm{\hat{p}^2}{\hat{x}}\hat{p}=-2i\hbar\hat{p}^2$ and $\comm{\hat{p}^2}{\hat{p}\hat{x}}=\hat{p}\comm{\hat{p}^2}{\hat{x}}=-2i\hbar\hat{p}^2$. Together, $\comm{\hat{p}^2}{\hat{D}}=-4i\hbar\hat{p}^2$. Similarly, $\comm{\hat{x}^2}{\hat{p}}=2i\hbar\hat{x}$, and since $\hat{x}^2$ commutes with $\hat{x}$, $\comm{\hat{x}^2}{\hat{x}\hat{p}}=\hat{x}\comm{\hat{x}^2}{\hat{p}}=2i\hbar\hat{x}^2$ and $\comm{\hat{x}^2}{\hat{p}\hat{x}}=\comm{\hat{x}^2}{\hat{p}}\hat{x}=2i\hbar\hat{x}^2$. Together, $\comm{\hat{x}^2}{\hat{D}}=4i\hbar\hat{x}^2$. Therefore the relation

$$ \comm{\hat{H}}{\hat{D}}=\frac{-4i\hbar\hat{p}^2}{2m}+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}\cdot4i\hbar\hat{x}^2=-4i\hbar\left(\frac{\hat{p}^2}{2m}-\frac12m\omega^2\hat{x}^2\right)=-4i\hbar\left(\hat{T}-\hat{V}\right) $$

holds.

(c) $\hat{D}$ is a Hermitian operator (Exercise 9.5) and has no explicit time dependence. In a stationary state of $\hat{H}$, the expectation value $\langle D\rangle$ is independent of time (Section 9.5.2), so $\dfrac{\dd\langle D\rangle}{\dd t}=0$. On the other hand, from the formula for the time dependence of an expectation value, $\dfrac{\dd\langle A\rangle}{\dd t}=\dfrac{i}{\hbar}\langle\comm{\hat{H}}{\hat{A}}\rangle$ (Chapter 9, Section 9.4.6), we get $\dfrac{\dd\langle D\rangle}{\dd t}=\dfrac{i}{\hbar}\langle\comm{\hat{H}}{\hat{D}}\rangle=\dfrac{i}{\hbar}\left(-4i\hbar\right)\left(\langle T\rangle-\langle V\rangle\right)=4\left(\langle T\rangle-\langle V\rangle\right)$ (since $i\cdot(-4i)=4$). Since this is $0$, $\langle T\rangle=\langle V\rangle$. From the total energy $E=\langle T\rangle+\langle V\rangle$, in a stationary state of the harmonic oscillator (energy $E$) we obtain $\langle T\rangle=\langle V\rangle=E/2$ (a special case of the virial theorem; Chapter 13).

Exercise 9.4: Probability current at a step potential, and reflection and transmission coefficients

Solution

(a) Since $V$ is finite at $x=0$ (it merely jumps to $V_0$), $\psi$ and $\psi'$ are continuous (Theorem 9.3). From $\psi(0^-)=1+A_{\mathrm R}$ and $\psi(0^+)=A_{\mathrm T}$ we get $1+A_{\mathrm R}=A_{\mathrm T}$ (Eq. (1)). From $\psi'(0^-)=ik(1-A_{\mathrm R})$ and $\psi'(0^+)=ik'A_{\mathrm T}$ we get $k(1-A_{\mathrm R})=k'A_{\mathrm T}$ (Eq. (2)). Substituting (1) into (2) gives $k(1-A_{\mathrm R})=k'(1+A_{\mathrm R})$; solving this for $A_{\mathrm R}$, we find that

$$ A_{\mathrm R}=\frac{k-k'}{k+k'},\qquad A_{\mathrm T}=1+A_{\mathrm R}=\frac{2k}{k+k'} $$

hold.

(b) $x\lt0$: By Example 9.8 (reading $r$ as $A_{\mathrm R}$), $J=\dfrac{\hbar k}{m}\left(1-\abs{A_{\mathrm R}}^2\right)$. $x\gt0$: $\psi=A_{\mathrm T}\,e^{ik'x}$ is a plane wave, and multiplying the probability density $\rho=\abs{A_{\mathrm T}}^2$ by the speed $v=\hbar k'/m$ gives $J=\dfrac{\hbar k'}{m}\abs{A_{\mathrm T}}^2$. In a stationary state $\partial\rho/\partial t=0$, so the continuity equation gives $\dd J/\dd x=0$; that is, $J$ is constant, independent of position. Therefore the values of $J$ on the left and on the right are equal, $k\left(1-\abs{A_{\mathrm R}}^2\right)=k'\abs{A_{\mathrm T}}^2$, that is, $1-\abs{A_{\mathrm R}}^2=\dfrac{k'}{k}\abs{A_{\mathrm T}}^2$. Checking with $A_{\mathrm R},A_{\mathrm T}$ from (a), we find $1-A_{\mathrm R}^2=\dfrac{(k+k')^2-(k-k')^2}{(k+k')^2}=\dfrac{4kk'}{(k+k')^2}$ and $\dfrac{k'}{k}A_{\mathrm T}^2=\dfrac{k'}{k}\cdot\dfrac{4k^2}{(k+k')^2}=\dfrac{4kk'}{(k+k')^2}$, which agree. This expresses the fact that the incident current splits into a reflected current and a transmitted current.

(c) For an electron, $k=\sqrt{2mE}/\hbar$: at $E=100\ \mathrm{eV}$ it is $5.123\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$ (Example 9.1), so at $E=10\ \mathrm{eV}$, $k=5.123\times10^{10}\times\sqrt{10/100}=1.620\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$. At $E-V_0=6\ \mathrm{eV}$, $k'=5.123\times10^{10}\times\sqrt{6/100}=1.255\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$. Then $A_{\mathrm R}=\dfrac{1.620-1.255}{1.620+1.255}=0.1270$ and $A_{\mathrm T}=\dfrac{2\times1.620}{1.620+1.255}=1.127$. The reflection coefficient is $R=\abs{A_{\mathrm R}}^2=0.0161$ (about $1.6\ \%$). The transmission coefficient is $T=\dfrac{k'}{k}\abs{A_{\mathrm T}}^2=\dfrac{1.255}{1.620}\times1.270=0.9839$ (about $98.4\ \%$). Since $R+T=0.0161+0.9839=1.0000$, probability is conserved. Note that $\abs{A_{\mathrm T}}=1.127\gt1$, but this is a ratio of amplitudes, and the particle current is evaluated by $T$, which includes the factor $k'/k$, so there is no contradiction (the wave on the transmitted side is slow, so the density is higher for the same current).

Exercise 9.5: Checking Hermiticity

Solution

(a) We have $\hat{D}_{\mathrm s}g=-i\hbar\left(xg'+\tfrac12g\right)$. Using integration by parts, $\displaystyle\int f^*xg'\dd x=\bigl[xf^*g\bigr]-\int\left(f^*+xf^{*\prime}\right)g\dd x$ (the boundary term is $0$), we get

$$ \int f^*\left(\hat{D}_{\mathrm s}g\right)\dd x=-i\hbar\left[-\int f^*g\dd x-\int xf^{*\prime}g\dd x+\frac12\int f^*g\dd x\right]=-i\hbar\left[-\int\left(\frac12f^*+xf^{*\prime}\right)g\dd x\right]=i\hbar\int\left(xf^{*\prime}+\frac12f^*\right)g\dd x $$

On the other hand, the complex conjugate of $\hat{D}_{\mathrm s}f=-i\hbar\left(xf'+\tfrac12f\right)$ is $\left(\hat{D}_{\mathrm s}f\right)^*=i\hbar\left(xf^{*\prime}+\tfrac12f^*\right)$, so $\displaystyle\int\left(\hat{D}_{\mathrm s}f\right)^*g\dd x=i\hbar\int\left(xf^{*\prime}+\tfrac12f^*\right)g\dd x$, which agrees with the result above. Therefore $\hat{D}_{\mathrm s}$ is a Hermitian operator. (We have $\hat{x}\hat{p}=\hat{D}_{\mathrm s}+\dfrac{i\hbar}{2}$; $\hat{D}_{\mathrm s}$ is Hermitian, but $\dfrac{i\hbar}{2}$ is a purely imaginary constant, so $\hat{x}\hat{p}$ by itself is not Hermitian.)

(b) By integration by parts, $\displaystyle\int_0^Lf^*(\hat{p}g)\dd x=\Bigl[-i\hbar f^*g\Bigr]_0^L+i\hbar\int_0^Lf^{*\prime}g\dd x=\Bigl[-i\hbar f^*g\Bigr]_0^L+\int_0^L(\hat{p}f)^*g\dd x$. Therefore

$$ \int_0^Lf^*(\hat{p}g)\dd x-\int_0^L(\hat{p}f)^*g\dd x=-i\hbar\Bigl[f^*(L)g(L)-f^*(0)g(0)\Bigr] $$

holds. For $f=1$ and $g=x$, $f^*g|_L=L$ and $f^*g|_0=0$, so the difference is $-i\hbar L\ne0$, and Hermiticity does not hold. If the wave function becomes $0$ at the boundary ($f(0)=f(L)=0$ or $g(0)=g(L)=0$), or is periodic ($f^*g$ is equal at both ends), then the right-hand side is $0$ and the operator is Hermitian.

Exercise 9.6: Oscillation of the position in a superposition of two states

Solution

For real $\psi_1,\psi_2$ and real $c_1,c_2$, $\abs{\Psi}^2=|c_1\psi_1e^{-iE_1t/\hbar}+c_2\psi_2e^{-iE_2t/\hbar}|^2=c_1^2\psi_1^2+c_2^2\psi_2^2+2c_1c_2\,\psi_1\psi_2\cos\omega_{21}t$ ($\omega_{21}=(E_2-E_1)/\hbar$). Multiplying by $x$ and integrating, and using $x_{mn}=\displaystyle\int\psi_mx\psi_n\dd x$, we obtain

$$ \langle x\rangle(t)=c_1^2x_{11}+c_2^2x_{22}+2c_1c_2\,x_{12}\cos\omega_{21}t $$

Therefore $\langle x\rangle$ oscillates at the angular frequency $\omega_{21}=(E_2-E_1)/\hbar$ (frequency $\nu_{21}=(E_2-E_1)/h$) with amplitude $2\abs{c_1c_2x_{12}}$. If $x_{12}=0$, it does not oscillate.

(a) $n=1,2$: $x_{12}=-\dfrac{16L}{9\pi^2}$ (found by integrating $\int_0^Lx\cos(q\pi x/L)\dd x$ by parts; Chapter 10, Section 10.5, Example 10.11), and the amplitude is $2\abs{c_1c_2}\times0.1801L$, which is largest for $c_1=c_2=1/\sqrt2$, where it equals $0.1801L=0.180\ \mathrm{nm}$ ($L=1\ \mathrm{nm}$). Since $E_2-E_1=3E_1=3\times0.3760=1.128\ \mathrm{eV}$, we have $\nu_{21}=\dfrac{1.128\times1.602\,177\times10^{-19}}{6.626\,070\times10^{-34}}=2.73\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$, and the period is $3.67\ \mathrm{fs}$. $\langle x\rangle$ oscillates.

(b) $n=1,3$: Both $\psi_1$ and $\psi_3$ are symmetric about the center of the well, $x=L/2$ ($\psi_n(L-x)=(-1)^{n+1}\psi_n(x)$, with $n$ odd). We have $x_{13}=\displaystyle\int_0^L\psi_1\left(x-\tfrac{L}{2}\right)\psi_3\dd x+\tfrac{L}{2}\int_0^L\psi_1\psi_3\dd x$, where the first term is $0$ because its integrand is an odd function about the center, and the second term is $0$ by the orthogonality of $\psi_1,\psi_3$. Hence $x_{13}=0$, and $\langle x\rangle=L/2$ stays constant and does not oscillate. (The probability density $\abs{\Psi}^2$ itself oscillates at $\omega_{31}$. $E_3-E_1=8E_1=3.01\ \mathrm{eV}$, $\nu_{31}=7.27\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$. However, it merely “breathes” symmetrically left and right, and $\langle x\rangle$ does not move.) Between two states with the same parity (evenness or oddness), the electric dipole ($\propto x$) does not oscillate, and no electromagnetic wave is radiated. This is the origin of the selection rule for the absorption and emission of light (Part IX).

Exercise 9.7: Dimensions of the wave function and the probability current

Solution

(a) In one dimension, $\int\abs{\psi}^2\dd x=1$ (dimensionless) gives $[\psi]^2\cdot\mathrm{m}=1$, so $[\psi]=\mathrm{m^{-1/2}}$. In three dimensions, $[\psi]^2\cdot\mathrm{m^3}=1$, so $[\psi]=\mathrm{m^{-3/2}}$. The probability current in one dimension is $J=\dfrac{\hbar}{m}\Imag\left(\psi^*\psi'\right)$: the dimension of $\dfrac{\hbar}{m}$ is $\dfrac{\mathrm{J\,s}}{\mathrm{kg}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}}}{\mathrm{kg}}=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, and the dimension of $\psi^*\psi'$ is $\mathrm{m^{-1/2}}\cdot\mathrm{m^{-1/2}}\cdot\mathrm{m^{-1}}=\mathrm{m^{-2}}$, so $[J]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\cdot\mathrm{m^{-2}}=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ (the probability passing through that point per unit time). In three dimensions, $\dfrac{\hbar}{m}$ is $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$ and $\psi^*\nabla\psi$ is $\mathrm{m^{-3/2}}\cdot\mathrm{m^{-3/2}}\cdot\mathrm{m^{-1}}=\mathrm{m^{-4}}$, so $[\bm{J}]=\mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$ (the probability passing through per unit area per unit time). This agrees with “velocity ($\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$) × probability density ($\mathrm{m^{-3}}$)”.

(b) Normalization: $\displaystyle\int\abs{\psi_{1s}}^2\dd^3r=\frac{1}{\pi a_0^3}\int_0^\infty e^{-2r/a_0}\,4\pi r^2\dd r=\frac{4}{a_0^3}\cdot\frac{a_0^3}{4}=1$ (we used the integral in the hint). The probability density at the position of the nucleus ($r=0$) is $\abs{\psi_{1s}(0)}^2=\dfrac{1}{\pi a_0^3}=\dfrac{1}{\pi\times(5.292\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m})^3}=\dfrac{1}{\pi\times1.482\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{m^3}}=2.15\times10^{30}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ ($=2.15\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{nm^{-3}}$; the probability of finding the electron inside a cube of side $0.01\ \mathrm{nm}$, with volume $10^{-6}\ \mathrm{nm^3}$, is about $2\times10^{-3}$). The dimension is $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, which agrees with $[\psi]^2=\mathrm{m^{-3}}$ from (a).

Exercise 9.8: Shift of the mean position due to an anharmonic term (the origin of thermal expansion)

Solution

(a) From $V=\tfrac12m\omega^2x^2+\beta x^3$ we get $V'=m\omega^2x+3\beta x^2$. Taking the average, $\langle V'\rangle=m\omega^2\langle x\rangle+3\beta\langle x^2\rangle$. Using $\langle x^2\rangle=\langle x\rangle^2+(\Delta x)^2$ (the definition of the variance, $(\Delta x)^2=\langle x^2\rangle-\langle x\rangle^2$) and substituting into Ehrenfest's theorem $m\dfrac{\dd^2\langle x\rangle}{\dd t^2}=-\langle V'\rangle$, we obtain

$$ m\frac{\dd^2\langle x\rangle}{\dd t^2}=-m\omega^2\langle x\rangle-3\beta\left[\langle x\rangle^2+(\Delta x)^2\right] $$

Since the term $3\beta x^2$ is second order in $x$, $\langle x^2\rangle$ appears, and the spread of the position, $(\Delta x)^2$, affects the force (with the harmonic term alone, $\langle V'\rangle=m\omega^2\langle x\rangle$, and the spread has no effect).

(b) In a stationary state, $\langle x\rangle$ is independent of time, so the left-hand side is $0$. Thus $m\omega^2\langle x\rangle=-3\beta\left[\langle x\rangle^2+(\Delta x)^2\right]$. Since $\langle x\rangle$ is of first order in $\beta$, $\langle x\rangle^2$ is of order $\beta^2$ and can be neglected to first order in $\beta$. For $(\Delta x)^2$, it suffices to use the zeroth-order value in $\beta$ (the value for the harmonic oscillator with $\beta=0$). Hence

$$ \langle x\rangle\doteqdot-\frac{3\beta(\Delta x)^2}{m\omega^2} $$

is obtained.

(c) In the ground state of the harmonic oscillator, $(\Delta x)^2=\dfrac{\hbar}{2m\omega}$ (Chapter 13), so $\langle x\rangle\doteqdot-\dfrac{3\beta}{m\omega^2}\cdot\dfrac{\hbar}{2m\omega}=-\dfrac{3\beta\hbar}{2m^2\omega^3}$. If $\beta\gt0$, the mean position shifts to the negative side: $\beta x^3$ raises $V$ for $x\gt0$ and lowers it for $x\lt0$, so the wall on the $x\gt0$ side is steep and the $x\lt0$ side is gentle. The mean position shifts toward the gentle side. That is, the shift of the mean position has the sign opposite to $\beta$. In an excited state (the $n$th), $(\Delta x)^2=(n+\tfrac12)\dfrac{\hbar}{m\omega}$, so the shift is $-\dfrac{3\beta\hbar}{m^2\omega^3}\left(n+\tfrac12\right)$, which grows in proportion to the vibrational quantum number (the square of the size of the vibration). The actual interatomic potential is steep on the near (repulsive) side and gentle on the far side, so it corresponds to the form with $\beta\lt0$ around the equilibrium point (on the far side, $x\gt0$, the potential is lower than the parabola), and the mean position shifts toward the far side. At high temperature, states with high $n$ are occupied, so the average interatomic distance increases with temperature. This is the quantum-mechanical origin of thermal expansion (Solid-State Physics (AD 06), the perturbation theory in Part V). For example, in the ground state with $\hbar=m=\omega=1$ and $\beta=0.005$, $\langle x\rangle\doteqdot-\dfrac{3\beta}{2}=-7.5\times10^{-3}$, which agrees with the result of first-order perturbation theory, in which $\beta x^3$ is treated as a perturbation.

← Back to Chapter 9, “The Schrödinger Equation — Wave Functions and Operators”

Chapter 10: The Infinite Potential Well — Particle in a Box

Exercise 10.1: A GaAs quantum well of width 12 nm

Solution

The levels of the infinite well are $E_n=\dfrac{n^2h^2}{8m^*L^2}$. Since $\dfrac{h^2}{8m_{\mathrm e}}=0.3760\ \mathrm{eV\,nm^2}$, for $m^*=0.067\,m_{\mathrm e}$ we get $\dfrac{h^2}{8m^*}=\dfrac{0.3760}{0.067}=5.612\ \mathrm{eV\,nm^2}$. With $L=12\ \mathrm{nm}$, $L^2=144\ \mathrm{nm^2}$, so

$$ E_n=\frac{5.612}{144}\,n^2\ \mathrm{eV}=0.03897\,n^2\ \mathrm{eV} $$ $$ E_1=39.0\ \mathrm{meV},\qquad E_2=4E_1=155.9\ \mathrm{meV},\qquad E_3=9E_1=350.8\ \mathrm{meV} $$

The energy of the $E_1\to E_2$ transition is $E_2-E_1=3E_1=116.9\ \mathrm{meV}=0.1169\ \mathrm{eV}$. The wavelength is

$$ \lambda=\frac{hc}{E_2-E_1}=\frac{1239.84\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}}{0.1169\ \mathrm{eV}}=1.06\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{nm}=10.6\ \mathrm{\mu m} $$

which lies in the mid-infrared region (on the longer-wavelength side of the 7.4 μm for $L=10\ \mathrm{nm}$ in Example 10.15; the wider the well, the smaller the level spacing and the longer the wavelength). In the infinite-well approximation, the levels are overestimated compared with those of the actual finite well.

Exercise 10.2: Levels of a rectangular well ($L_2=3L_1$)

Solution

The levels are $E=\dfrac{h^2}{8m}\left(\dfrac{n_1^2}{L_1^2}+\dfrac{n_2^2}{9L_1^2}\right)=E_1\left(n_1^2+\dfrac{n_2^2}{9}\right)=E_1\cdot\dfrac{9n_1^2+n_2^2}{9}$. We examine $(n_1,n_2)$ in increasing order of the numerator $9n_1^2+n_2^2$.

Rank$(n_1,n_2)$$9n_1^2+n_2^2$$E/E_1$Degeneracy
1$(1,1)$10$10/9=1.111$1
2$(1,2)$13$13/9=1.444$1
3$(1,3)$18$2$1
4$(1,4)$25$25/9=2.778$1
5$(1,5)$34$34/9=3.778$1
6$(2,1)$37$37/9=4.111$1
7$(2,2)$40$40/9=4.444$1
8$(1,6)$, $(2,3)$45$5$2

(The pairs that might otherwise come in between, $(1,7)$ with $9+49=58$, $(2,4)$ with $36+16=52$, and $(3,1)$ with $81+1=82$, are all larger than 45.) The only degenerate states are the two states $(1,6)$ and $(2,3)$ at $E=5E_1$. Since this rectangle has no symmetry under the interchange $x\leftrightarrow y$ ($L_1\ne L_2$), this degeneracy is an accidental degeneracy that cannot be explained by symmetry. The cause is that the square of the ratio of the sides, $(L_2/L_1)^2=9$, is a rational number (an integer), so $9n_1^2+n_2^2$ can take the same integer value for different $(n_1,n_2)$ ($9\cdot1+36=9\cdot4+9$).

Exercise 10.3: $\expval{x^2}$ and $\Delta x\,\Delta p$ in symmetric coordinates

Solution

$\psi_1(x)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt a}\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{2a}$ ($\abs{x}\le a$). Since the probability density $\abs{\psi_1}^2$ is an even function and $x$ is an odd function, $\expval{x}=\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a}x\abs{\psi_1}^2\dd x=0$.

$\expval{x^2}=\dfrac{1}{a}\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a}x^2\cos^2\dfrac{\pi x}{2a}\dd x=\dfrac{1}{2a}\int_{-a}^{a}x^2\left(1+\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{a}\right)\dd x=\dfrac{1}{2a}\left[\dfrac{2a^3}{3}+\int_{-a}^{a}x^2\cos qx\dd x\right]$ ($q=\pi/a$).

We evaluate the remaining integral by integrating by parts twice. First integration by parts: $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a}x^2\cos qx\dd x=\left[\frac{x^2\sin qx}{q}\right]_{-a}^{a}-\frac{2}{q}\int_{-a}^{a}x\sin qx\dd x=0-\frac{2}{q}\int_{-a}^{a}x\sin qx\dd x$ ($\sin qa=\sin\pi=0$). Second integration by parts: $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a}x\sin qx\dd x=\left[-\frac{x\cos qx}{q}\right]_{-a}^{a}+\int_{-a}^{a}\frac{\cos qx}{q}\dd x=\left(\frac{a}{q}\right)-\left(-\frac{a}{q}\right)+0=\frac{2a}{q}$ (at $x=a$, $-a\cos\pi/q=a/q$; at $x=-a$, $a\cos(-\pi)/q=-a/q$; and $\int\cos qx\dd x=[\sin qx/q]=0$). Hence $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a}x^2\cos qx\dd x=-\frac{2}{q}\cdot\frac{2a}{q}=-\frac{4a}{q^2}=-\frac{4a^3}{\pi^2}$.

$$ \expval{x^2}=\frac{1}{2a}\left[\frac{2a^3}{3}-\frac{4a^3}{\pi^2}\right]=a^2\left(\frac13-\frac{2}{\pi^2}\right)=0.1307\,a^2 $$

$\Delta x=\sqrt{\expval{x^2}-\expval{x}^2}=a\sqrt{\dfrac13-\dfrac{2}{\pi^2}}=0.3615\,a=0.1808\,L$ ($L=2a$). For the momentum, $\Delta p=\pi\hbar/L=\pi\hbar/(2a)$ ($n=1$, from the formula $\Delta p=n\pi\hbar/L$), so

$$ \Delta x\,\Delta p=0.3615\,a\times\frac{\pi\hbar}{2a}=0.568\,\hbar $$

which agrees with the value for $n=1$ in Example 10.7. This is only natural, since the spread $\Delta x$ does not change wherever the origin of the coordinate is placed (from $\expval{x^2}_{\text{center}}=\expval{x^2}_{\text{left end}}-L\expval{x}_{\text{left end}}+L^2/4$ one can verify that $L^2(1/12-1/2\pi^2)=a^2(1/3-2/\pi^2)$).

Exercise 10.4: Expansion of a triangular initial state

Solution

(1) Since the state is symmetric about the center, $\displaystyle\int_0^L\abs{\Psi}^2\dd x=2N^2\int_0^{L/2}x^2\dd x=2N^2\cdot\frac{(L/2)^3}{3}=\frac{N^2L^3}{12}=1$. Hence $N=\sqrt{12/L^3}$ ($N^2=12/L^3$).

(2) $c_n=\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{L}}\displaystyle\int_0^L\sin\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\,\Psi(x,0)\dd x$. Since $\Psi(L-x,0)=\Psi(x,0)$ and $\sin\dfrac{n\pi(L-x)}{L}=(-1)^{n+1}\sin\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}$, for even $n$ the integrand changes sign under $x\to L-x$, so the integral is $0$. For odd $n$ the two halves are equal, and $c_n=2\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{L}}\,N\displaystyle\int_0^{L/2}x\sin qx\dd x$ ($q=n\pi/L$). Integrating by parts:

$$ \int_0^{L/2}x\sin qx\dd x=\left[-\frac{x\cos qx}{q}\right]_0^{L/2}+\frac{1}{q}\int_0^{L/2}\cos qx\dd x=-\frac{L\cos(n\pi/2)}{2q}+\frac{\sin(n\pi/2)}{q^2} $$

For odd $n$, $\cos\dfrac{n\pi}{2}=0$ and $\sin\dfrac{n\pi}{2}=(-1)^{(n-1)/2}$, so the value is $\dfrac{(-1)^{(n-1)/2}L^2}{(n\pi)^2}$. Therefore

$$ c_n=2\sqrt{\frac{2}{L}}\sqrt{\frac{12}{L^3}}\cdot\frac{(-1)^{(n-1)/2}L^2}{(n\pi)^2}=\frac{2\sqrt{24}\,(-1)^{(n-1)/2}}{(n\pi)^2}=\frac{4\sqrt6\,(-1)^{(n-1)/2}}{(n\pi)^2}\quad(n\text{ odd}),\qquad c_n=0\ (n\text{ even}) $$

We have $c_1=\dfrac{4\sqrt6}{\pi^2}=0.9927$, $c_3=-\dfrac{4\sqrt6}{9\pi^2}=-0.1103$, $c_5=+0.0397$, …

(3) The probability of $n=1$ is $\abs{c_1}^2=\dfrac{96}{\pi^4}=0.9855$. By integration by parts (the boundary terms vanish because $\Psi(0)=\Psi(L)=0$), the expectation value of the energy is $\expval{E}=\expval{T}=\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2m}\displaystyle\int_0^L\abs{\Psi'}^2\dd x$. Since $\abs{\Psi'}=N$ (a constant), $\expval{E}=\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2m}N^2L=\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2m}\cdot\dfrac{12}{L^2}=\dfrac{6\hbar^2}{mL^2}$. Its ratio to the ground-state energy $E_1=\dfrac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2}$ is $\dfrac{12}{\pi^2}=1.216$. As a check: $\displaystyle\sum_n\abs{c_n}^2E_n=\sum_{n\text{ odd}}\frac{96}{\pi^4n^4}\cdot\frac{n^2\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2}=\frac{48\hbar^2}{\pi^2mL^2}\sum_{n\text{ odd}}\frac{1}{n^2}=\frac{48\hbar^2}{\pi^2mL^2}\cdot\frac{\pi^2}{8}=\frac{6\hbar^2}{mL^2}$ ($\sum_{n\text{ odd}}n^{-2}=\pi^2/8$), which agrees. Because of the kink at the center, the components with high $n$ ($c_3,c_5,\dots$) carry more weight than in the parabolic shape of Example 10.10 ($\expval{E}=1.013E_1$), and $\expval{E}$ is larger.

Exercise 10.5: Degeneracy in a cubic box

Solution

The positive integer solutions of $n_1^2+n_2^2+n_3^2=14$: $14=1+4+9$. The squares ($\le14$) are $1,4,9$, and this is the only triple of them whose sum is 14 ($9+4+1$). $(n_1,n_2,n_3)$ is a permutation of $(1,2,3)$, giving $3!=6$ possibilities, so the degeneracy is 6. All of these are carried into one another by the symmetry of the cube (interchange of $x,y,z$), so the degeneracy can be explained by symmetry.

$n_1^2+n_2^2+n_3^2=27$: the squares ($\le27$) are $1,4,9,16,25$. $27=25+1+1$ and $27=9+9+9$ (combinations such as $16+9+2$ and $16+4+7$ are not sums of squares). The permutations of $(5,1,1)$ give $3$ possibilities and $(3,3,3)$ gives $1$, so the degeneracy is $3+1=$ 4. The threefold degeneracy of $(1,1,5)$ is due to the symmetry of the cube (interchange of the axes), but the fact that $(3,3,3)$ has the same energy is a coincidence of numbers, $27=1+1+25=9+9+9$, and is an accidental degeneracy that cannot be explained by symmetry.

Exercise 10.6: HOMO–LUMO gap of a conjugated chain ($N=10$)

Solution

Since there are 10 $\pi$ electrons, the levels $n=1,\dots,5$ are filled with two electrons each; the HOMO is $n=5$ and the LUMO is $n=6$. The length of the chain is $L=(N-1)d=9\times0.1454\ \mathrm{nm}=1.309\ \mathrm{nm}$. $E_1=\dfrac{0.3760\ \mathrm{eV\,nm^2}}{(1.309\ \mathrm{nm})^2}=\dfrac{0.3760}{1.7124}=0.2196\ \mathrm{eV}$. The excitation energy is

$$ \Delta E=E_6-E_5=(36-25)E_1=11E_1=2.42\ \mathrm{eV} $$

(this is the formula $(N+1)E_1$ with $N=10$ substituted). The wavelength is $\lambda=\dfrac{1239.84}{2.415}=513\ \mathrm{nm}$ (green light). That is, the free-electron model predicts a molecule that absorbs green light (and appears reddish purple, the complementary color).

In reality, however, the absorption of a conjugated polyene with 10 carbon atoms lies in the near-ultraviolet region (at wavelengths in the 300s of nm) and does not reach the visible green. The excitation energy is much larger than the model's value of $2.4\ \mathrm{eV}$. That is, the free-electron model estimates the excitation energy to be smaller than the actual one (the absorption wavelength to be longer than the actual one). The cause is that, in an actual conjugated chain, the lengths of the double and single bonds alternate (bond alternation), so a gap opens between the HOMO and the LUMO, and the actual excitation energy becomes larger than the value of the model, which assumes that the $\pi$ electrons can move uniformly along the chain. This improvement is treated by the Hückel method (Chapter 40).

Exercise 10.7: Normalization of $\phi_n(p)$

Solution

With $\hbar=L=1$, $n=1$, and $p_1=\pi$, we have $\abs{\phi_1(p)}^2=\dfrac{4\pi\cos^2(p/2)}{(\pi^2-p^2)^2}$. At $p=\pm\pi$ both the denominator and the numerator are $0$ (a removable singularity), so in the numerical integration we shift the point slightly, as in $p\to p+10^{-11}$. Integrating from $-\infty$ to $\infty$ with scipy's quad gives

$$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\abs{\phi_1(p)}^2\dd p=1.0000000003 $$

which agrees with $1$ within an error of $10^{-9}$. This confirms Parseval's identity $\int\abs{\phi}^2\dd p=\int\abs{\psi_1}^2\dd x=1$.

Next, if we integrate only over $\abs{p}\lt P$, the missing part is the tail integral $2\displaystyle\int_P^\infty\abs{\phi_1}^2\dd p$. For $\abs{p}\gg p_1$, taking $\cos^2\to1/2$ and $(\pi^2-p^2)^2\to p^4$ gives $\abs{\phi_1}^2\approx\dfrac{2p_1^2}{\pi}p^{-4}=2\pi p^{-4}$ (the formula $\abs{\phi_n}^2\approx\dfrac{2\hbar p_n^2}{\pi L}p^{-4}$). Therefore

$$ 2\int_P^\infty\frac{2\pi}{p^4}\dd p=\frac{4\pi}{3P^3} $$

For $P=20$, the missing part is $\dfrac{4\pi}{3\times8000}=5.24\times10^{-4}$, so the estimate is $1-5.24\times10^{-4}=0.99948$. The numerical integral gives $0.99953$ (the missing part is $4.7\times10^{-4}$), which agrees with the estimate to within about 10% (the difference comes from replacing $\cos^2$ by its average $1/2$ and approximating the denominator). For $P=50$, the estimate $0.999966$ and the numerical value $0.999966$ agree well. We see that the normalization is satisfied roughly within the range $\abs{p}\lesssim20\hbar/L$, and that the missing part decreases in proportion to $P^{-3}$.

Exercise 10.8: Average energy per electron in the free-electron gas

Solution

At absolute zero, all states with $E\le E_{\mathrm F}$ are occupied (two electrons each, counting spin). Let $g_3(E)=C\sqrt{E}$ ($C$ is a constant); the spin factor 2 multiplies both the numerator and the denominator and cancels, so

$$ \expval{E}=\frac{\int_0^{E_{\mathrm F}}E\cdot C E^{1/2}\dd E}{\int_0^{E_{\mathrm F}}C E^{1/2}\dd E} =\frac{\dfrac{2}{5}E_{\mathrm F}^{5/2}}{\dfrac{2}{3}E_{\mathrm F}^{3/2}}=\frac{3}{5}E_{\mathrm F} $$

($\int_0^{E_{\mathrm F}}E^{3/2}\dd E=\dfrac{2}{5}E_{\mathrm F}^{5/2}$ and $\int_0^{E_{\mathrm F}}E^{1/2}\dd E=\dfrac{2}{3}E_{\mathrm F}^{3/2}$). For copper, $E_{\mathrm F}=7.03\ \mathrm{eV}$, so

$$ \expval{E}=\frac{3}{5}\times7.03\ \mathrm{eV}=4.22\ \mathrm{eV} $$

This value is far larger than the thermal energy at room temperature, $k_{\mathrm B}T\approx0.026\ \mathrm{eV}$. Because the electrons occupy all the states inside the Fermi sphere, we see that even at absolute zero the electrons have a large kinetic energy (a consequence of the Pauli exclusion principle). The kinetic energy of all the electrons is $\dfrac{3}{5}NE_{\mathrm F}$.

← Back to Chapter 10, “The Infinite Potential Well — Particle in a Box”

Chapter 11: The Finite Potential Well — Penetration and Bound States

Exercise 11.1: A shallow quantum well of width 2 nm

Solution

We have $\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2m^*}=\dfrac{0.038\,100}{0.067}=0.5687\ \mathrm{eV\,nm^2}$, and since the half-width is $a=1\ \mathrm{nm}$,

$$ z_0=a\sqrt{\frac{V_0}{\hbar^2/2m^*}}=1\ \mathrm{nm}\times\sqrt{\frac{0.3\ \mathrm{eV}}{0.5687\ \mathrm{eV\,nm^2}}}=\sqrt{0.5276}=0.7263 $$

Since $\dfrac{2z_0}{\pi}=0.462\lt1$, the number of bound states is $N=\lceil0.462\rceil=1$ ($z_0\lt\pi/2$). The only bound state is the even ground state, and it has $\xi\in(0,\pi/2)$. The function $g(\xi)=\xi\tan\xi-\sqrt{z_0^2-\xi^2}$ ($z_0^2=0.5276$) takes the value $0.2732-0.5269=-0.254$ at $\xi=0.5$ and $0.4105-0.4094=+0.001$ at $\xi=0.6$, so the solution lies just below $0.6$. Repeated bisection gives $\xi_1=0.5996$ and $\eta_1=\sqrt{0.5276-0.3595}=0.4099$ (check: $\xi_1\tan\xi_1=0.5996\times0.6836=0.4099=\eta_1$). The energy is

$$ E_1=V_0\frac{\xi_1^2}{z_0^2}=0.3\ \mathrm{eV}\times\frac{0.3595}{0.5276}=0.2045\ \mathrm{eV}=204.5\ \mathrm{meV} $$

The depth below the top of the wall (the binding energy) is $300-204.5=95.5\ \mathrm{meV}$, and since $E_1/V_0=0.68$, the level lies near the top of the wall. The level of the infinite well is $E_1^{\infty}=\dfrac{h^2}{8m^*L^2}=\dfrac{5.612}{4}\ \mathrm{eV}=1.403\ \mathrm{eV}$, which is higher than the wall height $0.3\ \mathrm{eV}$, so the infinite-well approximation cannot be used at all for this well. The actual level is about 15% of the infinite-well value. The penetration depth is $\dfrac{1}{\kappa_1}=\dfrac{a}{\eta_1}=\dfrac{1\ \mathrm{nm}}{0.4099}=2.44\ \mathrm{nm}$, which is longer than the width of the well, $2\ \mathrm{nm}$. Also, the probability of finding the particle outside the well is (Formula 11.1) $\dfrac{E_1/V_0}{1+\eta_1}=\dfrac{0.682}{1.410}=0.48$, so the particle is outside the well with a probability of about $48\ \%$.

Exercise 11.2: Recovering the levels of Chapter 10 in the limit $V_0\to\infty$

Solution

For the $n$th state, $\xi_n$ lies in the interval $\Bigl(\dfrac{(n-1)\pi}{2},\dfrac{n\pi}{2}\Bigr)$, and $\eta_n=\sqrt{z_0^2-\xi_n^2}\ge\sqrt{z_0^2-(n\pi/2)^2}$. As $z_0\to\infty$, $\eta_n\to\infty$ for fixed $n$. On the even branch ($n$ odd), $\xi\tan\xi=\eta_n$, so for the right-hand side to become infinite we must have $\tan\xi\to\infty$, that is, $\xi_n\to\dfrac{n\pi}{2}$ (the right end of the interval, an asymptote of $\tan$). On the odd branch ($n$ even), $-\xi\cot\xi=\eta_n\to\infty$ likewise requires $\xi_n\to\dfrac{n\pi}{2}$, the right end of the interval, where $\cot\xi\to-\infty$. In both cases $\xi_n\to\dfrac{n\pi}{2}$, and since $a=L/2$, we have

$$ E_n=\frac{\hbar^2\xi_n^2}{2ma^2}\to\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{n^2\pi^2/4}{L^2/4}=\frac{n^2\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2}=\frac{n^2h^2}{8mL^2} $$

which agrees with the levels of the infinite well of Chapter 10 ($\hbar=h/2\pi$).

Next we find the correction. In the phase form $\xi_n+\arctan\dfrac{\xi_n}{\eta_n}=\dfrac{n\pi}{2}$, when $z_0\gg\dfrac{n\pi}{2}$ we have $\xi_n\ll z_0$, so $\eta_n=\sqrt{z_0^2-\xi_n^2}\approx z_0$; also $\dfrac{\xi_n}{\eta_n}\ll1$, so $\arctan\dfrac{\xi_n}{\eta_n}\approx\dfrac{\xi_n}{z_0}$. Therefore $\xi_n\Bigl(1+\dfrac{1}{z_0}\Bigr)\approx\dfrac{n\pi}{2}$, that is, $\xi_n\approx\dfrac{n\pi/2}{1+1/z_0}$. The energy is $E_n\approx E_n^{\infty}\Bigl(1+\dfrac{1}{z_0}\Bigr)^{-2}\approx E_n^{\infty}\Bigl(1-\dfrac{2}{z_0}\Bigr)$. For $z_0=100$, the exact value of $\xi_1$ is $0.99010\times\dfrac{\pi}{2}=1.5552$, and the approximation above, $\dfrac{1.5708}{1.01}=1.5552$, agrees with it.

Exercise 11.3: Probability that the particle in the ground state is outside the well

Solution

The normalization integral for the even ground state, $\psi=A_1\cos kx$ ($\abs{x}\le a$) and $A_1\cos ka\,e^{-\kappa(\abs{x}-a)}$ ($\abs{x}\gt a$), is the sum of the contribution inside the well, $A_1^2\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a}\cos^2kx\dd x=A_1^2\Bigl(a+\dfrac{\sin2ka}{2k}\Bigr)$, and the contribution outside, $2A_1^2\cos^2ka\displaystyle\int_a^\infty e^{-2\kappa(x-a)}\dd x=A_1^2\dfrac{\cos^2ka}{\kappa}$. Therefore $P_{\text{out}}=\dfrac{\cos^2ka/\kappa}{a+\sin2ka/(2k)+\cos^2ka/\kappa}$.

From the quantization condition $\tan ka=\kappa/k$, we get $\cos^2ka=\dfrac{1}{1+\tan^2ka}=\dfrac{k^2}{k^2+\kappa^2}$ and $\sin ka\cos ka=\tan ka\cos^2ka=\dfrac{k\kappa}{k^2+\kappa^2}$, so $\dfrac{\sin2ka}{2k}=\dfrac{\sin ka\cos ka}{k}=\dfrac{\kappa}{k^2+\kappa^2}$. Letting $s=k^2+\kappa^2$, the denominator is $a+\dfrac{\kappa}{s}+\dfrac{k^2}{\kappa s}=a+\dfrac{\kappa^2+k^2}{\kappa s}=a+\dfrac{1}{\kappa}$ and the numerator is $\dfrac{k^2}{\kappa s}$, so we obtain

$$ P_{\text{out}}=\frac{k^2/(\kappa s)}{a+1/\kappa}=\frac{k^2/s}{\kappa a+1}=\frac{\xi^2/z_0^2}{1+\eta} $$

(because $k^2/s=\xi^2/(\xi^2+\eta^2)=\xi^2/z_0^2$). For $z_0\gg1$, the ground state has $\xi_1\to\pi/2$ (Exercise 11.2) and $\eta_1=\sqrt{z_0^2-\xi_1^2}\to z_0$, so $P_{\text{out}}\approx\dfrac{(\pi/2)^2}{z_0^2(1+z_0)}\approx\dfrac{\pi^2}{4z_0^3}$, which approaches $0$ in proportion to $z_0^{-3}$. For $z_0=10$, the approximate formula gives $\dfrac{\pi^2}{4\times1000}=2.47\times10^{-3}$, and the exact value is $\dfrac{1.4276^2}{100\times(1+9.8976)}=\dfrac{2.0380}{1089.8}=1.87\times10^{-3}$, so the approximate formula is about 30% larger. This is because the approximation sets $\xi_1\to\pi/2$, whereas at $z_0=10$, $\xi_1=1.4276$ is about 9% smaller than $\pi/2=1.5708$. Using the correction of Exercise 11.2, $\xi_1\approx\dfrac{\pi/2}{1+1/z_0}$, together with $\eta_1\approx z_0$, we get $P_{\text{out}}\approx\dfrac{(\pi/2)^2/(1+1/z_0)^2}{z_0^2(1+z_0)}=\dfrac{2.467/1.21}{100\times11}=1.85\times10^{-3}$, which agrees well with the exact value.

Exercise 11.4: A well of width 0.8 nm and wall height 5 eV

Solution

Using $a=0.4\ \mathrm{nm}$ and $\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2m_{\mathrm e}}=0.038\,100\ \mathrm{eV\,nm^2}$, we have

$$ z_0=0.4\times\sqrt{\frac{5}{0.038\,100}}=0.4\times11.456=4.582 $$

Since $\dfrac{2z_0}{\pi}=2.917$, $N=3$. Solving by bisection for $\xi_n$ in each interval ($n=1$: even, $n=2$: odd, $n=3$: even), we find $\xi_1=1.2863$, $\xi_2=2.5511$, $\xi_3=3.7528$, and $\eta_n=\sqrt{z_0^2-\xi_n^2}=4.398,\ 3.806,\ 2.629$. The energies are $E_n=V_0\xi_n^2/z_0^2$ ($z_0^2=20.997$), namely

$$ E_1=5\times\frac{1.6546}{20.997}=0.394\ \mathrm{eV},\quad E_2=5\times\frac{6.5082}{20.997}=1.550\ \mathrm{eV},\quad E_3=5\times\frac{14.083}{20.997}=3.354\ \mathrm{eV} $$

The levels of the infinite well are $E_n^{\infty}=n^2\dfrac{h^2}{8m_{\mathrm e}L^2}=n^2\times\dfrac{0.3760}{0.64}\ \mathrm{eV}=n^2\times0.5875\ \mathrm{eV}$, that is, $0.5875,\ 2.350,\ 5.288\ \mathrm{eV}$. The ratios are $E_n/E_n^{\infty}=0.671,\ 0.659,\ 0.634$. The $n=3$ level of the infinite well ($5.29\ \mathrm{eV}$) exceeds the wall height of $5\ \mathrm{eV}$, yet in the finite well it lies at $3.35\ \mathrm{eV}$. The deep-well approximation (with $\eta\approx z_0$, $E_1\approx E_1^{\infty}/(1+1/z_0)^2$) gives $0.5875/(1+1/4.582)^2=0.396\ \mathrm{eV}$, which reproduces $E_1$ well. From Formula 11.1, the probability outside the well for $n=1$ is

$$ P_{\text{out}}=\frac{E_1/V_0}{1+\eta_1}=\frac{0.0788}{1+4.398}=0.0146 $$

which is about $1.5\ \%$.

Exercise 11.5: Deriving the $\delta$ well as a limit of the finite well

Solution

We have $z_0^2=\dfrac{2ma^2V_0}{\hbar^2}=\dfrac{mV_0L^2}{2\hbar^2}$ ($a=L/2$), and substituting $V_0=\alpha/L$ gives $z_0^2=\dfrac{m\alpha L}{2\hbar^2}$. If we keep $\alpha$ constant and let $L\to0$, then $z_0^2\to0$, that is, $z_0\to0$, and we are in the limit of a weak well with $N=1$.

For the ground state (even), $\xi\lt z_0\ll1$, so we can set $\tan\xi\approx\xi$, which gives $\eta=\xi\tan\xi\approx\xi^2$. Putting $\xi^2=\eta$ into the equation of the circle, $\eta^2=z_0^2-\xi^2$, gives $\eta^2+\eta=z_0^2$, and for $\eta\ll1$ we can neglect $\eta^2$ to get $\eta\approx z_0^2$. Then $\kappa=\dfrac{\eta}{a}=\dfrac{2\eta}{L}\approx\dfrac{2z_0^2}{L}=\dfrac{2}{L}\cdot\dfrac{m\alpha L}{2\hbar^2}=\dfrac{m\alpha}{\hbar^2}$, and $L$ drops out. This approximation becomes exact as $L\to0$ ($z_0\to0$). First we fix how the energy is measured. In the finite well, $E$ is measured from the bottom of the well ($V=0$), so the top of the wall is at height $V_0$, and from $\kappa=\sqrt{2m(V_0-E)}/\hbar$ we get $E=V_0-\dfrac{\hbar^2\kappa^2}{2m}$. In the $\delta$ well, on the other hand, we take $V=0$ outside the well (everywhere except the origin), so the binding energy is a negative value $E_\delta$, and $\kappa=\sqrt{-2mE_\delta}/\hbar$. Since the top of the wall of the finite well ($V=V_0$) corresponds to the outside of the $\delta$ well ($V=0$), $E_\delta$ corresponds to the energy $E-V_0$ measured from the top of the wall of the finite well. That is, $E_\delta=E-V_0=-\dfrac{\hbar^2\kappa^2}{2m}$. Substituting $\kappa=\dfrac{m\alpha}{\hbar^2}$ gives $E_\delta=-\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2m}\Bigl(\dfrac{m\alpha}{\hbar^2}\Bigr)^2=-\dfrac{m\alpha^2}{2\hbar^2}$. This is the binding energy of the $\delta$ well, $E=-\dfrac{m\alpha^2}{2\hbar^2}$ (since $V_0=\alpha/L\to\infty$, $E$ measured from the bottom of the well diverges to $\infty$, but $E_\delta$ measured from the top of the wall settles to a finite value).

Exercise 11.6: The limit of the double $\delta$ well and the condition for the antibonding state to exist

Solution

(1) As $R\to0$, $e^{-\kappa R}\to1$, so for the bonding state $\kappa=\kappa_0(1+1)=2\kappa_0$ and $E=-\dfrac{\hbar^2(2\kappa_0)^2}{2m}=-\dfrac{2m\alpha^2}{\hbar^2}$ (four times the level $-\dfrac{m\alpha^2}{2\hbar^2}$ of an isolated well). This agrees with the energy $-\dfrac{m(2\alpha)^2}{2\hbar^2}$ of a single $\delta$ well of strength $2\alpha$ (the two wells overlap and become one).

(2) The antibonding state is the solution with $\kappa\gt0$ of $\kappa=\kappa_0(1-e^{-\kappa R})$. Let $f(\kappa)=\kappa_0(1-e^{-\kappa R})-\kappa$. Then $f(0)=0$, $f'(\kappa)=\kappa_0Re^{-\kappa R}-1$, $f'(0)=\kappa_0R-1$, and $f''(\kappa)=-\kappa_0R^2e^{-\kappa R}\lt0$ (concave down). As $\kappa\to\infty$, $f\to\kappa_0-\kappa\to-\infty$. If $f'(0)\gt0$ ($\kappa_0R\gt1$), $f$ increases from $\kappa=0$ and takes positive values, and then heads toward $-\infty$, so it has only one zero in $\kappa\gt0$. If $f'(0)\le0$, then $f$ is concave down and $f'(0)\le0$, so $f\lt0$ for $\kappa\gt0$, and there is no zero. Therefore the antibonding state exists only when $R\gt\dfrac{1}{\kappa_0}=\dfrac{\hbar^2}{m\alpha}$. This means that the separation of the wells is longer than the penetration depth $1/\kappa_0$ of the wave function of an isolated well.

(3) For $\hbar=m=\alpha=1$, $\kappa_0=1$ and $E=-\kappa^2/2$. For $R=3$, the bonding state is found by successive substitution into $\kappa=1+e^{-3\kappa}$ starting from $\kappa=1$: $1\to1.0498\to1.0429\to1.0438\to1.0437$. Thus $\kappa_{\text{bond}}=1.0437$ and $E_{\text{bond}}=-0.5446$. For the antibonding state, substituting into $\kappa=1-e^{-3\kappa}$ starting from $\kappa=0.9$ gives $0.9\to0.9328\to0.9391\to0.9402\to0.9404\to0.9405$. Thus $\kappa_{\text{anti}}=0.9405$ and $E_{\text{anti}}=-0.4423$. For $R=1.5$, a similar successive substitution (with somewhat slower convergence) gives $\kappa_{\text{bond}}=1.1723$, $E_{\text{bond}}=-0.6872$, $\kappa_{\text{anti}}=0.5828$, and $E_{\text{anti}}=-0.1698$ (since $R=1.5\gt1$, the antibonding state exists). The shifts from the level $-0.5$ of an isolated well are $-0.045$ and $+0.058$ for $R=3$, and $-0.187$ and $+0.330$ for $R=1.5$; they are larger for smaller $R$, and the rise of the antibonding level is larger than the drop of the bonding level.

Exercise 11.7: Quantum-well width and emission wavelength

Solution

Using the same method as in Example 11.9, for each of the electron (mass $0.067\,m_{\mathrm e}$ in the well, $0.092\,m_{\mathrm e}$ in the barrier, depth $\Delta E_{\mathrm c}=0.22\ \mathrm{eV}$) and the heavy hole ($0.45\,m_{\mathrm e}$ in the well, $0.55\,m_{\mathrm e}$ in the barrier, depth $\Delta E_{\mathrm v}=0.15\ \mathrm{eV}$), we find the ground-state solution of the BenDaniel–Duke condition $\xi\tan\xi=\dfrac{m_{\mathrm w}}{m_{\mathrm b}}\eta$ together with the ellipse $\xi^2+\dfrac{m_{\mathrm w}}{m_{\mathrm b}}\eta^2=z_0^2$.

Details for $L=8\ \mathrm{nm}$ ($a=4\ \mathrm{nm}$): for the electron, $\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2m_{\mathrm w}}=0.5687\ \mathrm{eV\,nm^2}$, so $z_0=4\times\sqrt{0.22/0.5687}=2.488$ ($z_0^2=6.19$), and $\dfrac{m_{\mathrm w}}{m_{\mathrm b}}=0.7283$. The solution is $\xi=1.0644$, $\eta=2.6352$ (check: $\xi\tan\xi=1.0644\times1.8030=1.919$, $0.7283\times2.6352=1.919$; ellipse: $1.133+0.7283\times6.944=6.19$). The energy is $E_{1\mathrm e}=0.5687\times\dfrac{1.0644^2}{16}\ \mathrm{eV}=0.04027\ \mathrm{eV}=40.3\ \mathrm{meV}$. For the heavy hole, $\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2m_{\mathrm w}}=\dfrac{0.038\,100}{0.45}=0.08467\ \mathrm{eV\,nm^2}$, so $z_0=4\times\sqrt{0.15/0.08467}=5.324$, and $\dfrac{m_{\mathrm w}}{m_{\mathrm b}}=\dfrac{0.45}{0.55}=0.8182$. The solution is $\xi=1.2994$, $\eta=5.7081$ (check: $\xi\tan\xi=1.2994\times3.5942=4.670$, $0.8182\times5.7081=4.670$), and $E_{1\mathrm{hh}}=0.08467\times\dfrac{1.2994^2}{16}\ \mathrm{eV}=8.93\ \mathrm{meV}$. Therefore $h\nu=1.424+0.0403+0.0089=1.4732\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $\lambda=\dfrac{1239.84}{1.4732}\ \mathrm{nm}=841.6\ \mathrm{nm}$.

Solving similarly for $L=4,\ 15\ \mathrm{nm}$ gives the following table.

Results of Exercise 11.7 (under the assumptions of Example 11.9)
$L$ [nm]$E_{1\mathrm e}$ [meV]$E_{1\mathrm{hh}}$ [meV]Total [meV]$h\nu$ [eV]$\lambda$ [nm]
490.325.8116.11.540805
840.38.949.21.473842
1515.93.018.91.443859

The narrower the well, the larger the confinement energy and the shorter the emission wavelength ($805\ \mathrm{nm}$ for $L=4\ \mathrm{nm}$ and $859\ \mathrm{nm}$ for $15\ \mathrm{nm}$). Combined with the results of Example 11.9 for 5, 10, and 20 nm ($819,\ 849,\ 864\ \mathrm{nm}$), this shows that the narrower the well becomes, the more rapidly the wavelength changes.

Exercise 11.8: Well sizes at which the second and third bound states appear

Solution

The $n$th bound state appears for $z_0\gt(n-1)\pi/2$ (Theorem 11.4). Since $z_0=\dfrac{L}{2}\dfrac{\sqrt{2mV_0}}{\hbar}$, the condition $z_0=(n-1)\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ reads $L\sqrt{2mV_0}/\hbar=(n-1)\pi$, that is, $V_0=\dfrac{(n-1)^2\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2}$.

(1) For $L=1\ \mathrm{nm}$ and $m=m_{\mathrm e}$, $\dfrac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2m_{\mathrm e}L^2}=\pi^2\times0.038\,100\ \mathrm{eV}=0.3760\ \mathrm{eV}$, so the second ($n=2$) state appears for $V_0\gt0.376\ \mathrm{eV}$ and the third ($n=3$) state for $V_0\gt4\times0.3760=1.504\ \mathrm{eV}$. These values are equal to $E_1^{\infty}$ and $E_2^{\infty}$ of the infinite well (for $V_0=1\ \mathrm{eV}$ in Example 11.4, $0.376\lt1\lt1.504$ and hence $N=2$).

(2) Solving $z_0=\dfrac{\pi}{2}(n-1)$ for $L$ gives $L=\dfrac{(n-1)\pi}{\sqrt{V_0/(\hbar^2/2m^*)}}$. For $V_0=0.3\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2m^*}=0.5687\ \mathrm{eV\,nm^2}$, $\sqrt{V_0/(\hbar^2/2m^*)}=\sqrt{0.5276}=0.7263\ \mathrm{nm^{-1}}$, so for $n=2$, $L=\dfrac{\pi}{0.7263}\ \mathrm{nm}=4.33\ \mathrm{nm}$, and for $n=3$, $L=\dfrac{2\pi}{0.7263}\ \mathrm{nm}=8.65\ \mathrm{nm}$. That is, the second bound state appears when the width exceeds $4.33\ \mathrm{nm}$, and the third bound state appears when it exceeds $8.65\ \mathrm{nm}$. This agrees with the fact that $N=3$ for $L=10\ \mathrm{nm}$ in Example 11.8 ($10\gt8.65$).

← Back to Chapter 11, “The Finite Potential Well — Penetration and Bound States”

Chapter 12: Tunneling — Step and Barrier Potentials

Exercise 12.1: Transmission coefficient of a thick barrier — exact and approximate formulas

Solution

(1) Since $V_0-E=3\ \mathrm{eV}$, $\kappa=\dfrac{\sqrt{2m_{\mathrm e}\times3\ \mathrm{eV}}}{\hbar}=8.874\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}=8.874\ \mathrm{nm^{-1}}$ (the same value as in Illustration 12.1 of Chapter 12). With $L=0.6\ \mathrm{nm}$,

$$ \kappa L=8.874\times0.6=5.324 $$

(2) We have $e^{5.324}=205.2$ and $e^{-5.324}=0.00487$, so $\sinh\kappa L=\dfrac{205.2-0.0049}{2}=102.6$ and $\sinh^2\kappa L=1.053\times10^{4}$. Substituting $4E(V_0-E)=4\times5\times3=60\ \mathrm{eV^2}$ and $V_0^2=64\ \mathrm{eV^2}$ into the formula for the transmission coefficient, $T=\left[1+\dfrac{V_0^2\sinh^2\kappa L}{4E(V_0-E)}\right]^{-1}$, we obtain

$$ T=\left[1+\frac{64\times1.053\times10^{4}}{60}\right]^{-1}=\left[1+1.123\times10^{4}\right]^{-1}=8.90\times10^{-5} $$

(3) The prefactor is $\dfrac{16E(V_0-E)}{V_0^2}=\dfrac{16\times5\times3}{64}=3.75$, and $e^{-2\kappa L}=e^{-10.648}=2.374\times10^{-5}$, so the approximate formula with the prefactor (the thick-barrier approximation) gives

$$ T\approx3.75\times2.374\times10^{-5}=8.90\times10^{-5} $$

which agrees with the exact value $8.90\times10^{-5}$ to four digits (the relative error is of the order of $e^{-2\kappa L}$, that is, $2\times10^{-5}$). Without the prefactor, $e^{-2\kappa L}=2.37\times10^{-5}$ is $0.27$ times the exact value ($1/3.75$), so it is smaller by only one order of magnitude.

Exercise 12.2: $R+T=1$ for the step potential, and the high-energy limit

Solution

(1) The probability current of the wave function $Ae^{ik_1x}+Be^{-ik_1x}$ for $x\lt0$ is $J=\dfrac{\hbar k_1}{m}\left(\abs{A}^2-\abs{B}^2\right)$, and that of $Ce^{ik_2x}$ for $x\gt0$ is $J=\dfrac{\hbar k_2}{m}\abs{C}^2$. In a stationary state the probability density does not depend on time, so the continuity equation gives $\dfrac{\dd J}{\dd x}=0$; that is, $J$ is a constant independent of $x$, and it is equal on the left and right of $x=0$: $k_1\left(\abs{A}^2-\abs{B}^2\right)=k_2\abs{C}^2$. Dividing both sides by $k_1\abs{A}^2$, we obtain

$$ 1-\abs{\frac{B}{A}}^2=\frac{k_2}{k_1}\abs{\frac{C}{A}}^2\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 1-R=T $$

and thus $R+T=1$ is proved.

(2) Since $k_2/k_1=\sqrt{1-V_0/E}=\sqrt{1-5/10}=0.7071$,

$$ R=\left(\frac{1-0.7071}{1+0.7071}\right)^2=(0.17157)^2=0.0294,\qquad T=\frac{4\times0.7071}{(1.7071)^2}=\frac{2.8284}{2.9142}=0.9706 $$

Thus $R+T=1.0000$.

(3) Let $\delta\equiv V_0/E\ll1$. Then $\dfrac{k_2}{k_1}=\sqrt{1-\delta}=1-\dfrac{\delta}{2}-\dfrac{\delta^2}{8}-\cdots$. Therefore $1-\dfrac{k_2}{k_1}\approx\dfrac{\delta}{2}$ and $1+\dfrac{k_2}{k_1}\approx2$, so that

$$ R=\left(\frac{1-k_2/k_1}{1+k_2/k_1}\right)^2\approx\left(\frac{\delta/2}{2}\right)^2=\left(\frac{\delta}{4}\right)^2=\left(\frac{V_0}{4E}\right)^2 $$

For $E=100\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $V_0=5\ \mathrm{eV}$, the approximate formula gives $\left(\dfrac{5}{400}\right)^2=1.56\times10^{-4}$. Computed exactly, $k_2/k_1=\sqrt{0.95}=0.97468$ gives $R=\left(\dfrac{0.02532}{1.97468}\right)^2=(0.012823)^2=1.64\times10^{-4}$, and the difference from the approximate formula is about $5\%$ (due to the next term $\delta^2/8$). The higher the energy, the more rapidly the reflection becomes smaller, as $E^{-2}$.

Exercise 12.3: The three energies of perfect transmission for a barrier with $E\gt V_0$

Solution

(1) The condition for $T=1$ is $\sin k'L=0$, that is, $k'L=n\pi$, and $E-V_0=\dfrac{\hbar^2k'^2}{2m_{\mathrm e}}=\dfrac{n^2\pi^2\hbar^2}{2m_{\mathrm e}L^2}=n^2\,\dfrac{h^2}{8m_{\mathrm e}L^2}$. For $L=0.5\ \mathrm{nm}$, $\dfrac{h^2}{8m_{\mathrm e}L^2}=\dfrac{0.3760\ \mathrm{eV\,nm^2}}{(0.5\ \mathrm{nm})^2}=1.504\ \mathrm{eV}$, so

$$ E_n=5+1.504\,n^2\ \mathrm{eV}\ \Longrightarrow\ E_1=6.504\ \mathrm{eV},\quad E_2=11.02\ \mathrm{eV},\quad E_3=18.54\ \mathrm{eV} $$

(2) For $E=8\ \mathrm{eV}$, $E-V_0=3\ \mathrm{eV}$, and $k'=\dfrac{\sqrt{2m_{\mathrm e}\times3\ \mathrm{eV}}}{\hbar}=8.874\ \mathrm{nm^{-1}}$, so $k'L=8.874\times0.5=4.437$. Since $4.437-\pi=1.296$, $\sin k'L=-\sin1.296=-0.9623$ and $\sin^2k'L=0.9260$. Substituting $4E(E-V_0)=4\times8\times3=96\ \mathrm{eV^2}$ and $V_0^2=25\ \mathrm{eV^2}$ into the formula for the reflection coefficient, $R=\left[1+\dfrac{4E(E-V_0)}{V_0^2\sin^2k'L}\right]^{-1}$, we obtain

$$ R=\left[1+\frac{96}{25\times0.9260}\right]^{-1}=\left[1+4.147\right]^{-1}=0.194 $$

Hence $T=0.806$. The value $k'L=4.437$ lies between $\pi$ ($E_1$) and $2\pi$ ($E_2$), close to $3\pi/2=4.71$, in the neighborhood where $\sin^2k'L$ is close to $1$ and the reflection is strongest.

Exercise 12.4: The $\alpha$ decay of radium $226$

Solution

Since $A_{\mathrm d}^{1/3}=222^{1/3}=6.055$ and $4^{1/3}=1.587$, $R_{\mathrm N}=1.2\times(6.055+1.587)=9.17\ \mathrm{fm}$.

(1) Turning point: $r_0=\dfrac{2Z\,e_0^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)}{E}=\dfrac{2\times86\times1.43996}{4.871}=\dfrac{247.67}{4.871}=50.85\ \mathrm{fm}$.

(2) $x^2=R_{\mathrm N}/r_0=9.17/50.85=0.1804$, so $x=0.4247$. Then $\sin^{-1}x=0.4386$ and $x\sqrt{1-x^2}=0.4247\times\sqrt{0.8196}=0.4247\times0.9053=0.3845$. The bracket is $\pi-2\times0.4386-2\times0.3845=3.1416-0.8772-0.7690=1.4954$. The prefactor is

$$ \frac{\sqrt{2\mu c^2E}\,r_0}{\hbar c}=\frac{\sqrt{2\times3661.4\times4.871}\times50.85}{197.327}=\frac{188.86\times50.85}{197.327}=48.67 $$

so $G=48.67\times1.4954=72.8$. The transmission coefficient is $T=e^{-72.8}=2.5\times10^{-32}$.

(3) $T_{1/2}=\dfrac{\ln2}{fT}=\dfrac{0.6931}{10^{21}\times2.48\times10^{-32}}=2.8\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{s}=\dfrac{2.8\times10^{10}}{3.156\times10^{7}}\ \text{yr}=8.8\times10^{2}\ \text{yr}$. This is about $0.55$ times the measured value of 1600 years, so the order of magnitude is right. (If we use the approximate formula $\pi-4x=1.443$, we get $G=70.2$, and the half-life comes out $e^{2.6}\approx13$ times too short.)

Exercise 12.5: In field emission, how much harder is it for electrons below the Fermi level to escape?

Solution

Let the energy of the electron be $E=-1\ \mathrm{eV}$ (taking the Fermi level as $0$). For the barrier potential $V(x)=W_0-e_0Fx$ we have $V(x)-E=(W_0-E)-e_0Fx=(W_0+1\ \mathrm{eV})-e_0Fx$, which is a triangular barrier of the same form, with height $W_0'=W_0-E=5.5\ \mathrm{eV}$. The turning point is $x_t=W_0'/(e_0F)=5.5/4=1.375\ \mathrm{nm}$. By the same calculation as in Section 12.7.3 (Chapter 12, Section 12.7.3; let $u=W_0'-e_0Fx$), the exponent in Formula 12.1 is

$$ G(E)=\frac{2}{\hbar}\int_0^{x_t}\sqrt{2m_{\mathrm e}\left(W_0'-e_0Fx\right)}\,\dd x=\frac{4\sqrt{2m_{\mathrm e}}}{3\hbar e_0}\,\frac{{W_0'}^{3/2}}{F}=b\,\frac{(W_0-E)^{3/2}}{F} $$

Here $b=6.831\ \mathrm{V\,nm^{-1}\,eV^{-3/2}}$ and ${W_0'}^{3/2}=5.5^{3/2}=12.90$, so for $F=4\ \mathrm{V/nm}$, $G(-1\ \mathrm{eV})=\dfrac{6.831\times12.90}{4}=22.03$. For an electron at the Fermi level, $W_0^{3/2}=9.546$ gives $G(0)=\dfrac{6.831\times9.546}{4}=16.30$ (Example 12.12). The difference of the exponents is $22.03-16.30=5.73$ (this is $16.30\times0.351=5.7$, from the ratio $(5.5/4.5)^{3/2}=1.351$), and the ratio of the transmission coefficients is

$$ \frac{T(-1\ \mathrm{eV})}{T(0)}=e^{-5.73}=3.3\times10^{-3} $$

That is, the ratio is about $1/300$. Each time the energy becomes $1\ \mathrm{eV}$ deeper, the transmission coefficient drops to about $1/300$ (to $1/e$ for every $0.175\ \mathrm{eV}$). On the other hand, the supply of electrons in the metal increases only gradually with depth (roughly in proportion to the depth, as we saw in Chapter 12, Section 12.7.3), and it cannot compete with the exponential decrease $e^{-\Delta/0.175\ \mathrm{eV}}$. Therefore most of the emission current is carried by electrons very close to the Fermi level (within about $0.2\ \mathrm{eV}$). This is why the field-emission current is described by the Fowler–Nordheim equation, which is determined only by the barrier height $W_0$ measured from the Fermi level.

Exercise 12.6: In STM, when the tip approaches by $0.05\ \mathrm{nm}$

Solution

$2m_{\mathrm e}W_0=2\times9.109\,384\times10^{-31}\times5.0\times1.602\,177\times10^{-19}=1.4595\times10^{-48}\ \mathrm{kg\,J}$, its square root is $1.2081\times10^{-24}$, and $\kappa=\dfrac{1.2081\times10^{-24}}{1.054\,572\times10^{-34}}=1.1456\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}=1.1456\ \text{Å}^{-1}$.

(1) When the separation decreases by $\Delta d=0.05\ \mathrm{nm}=0.5\ \text{Å}$, the current is multiplied by $e^{2\kappa\Delta d}=e^{2\times1.1456\times0.5}=e^{1.1456}=3.14$.

(2) When the separation changes by $\delta$, the current is multiplied by $e^{2\kappa\delta}$, so if a $1\%$ change, that is, $e^{2\kappa\delta}=1.01$, can be detected, then

$$ \delta=\frac{\ln1.01}{2\kappa}=\frac{0.00995}{2\times1.1456\ \text{Å}^{-1}}=0.00434\ \text{Å}=0.43\ \mathrm{pm} $$

Merely by measuring the current to $1\%$ accuracy, one can detect changes in the height of the tip finer than $1\ \mathrm{pm}$ (in a real instrument, vibration and noise determine the resolution).

Exercise 12.7: Ratio of the transmission coefficients of hydrogen and deuterium

Solution

(1) In the thick-barrier approximation $T\approx e^{-2\kappa L}$ (without the prefactor), since $\kappa=\sqrt{2m(V_0-E)}/\hbar\propto\sqrt{m}$, we have $\kappa_{\mathrm d}=\kappa_{\mathrm p}\sqrt{m_{\mathrm d}/m_{\mathrm p}}$. Therefore

$$ \frac{T_{\mathrm p}}{T_{\mathrm d}}=\frac{e^{-2\kappa_{\mathrm p}L}}{e^{-2\kappa_{\mathrm d}L}}=\exp\!\left[2(\kappa_{\mathrm d}-\kappa_{\mathrm p})L\right]=\exp\!\left[2\kappa_{\mathrm p}L\left(\sqrt{\frac{m_{\mathrm d}}{m_{\mathrm p}}}-1\right)\right] $$

The ratio is determined by the square root of the mass ratio, which enters the exponent. (The prefactor $16E(V_0-E)/V_0^2$ is the same for the two particles, so it cancels in the ratio.)

(2) $\kappa_{\mathrm p}=1.2024\times10^{11}\times\sqrt{0.25/0.3}=1.2024\times10^{11}\times0.9129=1.0976\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$. With $L=0.04\ \mathrm{nm}=4\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m}$, $2\kappa_{\mathrm p}L=8.781$. Since $\sqrt{m_{\mathrm d}/m_{\mathrm p}}=\sqrt{1.999}=1.4139$,

$$ \frac{T_{\mathrm p}}{T_{\mathrm d}}=\exp[8.781\times(1.4139-1)]=\exp[3.634]=37.9 $$

Thus the transmission coefficient of deuterium is about $1/38$ that of hydrogen. The ratio is smaller than the ratio $145$ in Example 12.5 ($0.3\ \mathrm{eV}$, $0.05\ \mathrm{nm}$) because the barrier is lower and thinner: when $2\kappa_{\mathrm p}L$ is smaller ($8.8$ compared with $12.0$), the difference in the exponent, $2\kappa_{\mathrm p}L\times0.414$, is also smaller.

Exercise 12.8: Transmission coefficient of a barrier with $E=V_0$

Solution

(1) As $E\to V_0$, $\kappa=\sqrt{2m(V_0-E)}/\hbar\to0$, so $\sinh\kappa L\approx\kappa L$. Then

$$ \frac{V_0^2\sinh^2\kappa L}{4E(V_0-E)}\approx\frac{V_0^2\kappa^2L^2}{4E(V_0-E)}=\frac{V_0^2L^2}{4E(V_0-E)}\cdot\frac{2m(V_0-E)}{\hbar^2}=\frac{mV_0^2L^2}{2\hbar^2E}\ \xrightarrow{E\to V_0}\ \frac{mV_0L^2}{2\hbar^2} $$

and we obtain $T=\left[1+\dfrac{mV_0L^2}{2\hbar^2}\right]^{-1}$.

(2) As $E\to V_0$ (from above), $k'=\sqrt{2m(E-V_0)}/\hbar\to0$, and $\sin k'L\approx k'L$.

$$ \frac{V_0^2\sin^2k'L}{4E(E-V_0)}\approx\frac{V_0^2k'^2L^2}{4E(E-V_0)}=\frac{V_0^2L^2}{4E(E-V_0)}\cdot\frac{2m(E-V_0)}{\hbar^2}=\frac{mV_0^2L^2}{2\hbar^2E}\ \xrightarrow{E\to V_0}\ \frac{mV_0L^2}{2\hbar^2} $$

This is the same value as in (1). The transmission coefficient is continuous across $E=V_0$, and the formula for $E\lt V_0$ and the formula for $E\gt V_0$ connect smoothly at $E=V_0$.

(3) $\dfrac{mV_0L^2}{2\hbar^2}=\dfrac{9.109\,384\times10^{-31}\times1.602\,177\times10^{-19}\times(0.5\times10^{-9})^2}{2\times(1.054\,572\times10^{-34})^2}=\dfrac{3.6487\times10^{-68}}{2.2242\times10^{-68}}=1.640$, so

$$ T=\frac{1}{1+1.640}=0.379,\qquad R=1-T=0.621 $$

(Letting $g=2mV_0L^2/\hbar^2=6.56$, we have $T=\dfrac{4}{g+4}$ and $R=\dfrac{g}{g+4}$, which give the same values.)

← Back to Chapter 12, “Tunneling — Step and Barrier Potentials”

Chapter 13: The Harmonic Oscillator — Series Solution and Hermite Polynomials

Exercise 13.1: The wave function for $n=3$

Solution

Let $A=\left(\dfrac{m\omega}{\pi\hbar}\right)^{1/4}$ and $X=\sqrt{m\omega/\hbar}\,x$. Since $H_3=8X^3-12X=4(2X^3-3X)$ and $C_3=\dfrac{A}{\sqrt{2^3\cdot3!}}=\dfrac{A}{\sqrt{48}}=\dfrac{A}{4\sqrt{3}}$, we have $4\times\dfrac{1}{4\sqrt3}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$, and therefore

$$ \psi_3=\frac{A}{\sqrt{3}}\,(2X^3-3X)\,e^{-X^2/2},\qquad E_3=\frac72\hbar\omega. $$

(1) Using $A^2\dd x=\dfrac{\dd X}{\sqrt{\pi}}$ and $(2X^3-3X)^2=4X^6-12X^4+9X^2$, we obtain

$$ \int\psi_3^2\dd x=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{\pi}}\int(4X^6-12X^4+9X^2)\,e^{-X^2}\dd X=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{\pi}}\left(4\cdot\frac{15\sqrt{\pi}}{8}-12\cdot\frac{3\sqrt{\pi}}{4}+9\cdot\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}\right)=\frac13\left(\frac{15}{2}-9+\frac92\right)=\frac13\cdot3=1. $$

(2) The nodes follow from $2X^3-3X=X(2X^2-3)=0$: $X=0,\ \pm\sqrt{3/2}=\pm1.225$, that is, $x=0,\ \pm1.225\,x_0$, three nodes in all ($n=3$ nodes). The energy is $E_3=(3+\tfrac12)\hbar\omega=\tfrac72\hbar\omega$ ($\varepsilon=7$).

(3) From $H_3=8X^3-12X$ we get $H_3'=24X^2-12$ and $H_3''=48X$. Then $H_3''-2XH_3'+6H_3=48X-2X(24X^2-12)+6(8X^3-12X)=48X-48X^3+24X+48X^3-72X=(48+24-72)X=0$. The equation is indeed satisfied.

Exercise 13.2: The probability in the forbidden region for $n=2$

Solution

Here $\lvert\psi_2\rvert^2\dd x=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{\pi}}(2X^2-1)^2e^{-X^2}\dd X$, and the turning point is $X_1\equiv X_{\mathrm t}=\sqrt{5}$. Since the function is even, we obtain

$$ P=2\int_{X_1}^\infty\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\pi}}(4X^4-4X^2+1)\,e^{-X^2}\dd X=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}}\left(4J_4-4J_2+J_0\right),\qquad J_{2k}=\int_{X_1}^\infty X^{2k}e^{-X^2}\dd X $$

Now $J_0=\dfrac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}\operatorname{erfc}(X_1)$. Integration by parts, $\displaystyle\int_{X_1}^\infty X^{2k-1}\cdot Xe^{-X^2}\dd X=\Bigl[-\tfrac12X^{2k-1}e^{-X^2}\Bigr]_{X_1}^\infty+\tfrac{2k-1}{2}J_{2k-2}$, gives $J_2=\dfrac{X_1}{2}e^{-X_1^2}+\dfrac12J_0$ and $J_4=\dfrac{X_1^3}{2}e^{-X_1^2}+\dfrac32J_2$. Therefore $4J_4=2X_1^3e^{-X_1^2}+6J_2$, and

$$ 4J_4-4J_2+J_0=2X_1^3e^{-X_1^2}+2J_2+J_0=2X_1^3e^{-X_1^2}+X_1e^{-X_1^2}+J_0+J_0=(2X_1^3+X_1)\,e^{-X_1^2}+\sqrt{\pi}\operatorname{erfc}(X_1). $$

Hence $P=\dfrac{(2X_1^3+X_1)\,e^{-X_1^2}}{\sqrt{\pi}}+\operatorname{erfc}(X_1)$. For $X_1=\sqrt{5}$: since $X_1^3=5\sqrt{5}$, $2X_1^3=10\sqrt{5}=22.36$; with $X_1=\sqrt{5}=2.236$, $2X_1^3+X_1=24.60$; and since $e^{-5}=6.738\times10^{-3}$,

$$ P=\frac{24.60\times6.738\times10^{-3}}{1.7725}+\operatorname{erfc}(\sqrt{5})=0.0935+0.0016=0.0951. $$

That is, the probability is about $9.5\ \%$. For $n=0,1,2$ the probabilities are $15.7\ \%,\ 11.2\ \%,\ 9.5\ \%$: the probability in the forbidden region decreases as $n$ grows, but only slowly ($6.0\ \%$ for $n=10$ and $4.3\ \%$ for $n=30$).

Exercise 13.3: $\expval{x^4}$ for $n=1$

Solution

Since $\psi_1^2=\sqrt{\dfrac{\alpha}{\pi}}\,2\alpha\,x^2e^{-\alpha x^2}$, we have $\expval{x^N}=2\alpha\sqrt{\dfrac{\alpha}{\pi}}\displaystyle\int x^{N+2}e^{-\alpha x^2}\dd x$. By the formulas (Formula 13.1 in Chapter 13) $a_4=\dfrac{3}{4\alpha^2}\sqrt{\dfrac{\pi}{\alpha}}$ and $a_6=\dfrac{15}{8\alpha^3}\sqrt{\dfrac{\pi}{\alpha}}$, we obtain

$$ \expval{x^2}=2\alpha\cdot\frac{3}{4\alpha^2}=\frac{3}{2\alpha},\qquad \expval{x^4}=2\alpha\cdot\frac{15}{8\alpha^3}=\frac{15}{4\alpha^2}. $$

Since $\alpha=m\omega/\hbar=1/x_0^2$, $\expval{x^2}=\dfrac32x_0^2$ ($=(n+\tfrac12)x_0^2$, which agrees with the value for $n=1$) and $\expval{x^4}=\dfrac{15}{4}x_0^4$. The ratio is $\dfrac{\expval{x^4}}{\expval{x^2}^2}=\dfrac{15/4}{9/4}=\dfrac53=1.67$, which is smaller than the value $3$ for $n=0$ (Gaussian distribution). This reflects the following difference: the probability density for $n=1$ has two peaks with the center hollowed out, and it carries less weight in its tails than a Gaussian one does.

The first-order change of the $n=1$ level due to the anharmonic term $\lambda x^4$ is $\Delta E_1\approx\lambda\expval{x^4}=\dfrac{15}{4}\lambda x_0^4$, which is five times the value $\dfrac34\lambda x_0^4$ for $n=0$. The higher the state, the greater its spread, so the effect of the anharmonic term becomes larger.

Exercise 13.4: The spring constant and zero-point energy of the HF molecule

Solution

(1) Since $\tilde{\nu}=4140\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}=4.14\times10^5\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$, we have $\omega=2\pi c\tilde{\nu}=2\pi\times2.998\times10^8\times4.14\times10^5=7.80\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

$$ k_0=\mu\omega^2=1.589\times10^{-27}\times(7.80\times10^{14})^2=1.589\times10^{-27}\times6.08\times10^{29}=9.66\times10^{2}\ \mathrm{N/m}. $$

(2) $\hbar\omega=hc\tilde{\nu}=1.2398\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV\,cm}\times4140\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}=0.5133\ \mathrm{eV}$. The zero-point energy is $\tfrac12\hbar\omega=0.2566\ \mathrm{eV}=0.2566\times96.485=24.8\ \mathrm{kJ/mol}$.

(3) $\hbar\omega=0.5133\times1.602\times10^{-19}=8.224\times10^{-20}\ \mathrm{J}$, and $x_0=\dfrac{\hbar}{\sqrt{\mu\,\hbar\omega}}=\dfrac{1.0546\times10^{-34}}{\sqrt{1.589\times10^{-27}\times8.224\times10^{-20}}}=\dfrac{1.0546\times10^{-34}}{1.143\times10^{-23}}=9.2\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}=9.2\ \mathrm{pm}$. This is about $10\ \%$ of the bond length of $91.7\ \mathrm{pm}$ (for HCl it is $8\ \%$, Example 13.3). $x_0$ is a rough measure of length; the standard deviation of the position in the ground state is $\Delta x=x_0/\sqrt{2}=6.5\ \mathrm{pm}$, about $7\ \%$ of the bond length. Even the zero-point vibration alone makes the bond length fluctuate by a little under $1$ part in 10.

Exercise 13.5: Finding $\expval{p^2}$ with the Hellmann–Feynman theorem

Solution

Regard the mass $m$ in $\hat{H}=\dfrac{\hat{p}^2}{2m}+\dfrac12m\omega^2\hat{x}^2$ as $\lambda$ (keeping $\omega$ constant). Then $\dfrac{\partial\hat{H}}{\partial m}=-\dfrac{\hat{p}^2}{2m^2}+\dfrac12\omega^2\hat{x}^2$. On the other hand, the eigenvalue $E_n=(n+\tfrac12)\hbar\omega$ does not contain $m$, so $\dfrac{\dd E_n}{\dd m}=0$. By the Hellmann–Feynman theorem $\dfrac{\dd E}{\dd\lambda}=\expval{\partial\hat{H}/\partial\lambda}$, we obtain

$$ 0=-\frac{\expval{p^2}}{2m^2}+\frac12\omega^2\expval{x^2}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad\expval{p^2}=m^2\omega^2\expval{x^2}. $$

Substituting $\expval{x^2}=\left(n+\tfrac12\right)\dfrac{\hbar}{m\omega}$ (from the Hellmann–Feynman theorem with $\omega$ taken as $\lambda$), we get $\expval{p^2}=m^2\omega^2\left(n+\tfrac12\right)\dfrac{\hbar}{m\omega}=\left(n+\tfrac12\right)m\hbar\omega$. This agrees with $\expval{p^2}=2m\expval{T}=mE_n$ obtained from the virial theorem.

Exercise 13.6: The momentum representation for $n=2$

Solution

Since $\dfrac{\dd^2}{\dd K^2}e^{-iKX}=(-iX)^2e^{-iKX}=-X^2e^{-iKX}$, we have $X^2e^{-iKX}=-\dfrac{\dd^2}{\dd K^2}e^{-iKX}$. Substituting this into $\mathcal{F}[X^2f](K)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int X^2f(X)\,e^{-iKX}\dd X$ and taking the differentiation with respect to $K$ outside the integral, we obtain $\mathcal{F}[X^2f]=-\dfrac{\dd^2}{\dd K^2}\mathcal{F}[f]$.

Using $\mathcal{F}[e^{-X^2/2}]=e^{-K^2/2}$ (the Fourier transform $\int e^{-X^2/2}e^{-iKX}\dd X=\sqrt{2\pi}\,e^{-K^2/2}$ of the Gaussian function with $\gamma=\tfrac12$, divided by $\sqrt{2\pi}$), we have $\dfrac{\dd}{\dd K}e^{-K^2/2}=-Ke^{-K^2/2}$ and $\dfrac{\dd^2}{\dd K^2}e^{-K^2/2}=(K^2-1)\,e^{-K^2/2}$, so

$$ \mathcal{F}\left[(2X^2-1)\,e^{-X^2/2}\right]=-2\,(K^2-1)\,e^{-K^2/2}-e^{-K^2/2}=-(2K^2-1)\,e^{-K^2/2}. $$

Since $H_2=4X^2-2=2(2X^2-1)$, we have $\mathcal{F}[H_2e^{-X^2/2}](K)=-H_2(K)\,e^{-K^2/2}=(-i)^2H_2(K)\,e^{-K^2/2}$ (with $(-i)^2=-1$). The normalization constant is common to $X$ and $K$, so the normalized function $u_2(X)=\dfrac{H_2(X)\,e^{-X^2/2}}{\sqrt{2^2\,2!\sqrt{\pi}}}$ satisfies $\mathcal{F}[u_2]=-u_2(K)$. For $\phi_2(p)$ in terms of physical quantities, using $\phi_n(p)=\sqrt{x_0/\hbar}\,\mathcal{F}[u_n](P)$ (with $P=p/\sqrt{m\hbar\omega}$) and $u_n(P)=\sqrt{x_0}\,\psi_n(p/m\omega)$, we obtain $\phi_2(p)=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{m\omega}}\,\psi_2\!\left(\dfrac{p}{m\omega}\right)$, and we have confirmed the factor $(-i)^2=-1$ of Theorem 13.6.

Exercise 13.7: Finding $H_n(0)$ from the generating function and comparing the probability density at the origin with the classical one

Solution

(1) Setting $X=0$ in the generating function $e^{2Xt-t^2}=\sum_nH_n(X)\dfrac{t^n}{n!}$ gives $e^{-t^2}=\sum_nH_n(0)\dfrac{t^n}{n!}$. The left-hand side is $\sum_m\dfrac{(-1)^mt^{2m}}{m!}$, so the odd-order coefficients are $0$, and comparing the coefficients of $t^{2m}$ gives $\dfrac{H_{2m}(0)}{(2m)!}=\dfrac{(-1)^m}{m!}$. Hence $H_{2m+1}(0)=0$ and $H_{2m}(0)=(-1)^m\dfrac{(2m)!}{m!}$ ($H_2(0)=-2$ and $H_4(0)=12$ agree with Table 13.1, and $H_6(0)=-120$ also follows from this formula $(-1)^m(2m)!/m!$).

(2) $\psi_n(0)^2=A^2\dfrac{H_n(0)^2}{2^nn!}$. For $n=0$ it is $A^2$. The ratio, for $n=2m$, is $\dfrac{H_{2m}(0)^2}{2^{2m}(2m)!}=\dfrac{[(2m)!]^2}{(m!)^2\,4^m\,(2m)!}=\dfrac{(2m)!}{4^m\,(m!)^2}$. For $m=1$ it is $\dfrac{2}{4}=\dfrac12$ ($\psi_2(0)^2$ is half of $\psi_0(0)^2$), and for $m=2$ it is $\dfrac{24}{16\cdot4}=\dfrac38=0.375$.

(3) For even $n=2m$, the probability density per $X=x/x_0$ is $\lvert u_n(0)\rvert^2=\dfrac{H_n(0)^2}{2^nn!\sqrt{\pi}}=\dfrac{(2m)!}{4^m(m!)^2\sqrt{\pi}}$ (dimensionless). We also write the classical probability density, per $X$, as $2P_{\mathrm{cl}}(0)=\dfrac{2}{\pi\sqrt{2n+1}}$.

$n$$\lvert u_n(0)\rvert^2$$2P_{\mathrm{cl}}(0)=\dfrac{2}{\pi\sqrt{2n+1}}$Ratio
10$0.13884$$0.13892$$0.9994$
20$0.09941$$0.09942$$0.9999$
100$0.04490$$0.04490$$1.0000$

For large even $n$, the quantum probability density at the origin (the height of the peaks of the oscillation of $\lvert\psi_n\rvert^2$) approaches exactly $2$ times the classical probability density (for odd $n$ the origin is a node, so $\lvert\psi_n(0)\rvert^2=0$, and there are peaks just outside the origin). Since $\lvert\psi_n\rvert^2$ oscillates finely between $0$ and about $2$ times the classical value, and its average is the classical value $P_{\mathrm{cl}}$, this is a quantitative confirmation of the correspondence principle (Section 13.4).

Exercise 13.8: Distribution of the probability among the regions for $n=10$, and comparison with the classical case

Solution

Classical: independent of $X_{\mathrm t}$, (a) $\dfrac{2}{\pi}\arcsin\dfrac12=\dfrac13=0.333$, (b) $\dfrac{2}{\pi}\left(\arcsin1-\arcsin\dfrac12\right)=\dfrac{2}{\pi}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)=\dfrac23=0.667$, (c) $0$.

Quantum ($n=10$, $X_{\mathrm t}=\sqrt{21}=4.583$): we integrate $\lvert\psi_{10}\rvert^2$ numerically with Python.

import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import quad
from scipy.special import eval_hermite, factorial

n = 10
psi2 = lambda X: (eval_hermite(n, X) * np.exp(-X**2/2))**2 / (2.0**n * factorial(n) * np.sqrt(np.pi))
Xt = np.sqrt(2*n + 1)
inner = quad(psi2, -Xt/2, Xt/2, limit=400)[0]        # (a) center
mid   = 2 * quad(psi2, Xt/2, Xt, limit=400)[0]        # (b) middle
print(inner, mid, 1 - inner - mid)                    # (c) outside = 1 - (a) - (b)

The results are (a) $0.352$, (b) $0.588$, (c) $0.060$. Compared with the classical $0.333,\ 0.667,\ 0$, (a) is larger by $0.019$, (b) is smaller by $0.079$, and the remainder penetrates into the forbidden region ($6.0\ \%$). For $n=30$, (a) becomes $0.340$, closer still to the classical value (Example 13.9). The biggest difference is that $6\ \%$ of the quantum probability appears in the classically forbidden region.
