Chapter 23: Spin — The Electron's Other Angular Momentum

Exercise 23.1: Eigenstates of the spin component along an arbitrary direction

Solution

(1) The elements of $\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{n}=\sin\theta\cos\varphi\,\sigma_x+\sin\theta\sin\varphi\,\sigma_y+\cos\theta\,\sigma_z$ are as follows: the $(1,2)$ element is $\sin\theta\cos\varphi-i\sin\theta\sin\varphi=\sin\theta\,e^{-i\varphi}$ and the $(2,1)$ element is $\sin\theta\,e^{i\varphi}$, so

$$ \bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{n}=\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&\sin\theta\,e^{-i\varphi}\\ \sin\theta\,e^{i\varphi}&-\cos\theta\end{bmatrix} $$

Squaring, the $(1,1)$ element is $\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta\,e^{-i\varphi}e^{i\varphi}=1$, the $(1,2)$ element is $\cos\theta\sin\theta\,e^{-i\varphi}-\sin\theta\,e^{-i\varphi}\cos\theta=0$, the $(2,1)$ element is likewise $0$, and the $(2,2)$ element is $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$, so that $(\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{n})^2=E$ (this is also the result of setting $\bm{a}=\bm{b}=\bm{n}$ in the formula $(\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{a})(\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{b})=\bm{a}\cdot\bm{b}\,E+i\bm{\sigma}\cdot(\bm{a}\times\bm{b})$). From $\lambda^2=1$ the eigenvalue $\lambda$ is $\pm1$, and since the trace is $\cos\theta-\cos\theta=0$, there is exactly one $+1$ and one $-1$. Therefore the eigenvalues of $\hat{S}_n=\tfrac\hbar2\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{n}$ are only $+\tfrac\hbar2$ and $-\tfrac\hbar2$, and whichever direction we measure the spin component along, the result is one of the two values $\pm\hbar/2$.

(2) Multiplying $\bm{u}=\bigl(\cos\tfrac\theta2,\ e^{i\varphi}\sin\tfrac\theta2\bigr)^{\mathsf T}$ by $\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{n}$ gives

$$ \begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta\cos\tfrac\theta2+\sin\theta\,e^{-i\varphi}e^{i\varphi}\sin\tfrac\theta2\\ \sin\theta\,e^{i\varphi}\cos\tfrac\theta2-\cos\theta\,e^{i\varphi}\sin\tfrac\theta2\end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix}\cos\bigl(\theta-\tfrac\theta2\bigr)\\ e^{i\varphi}\sin\bigl(\theta-\tfrac\theta2\bigr)\end{bmatrix}=\bm{u} $$

(we used the addition theorems $\cos\theta\cos\tfrac\theta2+\sin\theta\sin\tfrac\theta2=\cos\tfrac\theta2$ and $\sin\theta\cos\tfrac\theta2-\cos\theta\sin\tfrac\theta2=\sin\tfrac\theta2$). Hence $(\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{n})\bm{u}=\bm{u}$ and $\hat{S}_n\bm{u}=+\tfrac\hbar2\bm{u}$. The normalization is $\bm{u}^\dagger\bm{u}=\cos^2\tfrac\theta2+\abs{e^{i\varphi}}^2\sin^2\tfrac\theta2=1$. (Similarly, $\bm{v}=\bigl(-e^{-i\varphi}\sin\tfrac\theta2,\ \cos\tfrac\theta2\bigr)^{\mathsf T}$ is the eigenvector with eigenvalue $-\tfrac\hbar2$, and the two eigenvectors are orthogonal, since $\bm{u}^\dagger\bm{v}=-e^{-i\varphi}\cos\tfrac\theta2\sin\tfrac\theta2+e^{-i\varphi}\sin\tfrac\theta2\cos\tfrac\theta2=0$.)

(3) For $\theta=\pi/2$ and $\varphi=0$, $\bm{u}=\bigl(\cos\tfrac\pi4,\ \sin\tfrac\pi4\bigr)^{\mathsf T}=\dfrac1{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}$. Checking, $\sigma_x\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}$, so this is indeed the eigenvector of $\sigma_x$ with eigenvalue $+1$. The probability of obtaining $\uparrow$ ($\alpha$) when $\hat{S}_z$ is measured is the square of the absolute value of the $\alpha$ component:

$$ P(\uparrow)=\abs{\alpha^\dagger\bm{u}}^2=\left|\frac1{\sqrt2}\right|^2=\frac12 $$

(For $\downarrow$ it is also $\tfrac12$, and $\expval{\hat{S}_z}=\tfrac\hbar2\bigl(\tfrac12-\tfrac12\bigr)=0$.) For a general $\theta$, $P(\uparrow)=\abs{\cos\tfrac\theta2}^2=\cos^2\tfrac\theta2$ and $P(\downarrow)=\sin^2\tfrac\theta2$, and $\expval{\hat{S}_z}=\tfrac\hbar2\bigl(\cos^2\tfrac\theta2-\sin^2\tfrac\theta2\bigr)=\tfrac\hbar2\cos\theta$. This is nothing other than the expectation value of the $z$ component for a spin oriented along $\bm{n}$.

Exercise 23.2: Showing $(\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{a})(\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{b})=\bm{a}\cdot\bm{b}+i\bm{\sigma}\cdot(\bm{a}\times\bm{b})$ in components

Solution

Let $a_\pm=a_x\pm ia_y$ and $b_\pm=b_x\pm ib_y$. Then

$$ \bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{a}=a_x\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}+a_y\begin{bmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{bmatrix}+a_z\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}a_z&a_x-ia_y\\a_x+ia_y&-a_z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}a_z&a_-\\a_+&-a_z\end{bmatrix} $$

The same holds for $\bm{b}$. The four elements of the product are as follows.

$$ (\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{a})(\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{b})=\begin{bmatrix}a_zb_z+a_-b_+&a_zb_--a_-b_z\\a_+b_z-a_zb_+&a_+b_-+a_zb_z\end{bmatrix} $$

Let $\bm{c}=\bm{a}\times\bm{b}$ (so $c_x=a_yb_z-a_zb_y$, $c_y=a_zb_x-a_xb_z$, $c_z=a_xb_y-a_yb_x$), and let $c_\pm=c_x\pm ic_y$.

• The $(1,1)$ element: $a_-b_+=(a_x-ia_y)(b_x+ib_y)=a_xb_x+a_yb_y+i(a_xb_y-a_yb_x)=a_xb_x+a_yb_y+ic_z$. Therefore $(1,1)=a_xb_x+a_yb_y+a_zb_z+ic_z=\bm{a}\cdot\bm{b}+ic_z$.

• The $(2,2)$ element: $a_+b_-=(a_x+ia_y)(b_x-ib_y)=a_xb_x+a_yb_y-i(a_xb_y-a_yb_x)=a_xb_x+a_yb_y-ic_z$. Therefore $(2,2)=\bm{a}\cdot\bm{b}-ic_z$.

• The $(1,2)$ element: $a_zb_--a_-b_z=a_z(b_x-ib_y)-(a_x-ia_y)b_z=(a_zb_x-a_xb_z)-i(a_zb_y-a_yb_z)=c_y+ic_x=i(c_x-ic_y)=ic_-$.

• The $(2,1)$ element: $a_+b_z-a_zb_+=(a_x+ia_y)b_z-a_z(b_x+ib_y)=(a_xb_z-a_zb_x)+i(a_yb_z-a_zb_y)=-c_y+ic_x=i(c_x+ic_y)=ic_+$.

Collecting the above,

$$ (\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{a})(\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{b})=(\bm{a}\cdot\bm{b})\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}+i\begin{bmatrix}c_z&c_-\\c_+&-c_z\end{bmatrix}=(\bm{a}\cdot\bm{b})E+i\,\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{c} $$

and since $\bm{c}=\bm{a}\times\bm{b}$, the identity is proved. Check: for $\bm{a}=(1,0,0)$ and $\bm{b}=(0,1,0)$, we have $\bm{a}\cdot\bm{b}=0$ and $\bm{a}\times\bm{b}=(0,0,1)$, so the right-hand side is $i\sigma_z$, which agrees with $\sigma_x\sigma_y=i\sigma_z$.

Exercise 23.3: The number of Stern–Gerlach beams for an atom with orbital angular momentum $0$

Solution

(1) The number of beams is $2S+1$.

AtomGround term$S$Number of beams $2S+1$
H${}^2\mathrm{S}_{1/2}$$\tfrac12$2
N${}^4\mathrm{S}_{3/2}$$\tfrac32$4
Mn${}^6\mathrm{S}_{5/2}$$\tfrac52$6
Cr${}^7\mathrm{S}_3$$3$7

(The superscript at the upper left of the term symbol is $2S+1$, which is exactly the number of beams.)

(2) For an atom with $L=0$, the magnetic moment is carried by the spin alone, $\mu_z=-g_sM_S\mu_{\mathrm{B}}$ ($M_S=-S,\ldots,S$). With $g_s=2$, the maximum magnitude is $\abs{\mu_z}_{\max}=g_sS\mu_{\mathrm{B}}=2S\mu_{\mathrm{B}}$. For Ag ($S=\tfrac12$) it is $2\cdot\tfrac12\mu_{\mathrm{B}}=1\,\mu_{\mathrm{B}}$. For Cr ($S=3$) it is $2\cdot3\,\mu_{\mathrm{B}}=6\,\mu_{\mathrm{B}}$, and since the force $F_z=\mu_z\partial B_z/\partial z$ is also six times as large, the deflection of the outermost atomic beam is six times that of Ag. The seven beams of Cr correspond to $\mu_z=+6,+4,+2,0,-2,-4,-6\ (\mu_{\mathrm{B}})$ and are equally spaced (with a spacing corresponding to $2\mu_{\mathrm{B}}\,\partial B_z/\partial z$). Note also that for Cr ($S=3$), where the number of values of $M_S$ is odd, there is one undeflected atomic beam with $\mu_z=0$ at the center, whereas for H, N, and Mn, where $S$ is a half-integer, there is no central atomic beam and the number of beams is even.

Exercise 23.4: The numerical value of the Bohr magneton and unit conversion

Solution

(1) Using $e_0=1.602\,177\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, $\hbar=1.054\,572\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$, and $m_{\mathrm{e}}=9.109\,384\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$,

$$ \mu_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{e_0\hbar}{2m_{\mathrm{e}}}=\frac{(1.602\,177\times10^{-19})(1.054\,572\times10^{-34})}{2(9.109\,384\times10^{-31})}\ \frac{\mathrm{C\,J\,s}}{\mathrm{kg}}=9.274\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{J/T} $$

(the numerator is $1.689\,66\times10^{-53}$ and the denominator is $1.821\,88\times10^{-30}$).

(2) At $B=1\ \mathrm{T}$, $\mu_{\mathrm{B}}B=9.274\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{J}$.

  • eV: $\dfrac{9.274\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{J}}{1.602\,177\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J/eV}}=5.788\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV}=57.88\ \mu\mathrm{eV}$.
  • Wavenumber: $5.788\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV}\times8065.54\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}/eV}=0.4669\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ (equivalently, $=5.788\times10^{-5}/(1.239\,842\times10^{-4})\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$).
  • Frequency: $\dfrac{5.788\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV}}{4.135\,668\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{eV\,s}}=1.3996\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{Hz}=13.996\ \mathrm{GHz}$.
  • Temperature: $\dfrac{9.274\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{J}}{1.380\,649\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J/K}}=0.6717\ \mathrm{K}$.

For the electron spin ($g_s=2.0023$), the values are $g_s$ times these (about twice as large): $115.9\ \mu\mathrm{eV}$, $0.9348\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, $28.02\ \mathrm{GHz}$, and $1.345\ \mathrm{K}$. We see that even in a magnetic field of $1\ \mathrm{T}$, the Zeeman splitting energy is more than two orders of magnitude smaller than the thermal energy at room temperature ($k_{\mathrm B}T=25.9\ \mathrm{meV}$, at about $300\ \mathrm{K}$).

Exercise 23.5: Saturation magnetization of iron

Solution

(1) Since the unit cell (a cube of volume $a^3$) contains two atoms, and $a=2.866\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$,

$$ n=\frac{2}{a^3}=\frac{2}{(2.866\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m})^3}=\frac{2}{2.354\times10^{-29}\ \mathrm{m^3}}=8.50\times10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}} $$

(2) The magnetic moment of one atom is $\mu=2.22\,\mu_{\mathrm{B}}=2.22\times9.274\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{J/T}=2.059\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{A\,m^2}$, so

$$ M_{\mathrm s}=n\mu=(8.496\times10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}})(2.059\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{A\,m^2})=1.75\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{A/m} $$

(3) $\mu_0M_{\mathrm s}=(1.2566\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{N/A^2})(1.749\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{A/m})=2.20\ \mathrm{T}$. This agrees well with the measured value of the saturation magnetic flux density of iron (about $2.2\ \mathrm{T}$). It is one manifestation of the fact that almost all of the magnetic moment originates from the spin.

Exercise 23.6: Projection operators for spin

Solution

(1) $P_\uparrow=\tfrac12(E+\sigma_z)=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$ and $P_\downarrow=\tfrac12(E-\sigma_z)=\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$. Using $\sigma_z^2=E$,

$$ P_\uparrow^2=\frac14\bigl(E+2\sigma_z+\sigma_z^2\bigr)=\frac14\bigl(2E+2\sigma_z\bigr)=P_\uparrow,\qquad P_\downarrow^2=\frac14\bigl(E-2\sigma_z+\sigma_z^2\bigr)=P_\downarrow $$ $$ P_\uparrow+P_\downarrow=\frac12(E+\sigma_z)+\frac12(E-\sigma_z)=E,\qquad P_\uparrow P_\downarrow=\frac14\bigl(E-\sigma_z^2\bigr)=\frac14(E-E)=0 $$

(2) Computing with matrices, $P_\uparrow\alpha=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}=\alpha$, $P_\uparrow\beta=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\end{bmatrix}=0$, $P_\downarrow\alpha=0$, and $P_\downarrow\beta=\beta$. That is, $P_\uparrow$ picks out only the $\alpha$ component (eliminating the $\beta$ component), and $P_\downarrow$ picks out only the $\beta$ component.

(3) $\gamma^\dagger P_\uparrow\gamma=\begin{bmatrix}C_\alpha^*&C_\beta^*\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}C_\alpha\\C_\beta\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}C_\alpha^*&C_\beta^*\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}C_\alpha\\0\end{bmatrix}=\abs{C_\alpha}^2$. This is the probability that the spin of the electron is up in the state $\gamma$. Similarly, $\gamma^\dagger P_\downarrow\gamma=\abs{C_\beta}^2$ is the probability that it is down, and from $P_\uparrow+P_\downarrow=E$ the sum of the two is $\gamma^\dagger\gamma=1$.

Exercise 23.7: Normalization and probabilities of a spin orbital

Solution

(1) $\abs{\psi_+}^2=\abs{1+i}^2f^2=2A^2e^{-2r/a_0}$ and $\abs{\psi_-}^2=A^2e^{-2r/a_0}$. The angular integral is $4\pi$ and the radial integral is $\int_0^\infty r^2e^{-2r/a_0}\dd r=\dfrac{a_0^3}{4}$, so

$$ \int\abs{\psi_+}^2\dd V=2A^2\cdot4\pi\cdot\frac{a_0^3}{4}=2\pi a_0^3A^2,\qquad \int\abs{\psi_-}^2\dd V=A^2\cdot4\pi\cdot\frac{a_0^3}{4}=\pi a_0^3A^2 $$

From the normalization $2\pi a_0^3A^2+\pi a_0^3A^2=3\pi a_0^3A^2=1$, we obtain $A=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3\pi a_0^3}}$.

(2) $P(\uparrow)=\int\abs{\psi_+}^2\dd V=2\pi a_0^3A^2=\dfrac23$ ($P(\downarrow)=\dfrac13$).

(3) $\expval{\hat{S}_z}=\dfrac\hbar2\bigl[P(\uparrow)-P(\downarrow)\bigr]=\dfrac\hbar2\left(\dfrac23-\dfrac13\right)=\dfrac\hbar6$.

(Supplement: since $\psi_+/\psi_-=1+i$ is a constant independent of $r$, this wave function has the product form $\phi_{1s}(r)\,\dfrac{(1+i)\alpha+\beta}{\sqrt3}$, that is, it is a state in which the orientation of the spin does not depend on position.)

Exercise 23.8: ESR at Q band

Solution

The resonance condition is $h\nu=g\mu_{\mathrm{B}}B_{\mathrm{res}}$, that is, $B_{\mathrm{res}}=\dfrac{h\nu}{g\mu_{\mathrm{B}}}=\dfrac{\nu}{g\,(\mu_{\mathrm{B}}/h)}$. We use $\mu_{\mathrm{B}}/h=13.996\ \mathrm{GHz/T}$.

(1) For $g_s=2.0023$, $g_s\mu_{\mathrm{B}}/h=2.0023\times13.996\ \mathrm{GHz/T}=28.025\ \mathrm{GHz/T}$, so

$$ B_{\mathrm{res}}=\frac{34\ \mathrm{GHz}}{28.025\ \mathrm{GHz/T}}=1.213\ \mathrm{T} $$

Compared with the X-band value of $0.339\ \mathrm{T}$, this is $1.213/0.339=3.58$ times larger, which agrees with the frequency ratio $34/9.5=3.58$ (the resonance field is proportional to the frequency).

(2) For $g=2.10$, $g\mu_{\mathrm{B}}/h=2.10\times13.996=29.392\ \mathrm{GHz/T}$, and

$$ B_{\mathrm{res}}=\frac{34}{29.392}\ \mathrm{T}=1.157\ \mathrm{T} $$

The shift from the free-electron value is $1.157-1.213=-0.056\ \mathrm{T}$ (the larger $g$ is, the lower the field at which resonance occurs). A shift of $0.056\ \mathrm{T}=56\ \mathrm{mT}$ is large enough to be measured, and from the shift of the $g$ value we can learn about the environment around the electron (the contribution of the orbital angular momentum).

(3) The photon energy is $h\nu=(4.1357\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{eV\,s})(34\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}})=1.406\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV}=140.6\ \mu\mathrm{eV}$, and this equals the spin level splitting $g_s\mu_{\mathrm{B}}B_{\mathrm{res}}$. The NMR frequency of the proton is $\nu_{\mathrm{p}}=(42.577\ \mathrm{MHz/T})(1.213\ \mathrm{T})=51.65\ \mathrm{MHz}$.

← Back to Chapter 23, “Spin — The Electron's Other Angular Momentum”

Chapter 24: Ladder Operators and the Matrix Representation of Angular Momentum

Exercise 24.1: $\hat{J}_-\hat{J}_+$ and the coefficients of the ladder operators

Solution

(1) Expand the product, keeping the order of the factors.

$$ \hat{J}_-\hat{J}_+=\bigl(\hat{J}_x-i\hat{J}_y\bigr)\bigl(\hat{J}_x+i\hat{J}_y\bigr)=\hat{J}_x^2+i\hat{J}_x\hat{J}_y-i\hat{J}_y\hat{J}_x+\hat{J}_y^2=\hat{J}_x^2+\hat{J}_y^2+i\comm{\hat{J}_x}{\hat{J}_y} $$

Substituting $\comm{\hat{J}_x}{\hat{J}_y}=i\hbar\hat{J}_z$ gives $i\cdot i\hbar\hat{J}_z=-\hbar\hat{J}_z$, so $\hat{J}_-\hat{J}_+=\hat{J}_x^2+\hat{J}_y^2-\hbar\hat{J}_z$. Furthermore, since $\hat{J}_x^2+\hat{J}_y^2=\hat{J}^2-\hat{J}_z^2$,

$$ \hat{J}_-\hat{J}_+=\hat{J}^2-\hat{J}_z^2-\hbar\hat{J}_z $$

(2) Since $\hat{J}_+^\dagger=\hat{J}_-$, the square of the norm is

$$ \norm{\hat{J}_+\ket{j,m}}^2=\bra{j,m}\hat{J}_+^\dagger\hat{J}_+\ket{j,m}=\bra{j,m}\hat{J}_-\hat{J}_+\ket{j,m}=\bra{j,m}\bigl(\hat{J}^2-\hat{J}_z^2-\hbar\hat{J}_z\bigr)\ket{j,m} $$

Here $\ket{j,m}$ is an eigenstate of $\hat{J}^2$ and $\hat{J}_z$ (with eigenvalues $j(j+1)\hbar^2$ and $m\hbar$) and $\braket{j,m}{j,m}=1$, so the right-hand side is $\bigl[j(j+1)-m^2-m\bigr]\hbar^2=\bigl[j(j+1)-m(m+1)\bigr]\hbar^2=(j-m)(j+m+1)\hbar^2$ (since $j^2+j-m^2-m=(j-m)(j+m+1)$). The state $\hat{J}_+\ket{j,m}$ has the $\hat{J}_z$ eigenvalue $(m+1)\hbar$, that is, it is proportional to $\ket{j,m+1}$, so if we choose the phase of the coefficient to be a “positive real number,” we obtain

$$ \hat{J}_+\ket{j,m}=\hbar\sqrt{j(j+1)-m(m+1)}\,\ket{j,m+1} $$

Similarly, from $\hat{J}_+\hat{J}_-=\hat{J}^2-\hat{J}_z^2+\hbar\hat{J}_z$ we get $\norm{\hat{J}_-\ket{j,m}}^2=\hbar^2\bigl[j(j+1)-m(m-1)\bigr]$, and hence $\hat{J}_-\ket{j,m}=\hbar\sqrt{j(j+1)-m(m-1)}\,\ket{j,m-1}$.

(3) For $j=\tfrac12$ and $m=-\tfrac12$ we have $j(j+1)=\tfrac34$ and $m(m+1)=\bigl(-\tfrac12\bigr)\cdot\tfrac12=-\tfrac14$. Hence $\tfrac34+\tfrac14=1$, and the coefficient is $\hbar\sqrt1=\hbar$: $\hat{J}_+\ket{\tfrac12,-\tfrac12}=\hbar\ket{\tfrac12,\tfrac12}$, that is, $\hat{S}_+\beta=\hbar\alpha$. Also, for $m=\tfrac12$ we have $\tfrac34-\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac32=0$, so $\hat{S}_+\alpha=0$ (the top rung of the ladder).

Exercise 24.2: Eigenvectors of $\hat{J}_y$ for $j=1$ and measurement probabilities

Solution

$\hat{J}_y=\dfrac{\hbar}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}0&-i&0\\i&0&-i\\0&i&0\end{pmatrix}$. (1) Let $b=\dfrac{i\hbar}{\sqrt2}$. Then $\lambda E-\hat{J}_y=\begin{pmatrix}\lambda&b&0\\-b&\lambda&b\\0&-b&\lambda\end{pmatrix}$ (a tridiagonal matrix, with nonzero elements only on the diagonal and on the diagonals immediately next to it). Expanding along the first row, we obtain $$ \det\bigl(\lambda E-\hat{J}_y\bigr)=\lambda\begin{vmatrix}\lambda&b\\-b&\lambda\end{vmatrix}-b\begin{vmatrix}-b&b\\0&\lambda\end{vmatrix}=\lambda\bigl(\lambda^2+b^2\bigr)-b\bigl(-b\lambda\bigr)=\lambda^3+2b^2\lambda $$ Since $b^2=-\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2}$ (the product of adjacent elements $\Bigl(\dfrac{i\hbar}{\sqrt2}\Bigr)\Bigl(-\dfrac{i\hbar}{\sqrt2}\Bigr)=\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2}$ occurs in two places), we have $\lambda^3-\hbar^2\lambda=\lambda\bigl(\lambda^2-\hbar^2\bigr)=0$. The eigenvalues are $\lambda=0,\pm\hbar$.

(2) With $v=(v_1,v_2,v_3)^{\mathsf T}$, the three equations of $\hat{J}_yv=\lambda v$ are $-\dfrac{i}{\sqrt2}v_2=\dfrac{\lambda}{\hbar}v_1$, $\dfrac{i}{\sqrt2}(v_1-v_3)=\dfrac\lambda\hbar v_2$, and $\dfrac{i}{\sqrt2}v_2=\dfrac\lambda\hbar v_3$.

$\lambda=\hbar$: the first equation gives $v_2=i\sqrt2\,v_1$ ($1/(-i)=i$), and the third gives $v_3=\dfrac{i}{\sqrt2}v_2=\dfrac{i}{\sqrt2}\cdot i\sqrt2\,v_1=-v_1$. Letting $v_1=t$, we have $(t,i\sqrt2\,t,-t)$, and $\abs{v}^2=t^2(1+2+1)=1$ gives $t=\tfrac12$. Thus $v_+=\bigl(\tfrac12,\ \tfrac{i}{\sqrt2},\ -\tfrac12\bigr)^{\mathsf T}$.

$\lambda=0$: the first and third equations give $v_2=0$, and the second gives $v_3=v_1$. Thus $v_0=\bigl(\tfrac1{\sqrt2},\ 0,\ \tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigr)^{\mathsf T}$.

$\lambda=-\hbar$: the first equation gives $v_2=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{i}v_1=-i\sqrt2\,v_1$, and the third gives $v_3=-\dfrac{i}{\sqrt2}v_2=-\dfrac{i}{\sqrt2}\cdot(-i\sqrt2)\,v_1=-v_1$. Thus $v_-=\bigl(\tfrac12,\ -\tfrac{i}{\sqrt2},\ -\tfrac12\bigr)^{\mathsf T}$.

(3) The magnitudes of the inner products with $\ket{1,1}=(1,0,0)^{\mathsf T}$ are $\abs{v_{+,1}}=\tfrac12$, $\abs{v_{0,1}}=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}$, and $\abs{v_{-,1}}=\tfrac12$, so the probabilities are $+\hbar$: $\tfrac14$, $0$: $\tfrac12$, $-\hbar$: $\tfrac14$ (the sum is $1$). The expectation values are $\expval{\hat{J}_y}=\hbar\bigl(\tfrac14-\tfrac14\bigr)=0$ and $\expval{\hat{J}_y^2}=\hbar^2\bigl(\tfrac14+\tfrac14\bigr)=\tfrac12\hbar^2$ (in agreement with $[j(j+1)-m^2]\hbar^2/2=\tfrac12\hbar^2$). These are the same as the results for $\hat{L}_y$ ($l=1$) in the main text.

Exercise 24.3: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $\hat{J}_x$ for $j=\tfrac32$

Solution

Expand the determinant of $\lambda E-M=\begin{pmatrix}\lambda&-\sqrt3&0&0\\-\sqrt3&\lambda&-2&0\\0&-2&\lambda&-\sqrt3\\0&0&-\sqrt3&\lambda\end{pmatrix}$ along the first row (this is a tridiagonal matrix, with nonzero elements only on the diagonal and on the diagonals immediately next to it, so the first row has two elements that are not $0$):

$$ \det(\lambda E-M)=\lambda\begin{vmatrix}\lambda&-2&0\\-2&\lambda&-\sqrt3\\0&-\sqrt3&\lambda\end{vmatrix}+(-1)^{1+2}\bigl(-\sqrt3\bigr)\begin{vmatrix}-\sqrt3&-2&0\\0&\lambda&-\sqrt3\\0&-\sqrt3&\lambda\end{vmatrix} $$

The first $3\times3$ determinant, expanded along the first row, is $\lambda(\lambda^2-3)-(-2)(-2\lambda)=\lambda^3-7\lambda$ ($7=3+4$, the sum of the products of adjacent elements), and the other, expanded along the first column, is $-\sqrt3(\lambda^2-3)$. Therefore

$$ \det(\lambda E-M)=\lambda\bigl(\lambda^3-7\lambda\bigr)-3\bigl(\lambda^2-3\bigr)=\lambda^4-10\lambda^2+9=(\lambda^2-1)(\lambda^2-9) $$

so that $\lambda=\pm1,\pm3$, and the eigenvalues of $\hat{J}_x=\tfrac\hbar2M$ are $\pm\tfrac32\hbar,\ \pm\tfrac12\hbar$.

The eigenvector $v=(v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4)^{\mathsf T}$ is determined from $Mv=\lambda v$, that is, from $\sqrt3\,v_2=\lambda v_1$, $\sqrt3\,v_1+2v_3=\lambda v_2$, $2v_2+\sqrt3\,v_4=\lambda v_3$, and $\sqrt3\,v_3=\lambda v_4$.

$\lambda=3$: let $v_1=1$. The first equation gives $v_2=\sqrt3$, the second gives $2v_3=3\sqrt3-\sqrt3=2\sqrt3$, so $v_3=\sqrt3$, and the fourth gives $v_4=\sqrt3\cdot\sqrt3/3=1$. We have $(1,\sqrt3,\sqrt3,1)$, whose squared length is $1+3+3+1=8$, so $v_{3/2}=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}\bigl(1,\sqrt3,\sqrt3,1\bigr)^{\mathsf T}$.

$\lambda=1$: let $v_1=\sqrt3$. Then $v_2=\dfrac{1\cdot v_1}{\sqrt3}=1$, the second equation gives $3+2v_3=1$, so $v_3=-1$, and the fourth gives $v_4=\sqrt3\,v_3=-\sqrt3$. The squared length is $3+1+1+3=8$: $v_{1/2}=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}\bigl(\sqrt3,1,-1,-\sqrt3\bigr)^{\mathsf T}$.

$\lambda=-1$: $v_1=\sqrt3$ and $v_2=-1$; the second equation gives $3+2v_3=(-1)(-1)=1$, so $v_3=-1$; the fourth gives $\sqrt3\,v_3=-v_4$, so $v_4=\sqrt3$: $v_{-1/2}=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}\bigl(\sqrt3,-1,-1,\sqrt3\bigr)^{\mathsf T}$.

$\lambda=-3$: $v_1=1$ and $v_2=-\sqrt3$; the second equation gives $\sqrt3+2v_3=(-3)(-\sqrt3)=3\sqrt3$, so $v_3=\sqrt3$; the fourth gives $\sqrt3\cdot\sqrt3=-3v_4$, so $v_4=-1$: $v_{-3/2}=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}\bigl(1,-\sqrt3,\sqrt3,-1\bigr)^{\mathsf T}$.

These are mutually orthogonal (for example, $v_{3/2}\cdot v_{1/2}\propto\sqrt3+\sqrt3-\sqrt3-\sqrt3=0$). The probabilities of the outcomes of a measurement of $\hat{J}_x$ on $\ket{\tfrac32,\tfrac32}=(1,0,0,0)^{\mathsf T}$ are the squares of the first components: $+\tfrac32\hbar$: $\dfrac{1}{8}$, $+\tfrac12\hbar$: $\dfrac{3}{8}$, $-\tfrac12\hbar$: $\dfrac{3}{8}$, $-\tfrac32\hbar$: $\dfrac{1}{8}$ (the binomial distribution $\binom3k/2^3$). Check: $\expval{\hat{J}_x^2}=\hbar^2\Bigl(\dfrac18\cdot\dfrac94+\dfrac38\cdot\dfrac14+\dfrac38\cdot\dfrac14+\dfrac18\cdot\dfrac94\Bigr)=\dfrac34\hbar^2$, which agrees with $[j(j+1)-m^2]\hbar^2/2=\bigl(\tfrac{15}{4}-\tfrac94\bigr)\hbar^2/2=\tfrac34\hbar^2$.

Exercise 24.4: Eigenvalues of $\bm{n}\cdot\bm{\sigma}$ and the eigenvectors for $\bm{n}=(1,1,0)/\sqrt2$

Solution

(1) Squaring $\bm{n}\cdot\bm{\sigma}=n_x\sigma_x+n_y\sigma_y+n_z\sigma_z$ and using $\sigma_i^2=E$ and $\sigma_i\sigma_j+\sigma_j\sigma_i=0$ ($i\ne j$; for example, $\sigma_x\sigma_y=i\sigma_z$ and $\sigma_y\sigma_x=-i\sigma_z$), we get

$$ (\bm{n}\cdot\bm{\sigma})^2=\sum_in_i^2\sigma_i^2+\sum_{i\lt j}n_in_j\bigl(\sigma_i\sigma_j+\sigma_j\sigma_i\bigr)=\bigl(n_x^2+n_y^2+n_z^2\bigr)E=E $$

Multiplying the eigenvalue equation $(\bm{n}\cdot\bm{\sigma})\psi=\lambda\psi$ once more by $\bm{n}\cdot\bm{\sigma}$ gives $\psi=(\bm{n}\cdot\bm{\sigma})^2\psi=\lambda^2\psi$. Since $\psi\ne\bm{0}$, $\lambda^2=1$, and hence $\lambda=\pm1$.

(2) For $\bm{n}=(1,1,0)/\sqrt2$, $\bm{n}\cdot\bm{\sigma}=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{\sqrt2}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}0&1-i\\1+i&0\end{pmatrix}$. For $\lambda=+1$, the first row for the eigenvector $(a,b)^{\mathsf T}$ reads $-a+\dfrac{1-i}{\sqrt2}b=0$, so $b=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{1-i}a=\dfrac{\sqrt2(1+i)}{2}a=\dfrac{1+i}{\sqrt2}a=e^{i\pi/4}a$. Since $\abs{e^{i\pi/4}}=1$, normalizing gives $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\(1+i)/\sqrt2\end{pmatrix}$. This agrees with the formula in the theorem (for $\theta=\tfrac\pi2$ and $\varphi=\tfrac\pi4$, $(\cos\tfrac\theta2,e^{i\varphi}\sin\tfrac\theta2)=(1,e^{i\pi/4})/\sqrt2$). For $\lambda=-1$: the first row $a+\dfrac{1-i}{\sqrt2}b=0$ gives $b=-e^{i\pi/4}a$: $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix}$.

(3) For $\psi=(1,e^{i\varphi})^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2$ with $\varphi=\tfrac\pi4$, the formulas $\expval{\sigma_x}=\cos\varphi$, $\expval{\sigma_y}=\sin\varphi$, $\expval{\sigma_z}=0$ in the main text (Section 24.7.4) give $\expval{\sigma_x}=\expval{\sigma_y}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$ and $\expval{\sigma_z}=0$. Therefore $\expval{\hat{S}_x}=\expval{\hat{S}_y}=\dfrac{\hbar}{2\sqrt2}$ and $\expval{\hat{S}_z}=0$. The spin direction agrees: $(\expval{\sigma_x},\expval{\sigma_y},\expval{\sigma_z})=\bm{n}$.

Exercise 24.5: $\hat{L}_x^2+\hat{L}_y^2$ and the uncertainty in $\ket{l,m}$

Solution

(1) Taking the expectation value of $\hat{L}_x^2+\hat{L}_y^2=\hat{L}^2-\hat{L}_z^2$ in $\ket{l,m}$, we have $\hat{L}^2\to l(l+1)\hbar^2$ and $\hat{L}_z^2\to m^2\hbar^2$, so $\expval{\hat{L}_x^2+\hat{L}_y^2}=[l(l+1)-m^2]\hbar^2$.

(2) The operator $\hat{L}_x=\tfrac12(\hat{L}_++\hat{L}_-)$ shifts $m$ by $\pm1$, so $\expval{\hat{L}_x}=0$, and similarly $\expval{\hat{L}_y}=0$. Also, $\hat{L}_x^2-\hat{L}_y^2=\tfrac12(\hat{L}_+^2+\hat{L}_-^2)$ shifts $m$ by $\pm2$, so its expectation value is $0$ and $\expval{\hat{L}_x^2}=\expval{\hat{L}_y^2}=\tfrac12[l(l+1)-m^2]\hbar^2$. Therefore $\Delta L_x=\Delta L_y=\hbar\sqrt{[l(l+1)-m^2]/2}$, and the product is $\Delta L_x\,\Delta L_y=\tfrac12[l(l+1)-m^2]\hbar^2$. The lower bound of the Robertson inequality is $\tfrac12\abs{\expval{\comm{\hat{L}_x}{\hat{L}_y}}}=\tfrac12\hbar\abs{\expval{\hat{L}_z}}=\tfrac12\abs{m}\hbar^2$. Taking the difference, we get

$$ \Delta L_x\,\Delta L_y-\frac12\abs{m}\hbar^2=\frac{\hbar^2}{2}\bigl[l(l+1)-m^2-\abs{m}\bigr]=\frac{\hbar^2}{2}\bigl(l-\abs{m}\bigr)\bigl(l+\abs{m}+1\bigr) $$

(since $l(l+1)-\abs{m}(\abs{m}+1)=(l-\abs{m})(l+\abs{m}+1)$). Since $\abs{m}\le l$, we have $l-\abs{m}\ge0$ and $l+\abs{m}+1>0$, so the difference is at least $0$, and it equals $0$ only when $l-\abs{m}=0$, that is, only when $\abs{m}=l$.

(3) For $l=2$ ($l(l+1)=6$): $\Delta L_x\Delta L_y=\tfrac12(6-m^2)\hbar^2$. For $m=0$ this is $3\hbar^2$, for $m=\pm1$ it is $\tfrac52\hbar^2$, and for $m=\pm2$ it is $\hbar^2$. The lower bound $\tfrac12\abs{m}\hbar^2$ is $0,\ \tfrac12\hbar^2,\ \hbar^2$, respectively, and equality holds only for $m=\pm2$.

Exercise 24.6: Unitary transformations and commutation relations

Solution

(1) Inserting $U^\dagger U=E$ between the factors, we have

$$ \comm{U^\dagger AU}{U^\dagger BU}=U^\dagger AU\,U^\dagger BU-U^\dagger BU\,U^\dagger AU=U^\dagger ABU-U^\dagger BAU=U^\dagger\comm{A}{B}U $$

Multiplying both sides of $\comm{\hat{J}_x}{\hat{J}_y}=i\hbar\hat{J}_z$ by $U^\dagger$ from the left and by $U$ from the right gives $\comm{\hat{J}_x'}{\hat{J}_y'}=U^\dagger(i\hbar\hat{J}_z)U=i\hbar\hat{J}_z'$. The other two equations follow similarly. Also, $\bigl(U^\dagger\hat{J}_iU\bigr)^\dagger=U^\dagger\hat{J}_i^\dagger U=U^\dagger\hat{J}_iU$, so Hermiticity is preserved as well.

(2) The matrix $U=\dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_z}{\sqrt2}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ is both Hermitian and unitary ($U^2=E$), and $U^\dagger=U$. Using the anticommutation relation of the Pauli matrices, $\sigma_i\sigma_j+\sigma_j\sigma_i=2\delta_{ij}E$, we get $U^2=\tfrac12\bigl(\sigma_x^2+\sigma_z^2+\sigma_x\sigma_z+\sigma_z\sigma_x\bigr)=E$. Since $\sigma_y$ anticommutes with both $\sigma_x$ and $\sigma_z$, we have $\sigma_yU=-U\sigma_y$, and $U\sigma_yU=-U^2\sigma_y=-\sigma_y$. Next, $U\sigma_xU=\tfrac12(\sigma_x+\sigma_z)\sigma_x(\sigma_x+\sigma_z)=\tfrac12\bigl(E+\sigma_z\sigma_x\bigr)(\sigma_x+\sigma_z)=\tfrac12\bigl(\sigma_x+\sigma_z+\sigma_z+\sigma_z\sigma_x\sigma_z\bigr)$, and since $\sigma_z\sigma_x\sigma_z=-\sigma_x\sigma_z\sigma_z=-\sigma_x$, this continues as $=\tfrac12\bigl(2\sigma_z\bigr)=\sigma_z$. Similarly, $U\sigma_zU=\sigma_x$. Hence $(\hat{S}_x',\hat{S}_y',\hat{S}_z')=\tfrac\hbar2(\sigma_z,-\sigma_y,\sigma_x)=(\hat{S}_z,-\hat{S}_y,\hat{S}_x)$. For example, $\comm{\hat{S}_x'}{\hat{S}_y'}=\comm{\hat{S}_z}{-\hat{S}_y}=\comm{\hat{S}_y}{\hat{S}_z}=i\hbar\hat{S}_x=i\hbar\hat{S}_z'$, which agrees with the result of (1).

(3) The eigenvectors $\eta_{\pm x}=(1,\pm1)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2$ of the original $\hat{S}_x$ are represented in the new representation by $U^\dagger\eta_{\pm x}=U\eta_{\pm x}$. We have $U\eta_{+x}=\dfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}$ and $U\eta_{-x}=\dfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}$. On the other hand, the eigenvectors of $\hat{S}_x'=\hat{S}_z=\tfrac\hbar2\mathrm{diag}(1,-1)$ in the new representation are $(1,0)^{\mathsf T}$ (eigenvalue $+\tfrac\hbar2$) and $(0,1)^{\mathsf T}$ ($-\tfrac\hbar2$), which agree with $U\eta_{\pm x}$. The same physical state is expressed in a simple form in the new basis (in which $\hat{S}_x'$ is diagonal).

Exercise 24.7: The $4\pi$ periodicity of $\hat{R}_z(\Theta)$ and the neutron interferometer

Solution

(1) Since $\sigma_z$ is a diagonal matrix, its exponential can also be computed element by element along the diagonal:

$$ \hat{R}_z(\Theta)=\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{i\Theta}{2}\sigma_z\Bigr)=\begin{pmatrix}e^{-i\Theta/2}&0\\0&e^{i\Theta/2}\end{pmatrix} $$

For $\Theta=2\pi$: $e^{-i\pi}=-1$ and $e^{i\pi}=-1$, so $\hat{R}_z(2\pi)=-E$. For $\Theta=4\pi$: $e^{\mp2\pi i}=1$, so $\hat{R}_z(4\pi)=E$.

(2) The neutron splits into two paths, and the intensity is $\tfrac12$ in each path. If only the spin in one path is rotated by $\hat{R}_z(\Theta)$, the (normalized) amplitude of the recombined wave is $\tfrac12\bigl(\ket{\psi}+\hat{R}_z\ket{\psi}\bigr)$, and, letting $I_0$ be the intensity at $\Theta=0$,

$$ \frac{I}{I_0}=\frac14\norm{\ket{\psi}+\hat{R}_z\ket{\psi}}^2=\frac14\Bigl(\braket{\psi}{\psi}+\bra{\psi}\hat{R}_z^\dagger\hat{R}_z\ket{\psi}+2\Real\bra{\psi}\hat{R}_z\ket{\psi}\Bigr)=\frac14\bigl(2+2\Real\bra{\psi}\hat{R}_z\ket{\psi}\bigr) $$

(Here $\hat{R}_z$ is unitary, so $\norm{\hat{R}_z\ket{\psi}}=1$.) Letting $\ket{\psi}=(a,b)^{\mathsf T}$ ($\abs{a}^2+\abs{b}^2=1$), we obtain

$$ \bra{\psi}\hat{R}_z\ket{\psi}=\abs{a}^2e^{-i\Theta/2}+\abs{b}^2e^{i\Theta/2}=\cos\frac\Theta2-i\bigl(\abs{a}^2-\abs{b}^2\bigr)\sin\frac\Theta2 $$

and the real part is $\cos\dfrac\Theta2$ (it does not depend on the direction of the neutron spin). Hence

$$ \frac{I}{I_0}=\frac12\Bigl(1+\cos\frac\Theta2\Bigr)=\cos^2\frac\Theta4 $$

(half-angle formula $1+\cos2x=2\cos^2x$).

(3) Values of $\cos^2(\Theta/4)$ and $\cos^2(\Theta/2)$:

$\Theta$$90^\circ$$180^\circ$$360^\circ$$540^\circ$$720^\circ$
$\cos^2(\Theta/4)$$0.854$$0.500$$0$$0.500$$1$
$\cos^2(\Theta/2)$$0.500$$0$$1$$0$$1$

($\cos^2 22.5^\circ=(1+\cos45^\circ)/2=0.854$, $\cos^2135^\circ=0.500$.) If the spin returned to its original state after a rotation by $2\pi$, like an ordinary vector, the interference would return to its maximum value $1$ at $\Theta=360^\circ$ (as $\cos^2(\Theta/2)$, with period $2\pi$, does), but in fact it is $0$, and it returns to $1$ only at $720^\circ$. This is the result, observed through interference, of $\hat{R}_z(2\pi)=-E$ (the sign reversal of the state vector).

← Back to Chapter 24, “Ladder Operators and the Matrix Representation of Angular Momentum”

Chapter 25: Addition of Angular Momenta and the Eigenvalue Problem of $\hat{\bm{L}}\cdot\hat{\bm{S}}$

Exercise 25.1: Commutation relations of $\hat{\bm{L}}\cdot\hat{\bm{S}}$ ($x$ component)

Solution

(1) Since $\hat{\bm{J}}=\hat{\bm{L}}+\hat{\bm{S}}$, we have $[\hat{\bm{L}}\cdot\hat{\bm{S}},\hat{J}_x]=[\hat{\bm{L}}\cdot\hat{\bm{S}},\hat{L}_x]+[\hat{\bm{L}}\cdot\hat{\bm{S}},\hat{S}_x]$. Since $\hat{\bm{L}}\cdot\hat{\bm{S}}=\sum_i\hat{L}_i\hat{S}_i$ and $\hat{S}_i$ commutes with $\hat{L}_x$,

$$ [\hat{\bm{L}}\cdot\hat{\bm{S}},\hat{L}_x]=\sum_i\hat{S}_i\,[\hat{L}_i,\hat{L}_x]=\hat{S}_x\cdot0+\hat{S}_y\,[\hat{L}_y,\hat{L}_x]+\hat{S}_z\,[\hat{L}_z,\hat{L}_x] =\hat{S}_y\,(-i\hbar\hat{L}_z)+\hat{S}_z\,(i\hbar\hat{L}_y)=i\hbar\,(\hat{L}_y\hat{S}_z-\hat{L}_z\hat{S}_y). $$

Similarly, since $\hat{L}_i$ commutes with $\hat{S}_x$,

$$ [\hat{\bm{L}}\cdot\hat{\bm{S}},\hat{S}_x]=\sum_i\hat{L}_i\,[\hat{S}_i,\hat{S}_x]=\hat{L}_y\,[\hat{S}_y,\hat{S}_x]+\hat{L}_z\,[\hat{S}_z,\hat{S}_x]=\hat{L}_y\,(-i\hbar\hat{S}_z)+\hat{L}_z\,(i\hbar\hat{S}_y)=-i\hbar\,(\hat{L}_y\hat{S}_z-\hat{L}_z\hat{S}_y). $$

The sum of the two equations is $0$: $[\hat{\bm{L}}\cdot\hat{\bm{S}},\hat{J}_x]=0$. (The $y$ component is likewise $0$, by cyclically permuting the indices.)

(2) From $\hat{J}^2=\hat{L}^2+2\hat{\bm{L}}\cdot\hat{\bm{S}}+\hat{S}^2$ we have $[\hat{J}^2,\hat{L}_z]=[\hat{L}^2,\hat{L}_z]+2[\hat{\bm{L}}\cdot\hat{\bm{S}},\hat{L}_z]+[\hat{S}^2,\hat{L}_z]$. Here $[\hat{L}^2,\hat{L}_z]=0$, and since $\hat{S}^2$ commutes with $\hat{L}_z$, $[\hat{S}^2,\hat{L}_z]=0$. Therefore

$$ [\hat{J}^2,\hat{L}_z]=2[\hat{\bm{L}}\cdot\hat{\bm{S}},\hat{L}_z]=2i\hbar\,(\hat{L}_x\hat{S}_y-\hat{L}_y\hat{S}_x) $$

(here $[\hat{\bm{L}}\cdot\hat{\bm{S}},\hat{L}_z]=\hat{S}_x[\hat{L}_x,\hat{L}_z]+\hat{S}_y[\hat{L}_y,\hat{L}_z]=i\hbar(\hat{L}_x\hat{S}_y-\hat{L}_y\hat{S}_x)$). This operator is not $0$. For example, acting on $R\,Y_1^{0}\alpha$, we find from the result of the example in Section 25.4 that $[\hat{J}^2,\hat{L}_z]\,R\,Y_1^{0}\alpha=-\sqrt2\,\hbar^3\,R\,Y_1^{1}\beta\ne0$. Therefore $\hat{J}^2$ and $\hat{L}_z$ do not commute, and an eigenstate of $\hat{J}^2$ is, in general, not an eigenstate of $\hat{L}_z$ ($m$).

Exercise 25.2: The block for the f orbitals ($m_j=\tfrac32$)

Solution

Take as the basis $\phi_1=R\,Y_3^{1}\alpha$ ($m=1$) and $\phi_2=R\,Y_3^{2}\beta$ ($m=2$). We use the formulas $(\hat{\bm{L}}\cdot\hat{\bm{S}})R\,Y_l^m\alpha=\tfrac{\hbar^2}{2}\sqrt{(l-m)(l+m+1)}\,R\,Y_l^{m+1}\beta+\tfrac{m\hbar^2}{2}R\,Y_l^m\alpha$ and $(\hat{\bm{L}}\cdot\hat{\bm{S}})R\,Y_l^m\beta=\tfrac{\hbar^2}{2}\sqrt{(l+m)(l-m+1)}\,R\,Y_l^{m-1}\alpha-\tfrac{m\hbar^2}{2}R\,Y_l^m\beta$ with $l=3$.

$$ (\hat{\bm{L}}\cdot\hat{\bm{S}})\phi_1=\tfrac{\hbar^2}{2}\sqrt{(3-1)(3+1+1)}\,\phi_2+\tfrac{1\cdot\hbar^2}{2}\phi_1=\tfrac{\sqrt{10}}{2}\hbar^2\phi_2+\tfrac12\hbar^2\phi_1, $$ $$ (\hat{\bm{L}}\cdot\hat{\bm{S}})\phi_2=\tfrac{\hbar^2}{2}\sqrt{(3+2)(3-2+1)}\,\phi_1-\tfrac{2\hbar^2}{2}\phi_2=\tfrac{\sqrt{10}}{2}\hbar^2\phi_1-\hbar^2\phi_2 . $$

The matrix of the block is $\hbar^2\begin{bmatrix}\frac12&\frac{\sqrt{10}}{2}\\ \frac{\sqrt{10}}{2}&-1\end{bmatrix}$. From the trace $-\tfrac12$ and the determinant $-\tfrac12-\tfrac{10}{4}=-3$, the characteristic equation is $\lambda^2+\tfrac12\lambda-3=0$, that is, $(\lambda-\tfrac32)(\lambda+2)=0$, and the eigenvalues are $\lambda=\tfrac32\hbar^2$ and $-2\hbar^2$ (in units of $\hbar^2$: $\tfrac32,-2$).

Eigenvector $(a,b)$: the first row reads $(\tfrac12-\lambda)a+\tfrac{\sqrt{10}}{2}b=0$. For $\lambda=\tfrac32$ this is $-a+\tfrac{\sqrt{10}}{2}b=0$, so $b=\tfrac{2}{\sqrt{10}}a=\sqrt{\tfrac25}\,a$. From the normalization $a^2\bigl(1+\tfrac25\bigr)=1$ we get $a=\sqrt{\tfrac57}$ and $b=\sqrt{\tfrac27}$. For $\lambda=-2$ it reads $\tfrac52a+\tfrac{\sqrt{10}}{2}b=0$, so $b=-\sqrt{\tfrac52}\,a$, and from the normalization $a^2\bigl(1+\tfrac52\bigr)=1$ we get $a=\pm\sqrt{\tfrac27}$ and $b=\mp\sqrt{\tfrac57}$. Taking the coefficient of $Y_3^2\beta$ to be positive, we have $a=-\sqrt{\tfrac27}$ and $b=+\sqrt{\tfrac57}$.

Setting $l=3$ and $m_j=\tfrac32$ in Theorem 25.9, we have $2l+1=7$, $l+m_j+\tfrac12=5$, and $l-m_j+\tfrac12=2$, so

$$ \ket{\tfrac72,\tfrac32}=\sqrt{\tfrac57}\,Y_3^{1}\alpha+\sqrt{\tfrac27}\,Y_3^{2}\beta,\qquad \ket{\tfrac52,\tfrac32}=-\sqrt{\tfrac27}\,Y_3^{1}\alpha+\sqrt{\tfrac57}\,Y_3^{2}\beta $$

and these agree exactly with the eigenvectors above. The eigenvalues $\tfrac32\hbar^2=\tfrac{l}{2}\hbar^2$ ($j=\tfrac72$) and $-2\hbar^2=-\tfrac{l+1}{2}\hbar^2$ ($j=\tfrac52$) also follow the formulas for $l=3$.

Exercise 25.3: Constructing eigenstates from the general formula for CG coefficients and checking them

Solution

$l=1$, $m_j=-\tfrac12$. From $2l+1=3$, $l+m_j+\tfrac12=1$, and $l-m_j+\tfrac12=2$, the state with $j=l-\tfrac12=\tfrac12$ is

$$ \ket{\tfrac12,-\tfrac12}=-\sqrt{\tfrac23}\,R\,Y_1^{-1}\alpha+\sqrt{\tfrac13}\,R\,Y_1^{0}\beta . $$

Multiplying the matrix of Block ① $\hbar^2\begin{bmatrix}-\frac12&\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\\ \frac{\sqrt2}{2}&0\end{bmatrix}$ by the coefficient vector $v=\bigl(-\sqrt{\tfrac23},\ \sqrt{\tfrac13}\bigr)^{\mathsf T}$, the first component is $-\tfrac12\bigl(-\sqrt{\tfrac23}\bigr)+\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}=\tfrac12\sqrt{\tfrac23}+\tfrac12\sqrt{\tfrac23}=\sqrt{\tfrac23}$, and the second component is $\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\bigl(-\sqrt{\tfrac23}\bigr)=-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$. That is, the result is $\bigl(\sqrt{\tfrac23},\,-\sqrt{\tfrac13}\bigr)=-v$, and the eigenvalue is $-\hbar^2$. The normalization $\tfrac23+\tfrac13=1$ is also confirmed. For $j=\tfrac32$, $\ket{\tfrac32,-\tfrac12}=\sqrt{\tfrac13}\,R\,Y_1^{-1}\alpha+\sqrt{\tfrac23}\,R\,Y_1^{0}\beta$, and applying $\hat{\bm{L}}\cdot\hat{\bm{S}}$ to it multiplies it by $\tfrac12\hbar^2$ (first component: $-\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}+\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\sqrt{\tfrac23}=\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt3}$). The two states are orthogonal: $\sqrt{\tfrac13}\bigl(-\sqrt{\tfrac23}\bigr)+\sqrt{\tfrac23}\sqrt{\tfrac13}=0$.

$l=2$, $m_j=-\tfrac12$. From $2l+1=5$, $l+m_j+\tfrac12=2$, and $l-m_j+\tfrac12=3$, the state with $j=\tfrac32$ is

$$ \ket{\tfrac32,-\tfrac12}=-\sqrt{\tfrac35}\,R\,Y_2^{-1}\alpha+\sqrt{\tfrac25}\,R\,Y_2^{0}\beta . $$

Multiplying the block $\hbar^2\begin{bmatrix}-\frac12&\frac{\sqrt6}{2}\\ \frac{\sqrt6}{2}&0\end{bmatrix}$ of the d orbitals with $m_j=-\tfrac12$ by $v=\bigl(-\sqrt{\tfrac35},\ \sqrt{\tfrac25}\bigr)^{\mathsf T}$, the first component is $\tfrac12\sqrt{\tfrac35}+\tfrac{\sqrt6}{2}\sqrt{\tfrac25}=\tfrac12\sqrt{\tfrac35}+\sqrt{\tfrac35}=\tfrac32\sqrt{\tfrac35}$ ($\tfrac{\sqrt6}{2}\sqrt{\tfrac25}=\tfrac{\sqrt{12}}{2\sqrt5}=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{\sqrt5}$), and the second component is $\tfrac{\sqrt6}{2}\bigl(-\sqrt{\tfrac35}\bigr)=-\tfrac{\sqrt{18}}{2\sqrt5}=-\tfrac32\sqrt{\tfrac25}$. The result is $\bigl(\tfrac32\sqrt{\tfrac35},\,-\tfrac32\sqrt{\tfrac25}\bigr)=-\tfrac32\,v$, so the eigenvalue is $-\tfrac32\hbar^2$. The normalization is $\tfrac35+\tfrac25=1$.

Exercise 25.4: The ${}^3\mathrm{F}_J$ levels of a 3d2 ion

Solution

With $L=3$ and $S=1$, $L(L+1)+S(S+1)=12+2=14$, so $E_J=\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\bigl[J(J+1)-14\bigr]$. For $J=2,3,4$ ($\lvert L-S\rvert,\dots,L+S$),

$$ E_2=\tfrac\lambda2(6-14)=-4\lambda,\qquad E_3=\tfrac\lambda2(12-14)=-\lambda,\qquad E_4=\tfrac\lambda2(20-14)=+3\lambda . $$

The intervals are $E_3-E_2=3\lambda=\lambda\cdot3$ and $E_4-E_3=4\lambda=\lambda\cdot4$, which follow the Landé interval rule $E_J-E_{J-1}=\lambda J$ (ratio $3:4$). Center of gravity: $\sum(2J+1)E_J=5(-4\lambda)+7(-\lambda)+9(3\lambda)=(-20-7+27)\lambda=0$. Since 3d2 fills less than half of the shell, $\lambda>0$, and so $J=2$ is the lowest level (${}^3\mathrm{F}_2$ is the ground state).

Exercise 25.5: Addition of $1\otimes1$

Solution

(1) Since $j_1=j_2=1$, we have $J=0,1,2$. The number of pairs $(m_1,m_2)$ for each value of $m=m_1+m_2$ is as follows: for $m=\pm2$, one pair, $(\pm1,\pm1)$; for $m=\pm1$, two pairs, $(\pm1,0),(0,\pm1)$; for $m=0$, three pairs, $(1,-1),(0,0),(-1,1)$; the total is $1+2+3+2+1=9$. The highest value, $m=2$, occurs once $\to J=2$ (five states, $m=2,1,0,-1,-2$); of the remainder, $m=\pm1$ occur once each and $m=0$ occurs twice $\to J=1$ (three states); the one remaining $m=0$ state $\to J=0$ (one state). $9=5+3+1$.

(2) $\hat{J}_-\ket{1,m}=\sqrt2\hbar\ket{1,m-1}$ ($m=1,0$). We write $\ket{m_1,m_2}$ for the states. $\ket{2,2}=\ket{1,1}$. $\hat{J}_-\ket{2,2}=\hbar\sqrt{6-2}\ket{2,1}=2\hbar\ket{2,1}$, and the left-hand side is $\hat{J}_{1-}\ket{1,1}+\hat{J}_{2-}\ket{1,1}=\sqrt2\hbar(\ket{0,1}+\ket{1,0})$, so $\ket{2,1}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{1,0}+\ket{0,1})$. Next, $\hat{J}_-\ket{2,1}=\hbar\sqrt{6-0}\ket{2,0}=\sqrt6\hbar\ket{2,0}$, and the left-hand side is $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\sqrt2\hbar\bigl(\ket{0,0}+\ket{1,-1}+\ket{-1,1}+\ket{0,0}\bigr)=\hbar\bigl(\ket{1,-1}+2\ket{0,0}+\ket{-1,1}\bigr)$, so

$$ \ket{2,0}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}\bigl(\ket{1,-1}+2\ket{0,0}+\ket{-1,1}\bigr). $$

Among the states with $m=1$, the one orthogonal to $\ket{2,1}$ is the highest state of $J=1$, $\ket{1,1}_J=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{1,0}-\ket{0,1})$ (taking the component with $m_1=1$ to be positive). $\hat{J}_-\ket{1,1}_J=\sqrt2\hbar\ket{1,0}_J$, and the left-hand side is $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\sqrt2\hbar\bigl[(\ket{0,0}+\ket{1,-1})-(\ket{-1,1}+\ket{0,0})\bigr]=\hbar\bigl(\ket{1,-1}-\ket{-1,1}\bigr)$, so

$$ \ket{1,0}_J=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\bigl(\ket{1,-1}-\ket{-1,1}\bigr). $$

Among the three states with $m=0$, we look for the one, $\ket{0,0}=a\ket{1,-1}+b\ket{0,0}+c\ket{-1,1}$, that is orthogonal to both $\ket{2,0}$ and $\ket{1,0}_J$. Orthogonality to $\ket{1,0}_J$ gives $a-c=0$, and orthogonality to $\ket{2,0}$ gives $a+2b+c=0$. Hence $c=a$ and $b=-a$, and from the normalization $3a^2=1$ (taking the component with $m_1=1$ to be positive)

$$ \ket{0,0}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\bigl(\ket{1,-1}-\ket{0,0}+\ket{-1,1}\bigr). $$

(3) $\hat{\bm{J}}_1\cdot\hat{\bm{J}}_2=\tfrac{\hbar^2}{2}\bigl[J(J+1)-j_1(j_1+1)-j_2(j_2+1)\bigr]=\tfrac{\hbar^2}{2}\bigl[J(J+1)-4\bigr]$: this is $+\hbar^2$ for $J=2$, $-\hbar^2$ for $J=1$, and $-2\hbar^2$ for $J=0$. Weighted sum: $5\cdot1+3\cdot(-1)+1\cdot(-2)=0$.

Exercise 25.6: The spin exchange operator and the Pauli principle

Solution

(1) The Pauli matrices act as $\sigma_x\alpha=\beta$, $\sigma_x\beta=\alpha$, $\sigma_y\alpha=i\beta$, $\sigma_y\beta=-i\alpha$, $\sigma_z\alpha=\alpha$, $\sigma_z\beta=-\beta$. Acting with $\bm{\sigma}_1\cdot\bm{\sigma}_2=\sigma_{1x}\sigma_{2x}+\sigma_{1y}\sigma_{2y}+\sigma_{1z}\sigma_{2z}$ on each function, we obtain

$$ \begin{aligned} \bm{\sigma}_1\cdot\bm{\sigma}_2\,\alpha\alpha&=\beta\beta+(i\beta)(i\beta)+\alpha\alpha=\beta\beta-\beta\beta+\alpha\alpha=\alpha\alpha,\\ \bm{\sigma}_1\cdot\bm{\sigma}_2\,\alpha\beta&=\beta\alpha+(i\beta)(-i\alpha)+\alpha(-\beta)=\beta\alpha+\beta\alpha-\alpha\beta=2\beta\alpha-\alpha\beta,\\ \bm{\sigma}_1\cdot\bm{\sigma}_2\,\beta\alpha&=2\alpha\beta-\beta\alpha,\qquad \bm{\sigma}_1\cdot\bm{\sigma}_2\,\beta\beta=\beta\beta . \end{aligned} $$

(For the second term of $\alpha\beta$: $\sigma_{1y}\alpha=i\beta$ and $\sigma_{2y}\beta=-i\alpha$, so $(i\beta)(-i\alpha)=\beta\alpha$.) Therefore $\hat{P}_{12}=\tfrac12(1+\bm{\sigma}_1\cdot\bm{\sigma}_2)$ gives $\hat{P}_{12}\alpha\alpha=\alpha\alpha$, $\hat{P}_{12}\alpha\beta=\tfrac12(\alpha\beta+2\beta\alpha-\alpha\beta)=\beta\alpha$, $\hat{P}_{12}\beta\alpha=\alpha\beta$, and $\hat{P}_{12}\beta\beta=\beta\beta$, so it is indeed the operator that interchanges the two spins. The triplet $\alpha\alpha,\ \tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\alpha\beta+\beta\alpha),\ \beta\beta$ is invariant under the interchange and hence has eigenvalue $+1$, whereas the singlet $\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\alpha\beta-\beta\alpha)\to\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\beta\alpha-\alpha\beta)=-(\text{singlet})$ has eigenvalue $-1$.

(2) From $\bm{\sigma}_i=\tfrac{2}{\hbar}\hat{\bm{S}}_i$ we get $\bm{\sigma}_1\cdot\bm{\sigma}_2=\tfrac{4}{\hbar^2}\hat{\bm{S}}_1\cdot\hat{\bm{S}}_2$; hence $\hat{P}_{12}=\tfrac12+\tfrac{2}{\hbar^2}\hat{\bm{S}}_1\cdot\hat{\bm{S}}_2$, that is, $\dfrac{\hat{\bm{S}}_1\cdot\hat{\bm{S}}_2}{\hbar^2}=\dfrac{\hat{P}_{12}-\frac12}{2}$. Substituting this into $\hat{H}_{\mathrm{eff}}=\varepsilon_a+\varepsilon_b+U_{ab}-\tfrac{J_{ab}}{2}-\tfrac{2J_{ab}}{\hbar^2}\hat{\bm{S}}_1\cdot\hat{\bm{S}}_2$ gives

$$ \hat{H}_{\mathrm{eff}}=\varepsilon_a+\varepsilon_b+U_{ab}-\frac{J_{ab}}{2}-J_{ab}\Bigl(\hat{P}_{12}-\frac12\Bigr)=\varepsilon_a+\varepsilon_b+U_{ab}-J_{ab}\,\hat{P}_{12} $$

For the triplet ($\hat{P}_{12}=+1$) this gives $E_{\mathrm T}=\varepsilon_a+\varepsilon_b+U_{ab}-J_{ab}$, and for the singlet ($\hat{P}_{12}=-1$) $E_{\mathrm S}=\varepsilon_a+\varepsilon_b+U_{ab}+J_{ab}$, which reproduces the result in the main text. The Pauli principle postulates that the eigenvalue of the operation that interchanges both the spatial coordinates and the spins of the electrons is $-1$. Therefore, if $\hat{P}_{12}$ of the spin part is $+1$ (triplet), the spatial part must be $-1$ (antisymmetric), and if the spin part is $-1$ (singlet), the spatial part must be $+1$ (symmetric).

Exercise 25.7: The angle between $\bm{L}$ and $\bm{S}$ (vector model)

Solution

$\lvert\bm{S}\rvert=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\hbar$, $\lvert\bm{L}\rvert=\sqrt{l(l+1)}\,\hbar$, $\lvert\bm{J}\rvert=\sqrt{j(j+1)}\,\hbar$. We use $\bm{L}\cdot\bm{S}\to\tfrac{l}{2}\hbar^2$ ($j=l+\tfrac12$) or $-\tfrac{l+1}{2}\hbar^2$ ($j=l-\tfrac12$).

$l=2$. Since $\lvert\bm{L}\rvert=\sqrt6\hbar$, $\lvert\bm{L}\rvert\lvert\bm{S}\rvert=\sqrt6\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\hbar^2=\tfrac{3\sqrt2}{2}\hbar^2\approx2.121\hbar^2$. For $j=\tfrac52$: $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt2/2}=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{3}\approx0.4714$, $\theta\approx61.9^\circ$, $\lvert\bm{J}\rvert=\sqrt{35/4}\,\hbar=\tfrac{\sqrt{35}}{2}\hbar\approx2.96\hbar$. For $j=\tfrac32$: $\cos\theta=\dfrac{-3/2}{3\sqrt2/2}=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\approx-0.7071$, $\theta=135.0^\circ$, $\lvert\bm{J}\rvert=\sqrt{15/4}\,\hbar=\tfrac{\sqrt{15}}{2}\hbar\approx1.94\hbar$.

$l=3$. Since $\lvert\bm{L}\rvert=\sqrt{12}\hbar$, $\lvert\bm{L}\rvert\lvert\bm{S}\rvert=\sqrt{12}\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\hbar^2=3\hbar^2$. For $j=\tfrac72$: $\cos\theta=\dfrac{3/2}{3}=\tfrac12$, $\theta=60.0^\circ$, $\lvert\bm{J}\rvert=\sqrt{63/4}\,\hbar=\tfrac{\sqrt{63}}{2}\hbar\approx3.97\hbar$. For $j=\tfrac52$: $\cos\theta=\dfrac{-2}{3}\approx-0.6667$, $\theta\approx131.8^\circ$, $\lvert\bm{J}\rvert=\tfrac{\sqrt{35}}{2}\hbar\approx2.96\hbar$.

For $j=l+\tfrac12$, $\theta$ becomes smaller as $l$ increases: $65.9^\circ\ (l=1)$, $61.9^\circ\ (l=2)$, $60.0^\circ\ (l=3)$ (approaching $54.7^\circ$ as $l\to\infty$); for $j=l-\tfrac12$ it becomes smaller as well: $144.7^\circ,\ 135.0^\circ,\ 131.8^\circ$ (approaching $125.3^\circ$).

Exercise 25.8: Spin–orbit splitting of the 4f levels of Ce3+

Solution

(1) The 4f electron has $l=3$, and the spacing is $(l+\tfrac12)\zeta_{4f}=\tfrac72\zeta_{4f}=2.2\times10^3\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, so

$$ \zeta_{4f}=\frac27\times2.2\times10^3\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\approx629\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\ \ (\approx0.078\ \mathrm{eV}). $$

The shifts from the center of gravity are $E\bigl({}^2\mathrm{F}_{7/2}\bigr)=+\tfrac{l}{2}\zeta=+\tfrac32\zeta\approx+943\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ and $E\bigl({}^2\mathrm{F}_{5/2}\bigr)=-\tfrac{l+1}{2}\zeta=-2\zeta\approx-1257\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$. The difference is $943+1257=2200\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, and for the center of gravity (the average weighted by the degeneracy) we have $8\times943+6\times(-1257)\approx0$.

(2) We have $k_{\mathrm B}T=0.6950\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}/K}\times300\ \mathrm{K}=208.5\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, so $\Delta E/k_{\mathrm B}T=2200/208.5=10.55$. Multiplying the Boltzmann factor $e^{-10.55}=2.6\times10^{-5}$ by the degeneracy ratio $8/6$, we obtain

$$ \frac{N({}^2\mathrm{F}_{7/2})}{N({}^2\mathrm{F}_{5/2})}=\frac{8}{6}\,e^{-\Delta E/k_{\mathrm B}T}=\frac43\times2.6\times10^{-5}\approx3.5\times10^{-5} $$

Even at room temperature, almost all $\mathrm{Ce^{3+}}$ ions are in the ground multiplet ${}^2\mathrm{F}_{5/2}$ (the fraction in the upper level is about $3.5\times10^{-5}$, that is, only $0.0035\ \%$).

← Back to Chapter 25, “Addition of Angular Momenta and the Eigenvalue Problem of $\hat{\bm{L}}\cdot\hat{\bm{S}}$”

Chapter 26: The Physics of Spin–Orbit Interaction and Atoms in a Magnetic Field

Exercise 26.1: $\xi(r)$ and $\zeta_{2p}$ for the Coulomb potential

Solution

(1) Differentiating $V(r)=-\dfrac{Ze_0^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,r^{-1}$ gives $\dfrac{\dd V}{\dd r}=+\dfrac{Ze_0^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,r^{-2}$. Dividing by $r$, we obtain $\dfrac1r\dfrac{\dd V}{\dd r}=\dfrac{Ze_0^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^3}$. Therefore

$$ \xi(r)=\frac{1}{2m_{\mathrm{e}}^2c^2}\cdot\frac{Ze_0^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^3}=\frac{Ze_0^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0m_{\mathrm{e}}^2c^2}\,\frac1{r^3}. $$

(2) With $Z=1$ and $\expval{r^{-3}}_{2p}=\dfrac{1}{24a_0^3}$, we have $\zeta_{2p}=\hbar^2\expval{\xi}=\dfrac{\hbar^2e_0^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0m_{\mathrm{e}}^2c^2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{24a_0^3}$. From $\dfrac{e_0^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}=\alpha\hbar c$ in the hint, $\dfrac{e_0^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0}=\dfrac{\alpha\hbar c}{2}$, so

$$ \zeta_{2p}=\frac{\hbar^2}{m_{\mathrm{e}}^2c^2}\cdot\frac{\alpha\hbar c}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{24a_0^3}=\frac{\alpha\hbar^3}{48\,m_{\mathrm{e}}^2c\,a_0^3}. $$

Substituting $\dfrac{1}{a_0^3}=\dfrac{m_{\mathrm{e}}^3c^3\alpha^3}{\hbar^3}$ ($a_0=\hbar/(m_{\mathrm{e}}c\alpha)$), the $\hbar^3$ cancels and we obtain

$$ \zeta_{2p}=\frac{\alpha}{48}\cdot\frac{m_{\mathrm{e}}^3c^3\alpha^3}{m_{\mathrm{e}}^2c}=\frac{\alpha^4m_{\mathrm{e}}c^2}{48}=\frac{\alpha^2E_{\mathrm{h}}}{48} $$

(here $E_{\mathrm{h}}=\alpha^2m_{\mathrm{e}}c^2$). Numerically, $\zeta_{2p}=1.4490\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV}/48=3.02\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV}$, and the interval between $2p_{3/2}$ and $2p_{1/2}$ is $\tfrac32\zeta_{2p}=4.53\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV}$.

Exercise 26.2: Finding $\zeta_{np}$ from the doublets of K and Rb

Solution

(1) From the wavelengths in air we find the wavenumber $\tilde\nu=1/\lambda$. K: $\tilde\nu_2=1/(766.49\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{cm})=13\,046.48\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ and $\tilde\nu_1=1/(769.90\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{cm})=12\,988.70\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, so the interval is $57.78\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, and $57.78/8065.5\ \mathrm{eV}=7.164\ \mathrm{meV}$. Rb: $\tilde\nu_2=1/(780.03\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{cm})=12\,820.02\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ and $\tilde\nu_1=1/(794.76\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{cm})=12\,582.41\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, so the interval is $237.60\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}=29.46\ \mathrm{meV}$. (Table 26.2 uses the difference of the wavenumbers in vacuum ($57.71\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ for K), so it differs slightly in the last digit from the value in this solution, which was obtained from the wavelengths in air. The difference is $0.1$–$0.2\ \%$.)

(2) For a $p$ orbital, $\Delta E=\tfrac32\zeta$, so $\zeta_{4p}(\mathrm{K})=\tfrac23\times7.164=4.776\approx4.78\ \mathrm{meV}$ and $\zeta_{5p}(\mathrm{Rb})=\tfrac23\times29.46=19.64\approx19.6\ \mathrm{meV}$.

(3) From the hydrogen-like formula $\zeta=\dfrac{\alpha^2E_{\mathrm{h}}Z_{\mathrm{eff}}^4}{2n^3\cdot1\cdot\frac32\cdot2}=\dfrac{\alpha^2E_{\mathrm{h}}Z_{\mathrm{eff}}^4}{6n^3}$, using $\alpha^2E_{\mathrm{h}}=1.449\ \mathrm{meV}$, we find for K ($n=4$, $6n^3=384$): $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}^4=\dfrac{384\times4.776}{1.449}=1.27\times10^3$, $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}=5.96$. For Rb ($n=5$, $6n^3=750$): $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}^4=\dfrac{750\times19.64}{1.449}=1.02\times10^4$, $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}=10.0$. For Cs, $\zeta_{6p}=45.8\ \mathrm{meV}$ and $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}=14.2$. Therefore $\zeta$ increases as $4.8$, $19.6$, $45.8\ \mathrm{meV}$ for K, Rb, Cs (Rb is about $4.1$ times K, and Cs is about $2.3$ times Rb), and $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$ increases as $6.0$, $10.0$, $14.2$, almost in proportion to $Z=19,37,55$ ($Z_{\mathrm{eff}}/Z=0.31,0.27,0.26$).

Exercise 26.3: $g_J$ for ${}^3P_J$

Solution

Since $L=1$, $S=1$, and $S(S+1)-L(L+1)=2-2=0$, we have $g_J=1+\dfrac{J(J+1)}{2J(J+1)}=\dfrac32$ (for $J\ne0$). Concretely, for $J=2$: $1+\dfrac{6+2-2}{2\cdot6}=\dfrac32$. For $J=1$: $1+\dfrac{2+2-2}{2\cdot2}=\dfrac32$.

The Zeeman energy is $E=g_Jm_J\mu_{\mathrm{B}}B$, and the interval between adjacent values of $m_J$ is $g_J\mu_{\mathrm{B}}B=\tfrac32\mu_{\mathrm{B}}B$. For $J=2$ the five levels ($m_J=-2,\ldots,2$) lie at $-3,-\tfrac32,0,+\tfrac32,+3$ (in units of $\mu_{\mathrm{B}}B$), and for $J=1$ the three levels lie at $-\tfrac32,0,+\tfrac32$; in both cases the levels are equally spaced, with interval $\tfrac32\mu_{\mathrm{B}}B$.

$J=0$ has only the single state $m_J=0$, and $E=g_Jm_J\mu_{\mathrm{B}}B=0$ (the first-order expectation value of $\hat{H}_{\mathrm{Z}}$ is proportional to $\expval{\hat{J}_z}=0$). Since there is no total angular momentum, the magnetic moment is also 0, and the state does not couple to the magnetic field at first order (for $J=0$ in the formula $g_J=\dfrac32+\dfrac{S(S+1)-L(L+1)}{2J(J+1)}$ the denominator is 0, and the value has no meaning). Note that if we use $g_s=2.0023$, $g_J$ deviates from $\tfrac32$ by about $0.1\ \%$.

Exercise 26.4: Polarization of the four components of the Na D$_1$ line

Solution

The four transitions from the upper level ${}^2P_{1/2}$ ($m_{\mathrm{up}}=\pm\tfrac12$) to the lower level ${}^2S_{1/2}$ ($m_{\mathrm{low}}=\pm\tfrac12$) are classified according to $\Delta m_j=m_{\mathrm{up}}-m_{\mathrm{low}}$ as follows ($\Delta E=g_{\mathrm{up}}m_{\mathrm{up}}-g_{\mathrm{low}}m_{\mathrm{low}}$, $g_{\mathrm{up}}=\tfrac23$, $g_{\mathrm{low}}=2$, in units of $\mu_{\mathrm{B}}B$).

  • $(+\tfrac12\to+\tfrac12)$: $\Delta m_j=0$, $\pi$, $\Delta E=\tfrac13-1=-\tfrac23$
  • $(-\tfrac12\to-\tfrac12)$: $\Delta m_j=0$, $\pi$, $\Delta E=-\tfrac13+1=+\tfrac23$
  • $(+\tfrac12\to-\tfrac12)$: $\Delta m_j=+1$, $\sigma$, $\Delta E=\tfrac13+1=+\tfrac43$
  • $(-\tfrac12\to+\tfrac12)$: $\Delta m_j=-1$, $\sigma$, $\Delta E=-\tfrac13-1=-\tfrac43$

The $\pi$ components ($\pm\tfrac23$) are transitions in which the electric dipole oscillates parallel to the magnetic field, and they emit no light along the direction of the magnetic field. Therefore, viewed along the direction of the magnetic field, only the two $\sigma$ components ($\pm\tfrac43$) are seen, and they are circularly polarized in opposite senses. Viewed from a direction perpendicular to the magnetic field, all four lines are seen; the $\pi$ components are linearly polarized parallel to the magnetic field, and the $\sigma$ components are linearly polarized perpendicular to the magnetic field. The intensities of the four lines are nearly equal (the total radiated power of a $\pi$ component is half that of a $\sigma$ component, but in the perpendicular direction it is seen with twice the amount of light).

Exercise 26.5: Analytic solution of the $2\times2$ block for $m_j=+\tfrac12$

Solution

The sum of the diagonal elements is $b-\tfrac12$ and the determinant is $b\cdot(-\tfrac12)-\tfrac12=-\dfrac{b+1}{2}$, so the characteristic equation is $\lambda^2-(b-\tfrac12)\lambda-\dfrac{b+1}{2}=0$. The solution is $\lambda=\tfrac12\bigl[(b-\tfrac12)\pm\sqrt{(b-\tfrac12)^2+2(b+1)}\bigr]$, and the expression under the square root is $b^2-b+\tfrac14+2b+2=b^2+b+\tfrac94=(b+\tfrac12)^2+2$, so

$$ \frac{E_\pm(b)}{\zeta}=\frac12\Bigl[b-\frac12\pm\sqrt{\Bigl(b+\frac12\Bigr)^2+2}\Bigr]. $$

(1) For $b=0$: $\sqrt{\tfrac14+2}=\tfrac32$, and $E_+=\tfrac12\zeta$ ($j=\tfrac32$), $E_-=-\zeta$ ($j=\tfrac12$). Differentiating gives $\dfrac{\dd E_\pm}{\dd b}=\dfrac12\Bigl[1\pm\dfrac{b+\frac12}{\sqrt{(b+\frac12)^2+2}}\Bigr]$, and at $b=0$ this is $\dfrac12\Bigl[1\pm\dfrac{1/2}{3/2}\Bigr]=\dfrac12\Bigl[1\pm\dfrac13\Bigr]$; that is, the slope of $E_+$ is $\tfrac23$ and the slope of $E_-$ is $\tfrac13$ (these are the slopes with respect to $b$ in units of $\zeta$, which are the same as the slopes with respect to $\mu_{\mathrm{B}}B$). This agrees with $g_Jm_j$: for $j=\tfrac32$, $\tfrac43\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac23$; for $j=\tfrac12$, $\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac13$.

(2) For $b\gg1$, $\sqrt{(b+\frac12)^2+2}=(b+\tfrac12)\sqrt{1+\dfrac{2}{(b+\frac12)^2}}\approx b+\tfrac12+\dfrac{1}{b+\frac12}$. Therefore

$$ \frac{E_+}{\zeta}\approx\frac12\Bigl[2b+\frac{1}{b+\frac12}\Bigr]=b+\frac{1}{2b+1}\to b,\qquad \frac{E_-}{\zeta}\approx\frac12\Bigl[-1-\frac{1}{b+\frac12}\Bigr]=-\frac12-\frac{1}{2b+1}\to-\frac12 . $$

In the strong-field formula $b\,(m_l+2m_s)+m_lm_s$, the state corresponding to $E_+$ is $(m_l,m_s)=(0,\uparrow)$: $b\cdot(0+1)+0=b$, and the state corresponding to $E_-$ is $(+1,\downarrow)$: $b\cdot(1-1)+(1)(-\tfrac12)=-\tfrac12$; both agree.

(3) For $b=1$: $\sqrt{\tfrac94+2}=\sqrt{4.25}=2.0616$, $E_\pm/\zeta=\tfrac12\bigl[\tfrac12\pm2.0616\bigr]$; that is, $E_+=1.2808\zeta$ and $E_-=-0.7808\zeta$.

Exercise 26.6: The separation angle of the Kα doublet

Solution

(1) $\dfrac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda}=\dfrac{0.71359-0.70932}{0.70932}=6.02\times10^{-3}$. For $2\theta=60^\circ$ ($\theta=30^\circ$, $\tan\theta=0.5774$): $\Delta(2\theta)=2\times0.5774\times6.02\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{rad}=6.95\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{rad}=0.398^\circ$. For $2\theta=120^\circ$ ($\theta=60^\circ$, $\tan\theta=1.732$): $\Delta(2\theta)=2\times1.732\times6.02\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{rad}=2.085\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{rad}=1.19^\circ$ (solving Bragg's equation $2d\sin\theta=\lambda$ exactly gives $0.399^\circ$ and $1.21^\circ$; at low angles the first-order approximation agrees well, and at higher angles it deviates somewhat).

(2) $d_{211}=a/\sqrt{2^2+1^2+1^2}=2.8665/\sqrt6=1.1702\ \text{Å}$. For Kα$_1$: $\sin\theta_1=\dfrac{1.5405929}{2\times1.1702}=0.65825$, $\theta_1=41.165^\circ$, $2\theta_1=82.33^\circ$. For Kα$_2$: $\sin\theta_2=\dfrac{1.5444274}{2\times1.1702}=0.65989$, $\theta_2=41.290^\circ$, $2\theta_2=82.58^\circ$. The interval is $0.25^\circ$, which agrees with the value given by the first-order approximation formula $\Delta(2\theta)=2\tan\theta\,\dfrac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda}$, namely $2\tan\theta_1\dfrac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda}=2\times0.8744\times2.489\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{rad}=4.35\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{rad}=0.249^\circ\approx0.25^\circ$.

Exercise 26.7: The area ratio of the XPS doublet

Solution

The hole left after photoelectron emission can be in two states, $j=l\pm\tfrac12$, and the ratio of their degeneracies (numbers of states) $2j+1$ gives the area ratio of the doublet. For $p$ ($l=1$): $j=\tfrac32,\tfrac12$, giving $4:2=\mathbf{2:1}$. For $d$ ($l=2$): $j=\tfrac52,\tfrac32$, giving $6:4=\mathbf{3:2}$. For $f$ ($l=3$): $j=\tfrac72,\tfrac52$, giving $8:6=\mathbf{4:3}$. In general, $\dfrac{2(l+\frac12)+1}{2(l-\frac12)+1}=\dfrac{2l+2}{2l}=\dfrac{l+1}{l}$, which for $l=1,2,3$ equals $2,\tfrac32,\tfrac43$.

An $s$ orbital has $l=0$ and only the single value $j=\tfrac12$; since $\hat{\bm{L}}=\bm{0}$, there is no spin–orbit interaction, and the level does not split. Therefore the photoelectron peak of an $s$ level is a single line.

Exercise 26.8: The spin-only magnetic moment

Solution

The number of unpaired electrons $=2S$, and $\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}=2\sqrt{S(S+1)}\,\mu_{\mathrm{B}}$.

  • $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ ($3d^5$, high spin): all five $d$ electrons are unpaired ($t_{2g}^3e_g^2$), so $S=\tfrac52$. $\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}=2\sqrt{\tfrac52\cdot\tfrac72}=2\sqrt{\tfrac{35}{4}}=\sqrt{35}=5.92$.
  • $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$ ($3d^3$): $t_{2g}^3$ has three unpaired electrons, so $S=\tfrac32$. $\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}=2\sqrt{\tfrac32\cdot\tfrac52}=\sqrt{15}=3.87$.
  • $\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}$ ($3d^8$, octahedral): in $t_{2g}^6e_g^2$ the two $e_g$ electrons are unpaired, so $S=1$. $\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}=2\sqrt{1\cdot2}=2\sqrt2=2.83$.

The measured values for $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$ are almost equal to these, whereas for $\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}$ the measured value is somewhat larger, around $3$. This is because, in $\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}$, the spin–orbit interaction mixes in excited orbital states, so that a small orbital contribution remains (Section 26.7).

← Back to Chapter 26, “The Physics of Spin–Orbit Interaction and Atoms in a Magnetic Field”

Chapter 27: Time-Independent Perturbation Theory — Nondegenerate First- and Second-Order Perturbation

Exercise 27.1: The coefficients $d_k$ of the second-order wave function

Solution

(1) The basic equation at second order is obtained by substituting $\psi_n^{(1)}=\sum_ic_i\psi_i^{(0)}$, $\psi_n^{(2)}=\sum_id_i\psi_i^{(0)}$, $E_n^{(1)}=V_{nn}$ into the second-order equation $\hat{V}\psi_n^{(1)}+\hat{H}_0\psi_n^{(2)}=E_n^{(2)}\psi_n^{(0)}+E_n^{(1)}\psi_n^{(1)}+E_n^{(0)}\psi_n^{(2)}$ and rearranging:

$$ \sum_ic_i\bigl(\hat{V}-V_{nn}\bigr)\psi_i^{(0)}+\sum_id_i\bigl(E_i^{(0)}-E_n^{(0)}\bigr)\psi_i^{(0)}=E_n^{(2)}\psi_n^{(0)} $$

Multiply both sides from the left by $\bra{\psi_k^{(0)}}$ ($k\ne n$). By the orthonormality $\braket{\psi_k^{(0)}}{\psi_i^{(0)}}=\delta_{ki}$, the first term becomes $\sum_ic_i(V_{ki}-V_{nn}\delta_{ki})=\sum_ic_iV_{ki}-V_{nn}c_k$, the second term becomes $d_k(E_k^{(0)}-E_n^{(0)})$, and the right-hand side is $E_n^{(2)}\braket{\psi_k^{(0)}}{\psi_n^{(0)}}=0$. Since $c_n=0$ in intermediate normalization, the sum runs only over $i\ne n$, so

$$ d_k\bigl(E_k^{(0)}-E_n^{(0)}\bigr)=-\sum_{i\ne n}V_{ki}c_i+V_{nn}c_k . $$

Substituting $c_i=-V_{in}/(E_i^{(0)}-E_n^{(0)})$ and $c_k=-V_{kn}/(E_k^{(0)}-E_n^{(0)})$ and dividing by $E_k^{(0)}-E_n^{(0)}$, we obtain

$$ d_k=\sum_{i\ne n}\frac{V_{ki}V_{in}}{\bigl(E_k^{(0)}-E_n^{(0)}\bigr)\bigl(E_i^{(0)}-E_n^{(0)}\bigr)}-\frac{V_{nn}V_{kn}}{\bigl(E_k^{(0)}-E_n^{(0)}\bigr)^2}\qquad(k\ne n) $$

This is the required result.

(2) Take the lower state to be $n=1$. Since state 2 is the only one, the sum consists of the single term $i=2$. $E_2^{(0)}-E_1^{(0)}=\Delta=0.10\ \mathrm{eV}$, $V_{11}=v_1=0.01$, $V_{22}=v_2=0.03$, $V_{12}=V_{21}=V=0.02$ (in eV).

$$ c_2=-\frac{V_{21}}{\Delta}=-\frac{0.02}{0.10}=-0.2,\qquad d_2=\frac{V_{22}V_{21}}{\Delta\cdot\Delta}-\frac{V_{11}V_{21}}{\Delta^2}=\frac{(v_2-v_1)V}{\Delta^2}=\frac{0.02\times0.02}{0.010}=0.040 . $$

Therefore the perturbation series for the second component of the intermediate-normalized eigenvector is $t\simeq\lambda c_2+\lambda^2d_2$. For $\lambda=0.1$, through first order it is $-0.0200$, and through second order it is $-0.0200+0.0004=-0.0196$.

On the other hand, the exact matrix for $\lambda=0.1$ is $\begin{pmatrix}0.001&0.002\\0.002&0.103\end{pmatrix}$, and its lower eigenvalue is $E_-=\bigl(0.104-\sqrt{0.102^2+4\times0.002^2}\bigr)/2=9.6080\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV}$. Writing the eigenvector as $(1,t)^{\mathrm T}$, the first row $(0.001-E_-)+0.002\,t=0$ gives $t=(E_--0.001)/0.002=-0.019600$. The value through second order, $-0.0196$, agrees with the exact value to five digits (the first-order value $-0.0200$ has an error of 2%).

Exercise 27.2: A $\delta$-function perturbation at the center of the well

Solution

(1) $\psi_k^{(0)}=\sqrt{2/L}\sin(k\pi x/L)$, $E_k^{(0)}=k^2E_1$, $E_1=\pi^2\hbar^2/(2mL^2)$. By the property of the $\delta$ function, the matrix elements are

$$ V_{kn}=\lambda_0\psi_k^{(0)}(L/2)\psi_n^{(0)}(L/2)=\frac{2\lambda_0}{L}\sin\frac{k\pi}{2}\sin\frac{n\pi}{2}. $$

For $n=1$, $V_{k1}=\dfrac{2\lambda_0}{L}\sin\dfrac{k\pi}{2}$ (0 if $k$ is even, $\pm2\lambda_0/L$ if it is odd). Therefore $E_1^{(1)}=V_{11}=2\lambda_0/L$. In units of $E_1=\pi^2\hbar^2/(2mL^2)$, $\dfrac{E_1^{(1)}}{E_1}=\dfrac{2\lambda_0}{L}\cdot\dfrac{2mL^2}{\pi^2\hbar^2}=\dfrac{4m\lambda_0L}{\pi^2\hbar^2}=\dfrac{4\gamma}{\pi^2}$. Similarly, $V_{k1}/E_1=(4\gamma/\pi^2)\sin(k\pi/2)$, so the mixing coefficients are

$$ c_k=-\frac{V_{k1}}{E_k^{(0)}-E_1^{(0)}}=-\frac{4\gamma}{\pi^2}\,\frac{\sin(k\pi/2)}{k^2-1}\qquad(k=3,5,7,\dots;\ k\text{ even gives }0). $$

Since $\sin(3\pi/2)=-1$, $\sin(5\pi/2)=+1$, and $\sin(7\pi/2)=-1$, we get $c_3=+\dfrac{4\gamma}{8\pi^2}=\dfrac{\gamma}{2\pi^2}=0.0507\gamma$, $c_5=-\dfrac{\gamma}{6\pi^2}=-0.0169\gamma$, $c_7=+\dfrac{\gamma}{12\pi^2}=0.0084\gamma$. Because $\psi_3^{(0)}$ is negative at the center $x=L/2$ ($\sin(3\pi/2)=-1$), the admixture with $c_3\gt0$ reduces the amplitude at the center. This change goes in the direction in which a repulsive perturbation reduces the probability at the center.

(2) By the formula $E_1^{(2)}=-\sum_{k\ne1}\abs{V_{k1}}^2/(E_k^{(0)}-E_1^{(0)})$, the second-order energy keeps only the terms with odd $k$:

$$ \frac{E_1^{(2)}}{E_1}=-\Bigl(\frac{4\gamma}{\pi^2}\Bigr)^2\sum_{k=3,5,\dots}\frac{1}{k^2-1}. $$

Using $\dfrac{1}{k^2-1}=\dfrac12\Bigl(\dfrac{1}{k-1}-\dfrac{1}{k+1}\Bigr)$, the sum is $\dfrac12\Bigl[\bigl(\tfrac12-\tfrac14\bigr)+\bigl(\tfrac14-\tfrac16\bigr)+\bigl(\tfrac16-\tfrac18\bigr)+\cdots\Bigr]=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac12=\dfrac14$ (a telescoping sum). Hence $E_1^{(2)}/E_1=-\dfrac{16\gamma^2}{\pi^4}\cdot\dfrac14=-\dfrac{4\gamma^2}{\pi^4}$.

(3) Exact solution: the even-parity states have the form $\sin kx$ for $x\lt L/2$ and $\sin k(L-x)$ for $x\gt L/2$ ($k=\sqrt{2mE}/\hbar$). Continuity at $x=L/2$ and the jump of the derivative at the $\delta$ function, $\psi'(L/2^+)-\psi'(L/2^-)=(2m\lambda_0/\hbar^2)\psi(L/2)$, give $-2k\cos(kL/2)=(2m\lambda_0/\hbar^2)\sin(kL/2)$. Letting $q=kL/2$, we have $\tan q=-\dfrac{\hbar^2k}{m\lambda_0}=-\dfrac{2q}{\gamma}$, and the energy is $E=\dfrac{\hbar^2k^2}{2m}=\Bigl(\dfrac{2q}{\pi}\Bigr)^2E_1$. For $\gamma\to0$, $q\to\pi/2$; for $\gamma\to\infty$, $q\to\pi$ ($E\to4E_1$: a wall forms at the center and the well becomes two boxes).

For $\gamma=0.5$, solving $\tan q=-4q$ numerically in $\pi/2\lt q\lt\pi$ gives $q=1.7155$, $E_1/E_1^{(0)}=(2q/\pi)^2=1.1927$. Perturbation theory gives, through first order, $1+4\gamma/\pi^2=1.2026$ (error 0.8%), and through second order, $1.2026-4\gamma^2/\pi^4=1.2026-0.0103=1.1924$ (error 0.03%), so the second-order result agrees well with the exact value. For $\gamma=0.1$, the exact value is $1.04012$, through first order $1.04053$, and through second order $1.04012$.

Exercise 27.3: The $x^4$ perturbation of the harmonic oscillator for $n=0,1,2$

Solution

From the result of Example 27.5 in Chapter 27, $\mel{n}{(\hat{x}/b)^4}{n}=\tfrac14(6n^2+6n+3)$, we obtain $E_n^{(1)}=\tfrac14(6n^2+6n+3)\hbar\omega$. $n=0$: $\tfrac34$, $n=1$: $\tfrac{15}{4}$, $n=2$: $\tfrac{39}{4}$ (in units of $\hbar\omega$). The values through first order for $g=0.01$ and the values from numerical diagonalization are as follows (in units of $\hbar\omega$).

$n$$E^{(0)}$$gE^{(1)}$Through first orderExact (diagonalization)Difference (exact − first order)
00.50.00750.5075000.507256$-0.000244$
11.50.03751.5375001.535648$-0.001852$
22.50.09752.5975002.590846$-0.006654$

The difference is the correction of second and higher order, and it grows rapidly with $n$ (0.24, 1.9, 6.7 $\times10^{-3}$). The formula giving the second-order coefficient is $-(34n^3+51n^2+59n+21)/8$ (in units of $\hbar\omega$, the coefficient of $g^2$), which for $n=0,1,2$ gives $-\tfrac{21}{8},\ -\tfrac{165}{8},\ -\tfrac{615}{8}$. Adding it, for $g=0.01$ we obtain $n=0$: $0.5072375$, $n=1$: $1.5354375$, $n=2$: $2.5898125$, and the differences from the exact values (exact $-$ through second order) shrink to $+1.9\times10^{-5}$, $+2.1\times10^{-4}$, and $+1.0\times10^{-3}$, respectively. The correction is larger for higher levels not only because $\expval{x^4}$ grows as $n^2$ but also because the second-order coefficient grows as $n^3$. The range in which perturbation theory can be used is roughly $g\,n^2\ll1$.

Exercise 27.4: The shift of the 1s level of the hydrogen atom due to the size of the nucleus

Solution

(1) The potential energy of a point charge is $-\dfrac{e_0^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}$, and inside a uniform sphere (radius $R$) it is $-\dfrac{e_0^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{3R^2-r^2}{2R^3}$ (at $r=R$ the two agree, both being $-e_0^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0R)$, so the potential is continuous). The difference $\Delta V=V_{\text{sphere}}-V_{\text{point}}$ is $\dfrac{e_0^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\Bigl[\dfrac1r-\dfrac{3R^2-r^2}{2R^3}\Bigr]\gt0$ for $r\lt R$ and $0$ for $r\gt R$. The first-order energy is $E^{(1)}=\int\abs{\psi_{1\mathrm{s}}}^2\Delta V\dd^3r$. Since $R\ll a_0$, $\abs{\psi_{1\mathrm{s}}(r)}^2$ can be regarded as equal to $\abs{\psi_{1\mathrm{s}}(0)}^2=1/(\pi a_0^3)$ over the range $r\lt R$.

$$ E^{(1)}\simeq\frac{1}{\pi a_0^3}\,\frac{e_0^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int_0^R4\pi r^2\Bigl[\frac1r-\frac{3}{2R}+\frac{r^2}{2R^3}\Bigr]\dd r=\frac{4}{a_0^3}\,\frac{e_0^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\Bigl[\frac{R^2}{2}-\frac{R^2}{2}+\frac{R^2}{10}\Bigr] $$

($\int_0^Rr\dd r=R^2/2$, $\int_0^R\dfrac{3r^2}{2R}\dd r=R^2/2$, $\int_0^R\dfrac{r^4}{2R^3}\dd r=R^2/10$). Hence $E^{(1)}=\dfrac{2}{5}\dfrac{R^2}{a_0^3}\dfrac{e_0^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}=\dfrac25\Bigl(\dfrac{R}{a_0}\Bigr)^2E_{\mathrm h}$ ($E_{\mathrm h}=e_0^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0a_0)$). It is positive: because the nuclear charge is spread out, the attraction felt by the electron is weakened, and the level rises.

(2) $R=\sqrt{5/3}\,r_{\mathrm p}=1.291\times0.84\ \mathrm{fm}=1.084\ \mathrm{fm}$, $R/a_0=1.084\times10^{-15}/(5.292\times10^{-11})=2.049\times10^{-5}$, $(R/a_0)^2=4.20\times10^{-10}$. $E^{(1)}=0.4\times4.20\times10^{-10}\times27.211\ \mathrm{eV}=4.57\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{eV}$. In terms of frequency, $4.57\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{eV}\times2.418\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz/eV}=1.1\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{Hz}=1.1\ \mathrm{MHz}$. This is extremely small, $4.5\times10^{-10}$ times the level spacing $10.2\ \mathrm{eV}$, which confirms that perturbation theory is a good approximation ($R\ll a_0$). Note also that if the wave function is used exactly, including its $e^{-r/a_0}$ form, the correction becomes $\tfrac25R^2-\tfrac13R^3+\cdots$ (in units where $a_0=1$), and the $R^3$ term is only $\tfrac56(R/a_0)\sim2\times10^{-5}$ times the first term. Even though the size is tiny, spectroscopy of the hydrogen atom is carried out with extremely high precision, so this correction is observable.

Exercise 27.5: Second-order perturbation theory for the quantum-confined Stark effect

Solution

(1) $k=4$: $X_{41}=\dfrac{2}{L}\displaystyle\int_0^Lx\sin\frac{4\pi x}{L}\sin\frac{\pi x}{L}\dd x=\frac1L\int_0^Lx\Bigl[\cos\frac{3\pi x}{L}-\cos\frac{5\pi x}{L}\Bigr]\dd x$. With $\int_0^Lx\cos qx\dd x=\dfrac{\cos qL-1}{q^2}$ (integration by parts, $\sin qL=0$), setting $q=j\pi/L$ gives $\dfrac{((-1)^j-1)L^2}{j^2\pi^2}$. $j=3$: $-\dfrac{2L^2}{9\pi^2}$, $j=5$: $-\dfrac{2L^2}{25\pi^2}$.

$$ X_{41}=\frac1L\Bigl[-\frac{2L^2}{9\pi^2}+\frac{2L^2}{25\pi^2}\Bigr]=\frac{2L}{\pi^2}\Bigl(-\frac19+\frac1{25}\Bigr)=\frac{2L}{\pi^2}\cdot\Bigl(-\frac{16}{225}\Bigr)=-\frac{32L}{225\pi^2}=-0.01441\,L . $$

Putting $k=4$ into the general formula $-8kL/(\pi^2(k^2-1)^2)$ gives $-32L/(\pi^2\cdot225)$, which agrees.

(2) $E_1^{(2)}=-\dfrac{128}{\pi^6}\dfrac{me_0^2F^2L^4}{\hbar^2}S$, $S=\sum_{k=2,4,\dots}\dfrac{k^2}{(k^2-1)^5}$. The $k=2$ term is $\dfrac{4}{3^5}=\dfrac{4}{243}=0.016461$, and the exact sum is $S=\dfrac{\pi^2(15-\pi^2)}{3072}=0.016483$, so the fraction is $0.016461/0.016483=0.9987$, that is, $99.87\ \%$. With $k=2$ alone, the value of Example 27.11 is $-1.927\ \mathrm{meV}$ (the total is $-1.930\ \mathrm{meV}$).

(3) $E_1^{(2)}\propto mF^2$. From the electron value ($m^*=0.067\,m_{\mathrm e}$) $-1.93\ \mathrm{meV}$ at $F=100\ \mathrm{kV/cm}$, at $30\ \mathrm{kV/cm}$ (the electric field is $0.3$ times, so its square is $0.09$ times) we get $-1.93\times0.09=-0.174\ \mathrm{meV}$. For the hole ($0.45\,m_{\mathrm e}$ is an assumed value), the mass ratio is $0.45/0.067=6.72$ times, so at $30\ \mathrm{kV/cm}$ it is $-0.174\times6.72=-1.17\ \mathrm{meV}$. The total decrease of the transition energy for the electron and hole together is $0.174+1.17=1.34\ \mathrm{meV}$ (the change in the exciton binding energy was neglected).

The condition for the applicability of perturbation theory is $e_0F\abs{X_{21}}/(E_2-E_1)\ll1$. $e_0F\abs{X_{21}}=e_0F\times0.180L$ is independent of the mass, and is $5.4\ \mathrm{meV}$ at $30\ \mathrm{kV/cm}$ and $18.0\ \mathrm{meV}$ at $100\ \mathrm{kV/cm}$. The level spacing $E_2-E_1=3E_1$ is $3\times56.12=168.4\ \mathrm{meV}$ for the electron and $3\times56.12\times0.067/0.45=25.1\ \mathrm{meV}$ for the hole. Therefore the ratios are $0.032$ ($30\ \mathrm{kV/cm}$) and $0.107$ ($100\ \mathrm{kV/cm}$) for the electron, and $0.215$ and $0.72$ for the hole. For the hole at $100\ \mathrm{kV/cm}$ the ratio is $0.72$, and second-order perturbation theory must not be used. Indeed, in exact diagonalization the shift of the hole is $-10.7\ \mathrm{meV}$, and the second-order value $-13.0\ \mathrm{meV}$ is $21\ \%$ too large. At $30\ \mathrm{kV/cm}$, the second-order value is $-1.17\ \mathrm{meV}$ against the exact $-1.14\ \mathrm{meV}$ (error $2.5\ \%$).

Exercise 27.6: Checking the third-order energy

Solution

(1) The formula is $E_1^{(3)}=\sum_{k,i\ne1}\dfrac{V_{1k}V_{ki}V_{i1}}{(E_1-E_k)(E_1-E_i)}-V_{11}\sum_{k\ne1}\dfrac{\abs{V_{k1}}^2}{(E_1-E_k)^2}$. For a two-level system only the single term $k=i=2$ remains, and since $E_1-E_2=-\Delta$,

$$ E_1^{(3)}=\frac{V_{12}V_{22}V_{21}}{\Delta^2}-\frac{V_{11}V_{21}^2}{\Delta^2}=\frac{(v_2-v_1)V^2}{\Delta^2}. $$

The numerical value is $\dfrac{(0.03-0.01)\times0.02^2}{0.10^2}=8.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV}=0.80\ \mathrm{meV}$. This also agrees with the coefficient of $\lambda^3$ in the general exact solution (the expansion of the lower eigenvalue $\bigl[\Delta+\lambda(v_1+v_2)-\sqrt{(\Delta+\lambda(v_2-v_1))^2+4\lambda^2V^2}\bigr]/2$).

(2) $\lambda=0.1$: $E^{(0)}=0$, $\lambda E^{(1)}=\lambda v_1=1.000\times10^{-3}$, $\lambda^2E^{(2)}=-\lambda^2V^2/\Delta=-4.0\times10^{-5}$, $\lambda^3E^{(3)}=8.0\times10^{-7}$ (eV). The sum through second order is $9.600\times10^{-4}$, and adding the third order gives $9.608\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV}$, which agrees with the exact value $9.6080\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV}$ to four digits (the error of $8\times10^{-7}$ through second order is reduced to about $10^{-9}$ by the third order).

(3) For state 2 of the three-level model of Example 27.7, $E^{(0)}=1.000$, $E^{(1)}=0.020$, $E^{(2)}=-6.667\times10^{-4}$ (eV). Numerical diagonalization of the matrix $\hat{H}_0+0.01\hat{V}$ for $\lambda=0.01$ gives the middle eigenvalue $E=1.0001999\ldots$, and $\bigl(E-E^{(0)}-\lambda E^{(1)}-\lambda^2E^{(2)}\bigr)/\lambda^3=-2.3237\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV}$. This agrees with the value from the formula, $E_2^{(3)}=-2.3222\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV}$, to $0.07\ \%$, and the difference is due to the $\lambda^4$ term ($E^{(4)}\lambda$). For $\lambda=0.02$ it is $-2.3252\times10^{-3}$, and the smaller $\lambda$ is, the closer it gets to the value from the formula.

Exercise 27.7: The radius of convergence and partial sums for the two-level model

Solution

(1) With $E_-=\bigl(\Delta-\sqrt{\Delta^2+4\lambda^2V^2}\bigr)/2$, let $t=(\lambda V/\Delta)^2$; then $E_-=\dfrac\Delta2\bigl(1-\sqrt{1+4t}\bigr)$. From $\sqrt{1+4t}=1+2t-2t^2+4t^3-\cdots$ (using $\sqrt{1+x}=1+\tfrac x2-\tfrac{x^2}{8}+\tfrac{x^3}{16}-\cdots$ with $x=4t$), we get $E_-=\dfrac\Delta2\bigl(-2t+2t^2-4t^3+\cdots\bigr)=-\Delta\bigl(t-t^2+2t^3-\cdots\bigr)$. The general-term formula $-\Delta(-1)^{k-1}C_{k-1}t^k$ agrees with this: $k=1$: $-\Delta C_0t=-\Delta t$, $k=2$: $+\Delta C_1t^2=+\Delta t^2$, and $k=3$: $-\Delta C_2t^3=-2\Delta t^3$ ($C_0=C_1=1$, $C_2=2$).

(2) The radius of convergence is $\lambda_{\mathrm c}=\Delta/(2V)=0.10/0.12=0.833$. For $V=0.06\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $\Delta=0.10\ \mathrm{eV}$, the terms $-\Delta(-1)^{k-1}C_{k-1}(\lambda\times0.6)^{2k}$ at $\lambda=0.5$, where $t=0.09$, are:

second order: $-\Delta t=-9.000\ \mathrm{meV}$, fourth order: $+\Delta t^2=+0.810$, sixth order: $-2\Delta t^3=-0.1458$, eighth order: $+5\Delta t^4=+0.0328$, …. The partial sums are $-9.000,\ -8.190,\ -8.336,\ -8.303,\ -8.311,\ -8.309,\ \dots$, and they converge to the exact value $\bigl(0.10-\sqrt{0.01+4\times0.25\times0.0036}\bigr)/2=-8.3095\ \mathrm{meV}$ (the ratio of successive terms is $4\lambda^2V^2/\Delta^2=0.36\lt1$).

For $\lambda=1$, $t=0.36$: second order: $-36.00$, fourth order: $+12.96$, sixth order: $-9.331$ (partial sums $-36.00,\ -23.04,\ -32.37$). The partial sums oscillate above and below the exact value $-28.10\ \mathrm{meV}$ with an amplitude of $\pm4\sim8\ \mathrm{meV}$ and do not converge even when the order is raised (the limit of the ratio of successive terms is $4\times0.36=1.44\gt1$). Therefore the series converges for $\lambda=0.5$, whereas $\lambda=1$ lies outside the radius of convergence $0.833$.

Exercise 27.8: The second-order correction for the step

Solution

With the exact matrix element $V_{k1}=V_0\Bigl[\dfrac{\sin((k-1)\pi\delta/L)}{(k-1)\pi}-\dfrac{\sin((k+1)\pi\delta/L)}{(k+1)\pi}\Bigr]$ ($\delta/L=0.05$) and $V_0/E_1=5.345$, each term is $-\bigl(\tfrac{V_0}{E_1}\tilde{V}_{k1}\bigr)^2/(k^2-1)$ (in units of $E_1$, with $\tilde{V}_{k1}=V_{k1}/V_0$).

(1) The values of the three terms are $k=2$: $-2.514\times10^{-5}$, $k=3$: $-2.069\times10^{-5}$, and $k=4$: $-1.895\times10^{-5}$, and their sum is $-6.48\times10^{-5}E_1$ ($-0.0036\ \mathrm{meV}$). This is only about $30\ \%$ of the total, $-2.1415\times10^{-4}E_1$. The sum converges very slowly with respect to $k$:

Upper limit of $k$4102040100400
$E_1^{(2)}/E_1\ (\times10^{-4})$$-0.648$$-1.530$$-2.088$$-2.135$$-2.141$$-2.1415$

The sum reaches about $97.5\ \%$ of the total by $k\simeq L/\delta=20$ and $99.7\ \%$ at $k=40$. This is because, although the denominator grows with the level spacing ($E_k\propto k^2$), the width $\delta$ of the step is short, and so the matrix element $V_{k1}$ hardly decreases until $k\simeq L/(\pi\delta)\simeq6$ is exceeded.

(2) With the Taylor-approximated matrix element $V_{k1}\simeq\varepsilon E_1k$, the term is $-\varepsilon^2E_1k^2/(k^2-1)=-\varepsilon^2E_1\bigl(1+\tfrac{1}{k^2-1}\bigr)$ ($\varepsilon^2=1.93\times10^{-5}$), which does not go to 0 even as $k\to\infty$ but approaches the constant value $-\varepsilon^2E_1$. Therefore the sum grows in proportion to the upper limit of $k$ (each term is about $-2\times10^{-5}E_1$); it is a divergent sum and gives no meaningful value. The Taylor approximation can be used only for $(k\pm1)\pi\delta/L\ll1$, that is, for $k\ll L/(\pi\delta)\simeq6$, and the exact matrix elements are needed for the sum in second-order perturbation theory.

(3) $E_1^{(2)}=-2.1415\times10^{-4}E_1=-2.1415\times10^{-4}\times56.12\ \mathrm{meV}=-0.0120\ \mathrm{meV}$. The first-order energy (from the exact integral) is $E_1^{(1)}/E_1=4.375\times10^{-3}$ (with the Taylor approximation, $4.396\times10^{-3}$), and adding the second-order term gives $E_1/E_1^{(0)}=1+4.375\times10^{-3}-2.14\times10^{-4}=1.004161$. The difference from the numerically diagonalized value $1.004171$ is $1.0\times10^{-5}$ (the contribution of third order and higher), and including the second-order term reduces the error from $2.0\times10^{-4}$ at first order to $1.0\times10^{-5}$.
