Chapter 38: Chemical Bonding (1) — The Valence Bond Method and Hybrid Orbitals

Exercise 38.1: Slater determinant representation of the triplet

Solution

Let the spin orbitals be $\chi_{\mathrm A}=A\alpha$, $\bar{\chi}_{\mathrm A}=A\beta$, $\chi_{\mathrm B}=B\alpha$, $\bar{\chi}_{\mathrm B}=B\beta$, and let $\Phi_1=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\bigl[\chi_{\mathrm A}(1)\bar{\chi}_{\mathrm B}(2)-\bar{\chi}_{\mathrm B}(1)\chi_{\mathrm A}(2)\bigr]$ and $\Phi_2=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\bigl[\chi_{\mathrm B}(1)\bar{\chi}_{\mathrm A}(2)-\bar{\chi}_{\mathrm A}(1)\chi_{\mathrm B}(2)\bigr]$. Expanding into four terms, we obtain

$$ \Psi_-\frac{\alpha(1)\beta(2)+\alpha(2)\beta(1)}{\sqrt2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\bigl[A(1)B(2)\alpha(1)\beta(2)+A(1)B(2)\alpha(2)\beta(1)-A(2)B(1)\alpha(1)\beta(2)-A(2)B(1)\alpha(2)\beta(1)\bigr]. $$

The first term is $[A\alpha](1)[B\beta](2)=\chi_{\mathrm A}(1)\bar{\chi}_{\mathrm B}(2)$, and the fourth term is $-[B\beta](1)[A\alpha](2)=-\bar{\chi}_{\mathrm B}(1)\chi_{\mathrm A}(2)$. The sum of these two terms is $\sqrt2\,\Phi_1$. The second term is $[A\beta](1)[B\alpha](2)=\bar{\chi}_{\mathrm A}(1)\chi_{\mathrm B}(2)$, and the third term is $-[B\alpha](1)[A\beta](2)=-\chi_{\mathrm B}(1)\bar{\chi}_{\mathrm A}(2)$. The sum of these two terms is $-\bigl[\chi_{\mathrm B}(1)\bar{\chi}_{\mathrm A}(2)-\bar{\chi}_{\mathrm A}(1)\chi_{\mathrm B}(2)\bigr]=-\sqrt2\,\Phi_2$. Therefore

$$ \Psi_-\frac{\alpha(1)\beta(2)+\alpha(2)\beta(1)}{\sqrt2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\bigl(\sqrt2\,\Phi_1-\sqrt2\,\Phi_2\bigr)=\Phi_1-\Phi_2 . $$

Normalization: $\braket{\Phi_1}{\Phi_1}=\braket{\Phi_2}{\Phi_2}=1$ and $\braket{\Phi_1}{\Phi_2}=S^2$ (Example 38.3), so $\braket{\Phi_1-\Phi_2}{\Phi_1-\Phi_2}=1+1-2S^2=2(1-S^2)$. The normalized triplet is $(\Phi_1-\Phi_2)/\sqrt{2(1-S^2)}$, and its normalization constant $1/\sqrt{2(1-S^2)}$ is equal to the normalization constant $N_-$ of the spatial function $\Psi_-$.

Energy: Since the Hamiltonian does not contain the spin, the three states $\Psi_-\alpha\alpha$, $\Psi_-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\alpha\beta+\beta\alpha)$, and $\Psi_-\beta\beta$ all have the same spatial function $\Psi_-$. In the expectation value of the energy, the spin-function part (which is normalized) factors out, and the expectation value becomes the energy $E_-$ of the spatial function $\Psi_-$. Therefore the three states have the same energy $E_-$ (they are threefold degenerate, which is the origin of the name “triplet”).

Exercise 38.2: Energy difference between the singlet and the triplet

Solution

(1) We use $E_\pm-2E_{\mathrm H}=\dfrac{Q\pm X}{1\pm S^2}$.

$$ E_--E_+=\frac{Q-X}{1-S^2}-\frac{Q+X}{1+S^2}=\frac{(Q-X)(1+S^2)-(Q+X)(1-S^2)}{(1-S^2)(1+S^2)}. $$

The numerator is $Q+QS^2-X-XS^2-Q+QS^2-X+XS^2=2QS^2-2X$ and the denominator is $1-S^4$, so

$$ E_--E_+=\frac{2\,(QS^2-X)}{1-S^4}. $$

(2) For $S=0.7529$ we have $S^2=0.56692$, $S^4=0.32141$, and $1-S^4=0.67859$. Since $2QS^2=2\times(-0.00227)\times0.56692=-0.00257$ and $-2X=+0.32600$, the numerator is $0.32343$.

$$ E_--E_+=\frac{0.32343}{0.67859}=0.47660\,E_{\mathrm h}=0.47660\times27.2114\ \mathrm{eV}=12.97\ \mathrm{eV}. $$

(This agrees with $10.10-(-2.87)=12.97\ \mathrm{eV}$ obtained in Example 38.2.) The quantity $-2X/(1-S^4)=0.32600/0.67859=0.4804\,E_{\mathrm h}$ is nearly equal to $E_--E_+=0.4766\,E_{\mathrm h}$ (about 101%; the $2QS^2$ term cancels it by only a little under 1%), so $E_--E_+$ is almost entirely the contribution of $-2X$.

(3) As $R$ becomes large, $S\to0$, and $S^4$ in the denominator is negligible compared with 1. Moreover, $Q$ is even smaller than $X$, so $QS^2$ in the numerator is also negligible compared with $X$. Therefore $E_--E_+\to-2X$. Since $X\lt0$, $E_--E_+\gt0$; that is, the triplet is higher. (Numerically, at $R=3\,a_0$, $E_--E_+=0.0791\,E_{\mathrm h}$ and $-2X=0.0796\,E_{\mathrm h}$, which are nearly equal.)

Since $\mathcal{J}=E_{\mathrm T}-E_{\mathrm S}=E_--E_+\gt0$, the singlet ($\Psi_+$, antiparallel spins) is stable. That is, the two spins align antiferromagnetically.

Exercise 38.3: Nodal planes of the two $\pi$ bonds of the nitrogen molecule

Solution

(1) We have $A_x(i)=g_{\mathrm A}(r_{\mathrm{A}i})\,x_i$ and $B_x(i)=g_{\mathrm B}(r_{\mathrm{B}i})\,x_i$ ($i=1,2$; $x_i$ is the $x$ coordinate of electron $i$; a coordinate perpendicular to the bond axis is the same measured from either nucleus), so

$$ \Psi_{\pi x}(1,2)=g_{\mathrm A}(r_{\mathrm{A}1})x_1\,g_{\mathrm B}(r_{\mathrm{B}2})x_2+g_{\mathrm A}(r_{\mathrm{A}2})x_2\,g_{\mathrm B}(r_{\mathrm{B}1})x_1=x_1x_2\bigl[g_{\mathrm A}(r_{\mathrm{A}1})g_{\mathrm B}(r_{\mathrm{B}2})+g_{\mathrm A}(r_{\mathrm{A}2})g_{\mathrm B}(r_{\mathrm{B}1})\bigr]. $$

The expression in the square brackets does not vanish, because the radial parts $g_{\mathrm A}$ and $g_{\mathrm B}$ have the same sign (for example, the radial part of a 2p orbital is positive near the origin). Therefore $\Psi_{\pi x}=0$ holds only when $x_1=0$ or $x_2=0$, and the nodal plane is $x=0$ (the $yz$ plane). This plane contains the bond axis (the $z$ axis).

(2) The function of the electron pair of the $\pi_y$ bond, $\Psi_{\pi y}(1,2)=A_y(1)B_y(2)+A_y(2)B_y(1)$ (with $A_y=g_{\mathrm A}\,y$ and $B_y=g_{\mathrm B}\,y$), can likewise be factorized as $y_1y_2\bigl[g_{\mathrm A}(r_{\mathrm{A}1})g_{\mathrm B}(r_{\mathrm{B}2})+g_{\mathrm A}(r_{\mathrm{A}2})g_{\mathrm B}(r_{\mathrm{B}1})\bigr]$, and its nodal plane is $y=0$ (the $zx$ plane). This plane also contains the bond axis. The normals of the two nodal planes $x=0$ and $y=0$ (the $x$ axis and the $y$ axis) are orthogonal, so the angle between the planes is $90^\circ$.

(3) We have $\Psi_\sigma=A_z(1)B_z(2)+A_z(2)B_z(1)$, with $A_z=g_{\mathrm A}\,(z-z_{\mathrm A})$ and $B_z=g_{\mathrm B}\,(z-z_{\mathrm B})$. These do not depend on the azimuthal angle around the bond axis ($x,y$ appear only through $r_{\mathrm A},r_{\mathrm B}$), so a factor that represents a “plane containing the bond axis,” such as $x_1$ or $x_2$, cannot be pulled out. In fact, even if electron 1 is placed on the plane $x_1=0$ or on the plane $y_1=0$, $\Psi_\sigma$ is in general not zero. Note also that if electron 1 is placed on the plane $z=z_{\mathrm A}$, then $A_z(1)$ in the first term vanishes, but the second term $A_z(2)B_z(1)$ is in general not zero, so the planes $z=z_{\mathrm A}$ and $z=z_{\mathrm B}$ are not nodal planes of $\Psi_\sigma$. $\Psi_\sigma=0$ holds only on the five-dimensional surface in the six-dimensional configuration space that satisfies $A_z(1)B_z(2)=-A_z(2)B_z(1)$, and there is no nodal plane containing the bond axis, such as $x=0$ and $y=0$ for $\Psi_\pi$. The number of nodal planes containing the bond axis is 0 for a $\sigma$ bond and 1 for a $\pi$ bond, in agreement with the classification in Table 38.3.

Exercise 38.4: Orthonormality of the sp² hybrid orbitals

Solution

The rows of the matrix are $\eta_1\leftrightarrow\bigl(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3},\,0,\,\sqrt{\tfrac23},\,0\bigr)$, $\eta_2\leftrightarrow\bigl(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3},\,\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2},\,-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt6},\,0\bigr)$, $\eta_3\leftrightarrow\bigl(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3},\,-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2},\,-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt6},\,0\bigr)$, and $\phi_{2p_z}\leftrightarrow(0,0,0,1)$. We compute the inner products of the rows (the components of $UU^{\mathrm T}$).

$$ \begin{aligned} \eta_1\cdot\eta_1&=\tfrac13+\tfrac23=1,\\ \eta_2\cdot\eta_2&=\tfrac13+\tfrac12+\tfrac16=1,\qquad\eta_3\cdot\eta_3=\tfrac13+\tfrac12+\tfrac16=1,\\ \eta_1\cdot\eta_2&=\tfrac13+0+\sqrt{\tfrac23}\left(-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}\right)=\tfrac13-\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{18}}=\tfrac13-\tfrac13=0,\qquad\eta_1\cdot\eta_3=0\ (\text{similarly}),\\ \eta_2\cdot\eta_3&=\tfrac13-\tfrac12+\tfrac16=0. \end{aligned} $$

Also, the row of $\phi_{2p_z}$ is orthogonal to the other three rows because their fourth components are all 0, and $(0,0,0,1)\cdot(0,0,0,1)=1$. Hence $UU^{\mathrm T}=1$, and $U$ is an orthogonal matrix. (In Python, U@U.T coincides with the identity matrix.)

Sum of the three: the coefficient of $\phi_{2s}$ is $3\times\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}=\sqrt3$, the coefficient of $\phi_{2p_x}$ is $0+\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}=0$, the coefficient of $\phi_{2p_y}$ is $\sqrt{\tfrac23}-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}=\sqrt{\tfrac23}-\tfrac{2}{\sqrt6}=\sqrt{\tfrac23}-\sqrt{\tfrac46}=0$, and the coefficient of $\phi_{2p_z}$ is 0, so

$$ \eta_1+\eta_2+\eta_3=\sqrt3\,\phi_{2s}\qquad\left(\phi_{2s}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}(\eta_1+\eta_2+\eta_3)\right). $$

This agrees with the fact that the 2s orbital is distributed among the three hybrid orbitals in shares of $\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right)^2=\tfrac13$ each (s component $33.3\ \%$).

Exercise 38.5: Hybridization ratio of ammonia

Solution

With Coulson's condition $\lambda^2=-1/\cos\theta$ and $\theta=107.8^\circ$: since $\cos107.8^\circ=-0.30570$, we get $\lambda^2=1/0.30570=3.271$. The s fraction is $\dfrac{1}{1+3.271}=0.2341$ ($23.4\ \%$), and the p fraction is $0.7659$ ($76.6\ \%$). The hybridization type is sp$^{3.27}$.

The single 2s orbital of N is used up completely by the four hybrid orbitals (three N–H bonds and one lone pair), so $\sum_is_i=1$. The three bonds use $3\times0.2341=0.7024$, so the s fraction of the lone pair is $s_{\mathrm{lp}}=1-0.7024=0.2976$ ($29.8\ \%$), and its p fraction is $0.7024$ (p/s $=2.36$). The total of the p fractions is $3\times0.7659+0.7024=3.000$, which uses up exactly the three 2p orbitals.

The angle between an N–H bond and the lone pair is given by the formula for the angle between two orthogonal hybrid orbitals with different s fractions, $\cos\theta_{ij}=-\sqrt{\dfrac{s_is_j}{(1-s_i)(1-s_j)}}$, with $s_i=0.2341$ and $s_j=0.2976$:

$$ \cos\theta=-\sqrt{\frac{0.2341\times0.2976}{0.7659\times0.7024}}=-\sqrt{\frac{0.06967}{0.53796}}=-\sqrt{0.12951}=-0.3599,\qquad\theta=111.1^\circ . $$

The angle between a bond and the lone pair is wider than the angle of $107.8^\circ$ between the N–H bonds (the lone pair has more s component and presses the bonds together).

Exercise 38.6: Rotation of ethylene and the $\pi$ bond

Solution

Take the C=C axis as the $y$ axis (the skeleton of in-plane $\sigma$ bonds lies in the $xy$ plane, and $2p_z$ is perpendicular to the plane). Consider the overlap between the $2p_z$ orbital of carbon atom A and the orbital $p_z'^{\mathrm B}$ obtained by rotating the $2p_z$ orbital of carbon atom B about the $y$ axis by the twist angle $\tau$. A rotation about the $y$ axis mixes the $z$ and $x$ components, so the rotated orbital is $p_z'^{\mathrm B}=\cos\tau\,p_z^{\mathrm B}+\sin\tau\,p_x^{\mathrm B}$. Therefore

$$ S_\pi(\tau)=\braket{p_z^{\mathrm A}}{p_z'^{\mathrm B}}=\cos\tau\,\braket{p_z^{\mathrm A}}{p_z^{\mathrm B}}+\sin\tau\,\braket{p_z^{\mathrm A}}{p_x^{\mathrm B}}. $$

The integrand of the second term is $z\,x\,g_{\mathrm A}(r_{\mathrm A})g_{\mathrm B}(r_{\mathrm B})$, which is an odd function under $z\to-z$ (reflection in the plane), so its integral over all space is 0. Hence $S_\pi(\tau)=S_\pi(0)\cos\tau$. It is maximal at $\tau=0$ (planar), half as large at $\tau=60^\circ$, and 0 at $\tau=90^\circ$ (the $\pi$ bond is broken).

Suppose that the barrier at $\tau=90^\circ$, where the $\pi$ bond is almost completely broken, is $E=2.7\ \mathrm{eV}$ ($2.7\times96.485=260\ \mathrm{kJ}$ per mole). At room temperature, $k_{\mathrm B}T=8.617\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV/K}\times300\ \mathrm{K}=0.02585\ \mathrm{eV}$, so $E/k_{\mathrm B}T=2.7/0.02585=104.4$, and we obtain

$$ e^{-E/k_{\mathrm B}T}=e^{-104.4}=4.4\times10^{-46}. $$

Only with such a tiny probability can thermal motion carry a molecule over the barrier to rotation. Therefore rotation about the C=C double bond virtually never occurs, and the cis and trans isomers, which differ in the positions of the substituents, can exist stably as separate molecules (isomers) that never change into one another. Cis–trans conversion occurs only under special conditions, such as light or a catalyst.

Exercise 38.7: Carbyne and polyacetylene

Solution

Polyacetylene (each carbon of the main chain is bonded to the two neighboring carbon atoms and one hydrogen atom, three atoms in all): (1) The hybridization type is sp². (2) There are three $\sigma$ bonds (two C–C and one C–H); three of the four valence electrons are used for the $\sigma$ bonds, and the remaining one becomes a $\pi$ electron (in the $2p_z$ orbital). (3) The three $\sigma$ bonds lie in the same plane at about $120^\circ$ to one another, so the carbon skeleton is a planar zigzag chain (trans form). (4) The $\pi$ electrons are in the $2p_z$ orbitals perpendicular to the plane; they form $\pi$ bonds between neighbors along the chain (conjugation, in which single and double bonds alternate) and spread above and below the plane of the chain. There is one $\pi$ electron per carbon atom.

Carbyne (each carbon is bonded only to the two neighboring carbon atoms): (1) The hybridization type is sp. (2) There are two $\sigma$ bonds (to the neighboring carbons); two of the four valence electrons are used for the $\sigma$ bonds, and the remaining two become $\pi$ electrons (one each in $2p_x$ and $2p_y$). (3) The two $\sigma$ bonds point in exactly opposite directions, so the skeleton is a straight line ($180^\circ$). (4) $2p_x$ and $2p_y$ form two mutually orthogonal $\pi$-bond systems, and the combined electron density spreads with cylindrical symmetry around the bond axis, as in Example 38.11. There are two $\pi$ electrons per carbon atom (whether the chain is the alternating sequence of triple and single bonds, $-\mathrm{C}{\equiv}\mathrm{C}-$, or the sequence of double bonds, $=\mathrm{C}{=}\mathrm{C}=$, each carbon has two $\sigma$ bonds + two $\pi$ electrons).

In short, the difference is that polyacetylene is “a planar chain with one $\pi$-electron system (above and below the plane)” and carbyne is “a linear chain with two orthogonal $\pi$-electron systems (cylindrical).”

Exercise 38.8: Hybridization ratio of hydrogen sulfide

Solution

Since $\cos92.1^\circ=-0.03664$, the hybrid orbital of the S–H bond has $\lambda^2=-1/\cos\theta=1/0.03664=27.29$. The s fraction is $\dfrac{1}{1+27.29}=0.03535$ ($3.5\ \%$), and the p fraction is $96.5\ \%$ (sp$^{27}$). The bonds are made of almost pure 3p orbitals.

The sum of the s fractions of the four hybrid orbitals is 1: the two bonds use $2\times0.03535=0.0707$, so the two lone-pair hybrid orbitals share the remaining $0.9293$, each having $s_{\mathrm{lp}}=0.4647$ ($46.5\ \%$) and a p fraction of $53.5\ \%$ (p/s $=1.15$). The total of the p fractions is $2\times0.9647+2\times0.5353=3.000$.

Angle between the lone pairs: $\cos\theta=-\dfrac{s_{\mathrm{lp}}}{1-s_{\mathrm{lp}}}=-\dfrac{0.4647}{0.5353}=-0.8681$, $\theta=150.2^\circ$. Angle between an S–H bond and a lone pair: $\cos\theta=-\sqrt{\dfrac{0.03535\times0.4647}{0.96465\times0.5353}}=-\sqrt{0.03181}=-0.1784$, $\theta=100.3^\circ$.

Compared with $\mathrm{H_2O}$ (s component of the bonds $20.0\ \%$, of the lone pairs $30.0\ \%$, angle between the lone pairs $115.3^\circ$), in sulfur the bonds have almost no s component (bond angle $92.1^\circ$, nearly $90^\circ$), and the s component gathers in the lone pairs ($46.5\ \%$, nearly sp). That is, the $3s$ electrons of sulfur are hardly used for bonding and enter, as lone pairs, orbitals of strong s character. In oxygen, some s component also mixes into the bonds, and the bond angle widens.

Chapter 39: Chemical Bonding (2) — The Molecular Orbital Method, the Hydrogen Molecular Ion, and Overlap Integrals

Exercise 39.1: LCAO molecular orbitals of $\mathrm{H_2^+}$ at $R=1.4\,a_0$ (the equilibrium internuclear distance of $\mathrm{H_2}$)

Solution

$R=1.4\,a_0$ is close to the equilibrium internuclear distance of the hydrogen molecule $\mathrm{H_2}$ ($0.741\ \text{Å}$). Here we evaluate the LCAO molecular orbitals of $\mathrm{H_2^+}$ at this distance.

(1) Since $S=0.7529$, we have $C_+=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\times1.7529}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3.5058}}=0.5341$ and $C_-=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\times0.2471}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{0.4942}}=1.4225$.

(2) In atomic units, $\phi_{1s}(r)=e^{-r}/\sqrt\pi$. At the position of nucleus B, $r_B=0$ and $r_A=R=1.4$, so $\phi_B=1/\sqrt\pi=0.5642$ and $\phi_A=e^{-1.4}/\sqrt\pi=0.2466\times0.5642=0.1391$. At the midpoint, $r_A=r_B=0.7$, and $\phi_A=\phi_B=e^{-0.7}/\sqrt\pi=0.4966\times0.5642=0.2802$. Therefore

$$ \psi_+(\text{nucleus B})=0.5341\times(0.1391+0.5642)=0.3756,\qquad \psi_-(\text{nucleus B})=1.4225\times(0.1391-0.5642)=-0.6047, $$ $$ \psi_+(\text{midpoint})=0.5341\times(0.2802+0.2802)=0.2993\qquad(\text{units }a_0^{-3/2}) $$

hold.

(3) At the midpoint, $\phi_A=\phi_B\equiv\phi_{\mathrm m}$, so $\psi_+^2=C_+^2(2\phi_{\mathrm m})^2=\dfrac{4\phi_{\mathrm m}^2}{2(1+S)}=\dfrac{2}{1+S}\phi_{\mathrm m}^2$. The average of the 1s densities of the two atoms is $\tfrac12(\phi_{\mathrm m}^2+\phi_{\mathrm m}^2)=\phi_{\mathrm m}^2$, so the ratio is $\dfrac{2}{1+S}=\dfrac{2}{1.7529}=1.141$. Numerically as well, $\psi_+^2=0.2993^2=0.08956$ and $\phi_{\mathrm m}^2=0.2802^2=0.07849$, which give the ratio $1.141$.

(4) The electron density is $\abs{\psi_+}^2=\dfrac{\phi_A^2+\phi_B^2}{2(1+S)}+\dfrac{2\phi_A\phi_B}{2(1+S)}$. Integrating over all space, the first term gives $\dfrac{1+1}{2(1+S)}=\dfrac{1}{1+S}=0.570$ (0.570 of an electron) and the second term gives $\dfrac{2S}{2(1+S)}=\dfrac{S}{1+S}=0.430$ (0.430 of an electron); the total is $\dfrac{1+S}{1+S}=1$, which confirms that the orbital is normalized. Compared with the LCAO equilibrium of $\mathrm{H_2^+}$ ($S=0.46$: $0.685$ and $0.315$), at the $\mathrm{H_2}$ distance, where the overlap is larger, the contribution of the interference term is larger.

Exercise 39.2: Expansion of the overlap integral about $R=0$

Solution

(1) Multiply $e^{-R}=1-R+\dfrac{R^2}{2}-\dfrac{R^3}{6}+\dfrac{R^4}{24}-\cdots$ by $1+R+\dfrac{R^2}{3}$ and collect the coefficient of each power.

  • $R^0$: $1$
  • $R^1$: $1\cdot(-1)+1\cdot1=0$
  • $R^2$: $1\cdot\dfrac12+1\cdot(-1)+\dfrac13\cdot1=\dfrac12-1+\dfrac13=-\dfrac16$
  • $R^3$: $1\cdot\Bigl(-\dfrac16\Bigr)+1\cdot\dfrac12+\dfrac13\cdot(-1)=-\dfrac16+\dfrac12-\dfrac13=0$
  • $R^4$: $1\cdot\dfrac1{24}+1\cdot\Bigl(-\dfrac16\Bigr)+\dfrac13\cdot\dfrac12=\dfrac1{24}-\dfrac16+\dfrac16=\dfrac1{24}$

Hence $S(R)=1-\dfrac{R^2}{6}+\dfrac{R^4}{24}-\cdots$. Since the first-order and third-order terms in $R$ vanish, the slope at $R=0$ is 0.

(2) The condition that the coefficient of $R^2$ in $e^{-\alpha R^2/2}=1-\dfrac{\alpha}{2}R^2+\cdots$ agree with $-\dfrac16$ is $\dfrac\alpha2=\dfrac16$, that is, $\alpha=\dfrac13=0.3333$. The resulting values are: $R=1$: $e^{-1/6}=0.8465$ (exact $S(1)=0.8584$, ratio $0.986$); $R=2$: $e^{-4/6}=0.5134$ ($S(2)=0.5865$, ratio $0.875$); $R=3$: $e^{-9/6}=0.2231$ ($S(3)=0.3485$, ratio $0.640$). Matching the curvature at $R=0$ gives values smaller than the exact ones in the region of large $R$. For the Gaussian function with $\alpha=0.27095$, which maximizes the overlap, the ratios at the same $R$ are $1.017$, $0.992$, $0.848$, and overall this one fits better.

(3) By the product rule, $\dfrac{\dd}{\dd R}\Bigl(1+R+\dfrac{R^2}{3}\Bigr)=1+\dfrac{2R}{3}$ and $\dfrac{\dd}{\dd R}e^{-R}=-e^{-R}$, so

$$ \frac{\dd S}{\dd R}=e^{-R}\Bigl[\Bigl(1+\frac{2R}{3}\Bigr)-\Bigl(1+R+\frac{R^2}{3}\Bigr)\Bigr]=e^{-R}\Bigl(-\frac R3-\frac{R^2}{3}\Bigr)=-\frac{R(1+R)}{3}e^{-R} $$

holds. Since this is negative for $R>0$, $S$ decreases monotonically.

Exercise 39.3: The Jacobian and volume in confocal ellipsoidal coordinates

Solution

(1) Since $\rho^2=x^2+y^2=\dfrac{R^2}{4}\sinh^2\mu\sin^2\nu$ and $z=\dfrac R2\cosh\mu\cos\nu$, we have

$$ r_B^2=\rho^2+\Bigl(z-\frac R2\Bigr)^2=\frac{R^2}{4}\Bigl[\sinh^2\mu\sin^2\nu+(\cosh\mu\cos\nu-1)^2\Bigr] $$

Substitute $\sinh^2\mu\sin^2\nu=(\cosh^2\mu-1)(1-\cos^2\nu)=\cosh^2\mu-\cosh^2\mu\cos^2\nu-1+\cos^2\nu$ and add $(\cosh\mu\cos\nu-1)^2=\cosh^2\mu\cos^2\nu-2\cosh\mu\cos\nu+1$. Then $\cosh^2\mu\cos^2\nu$ and the constants $\mp1$ cancel each other, and the contents of the bracket become $\cosh^2\mu+\cos^2\nu-2\cosh\mu\cos\nu=(\cosh\mu-\cos\nu)^2$. Since $\cosh\mu\ge1\ge\cos\nu$, $r_B=\dfrac R2(\cosh\mu-\cos\nu)$.

(2) Since $\partial(x,y,z)/\partial(\mu,\nu,\varphi)=\Bigl(\dfrac R2\Bigr)^3\sinh\mu\sin\nu(\sinh^2\mu+\sin^2\nu)$, the determinant of the matrix for the transformation in the opposite direction ($\partial(\mu,\nu,\varphi)/\partial(x,y,z)$) is its reciprocal:

$$ \frac{\partial(\mu,\nu,\varphi)}{\partial(x,y,z)}=\frac{1}{(R/2)^3\sinh\mu\sin\nu\,(\sinh^2\mu+\sin^2\nu)} $$

(the two matrices are inverse matrices of each other, and $\det(A^{-1})=1/\det A$).

(3) Since $R=4\,a_0$, $R/2=2\,a_0$, $u_0=\cosh0.5=1.127\,63$, $u_0^3=1.433\,82$, and $u_0^3-u_0=0.306\,20$. Integrating the volume element gives $V=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\Bigl(\dfrac R2\Bigr)^3(u_0^3-u_0)=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\times8\times0.306\,20=10.26\,a_0^3$. The semi-axes are, in the $z$ direction, $\dfrac R2\cosh\mu_0=2\times1.127\,63=2.2553\,a_0$, and in the $x,y$ directions, $\dfrac R2\sinh\mu_0=2\times0.521\,10=1.0422\,a_0$; then $\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\times2.2553\times1.0422^2=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\times2.4496=10.26\,a_0^3$, which agrees.

Exercise 39.4: Overlap integral between a 1s orbital and a 2s orbital (Advanced)

Solution

The product of the orbitals is $\phi_{1s}(r_A)\phi_{2s}(r_B)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt\pi}\dfrac{1}{4\sqrt{2\pi}}(2-r_B)\,e^{-r_A-r_B/2}$. Let $\xi=\cosh\mu$ and $\eta=\cos\nu$. Then $r_A=\dfrac R2(\xi+\eta)$ and $r_B=\dfrac R2(\xi-\eta)$, so the exponent is $r_A+\dfrac{r_B}{2}=\dfrac R2\Bigl(\dfrac32\xi+\dfrac12\eta\Bigr)=a\xi+c\eta$ ($a=\dfrac{3R}{4}$, $c=\dfrac R4$). The volume element is $\dd V=\Bigl(\dfrac R2\Bigr)^3(\xi^2-\eta^2)\,\dd\xi\,\dd\eta\,\dd\varphi$ (here $\dd\xi=\sinh\mu\,\dd\mu$ and $\dd\eta=-\sin\nu\,\dd\nu$; since $\nu:0\to\pi$ corresponds to $\eta:1\to-1$, the direction is reversed and the integral becomes $\int_{-1}^1\dd\eta$), and the $\varphi$ integral gives $2\pi$, so

$$ S_{1s,2s}=\frac{1}{4\sqrt2\,\pi}\cdot2\pi\Bigl(\frac R2\Bigr)^3\int_1^\infty\!\!\dd\xi\int_{-1}^{1}\!\!\dd\eta\,(\xi^2-\eta^2)\Bigl(2-\frac R2(\xi-\eta)\Bigr)e^{-a\xi-c\eta} $$

(here the coefficient is $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt\pi}\dfrac{1}{4\sqrt{2\pi}}=\dfrac{1}{4\sqrt2\,\pi}$, and $\dfrac{1}{4\sqrt2\pi}\cdot2\pi=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}$). Expanding the polynomial part of the integrand gives

$$ (\xi^2-\eta^2)\Bigl(2-\frac R2\xi+\frac R2\eta\Bigr)=2\xi^2-\frac R2\xi^3+\frac R2\xi^2\eta-2\eta^2+\frac R2\xi\eta^2-\frac R2\eta^3 $$

Let $A_m=\displaystyle\int_1^\infty\xi^me^{-a\xi}\dd\xi$ and $B_n=\displaystyle\int_{-1}^1\eta^ne^{-c\eta}\dd\eta$. Then the integral is $2A_2B_0-\dfrac R2A_3B_0+\dfrac R2A_2B_1-2A_0B_2+\dfrac R2A_1B_2-\dfrac R2A_0B_3$. By integration by parts, $A_0=\dfrac{e^{-a}}{a}$, $A_1=e^{-a}\Bigl(\dfrac1a+\dfrac1{a^2}\Bigr)$, $A_2=e^{-a}\Bigl(\dfrac1a+\dfrac2{a^2}+\dfrac2{a^3}\Bigr)$, $A_3=e^{-a}\Bigl(\dfrac1a+\dfrac3{a^2}+\dfrac6{a^3}+\dfrac6{a^4}\Bigr)$, $B_0=\dfrac{2\sinh c}{c}$, $B_1=-\dfrac{2\cosh c}{c}+\dfrac{B_0}{c}$, $B_2=\dfrac{2\sinh c}{c}+\dfrac{2}{c}B_1$, and $B_3=-\dfrac{2\cosh c}{c}+\dfrac3cB_2$. Combining these and simplifying, we obtain

$$ S_{1s,2s}(R)=\frac{16\sqrt2}{27R}\Bigl[\bigl(-3R^2+22R-64\bigr)e^{-R/2}+\bigl(10R+64\bigr)e^{-R}\Bigr] $$

For $R=2\,a_0$, we have $a=1.5$ and $c=0.5$, and $A_0=0.14875$, $A_1=0.24792$, $A_2=0.47932$, $A_3=1.10739$, $B_0=2.08438$, $B_1=-0.34174$, $B_2=0.71742$, $B_3=-0.20601$; the six terms are $2A_2B_0=1.99818$, $-\dfrac R2A_3B_0=-2.30823$, $\dfrac R2A_2B_1=-0.16380$, $-2A_0B_2=-0.21343$, $\dfrac R2A_1B_2=0.17786$, and $-\dfrac R2A_0B_3=0.03064$, and their sum is $-0.47879$. Multiplying by the prefactor $\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}\Bigl(\dfrac R2\Bigr)^3=0.35355$ gives

$$ S_{1s,2s}(2\,a_0)=0.35355\times(-0.47879)=-0.1693 $$

Checking with the final formula, $\dfrac{16\sqrt2}{54}\Bigl[(-12+44-64)e^{-1}+(20+64)e^{-2}\Bigr]=0.41903\times\bigl[-32\times0.36788+84\times0.13534\bigr]=0.41903\times(-11.772+11.369)=-0.169$, which agrees.

Next, we verify from the final formula that $S_{1s,2s}\to0$ as $R\to0$. Let $g(R)\equiv(-3R^2+22R-64)\,e^{-R/2}+(10R+64)\,e^{-R}$; then $S_{1s,2s}=\dfrac{16\sqrt2}{27R}\,g(R)$. Substituting $e^{-R/2}=1-\dfrac R2+\dfrac{R^2}{8}-\dfrac{R^3}{48}+\dfrac{R^4}{384}-\cdots$ and $e^{-R}=1-R+\dfrac{R^2}{2}-\dfrac{R^3}{6}+\dfrac{R^4}{24}-\cdots$, we collect the coefficient of each power of $R$.

  • $R^0$: $-64+64=0$
  • $R^1$: $\bigl(22+32\bigr)+\bigl(10-64\bigr)=54-54=0$
  • $R^2$: $\bigl(-3-11-8\bigr)+\bigl(-10+32\bigr)=-22+22=0$
  • $R^3$: $\Bigl(\dfrac32+\dfrac{11}{4}+\dfrac43\Bigr)+\Bigl(5-\dfrac{32}{3}\Bigr)=\dfrac{67}{12}-\dfrac{17}{3}=-\dfrac1{12}$
  • $R^4$: $\Bigl(-\dfrac38-\dfrac{11}{24}-\dfrac16\Bigr)+\Bigl(-\dfrac53+\dfrac83\Bigr)=-1+1=0$

(Breakdown of the $R^3$ term: the sum of $(-3R^2)\times\bigl(-\tfrac R2\bigr)$, $22R\times\tfrac{R^2}{8}$, and $-64\times\bigl(-\tfrac{R^3}{48}\bigr)$ is $\tfrac{67}{12}$, and the sum of $10R\times\tfrac{R^2}{2}$ and $64\times\bigl(-\tfrac{R^3}{6}\bigr)$ is $5-\tfrac{32}{3}=-\tfrac{17}{3}$.) In this way all the terms from $R^0$ through $R^2$ cancel each other, and the first term that remains is $g(R)=-\dfrac{R^3}{12}+O(R^5)$. Therefore

$$ S_{1s,2s}(R)=\frac{16\sqrt2}{27R}\Bigl(-\frac{R^3}{12}\Bigr)+\cdots=-\frac{4\sqrt2}{81}R^2+\frac{19\sqrt2}{1620}R^4-\cdots $$

and $S_{1s,2s}\to0$ as $R\to0$ (numerically as well, at $R=0.1$, $S_{1s,2s}=-6.97\times10^{-4}$ and $-\dfrac{4\sqrt2}{81}R^2=-6.98\times10^{-4}$).

On the sign: $S_{1s,2s}$ becomes 0 as $R\to0$ (the 1s and 2s orbitals on the same center are orthogonal) and is negative when $R$ is large. This sign is reversed by the choice of phase of the 2s orbital (multiplying $(2-r)$ by $-1$ gives the same orbital), so what has physical meaning is the absolute value $\abs{S}$. The $2s$ orbital has a node at $r=2\,a_0$, positive inside and negative outside. Since the 1s orbital is concentrated near nucleus A, as nucleus B moves away, the 1s orbital moves away from the positive inner core of the 2s orbital, and its overlap with the negative outer region of the 2s orbital grows. For this reason, in the region of small $R$, it starts out negative as $S_{1s,2s}\simeq-\dfrac{4\sqrt2}{81}R^2$ (the result of the expansion above).

Exercise 39.5: $\mathrm{H_2^+}$ with the orbital exponent $\zeta$ as a variational parameter

Solution

(1) $\phi_\zeta(\bm r)=\zeta^{3/2}\phi_1(\zeta\bm r)$ ($\phi_1$ is the 1s orbital with $\zeta=1$). Changing the integration variable to $\bm r'=\zeta\bm r$ makes all lengths $\zeta$ times as large, so the overlap integral is $S=S_1(\zeta R)=(1+\rho+\rho^2/3)e^{-\rho}$ ($\rho=\zeta R$), integrals containing $1/r$ are multiplied by $\zeta$, and $J'_\zeta(R)=\zeta J'_1(\zeta R)=\zeta\Bigl[\dfrac1{\zeta R}-\Bigl(1+\dfrac1{\zeta R}\Bigr)e^{-2\zeta R}\Bigr]=\dfrac1R-\Bigl(\dfrac1R+\zeta\Bigr)e^{-2\zeta R}$ and $K'_\zeta=\zeta K'_1(\zeta R)=\zeta(1+\rho)e^{-\rho}$.

The electron's Hamiltonian can be written as $-\tfrac12\nabla^2-\tfrac1{r_A}-\tfrac1{r_B}=\bigl(-\tfrac12\nabla^2-\tfrac\zeta{r_A}\bigr)-\tfrac{1-\zeta}{r_A}-\tfrac1{r_B}$. Since $\bigl(-\tfrac12\nabla^2-\tfrac\zeta{r_A}\bigr)\phi^A_\zeta=-\tfrac{\zeta^2}2\phi^A_\zeta$ and $\bra{\phi^A_\zeta}\tfrac1{r_A}\ket{\phi^A_\zeta}=\zeta$, we have

$$ H_{AA}=-\frac{\zeta^2}{2}-(1-\zeta)\zeta-J'_\zeta+\frac1R $$

Also, using $\bigl(-\tfrac12\nabla^2-\tfrac\zeta{r_B}\bigr)\phi^B_\zeta=-\tfrac{\zeta^2}2\phi^B_\zeta$ and noting that $\bra{\phi^A_\zeta}\tfrac1{r_B}\ket{\phi^B_\zeta}=\bra{\phi^A_\zeta}\tfrac1{r_A}\ket{\phi^B_\zeta}=K'_\zeta$ (by the symmetry between A and B), we obtain

$$ H_{AB}=\Bigl(-\frac{\zeta^2}{2}+\frac1R\Bigr)S-(1-\zeta)K'_\zeta-K'_\zeta=\Bigl(-\frac{\zeta^2}{2}+\frac1R\Bigr)S-(2-\zeta)K'_\zeta $$

(here $\tfrac1RS$ is the internuclear repulsion). $E_+(R,\zeta)=(H_{AA}+H_{AB})/(1+S)$. At $\zeta=1$, $H_{AA}=-\tfrac12-J'+\tfrac1R$ and $H_{AB}=(-\tfrac12+\tfrac1R)S-K'$, which agree with the equations in the main text.

(2) Varying $\zeta$ at $R=2$ to minimize $E_+$ gives $E_+=-0.5865\,E_{\mathrm h}$ at $\zeta=1.239$. This is $0.0327\,E_{\mathrm h}$ ($0.89\ \mathrm{eV}$) lower than the value $-0.5538$ at $\zeta=1$. For example, at $\zeta=1.24$ ($\rho=\zeta R=2.48$), $S=(1+2.48+2.0501)e^{-2.48}=0.4631$, $J'_\zeta=0.5-(0.5+1.24)e^{-4.96}=0.4878$, and $K'_\zeta=1.24\times3.48\times e^{-2.48}=0.3614$, so that $H_{AA}=-\dfrac{1.5376}{2}-(1-1.24)\times1.24-0.4878+0.5=-0.7688+0.2976-0.4878+0.5=-0.4590$ and $H_{AB}=(-0.7688+0.5)\times0.4631-(2-1.24)\times0.3614=-0.1245-0.2747=-0.3992$, and $E_+=\dfrac{-0.4590-0.3992}{1.4631}=-0.5865$.

(3) Varying $R$ as well in the search for the minimum, we find $R_{\mathrm e}=2.003\,a_0$, $\zeta=1.238$, and $E=-0.5865\,E_{\mathrm h}$, so the bond energy is $D_{\mathrm e}=0.0865\,E_{\mathrm h}=2.35\ \mathrm{eV}$. Compared with the case in which $\zeta=1$ is held fixed ($R_{\mathrm e}=2.49\,a_0$, $D_{\mathrm e}=1.76\ \mathrm{eV}$), $R_{\mathrm e}$ almost coincides with the exact value $1.997\,a_0$, and $D_{\mathrm e}$ also approaches the exact value $2.79\ \mathrm{eV}$. This is the effect of the orbital contracting ($\zeta>1$) and the electron gathering near the nuclei.

Exercise 39.6: Overlap integral between $p_z$-type Gaussian functions ($\sigma$ type)

Solution

(1) In Theorem 39.1, the product of the exponential parts is $e^{-\alpha r^2}e^{-\alpha\abs{\bm{r}-R\bm{e}_z}^2}=e^{-\alpha R^2/2}\,e^{-2\alpha\abs{\bm{r}-\bm{R}_P}^2}$ (since $\alpha_A=\alpha_B=\alpha$, we have $p=2\alpha$, $\bm{R}_P=\tfrac{R}{2}\bm{e}_z$, and $\dfrac{\alpha_A\alpha_B}{p}R^2=\dfrac{\alpha R^2}{2}$). Letting $\bm{r}'=\bm{r}-\bm{R}_P$, we have $z=z'+R/2$ and $z-R=z'-R/2$, so $z(z-R)=z'^2-R^2/4$, and

$$ S_{pp}=N_p^2\,e^{-\alpha R^2/2}\int\Bigl(z'^2-\frac{R^2}{4}\Bigr)e^{-2\alpha r'^2}\dd V'. $$

Using $\displaystyle\int e^{-\gamma r'^2}\dd V'=(\pi/\gamma)^{3/2}$ and $\displaystyle\int z'^2e^{-\gamma r'^2}\dd V'=\dfrac{1}{2\gamma}(\pi/\gamma)^{3/2}$ ($\gamma=2\alpha$), we obtain

$$ S_{pp}=N_p^2\Bigl(\frac{\pi}{2\alpha}\Bigr)^{3/2}e^{-\alpha R^2/2}\Bigl(\frac{1}{4\alpha}-\frac{R^2}{4}\Bigr). $$

Since $N_p^2=\Bigl(\dfrac{2\alpha}{\pi}\Bigr)^{3/2}\cdot4\alpha$, we have $N_p^2\Bigl(\dfrac{\pi}{2\alpha}\Bigr)^{3/2}=4\alpha$, and so

$$ S_{pp}(R)=4\alpha\Bigl(\frac{1}{4\alpha}-\frac{R^2}{4}\Bigr)e^{-\alpha R^2/2}=\bigl(1-\alpha R^2\bigr)\,e^{-\alpha R^2/2}. $$

At $R=0$, $S_{pp}=1$ (the same function overlaps itself, so this agrees with the normalization).

(2) $S_{pp}=0$ when $1-\alpha R^2=0$, that is, when $R=1/\sqrt\alpha$. For $R$ smaller than this, $S_{pp}\gt0$; for larger values, $S_{pp}\lt0$. The reason for the sign is that the negative lobe of the function on B (the $-z$ side of B) faces the positive lobe on A (the $+z$ side of A). When the nuclei move apart and the overlap between the facing lobes (the positive lobe of A and the negative lobe of B) becomes dominant, the product is negative. Therefore, the combination that makes the facing lobes the same sign is $\phi^p_A-\phi^p_B$; this is the $\sigma$ bonding combination, and it has the overlap $\displaystyle\int\phi^p_A\bigl(-\phi^p_B\bigr)\dd V=-S_{pp}\gt0$. Since $\dfrac{\dd S_{pp}}{\dd R}=\alpha R\,(\alpha R^2-3)\,e^{-\alpha R^2/2}$, the minimum value $S_{pp}=-2e^{-3/2}=-0.446$ is attained at $R=\sqrt{3/\alpha}$ (in contrast to the $s$-type $S^{\mathrm G}=e^{-\alpha R^2/2}$, which decreases monotonically).

(3) $\alpha R^2=0.4\times2.89=1.156$ and $S_{pp}=(1-1.156)\,e^{-0.578}=-0.156\times0.5609=-0.0875$. Since this $R$ is slightly larger than $1/\sqrt\alpha=1.58\,a_0$, the sign is negative.

Exercise 39.7: Sign reversal and minimum of $T_{AB}$

Solution

For $\alpha=0.5$, $T_{AB}=0.25\,(3-0.5R^2)\,e^{-0.25R^2}$. At $R=0$: $0.25\times3=0.75$. At $R=1$: $0.25\times2.5\times e^{-0.25}=0.625\times0.7788=0.4868$. At $R=2$: $0.25\times(3-2)\times e^{-1}=0.25\times0.3679=0.0920$ (in units of $E_{\mathrm h}$).

$T_{AB}=0$ when $3-\alpha R^2=0$, that is, when $R=\sqrt{3/\alpha}$ ($\sqrt6=2.449\,a_0$ for $\alpha=0.5$). To find the minimum value, let $y=\alpha R^2$ and differentiate $T_{AB}=\dfrac\alpha2(3-y)e^{-y/2}$ with respect to $y$:

$$ \frac{\dd T_{AB}}{\dd y}=\frac\alpha2e^{-y/2}\Bigl[-1-\frac{3-y}{2}\Bigr]=\frac\alpha4e^{-y/2}\,(y-5)=0\ \ \Longrightarrow\ \ y=5 $$

From this, the minimum occurs at $R=\sqrt{5/\alpha}$ (decreasing for $y<5$ and increasing for $y>5$), and the minimum value is $T_{AB}=\dfrac\alpha2(3-5)e^{-5/2}=-\alpha\,e^{-5/2}=-0.0821\,\alpha$. For $\alpha=0.5$, $R=\sqrt{10}=3.162\,a_0$ and $T_{AB}=-0.0410\,E_{\mathrm h}$; for $\alpha=0.27095$, $R=4.30\,a_0$ and $T_{AB}=-0.0222\,E_{\mathrm h}$ (the minimum in Figure 39.9 of the main text). Since $T_{AB}\to0$ as $R\to\infty$, the negative values become smaller in absolute value beyond $R=\sqrt{5/\alpha}$.

Exercise 39.8: Kinetic energy of the STO-3G hydrogen atom

Solution

For $R=0$, Theorem 39.2 gives $T_{ij}=\dfrac{3\alpha_i\alpha_j}{\alpha_i+\alpha_j}S^{\mathrm G}_{ij}$ and $S^{\mathrm G}_{ij}=\dfrac{(4\alpha_i\alpha_j)^{3/4}}{(\alpha_i+\alpha_j)^{3/2}}$. For the exponents $\alpha=(3.42525,\ 0.623914,\ 0.168855)$, the values of the 3×3 matrices are as follows.

$$ S^{\mathrm G}_{ij}(0)=\begin{pmatrix}1&0.6136&0.2753\\0.6136&1&0.7410\\0.2753&0.7410&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T_{ij}(0)=\begin{pmatrix}5.1379&0.9715&0.1329\\0.9715&0.9359&0.2954\\0.1329&0.2954&0.2533\end{pmatrix} $$

(For example, $T_{11}=\dfrac{3\times3.42525}{2}\times1=5.1379$ and $T_{12}=\dfrac{3\times3.42525\times0.623914}{4.049164}\times0.6136=1.5834\times0.6136=0.9715$.) The products $d_id_j$ of the coefficients form the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0.02382&0.08262&0.06862\\0.08262&0.28658&0.23803\\0.06862&0.23803&0.19770\end{pmatrix}$. For $T_{11}=\sum_{ij}d_id_jT_{ij}$, the diagonal terms give $0.12237+0.26820+0.05007=0.44064$ and the off-diagonal terms ($i\ne j$, counted twice) give $2\times(0.08026+0.00912+0.07031)=0.31938$, so

$$ T_{11}=0.44064+0.31938=0.7600\,E_{\mathrm h} $$

Here the function is normalized, since $\sum d_id_jS_{ij}=1.0000$.

For $R=1.4\,a_0$, we apply Formula 39.7 and Theorem 39.2 to each of the nine pairs $(i,j)$. $S^{\mathrm G}_{ij}(1.4)$ is $\begin{pmatrix}0.0349&0.2181&0.2008\\0.2181&0.5426&0.5711\\0.2008&0.5711&0.8475\end{pmatrix}$, and $T_{ij}(1.4)$ is $\begin{pmatrix}-0.2216&0.1072&0.0766\\0.1072&0.3008&0.1881\\0.0766&0.1881&0.1910\end{pmatrix}$. (For example, for $T_{11}(1.4)$ we have $\dfrac{\alpha_1\alpha_1}{\alpha_1+\alpha_1}=\dfrac{3.42525}{2}=1.7126$, $3-2\times1.7126\times1.4^2=3-6.7135=-3.7135$, and $S^{\mathrm G}_{11}(1.4)=e^{-1.7126\times1.96}=e^{-3.3567}=0.0349$, from which $T_{11}(1.4)=1.7126\times(-3.7135)\times0.0349=-0.2216$.) We multiply by $d_id_j$ and add. For the overlap integral, the diagonal terms ($i=j$) give $0.02382\times0.0349+0.28658\times0.5426+0.19770\times0.8475=0.00083+0.15549+0.16755=0.32387$, and the off-diagonal terms ($i\ne j$, counted twice) give $2\times(0.08262\times0.2181+0.06862\times0.2008+0.23803\times0.5711)=2\times(0.01802+0.01378+0.13593)=0.33546$, for a total of $0.32387+0.33546=0.65933\approx0.6593$. For the kinetic energy, the diagonal terms give $0.02382\times(-0.2216)+0.28658\times0.3008+0.19770\times0.1910=-0.00528+0.08620+0.03776=0.11868$, and the off-diagonal terms give $2\times(0.08262\times0.1072+0.06862\times0.0766+0.23803\times0.1881)=2\times(0.00886+0.00526+0.04477)=0.11778$, for a total of $0.23646$. Therefore the overlap integral and the kinetic energy are

$$ S_{12}=0.6593,\qquad T_{12}=0.2365\,E_{\mathrm h} $$

at this internuclear distance.

Chapter 40: Chemical Bonding (3) — Molecular Orbitals of Homonuclear Diatomic Molecules and the Hückel Method

Exercise 40.1: $\mathrm{N_2}$, $\mathrm{O_2}$, $\mathrm{F_2}$ and their ions

Solution

(1) The bonding MOs ($\sigma_{\mathrm g}2s$: 2, $\pi_{\mathrm u}2p$: 4, $\sigma_{\mathrm g}2p$: 2) hold at most eight electrons in any of these molecules, and, as in $\mathrm{N_2}$, all the bonding orbitals are filled first.
$\mathrm{N_2}$ (10 electrons): the only electrons in antibonding orbitals are the two in $\sigma_{\mathrm u}^{*}2s$. $b=(8-2)/2=3$.
$\mathrm{O_2}$ (12 electrons): two electrons in $\sigma_{\mathrm u}^{*}2s$ and two in $\pi_{\mathrm g}^{*}2p$ give four antibonding electrons. $b=(8-4)/2=2$.
$\mathrm{F_2}$ (14 electrons): $\pi_{\mathrm g}^{*}2p$ is filled, giving six antibonding electrons. $b=(8-6)/2=1$.
The bond lengths are 109.8 pm for $b=3$, 120.8 pm for $b=2$, and 141.2 pm for $b=1$: the smaller the bond order, the longer the bond (the weaker the bond becomes).
(2) Relative to $\mathrm{O_2}$, the only electrons added or removed are those in the antibonding $\pi_{\mathrm g}^{*}2p$ orbital (two in $\mathrm{O_2}$). The number of bonding electrons stays at eight.

SpeciesValence electrons$\pi_{\mathrm g}^{*}$ electrons$n_{\mathrm a}$$b=(8-n_{\mathrm a})/2$Unpaired electronsBond length (approx.)
$\mathrm{O_2^+}$1112+1=32.51112 pm
$\mathrm{O_2}$122422121 pm
$\mathrm{O_2^-}$133 ($\uparrow\downarrow$, $\uparrow$)51.51about 130 pm
$\mathrm{O_2^{2-}}$144610about 149 pm

In order of decreasing bond length, $\mathrm{O_2^{2-}}\;(149)\gt\mathrm{O_2^-}\;(130)\gt\mathrm{O_2}\;(121)\gt\mathrm{O_2^+}\;(112\ \mathrm{pm})$. This is the reverse of the order of decreasing bond order.

Exercise 40.2: Nitric oxide $\mathrm{NO}$

Solution

(1) There are $5+6=11$ valence electrons. Filling the orbitals in the order of $\mathrm{N_2}$ gives $$(\sigma2s)^2(\sigma^{*}2s)^2(\pi2p)^4(\sigma2p)^2(\pi^{*}2p)^1.$$ There are $2+4+2=8$ bonding electrons and $2+1=3$ antibonding electrons, so $b=(8-3)/2=2.5$. The single $\pi^{*}$ electron is unpaired, so there is one unpaired electron (paramagnetic, a radical).
(2) $\mathrm{NO^+}$ (10 electrons): the $\pi^{*}$ electron is gone, and $b=(8-2)/2=3$ (isoelectronic with $\mathrm{N_2}$ and $\mathrm{CO}$). $\mathrm{NO^-}$ (12 electrons): with $(\pi^{*}2p)^2$, $b=(8-4)/2=2$; the two electrons enter the two $\pi^{*}$ orbitals with parallel spins, giving two unpaired electrons (isoelectronic with $\mathrm{O_2}$). The measured bond lengths are 115.1 pm for $\mathrm{NO}$ and 106.3 pm for $\mathrm{NO^+}$: removing an antibonding electron raises the bond order from 2.5 to 3, and the bond shrinks by about 9 pm. $\mathrm{NO^+}$ is even shorter than $\mathrm{N_2}$ ($b=3$, 109.8 pm), but the bond length is not determined by the bond order alone; differences in the size of the atomic orbitals and in the uneven distribution of charge also play a role.
(3) The electron that can be removed from $\mathrm{NO}$ is the $\pi^{*}$ electron in the highest occupied orbital. This orbital is an antibonding orbital built from the N and O $2p$ orbitals; the contribution of N, the atom with the higher AO energy, is large, and the orbital lies higher than the $\pi_{\mathrm g}^{*}$ of $\mathrm{O_2}$ (which is made of O $2p$ orbitals only, and these lie deeper than those of N). Moreover, removing an antibonding electron strengthens the bond ($b:\,2.5\to3$), which favors ionization. In contrast, in $\mathrm{N_2}$ the electron is taken from the bonding/nonbonding $\sigma_{\mathrm g}2p$ orbital, which requires 15.6 eV, and in $\mathrm{O_2}$ 12.07 eV is required. The ease with which $\mathrm{NO}$ becomes $\mathrm{NO^+}$ (the nitrosonium ion), at 9.26 eV, lies behind the roles of $\mathrm{NO}$ as a ligand in metal complexes ($\mathrm{NO^+}$ type) and as a signaling molecule in living organisms.

Exercise 40.3: The allyl cation, radical, and anion

Solution

The levels and orbitals of the allyl system are $\psi_1$: $E=\alpha+\sqrt2\beta$, $(c_1,c_2,c_3)=(\tfrac12,\tfrac1{\sqrt2},\tfrac12)$; $\psi_2$: $E=\alpha$, $(\tfrac1{\sqrt2},0,-\tfrac1{\sqrt2})$; $\psi_3$: $E=\alpha-\sqrt2\beta$, $(\tfrac12,-\tfrac1{\sqrt2},\tfrac12)$. The values of $c_\mu^2$ for each orbital are $\psi_1$: $(\tfrac14,\tfrac12,\tfrac14)$; $\psi_2$: $(\tfrac12,0,\tfrac12)$; $\psi_3$: $(\tfrac14,\tfrac12,\tfrac14)$.

Electron configuration$E_\pi$Delocalization energy$q_1,q_2,q_3$
Cation (two electrons)$\psi_1^2$$2\alpha+2\sqrt2\beta=2\alpha+2.828\beta$$(2\sqrt2-2)\lvert\beta\rvert=0.828\lvert\beta\rvert$0.5, 1, 0.5
Radical (three electrons)$\psi_1^2\psi_2^1$$3\alpha+2.828\beta$$0.828\lvert\beta\rvert$1, 1, 1
Anion (four electrons)$\psi_1^2\psi_2^2$$4\alpha+2.828\beta$$0.828\lvert\beta\rvert$1.5, 1, 1.5

$E_\pi=\sum_in_iE_i$: for the cation, $2(\alpha+\sqrt2\beta)$; for the radical, adding one electron in $\psi_2$ ($E=\alpha$) gives $3\alpha+2\sqrt2\beta$; for the anion, adding two electrons in $\psi_2$ gives $4\alpha+2\sqrt2\beta$. Using as the localized reference an ethylene-type double bond ($2\alpha+2\beta$) and isolated $2p_z$ electrons ($\alpha$ each), we get cation: $2\alpha+2\beta$, radical: $3\alpha+2\beta$, anion: $4\alpha+2\beta$. In every case the difference is $(2\sqrt2-2)\beta$, of magnitude $0.828\lvert\beta\rvert$, and since the electrons in the nonbonding $\psi_2$ have no effect on $E$, it is the same for the three species.
Charge density $q_\mu=\sum_in_ic_{i\mu}^2$: for the cation, $2\times(\tfrac14,\tfrac12,\tfrac14)=(0.5,1,0.5)$. Since a neutral carbon has $q=1$, a positive charge of $+0.5$ sits on the two ends, half each (a superposition of two resonance structures). For the anion, $(0.5,1,0.5)+2\times(\tfrac12,0,\tfrac12)=(1.5,1,1.5)$: the negative charge $-0.5$ is split between the two ends. For the radical, $(0.5,1,0.5)+(\tfrac12,0,\tfrac12)=(1,1,1)$, so there is no charge imbalance.
The unpaired electron of the radical is in $\psi_2$, and the spin density is $c_{2\mu}^2=(\tfrac12,0,\tfrac12)$: half on each of the end carbons and 0 on the central carbon. This is consistent with the hyperfine structure of the allyl radical observed by electron spin resonance (ESR) (large for the H atoms at the ends, small for the central H).

Exercise 40.4: The Hückel method for naphthalene

Solution

We name the carbons $\mathrm{C_1,C_2,C_3,C_4}$ in ring A, $\mathrm{C_{4a}}$ at the fusion bond, $\mathrm{C_5,C_6,C_7,C_8}$ in ring B, and $\mathrm{C_{8a}}$ at the fusion bond (the bonds are 1–2, 2–3, 3–4, 4–4a, 4a–5, 5–6, 6–7, 7–8, 8–8a, 8a–1, 4a–8a). The molecule has two mirror planes: $\sigma_{\mathrm a}$ (which interchanges the two rings: $1\leftrightarrow8$, $2\leftrightarrow7$, $3\leftrightarrow6$, $4\leftrightarrow5$, while $\mathrm{4a},\mathrm{8a}$ are unchanged) and $\sigma_{\mathrm b}$ ($\mathrm{4a}\leftrightarrow\mathrm{8a}$, $1\leftrightarrow4$, $2\leftrightarrow3$, $5\leftrightarrow8$, $6\leftrightarrow7$). Sorting the linear combinations of the ten 2$p_z$ orbitals by their parity under the two reflections ($++$, $-+$, $+-$, $--$), we find by Law 40.1 that the matrix elements between different parities vanish, and the matrix $A$ (the eigenvalue problem for $x=(E-\alpha)/\beta$) splits into four blocks.

The elements of the adjacency matrix $A$ are 1 for pairs of bonded carbons (the 11 bonds listed above) and 0 otherwise. The matrix elements for the new basis functions $u_k$ and the like are computed from $\langle u|A|u'\rangle=\sum_{\mu\nu}c_\mu c'_\nu A_{\mu\nu}$ ($c_\mu$ and $c'_\nu$ are the coefficients of the respective basis functions).

(a) $\sigma_{\mathrm a}$ even, $\sigma_{\mathrm b}$ even (three dimensions): $u_1=(\phi_{4a}+\phi_{8a})/\sqrt2$, $u_2=\tfrac12(\phi_1+\phi_4+\phi_5+\phi_8)$, $u_3=\tfrac12(\phi_2+\phi_3+\phi_6+\phi_7)$.
$\langle u_1|A|u_1\rangle=\tfrac12(A_{4a,8a}+A_{8a,4a})=1$,
$\langle u_1|A|u_2\rangle=\tfrac1{2\sqrt2}\bigl(A_{4a,4}+A_{4a,5}+A_{8a,1}+A_{8a,8}\bigr)=\tfrac{4}{2\sqrt2}=\sqrt2$,
$\langle u_1|A|u_3\rangle=0$ (4a and 8a are not adjacent to 2, 3, 6, or 7),
$\langle u_2|A|u_2\rangle=0$ (1, 4, 5, and 8 are not adjacent to one another),
$\langle u_2|A|u_3\rangle=\tfrac14(A_{12}+A_{43}+A_{56}+A_{87})=1$,
$\langle u_3|A|u_3\rangle=\tfrac14\cdot2(A_{23}+A_{67})=1$. $$\begin{vmatrix}1-x&\sqrt2&0\\ \sqrt2&-x&1\\0&1&1-x\end{vmatrix}=(1-x)(x^2-x-3)=0\;\Rightarrow\;x=1,\ \tfrac{1\pm\sqrt{13}}{2}=2.303,\ -1.303.$$ (b) $\sigma_{\mathrm a}$ even, $\sigma_{\mathrm b}$ odd (three dimensions): $v_1=(\phi_{8a}-\phi_{4a})/\sqrt2$, $v_2=\tfrac12(\phi_1-\phi_4-\phi_5+\phi_8)$, $v_3=\tfrac12(\phi_2-\phi_3-\phi_6+\phi_7)$.
$\langle v_1|A|v_1\rangle=\tfrac12(-A_{8a,4a}-A_{4a,8a})=-1$,
$\langle v_1|A|v_2\rangle=\tfrac1{2\sqrt2}\bigl(A_{8a,1}+A_{8a,8}+A_{4a,4}+A_{4a,5}\bigr)=\sqrt2$ (the coefficient of $\phi_{8a}$ is $+1$ and the coefficients of $\phi_1$ and $\phi_8$ are also $+1$; the coefficient of $\phi_{4a}$ is $-1$ and the coefficients of $\phi_4$ and $\phi_5$ are also $-1$; hence all four terms are $+1$),
$\langle v_1|A|v_3\rangle=0$, $\langle v_2|A|v_2\rangle=0$,
$\langle v_2|A|v_3\rangle=\tfrac14\bigl(A_{12}+(-1)(-1)A_{43}+(-1)(-1)A_{56}+A_{87}\bigr)=1$,
$\langle v_3|A|v_3\rangle=\tfrac14\bigl(2A_{23}(+1)(-1)+2A_{67}(-1)(+1)\bigr)=-1$. $$\begin{vmatrix}-1-x&\sqrt2&0\\ \sqrt2&-x&1\\0&1&-1-x\end{vmatrix}=(1+x)(3-x-x^2)=0\;\Rightarrow\;x=-1,\ \tfrac{-1\pm\sqrt{13}}{2}=1.303,\ -2.303.$$ (c) $\sigma_{\mathrm a}$ odd, $\sigma_{\mathrm b}$ even (two dimensions): $w_1=\tfrac12(\phi_1+\phi_4-\phi_5-\phi_8)$, $w_2=\tfrac12(\phi_2+\phi_3-\phi_6-\phi_7)$.
$\langle w_1|A|w_1\rangle=0$, $\langle w_1|A|w_2\rangle=\tfrac14\bigl(A_{12}+A_{43}+(-1)(-1)A_{56}+(-1)(-1)A_{87}\bigr)=1$, $\langle w_2|A|w_2\rangle=\tfrac14\bigl(2A_{23}+2(-1)(-1)A_{67}\bigr)=1$: $\begin{vmatrix}-x&1\\1&1-x\end{vmatrix}=x^2-x-1=0\;\Rightarrow\;x=\tfrac{1\pm\sqrt5}{2}=1.618,\ -0.618$.
(d) Odd in both (two dimensions): $z_1=\tfrac12(\phi_1-\phi_4+\phi_5-\phi_8)$, $z_2=\tfrac12(\phi_2-\phi_3+\phi_6-\phi_7)$.
$\langle z_1|A|z_1\rangle=0$, $\langle z_1|A|z_2\rangle=\tfrac14\bigl(A_{12}+(-1)(-1)A_{43}+A_{56}+(-1)(-1)A_{87}\bigr)=1$, $\langle z_2|A|z_2\rangle=\tfrac14\bigl(2A_{23}(+1)(-1)+2A_{67}(+1)(-1)\bigr)=-1$: $\begin{vmatrix}-x&1\\1&-1-x\end{vmatrix}=x^2+x-1=0\;\Rightarrow\;x=\tfrac{-1\pm\sqrt5}{2}=0.618,\ -1.618$.

Arranging the 10 eigenvalues in descending order, we have $x=2.303,\ 1.618,\ 1.303,\ 1,\ 0.618,\ -0.618,\ -1,\ -1.303,\ -1.618,\ -2.303$ (distributed symmetrically above and below $\alpha$). The 10 π electrons fill the lower five orbitals.
The HOMO is $x=0.618=(\sqrt5-1)/2$: $E_{\mathrm{HOMO}}=\alpha+0.618\beta$. The LUMO is $x=-0.618$: $\alpha-0.618\beta$. The gap is $2\times0.618\lvert\beta\rvert=1.236\lvert\beta\rvert$ (the same value as for butadiene).
$E_\pi=2\beta\,(2.303+1.618+1.303+1+0.618)+10\alpha=10\alpha+13.683\beta$ (analytically, $\sum x_{\text{occ}}=\sqrt{13}+1+\sqrt5=6.842$). Five localized double bonds give $5(2\alpha+2\beta)=10\alpha+10\beta$, so the delocalization energy is $3.683\lvert\beta\rvert$ (larger than the $2\lvert\beta\rvert$ of benzene, but per ring it is $1.84\lvert\beta\rvert$, which is smaller than that of benzene).

Exercise 40.5: Pyridine (the Hückel method with a heteroatom)

Solution

Going around the ring, we label N as 1 and the carbons $\mathrm{C_2},\dots,\mathrm{C_6}$, so that $\mathrm{C_4}$ is opposite N. The mirror plane through N and $\mathrm{C_4}$ interchanges $\mathrm{C_2}\leftrightarrow\mathrm{C_6}$ and $\mathrm{C_3}\leftrightarrow\mathrm{C_5}$. The diagonal element of nitrogen is $\alpha_{\mathrm N}=\alpha+h\beta$ ($h=0.5$), so with $x=(E-\alpha)/\beta$ the diagonal element in the N row is $h=0.5$.
The even (symmetric) basis consists of $\phi_{\mathrm N}$, $s_2=(\phi_2+\phi_6)/\sqrt2$, $s_3=(\phi_3+\phi_5)/\sqrt2$, and $\phi_4$. From the N–$\mathrm{C_2}$ and N–$\mathrm{C_6}$ bonds, $\langle\mathrm N|A|s_2\rangle=\tfrac{2}{\sqrt2}=\sqrt2$, $\langle s_2|A|s_3\rangle=\tfrac12(A_{23}+A_{65})=1$, and $\langle s_3|A|\phi_4\rangle=\tfrac{2}{\sqrt2}=\sqrt2$. $$M_{\text{even}}=\begin{pmatrix}0.5&\sqrt2&0&0\\ \sqrt2&0&1&0\\0&1&0&\sqrt2\\0&0&\sqrt2&0\end{pmatrix}.$$ The secular equation is $2x^4-x^3-10x^2+3x+8=0$ ($x^4-0.5x^3-5x^2+1.5x+4=0$). Solving it numerically gives $x=2.107,\ 1.167,\ -0.841,\ -1.934$.
The odd (antisymmetric) basis consists of $a_2=(\phi_2-\phi_6)/\sqrt2$ and $a_3=(\phi_3-\phi_5)/\sqrt2$ (the components on N and $\mathrm{C_4}$ are 0), and the matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Hence $x=\pm1$.
The six eigenvalues taken together are $x=2.107,\ 1.167,\ 1,\ -0.841,\ -1,\ -1.934$ (the degeneracies of benzene, $2,1,1,-1,-1,-2$, have been lifted).
To obtain the charge densities, we find the coefficients of the three occupied orbitals. From rows 1–3 of $M_{\text{even}}c=xc$, the eigenvector $(c_{\mathrm N},c_{s2},c_{s3},c_4)$ of the even block is determined in turn, with $c_{\mathrm N}=1$, as $c_{s2}=(x-0.5)/\sqrt2$, $c_{s3}=x\,c_{s2}-\sqrt2$, and $c_4=(x\,c_{s3}-c_{s2})/\sqrt2$, and finally it is normalized.
$x=2.107$: $(1,\ 1.137,\ 0.981,\ 0.658)$. The sum of squares is $3.688$, and dividing by $\sqrt{3.688}=1.920$ gives $(c_{\mathrm N},c_{s2},c_{s3},c_4)=(0.521,\ 0.592,\ 0.511,\ 0.343)$ (the overall sign is arbitrary).
$x=1.167$: $(1,\ 0.472,\ -0.864,\ -1.046)$. The sum of squares is $3.063$, and dividing by $\sqrt{3.063}=1.750$ gives $(0.571,\ 0.270,\ -0.493,\ -0.598)$.
$x=1$ (odd block): the eigenvector in $(a_2,a_3)$ is $(1,1)/\sqrt2$. $a_2$ and $a_3$ contain no components on N and $\mathrm{C_4}$.
The coefficient $c_{s2}$ of the basis function $s_2=(\phi_2+\phi_6)/\sqrt2$ is distributed to $\phi_2$ and $\phi_6$ as $c_{s2}/\sqrt2$ each, and the coefficient $1/\sqrt2$ of $a_2=(\phi_2-\phi_6)/\sqrt2$ gives $+\tfrac12$ to $\phi_2$ and $-\tfrac12$ to $\phi_6$ (similarly for $\phi_3$ and $\phi_5$). Therefore, the charge density on each atom, $q_\mu=2\sum_{\text{occ}}c_{i\mu}^2$, is
N: $q_{\mathrm N}=2\,(0.521^2+0.571^2+0^2)=2\,(0.2711+0.3265)=1.195$,
$\mathrm{C_2}$ ($=\mathrm{C_6}$): $q=2\bigl[(0.592^2+0.270^2)/2+(1/2)^2\bigr]=2\,(0.1752+0.0363+0.25)=0.923$,
$\mathrm{C_3}$ ($=\mathrm{C_5}$): $q=2\bigl[(0.511^2+0.493^2)/2+(1/2)^2\bigr]=2\,(0.1305+0.1217+0.25)=1.004$,
$\mathrm{C_4}$: $q=2\,(0.343^2+0.598^2+0^2)=2\,(0.1175+0.3574)=0.950$.
The sum of the six values is $1.195+2(0.923)+2(1.004)+0.950=6.00$, which agrees with the total number of π electrons.
(2) The six π electrons occupy the lower three levels ($x=2.107,\ 1.167,\ 1$): $E_\pi=6\alpha+2(2.107+1.167+1)\beta=6\alpha+8.549\beta$. Compared with the benzene value $6\alpha+8\beta$, this is lower (more stable) by $0.549\lvert\beta\rvert$. This is because the nitrogen level is lowered by $0.5\lvert\beta\rvert$ (electronegativity) and the electrons are drawn toward nitrogen. The charge densities above are N: $q=1.195$, $\mathrm{C_{2,6}}$: 0.923, $\mathrm{C_{3,5}}$: 1.004, and $\mathrm{C_4}$: 0.950; electrons gather on nitrogen, and the π-electron densities at $\mathrm{C_2}$, $\mathrm{C_6}$, and $\mathrm{C_4}$ decrease (this agrees with the chemical tendency that these positions are readily attacked by nucleophiles). The HOMO is $x=1$ (an $a_2$-type orbital with nodes at N and $\mathrm{C_4}$) and the LUMO is $x=-0.841$ (which has a component on N); the HOMO–LUMO spacing is $1.841\lvert\beta\rvert$, smaller than the $2\lvert\beta\rvert$ of benzene.

Exercise 40.6: The $2\times2$ problem with overlap integral $S\ne0$

Solution

(1) The secular equation is $(\alpha-E)^2-(\beta-ES)^2=0$. This factorizes as $\bigl[(\alpha-E)-(\beta-ES)\bigr]\bigl[(\alpha-E)+(\beta-ES)\bigr]=0$.
$(\alpha-E)+(\beta-ES)=0$: from $\alpha+\beta=E(1+S)$ we get $E_{\mathrm b}=\dfrac{\alpha+\beta}{1+S}$ (bonding; since $\beta\lt0$, it lies lower than $\alpha$).
$(\alpha-E)-(\beta-ES)=0$: from $\alpha-\beta=E(1-S)$ we get $E_{\mathrm a}=\dfrac{\alpha-\beta}{1-S}$ (antibonding).
(2) $\alpha=0$, $\beta=-2$, $S=0.25$: $E_{\mathrm b}=\dfrac{-2}{1.25}=-1.6\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $E_{\mathrm a}=\dfrac{2}{0.75}=+2.667\ \mathrm{eV}$. Compared with $\mp2$ eV for $S=0$, the bonding level drops by only 1.6 eV, but the antibonding level rises by 2.667 eV. The ratio is $E_{\mathrm a}/\lvert E_{\mathrm b}\rvert=(1+S)/(1-S)=1.667$: the antibonding level moves $\dfrac{1+S}{1-S}$ times as far.
(3) The total energy of the four electrons (two each in $E_{\mathrm b}$ and $E_{\mathrm a}$) is $$2E_{\mathrm b}+2E_{\mathrm a}=\frac{2(\alpha+\beta)(1-S)+2(\alpha-\beta)(1+S)}{1-S^2}=\frac{4\alpha-4\beta S}{1-S^2}.$$ The difference from the energy $4\alpha$ of the four electrons of two isolated atoms is $$\frac{4\alpha-4\beta S}{1-S^2}-4\alpha=\frac{4\alpha S^2-4\beta S}{1-S^2}=\frac{4S(\alpha S-\beta)}{1-S^2}.$$ If $\beta\lt0$ and $\lvert\beta\rvert\gt\lvert\alpha\rvert S$ (usually satisfied; always satisfied if $\alpha=0$), then $\alpha S-\beta\gt0$, and this difference is positive. That is, the destabilization of the antibonding orbital exceeds the stabilization of the bonding orbital, and the four electrons (two closed shells) repel each other. For $\alpha=0$, $\beta=-2$, $S=0.25$ we get $2(-1.6)+2(2.667)=+2.13\ \mathrm{eV}$ (from the formula, $4\times0.25\times2/(1-0.0625)=2.13\ \mathrm{eV}$). The fact that $\mathrm{He_2}$ and $\mathrm{Be_2}$ do not form bonds (repulsion between closed shells) appears as an effect of $S\ne0$. For $S=0$ (the Hückel approximation), this repulsion becomes 0.

Exercise 40.7: Linear chain and ring for $N=7$ (Python)

Solution

(1) The Python code that builds the adjacency matrix and finds the eigenvalues is as follows.

import numpy as np
def chain(N):
    A = np.zeros((N, N))
    for i in range(N - 1):
        A[i, i+1] = A[i+1, i] = 1
    return A
def ring(N):
    A = chain(N)
    A[0, N-1] = A[N-1, 0] = 1
    return A
N = 7
xc = np.sort(np.linalg.eigvalsh(chain(N)))[::-1]      # descending order (in order of increasing energy)
xr = np.sort(np.linalg.eigvalsh(ring(N)))[::-1]
print(xc)                                                # 1.848, 1.414, 0.765, 0, -0.765, -1.414, -1.848
print([2*np.cos(j*np.pi/(N+1)) for j in range(1, N+1)])  # linear chain formula 2cos(jπ/(N+1))
print(xr)                                                # 2, 1.247, 1.247, -0.445, -0.445, -1.802, -1.802
print(sorted(2*np.cos(2*np.pi*np.arange(N)/N), reverse=True))  # ring formula 2cos(2πj/N)

The linear chain gives $1.848,\,1.414,\,0.765,\,0,\,-0.765,\,-1.414,\,-1.848$ and the ring gives $2,\,1.247\,(\times2),\,-0.445\,(\times2),\,-1.802\,(\times2)$; these agree with $2\cos\dfrac{j\pi}{8}$ ($j=1,\dots,7$) and $2\cos\dfrac{2\pi j}{7}$ ($j=0,\dots,6$), respectively.
(2) The six electrons occupy $x=2$ (two electrons) and the doubly degenerate level $x=1.247$ (four electrons). $$E_\pi=2(\alpha+2\beta)+4(\alpha+1.247\beta)=6\alpha+8.988\beta.$$ The difference from the value $6\alpha+6\beta$ for three localized double bonds is $2.988\lvert\beta\rvert$. There are six electrons ($=4\cdot1+2$, $n=1$), and the orbitals $x=2,\,1.247\,(\times2)$ are filled, giving a closed shell (the neutral seven-membered ring has seven electrons and is an open-shell radical, with only one electron in the doubly degenerate level $x=-0.445$, and is unstable). Therefore, $\mathrm{C_7H_7^+}$ is an aromatic ion that satisfies the $4n+2$ rule.
(3) For $N=20$, xs = np.sort(np.linalg.eigvalsh(chain(20)))[::-1]; xs[9]-xs[10] gives $0.2989$. This agrees with the formula $4\sin\dfrac{\pi}{42}=0.2989$, and also agrees well with the approximate formula $\dfrac{2\pi}{21}=0.2992$.

Exercise 40.8: Why the gap of a polyene goes to 0 as $N\to\infty$, and the real gap

Solution

(1) For a linear chain with even $N$, the HOMO is $j=N/2$ and the LUMO is $j=N/2+1$. With $E_j=\alpha+2\beta\cos\dfrac{j\pi}{N+1}$ and $\beta=-\lvert\beta\rvert$, let $\dfrac{(N/2)\pi}{N+1}=\dfrac\pi2-\varepsilon$ and $\dfrac{(N/2+1)\pi}{N+1}=\dfrac\pi2+\varepsilon$ ($\varepsilon=\dfrac{\pi}{2(N+1)}$). Since $\cos(\tfrac\pi2\mp\varepsilon)=\pm\sin\varepsilon$, $$E_{\mathrm{LUMO}}-E_{\mathrm{HOMO}}=2\lvert\beta\rvert\bigl[\cos(\tfrac\pi2-\varepsilon)-\cos(\tfrac\pi2+\varepsilon)\bigr]=2\lvert\beta\rvert\,(\sin\varepsilon+\sin\varepsilon)=4\lvert\beta\rvert\sin\frac{\pi}{2(N+1)}.$$ As $N\to\infty$, $\varepsilon\to0$ and $\sin\varepsilon\approx\varepsilon$, so the spacing is $\approx2\pi\lvert\beta\rvert/(N+1)\to0$.
(2) The $N$ levels lie in a range of width $4\lvert\beta\rvert$ ($\alpha\pm2\beta$), so the level spacing is $4\lvert\beta\rvert/N$ on average, which goes to 0 as $N\to\infty$. Near the center of the band the levels are nearly equally spaced, and the spacing is $dE/dj=2\lvert\beta\rvert\sin\dfrac{j\pi}{N+1}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{N+1}\to\dfrac{2\pi\lvert\beta\rvert}{N+1}$ ($j\approx N/2$). Therefore, the HOMO and LUMO are adjacent levels near the center, and the fact that their spacing approaches 0 means that a uniform half-filled chain becomes a metal without a gap. In the free-electron model of Chapter 10, if we match the fixed ends of the linear chain in the main text ($\mu=0$ and $\mu=N+1$) and take the length of the box as $L=(N+1)d$ ($d$ is the bond length), then the HOMO is $n=N/2$ and the LUMO is $n=N/2+1$, and $\Delta E=\bigl[(N/2+1)^2-(N/2)^2\bigr]\dfrac{h^2}{8m_{\mathrm e}L^2}=(N+1)\dfrac{h^2}{8m_{\mathrm e}L^2}=\dfrac{h^2}{8m_{\mathrm e}d^2\,(N+1)}\propto\dfrac1{N+1}$, so the gap approaches 0 with the same $1/N$ dependence (even if we place the walls at the positions of the two terminal carbons and take $L=(N-1)d$, the $1/N$ dependence for large $N$ does not change).
(3) A real chain has bonds that alternate between strong and weak (bond alternation). If we let the resonance integrals of adjacent bonds be alternately $\beta(1+\delta)$ and $\beta(1-\delta)$, the unit cell contains two carbons (length $2a$). Number the carbons of the $m$th unit cell $2m-1$ and $2m$ (the bond between $2m-1$ and $2m$ is $\beta(1+\delta)$, and the bond between $2m$ and $2m+1$ is $\beta(1-\delta)$), and substitute the Bloch-wave form $c_{2m-1}=A\,e^{i\,2mka}$, $c_{2m}=B\,e^{i\,2mka}$ into the secular equation $(E-\alpha)c_\mu=\beta_{\mu,\mu-1}c_{\mu-1}+\beta_{\mu,\mu+1}c_{\mu+1}$.
For carbon $2m-1$ (its neighbors are $2m-2$, with $\beta(1-\delta)$, and $2m$, with $\beta(1+\delta)$): $(E-\alpha)A\,e^{i2mka}=\beta\bigl[(1-\delta)B\,e^{i(2m-2)ka}+(1+\delta)B\,e^{i2mka}\bigr]$, so $$(E-\alpha)A=\beta\bigl[(1+\delta)+(1-\delta)e^{-i2ka}\bigr]B.$$ For carbon $2m$ (its neighbors are $2m-1$, with $\beta(1+\delta)$, and $2m+1$, with $\beta(1-\delta)$): $(E-\alpha)B\,e^{i2mka}=\beta\bigl[(1+\delta)A\,e^{i2mka}+(1-\delta)A\,e^{i(2m+2)ka}\bigr]$, so $$(E-\alpha)B=\beta\bigl[(1+\delta)+(1-\delta)e^{i2ka}\bigr]A.$$ Multiplying the two equations side by side and canceling $AB$, we obtain $$(E-\alpha)^2=\beta^2\bigl|(1+\delta)+(1-\delta)e^{i2ka}\bigr|^2=\beta^2\bigl[(1+\delta)^2+(1-\delta)^2+2(1-\delta^2)\cos2ka\bigr]=\beta^2\bigl[2(1+\delta^2)+2(1-\delta^2)\cos2ka\bigr].$$ At the zone boundary $k=\pi/2a$ (the Fermi wavenumber at half filling), $\cos2ka=\cos\pi=-1$, so $(E-\alpha)^2=\beta^2\,(2+2\delta^2-2+2\delta^2)=4\delta^2\beta^2$ and $E=\alpha\pm2\delta\lvert\beta\rvert$. Therefore, a gap $E_{\mathrm g}=4\delta\lvert\beta\rvert$ opens between the top of the lower band and the bottom of the upper band (for $\delta=0$, there is a degeneracy $E=\alpha$ at the zone boundary, and the gap is 0). With $E_{\mathrm g}=1.5\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $\lvert\beta\rvert=2.5\ \mathrm{eV}$, $$\delta=\frac{E_{\mathrm g}}{4\lvert\beta\rvert}=\frac{1.5}{10}=0.15.$$ The ratio of the resonance integrals of adjacent bonds is $(1+\delta)/(1-\delta)=1.15/0.85=1.35$. In numerical calculations, the HOMO–LUMO spacing of the chain with $\delta=0.15$ is $0.739\lvert\beta\rvert$ ($1.85\ \mathrm{eV}$) for $N=22$, $0.611\lvert\beta\rvert$ for $N=100$, and $0.601\lvert\beta\rvert$ ($1.50\ \mathrm{eV}$) for $N=400$, converging to $4\delta\lvert\beta\rvert=0.6\lvert\beta\rvert$. The spacing of the uniform chain with $N=22$ is only $0.273\lvert\beta\rvert=0.68\ \mathrm{eV}$, which differs greatly from the prediction for the uniform chain that the gap approaches 0.

Chapter 41: From Molecular Orbitals to Crystal Bands (1) — The One-Dimensional Atomic Chain, Density of States, Effective Mass, and Electrical Conduction

Exercise 41.1: Sign of $\beta$ for a chain of $p$ orbitals

Solution

(1) The $k=0$ Bloch sum is $\psi_0=\sum_n\phi_n$, and the $p_x$ orbitals of all the atoms have the same orientation (the right lobe is $+$, the left lobe is $-$). The right lobe ($+$) of atom $n$ faces the left lobe ($-$) of atom $n+1$, so the sign of the wave function is opposite between neighboring atoms, and a node forms between the atoms. Therefore $k=0$ is antibonding. In this case $S=\braket{\phi_n}{\phi_{n+1}}\lt 0$, which agrees in sign with the given value $S=-0.20$.

(2) $\beta\approx\alpha S=(-6.0\ \mathrm{eV})\times(-0.20)=+1.2\ \mathrm{eV}$ (positive). $E(k)=\alpha+2\beta\cos ka=-6.0+2.4\cos ka\ \mathrm{eV}$, and the bandwidth is $4|\beta|=4.8\ \mathrm{eV}$. The maximum is at $k=0$, where $E(0)=\alpha+2\beta=-3.6\ \mathrm{eV}$; the minimum is at $k=\pm\pi/a$, where $E(\pi/a)=\alpha-2\beta=-8.4\ \mathrm{eV}$; and at $k=\pm\pi/2a$, $E=\alpha=-6.0\ \mathrm{eV}$. It is a hill-shaped band that is upside down relative to that of a chain of $s$ orbitals, and the most stable state is at $k=\pm\pi/a$ (adjacent lobes have the same sign: bonding).

Exercise 41.2: The band in the presence of an overlap integral

Solution

(1) Substitute $\alpha=0$, $\beta=-1.0\ \mathrm{eV}$, and $S=0.20$ into $E(k)=\dfrac{\alpha+2\beta\cos ka}{1+2S\cos ka}$. For $k=0$: $E(0)=\dfrac{2\beta}{1+2S}=\dfrac{-2.0}{1.4}=-1.429\ \mathrm{eV}$. For $k=\pm\pi/a$: since $\cos\pi=-1$, $E(\pi/a)=\dfrac{-2\beta}{1-2S}=\dfrac{2.0}{0.6}=+3.333\ \mathrm{eV}$.

(2) For $S=0$, $E(0)=-2.0$ and $E(\pi/a)=+2.0\ \mathrm{eV}$ (with $\alpha=0$ as the reference). With overlap, the bonding level is raised by $0.571\ \mathrm{eV}$, from $-2.0\to-1.429$ (the stabilization is weakened), and the antibonding level is raised by $1.333\ \mathrm{eV}$, from $+2.0\to+3.333$. Measured from $\alpha$, the bonding level is lowered by $1.429\ \mathrm{eV}$ and the antibonding level is raised by $3.333\ \mathrm{eV}$, so the rise of the antibonding level is about $2.3$ times larger. With overlap, the width by which the antibonding orbital is pushed up is larger than the width by which the bonding orbital is pushed down.

(3) The bandwidth is $3.333-(-1.429)=4.762\ \mathrm{eV}$ (wider than the $4.0\ \mathrm{eV}$ for $S=0$).

Exercise 41.3: Normalization of the density of states and the one-quarter point

Solution

(1) Let $E-\alpha=2|\beta|\sin\varphi$ ($-\pi/2\le\varphi\le\pi/2$). Then $\mathrm{d}E=2|\beta|\cos\varphi\,\mathrm{d}\varphi$ and $\sqrt{4\beta^2-(E-\alpha)^2}=2|\beta|\sqrt{1-\sin^2\varphi}=2|\beta|\cos\varphi$. Therefore

$$ \int_{\alpha-2|\beta|}^{\alpha+2|\beta|}D(E)\,\mathrm{d}E=\frac1\pi\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\frac{2|\beta|\cos\varphi}{2|\beta|\cos\varphi}\,\mathrm{d}\varphi=\frac1\pi\cdot\pi=1 . $$

(2) The fraction of states from the bottom up to $E$ is, with $x=(E-\alpha)/(2|\beta|)=\sin\varphi$, $F(E)=\dfrac1\pi\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/2}^{\varphi}\mathrm{d}\varphi'=\dfrac1\pi\Bigl(\arcsin x+\dfrac\pi2\Bigr)$. Setting $F=\dfrac14$ gives $\arcsin x=-\dfrac\pi4$ and $x=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$, and hence $E_{1/4}-\alpha=-\sqrt2\,|\beta|=-1.414|\beta|$. The distance from the bottom ($-2|\beta|$) is $0.586|\beta|$, so $25\%$ of all the states lie within a range of only $14.6\%$ of the bandwidth $4|\beta|$.

(3) $D(E_{1/4})=\dfrac{1}{\pi\sqrt{4\beta^2-2\beta^2}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2\,\pi|\beta|}=\dfrac{0.225}{|\beta|}$. At the center, $D(\alpha)=\dfrac{1}{2\pi|\beta|}=\dfrac{0.159}{|\beta|}$. The ratio is $\sqrt2=1.41$, so the density of states at $E_{1/4}$ is about $1.4$ times that at the center.

Exercise 41.4: Fermi velocity of a half-filled chain

Solution

With one electron per atom the band is half filled, and the states with $|k|\lt \pi/2a$ are occupied. $k_{\mathrm F}=\dfrac{\pi}{2a}=\dfrac{\pi}{2\times3.0\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}}=5.2\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$. The velocity is $v(k)=\dfrac{1}{\hbar}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm{d}k}=\dfrac{2|\beta|a}{\hbar}\sin ka$, and since $\sin=1$ at $k_{\mathrm F}a=\pi/2$,

$$ v_{\mathrm F}=\frac{2|\beta|a}{\hbar}=\frac{2\times2.0\times1.602\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\times3.0\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}}{1.0546\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}}=1.8\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m/s}. $$

The effective mass is $m^*=\hbar^2\big/(\mathrm{d}^2E/\mathrm{d}k^2)$ with $\mathrm{d}^2E/\mathrm{d}k^2=2|\beta|a^2\cos ka$; at $k_{\mathrm F}a=\pi/2$ we have $\cos=0$, so $m^*\to\infty$. The Fermi level of the half-filled band lies at an inflection point, where the velocity is at its maximum (the acceleration is 0). For this reason, we cannot substitute $m^*(k_{\mathrm F})$ into $\sigma=ne_0^2\tau/m^*$. This is because $\Delta v=(\hbar/m^*)\Delta k$ is an approximation that holds only near the bottom of a band with a constant effective mass (a parabolic band). The conductivity depends on the distribution of all the occupied states taken together; in one dimension it is determined solely by the velocities at the two Fermi points, and the current flowing through the chain is $I=(2e_0^2\tau/\pi\hbar)\,v_{\mathrm F}E_x$ (the Caution in Chapter 41, Section 41.8.3). If we write this current as $n_1e_0^2\tau/m_{\mathrm{eff}}$ ($n_1=1/a$) and thereby define the mass $m_{\mathrm{eff}}$, then $m_{\mathrm{eff}}=\pi\hbar^2/(4|\beta|a^2)=(\pi/2)\,m_0$. From $m_0=\hbar^2/(2|\beta|a^2)=7.620\ \mathrm{eV\,\text{Å}^2}\big/(2\times2.0\ \mathrm{eV}\times9.0\ \text{Å}^2)\times m_{\mathrm e}=0.21\,m_{\mathrm e}$ we get $m_{\mathrm{eff}}=0.33\,m_{\mathrm e}$, which is a finite value.

Exercise 41.5: Conductivity and drift velocity of a metal

Solution

$\sigma=\dfrac{ne_0^2\tau}{m^*}=\dfrac{1.0\times10^{29}\times(1.602\times10^{-19})^2\times10\times10^{-15}}{9.109\times10^{-31}}\ \mathrm{S/m}=2.82\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{S/m}$. The resistivity is $\rho=1/\sigma=3.55\times10^{-8}\ \Omega\,\mathrm{m}$. The mobility is $\mu=\dfrac{e_0\tau}{m^*}=\dfrac{1.602\times10^{-19}\times10^{-14}}{9.109\times10^{-31}}=1.76\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^2\,V^{-1}\,s^{-1}}=17.6\ \mathrm{cm^2\,V^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$.

For $E_x=1\ \mathrm{V/cm}=100\ \mathrm{V/m}$, the magnitude of the drift velocity is $|v_{\mathrm d}|=\mu E_x=1.76\times10^{-3}\times100=0.176\ \mathrm{m/s}$, and the current density is $j=\sigma E_x=2.82\times10^{7}\times100=2.8\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{A/m^2}$ ($=2.8\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{A/mm^2}$). The drift velocity is far slower than the Fermi velocity (of order $10^6\ \mathrm{m/s}$).

Exercise 41.6: Difference between electron and hole mobilities

Solution

Substitute values such as $\mu=480\ \mathrm{cm^2\,V^{-1}\,s^{-1}}=0.048\ \mathrm{m^2\,V^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$ into $\tau=\mu m^*/e_0$. Holes in Si: $\tau_{\mathrm h}=\dfrac{0.048\times0.52\times9.109\times10^{-31}}{1.602\times10^{-19}}=1.42\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{s}$. Holes in Ge: from $\mu=0.19\ \mathrm{m^2\,V^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$, $\tau_{\mathrm h}=\dfrac{0.19\times0.3\times9.109\times10^{-31}}{1.602\times10^{-19}}=3.24\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{s}$.

The ratio of the mobilities in Si is $\dfrac{\mu_{\mathrm e}}{\mu_{\mathrm h}}=\dfrac{1350}{480}=2.81$. On the other hand, since $\mu=e_0\tau/m^*$, $\dfrac{\mu_{\mathrm e}}{\mu_{\mathrm h}}=\dfrac{m_{\mathrm h}^*}{m_c}\cdot\dfrac{\tau_{\mathrm e}}{\tau_{\mathrm h}}=\dfrac{0.52}{0.26}\times\dfrac{2.0\times10^{-13}}{1.42\times10^{-13}}=2.0\times1.41=2.8$, which agrees with it. Of the mobility ratio $2.8$, the difference in mass (the hole is $2.0$ times heavier) is the main part, and the remainder is the difference in relaxation time (that of the electron is $1.4$ times longer).

Exercise 41.7: A chain of two kinds of atoms in alternation

Solution

(1) The unit cell (of length $a$) contains one atom each of A and B, and the resonance integrals of A$_n$–B$_n$ (inside the cell) and of B$_n$–A$_{n+1}$ (between cells) are both $\beta$. Take as the basis the Bloch sum of A, $\psi_{\mathrm A}=\sum_ne^{ikna}\phi_{\mathrm A,n}$, and the Bloch sum of B, $\psi_{\mathrm B}=\sum_ne^{ikna}\phi_{\mathrm B,n}$. The diagonal elements are $\alpha_{\mathrm A}=\alpha+\Delta/2$ and $\alpha_{\mathrm B}=\alpha-\Delta/2$. The off-diagonal element is $\dfrac1N\langle\psi_{\mathrm A}|\hat{H}|\psi_{\mathrm B}\rangle=\beta+\beta\,e^{-ika}=\beta(1+e^{-ika})$ (the two terms $m=n$ and $m=n+1$). Using $|1+e^{-ika}|^2=2+2\cos ka=4\cos^2(ka/2)$, the secular equation is

$$ \Bigl(\alpha+\frac\Delta2-E\Bigr)\Bigl(\alpha-\frac\Delta2-E\Bigr)-4\beta^2\cos^2\frac{ka}{2}=0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ (E-\alpha)^2=\Bigl(\frac\Delta2\Bigr)^2+4\beta^2\cos^2\frac{ka}{2} $$

which gives $E_\pm(k)=\alpha\pm\sqrt{(\Delta/2)^2+4\beta^2\cos^2(ka/2)}$.

(2) For $\Delta=0$, $E_\pm=\alpha\pm2|\beta||\cos(ka/2)|$. This is the same as the $E=\alpha+2\beta\cos k'(a/2)$ of a uniform chain (interatomic spacing $a/2$) folded into the zone for period $a$, and there is no gap.

(3) At $ka=\pi$, $\cos(ka/2)=0$ and $E_\pm=\alpha\pm\Delta/2$. Hence the gap is $E_{\mathrm g}=\Delta$. Setting $ka=\pi-qa$, we have $\cos(ka/2)=\sin(qa/2)\approx qa/2$ and $4\beta^2\cos^2\approx\beta^2a^2q^2$. Thus $E_+\approx\alpha+\sqrt{\Delta^2/4+\beta^2a^2q^2}\approx\alpha+\dfrac\Delta2+\dfrac{\beta^2a^2}{\Delta}q^2$. Since $\mathrm{d}^2E/\mathrm{d}q^2=2\beta^2a^2/\Delta$, the effective mass is $m^*=\dfrac{\hbar^2}{\mathrm{d}^2E/\mathrm{d}q^2}=\dfrac{\hbar^2\Delta}{2\beta^2a^2}=\dfrac{E_{\mathrm g}}{2v_0^2}$ ($v_0=|\beta|a/\hbar$). The effective mass is proportional to the gap.

(4) From $m^*=E_{\mathrm g}/(2v_0^2)$, $v_0=\sqrt{\dfrac{E_{\mathrm g}}{2m^*}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{1.43\times1.602\times10^{-19}}{2\times0.07\times9.109\times10^{-31}}}=1.34\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m/s}$. $E_{\mathrm P}=2m_{\mathrm e}v_0^2=E_{\mathrm g}\dfrac{m_{\mathrm e}}{m^*}=\dfrac{1.43}{0.07}\ \mathrm{eV}=20.4\ \mathrm{eV}$. (For example, if the length of the unit cell is $a=4\ \text{Å}$, then $|\beta|=\hbar v_0/a=2.2\ \mathrm{eV}$.)

Exercise 41.8: Checking the periodicity from the Bloch sum

Solution

(1) Replacing $k$ by $k'=k+2\pi/a$, the coefficient on each atom becomes $e^{ik'na}=e^{ikna}\,e^{i(2\pi/a)na}=e^{ikna}\,e^{2\pi in}=e^{ikna}$ (since $n$ is an integer, $e^{2\pi in}=1$). Since the coefficients do not change, $\psi_{k+2\pi/a}=\psi_k$, and this is the same state. Hence it suffices to consider $k$ over one period of length $2\pi/a$ (the first Brillouin zone).

(2) Using $\phi_n(x+a)=\phi_{n-1}(x)$, we have $\psi_k(x+a)=\sum_ne^{ikna}\phi_{n-1}(x)=e^{ika}\sum_{n'}e^{ikn'a}\phi_{n'}(x)=e^{ika}\psi_k(x)$. Hence $|\psi_k(x+a)|^2=|e^{ika}|^2|\psi_k(x)|^2=|\psi_k(x)|^2$ (since $k$ is real, $|e^{ika}|=1$). The probability density is a periodic function with period $a$, so the way the electron is found around neighboring atoms (the probability density) is the same. Only the phase $e^{ika}$ differs from one atom to the next.

Chapter 42: From Molecular Orbitals to Crystal Bands (2) — Band Diagrams of Two- and Three-Dimensional Lattices and Bands of p Orbitals

Exercise 42.1: Numerical values for the two-dimensional $s$ band

Solution

(1) When $\alpha=0$ and $\beta=-1.5\ \mathrm{eV}$, Eq. (42.10) of Chapter 42 gives $E=\alpha+2\beta(\cos k_xa+\cos k_ya)=-3\,(\cos k_xa+\cos k_ya)\ \mathrm{eV}$ ($2\beta=-3\ \mathrm{eV}$).

  • $\Gamma=(0,0)$: $E=-3\times(1+1)=-6\ \mathrm{eV}$.
  • X$=(\pi/a,0)$: $E=-3\times(-1+1)=0$.
  • M$=(\pi/a,\pi/a)$: $E=-3\times(-1-1)=+6\ \mathrm{eV}$.
  • $(\pi/2a,\pi/2a)$: since $\cos(\pi/2)=0$, $E=0$ (on the Fermi surface of the half-filled band).

The bandwidth is $6-(-6)=12\ \mathrm{eV}=8\abs{\beta}$.

(2) The group velocity is $\bm{v}=\hbar^{-1}\nabla_{\bm{k}}E=\dfrac{2\abs{\beta}a}{\hbar}(\sin k_xa,\ \sin k_ya)$. At $(\pi/2a,\pi/2a)$, $\sin(\pi/2)=1$, so each component is

$$ \frac{2\abs{\beta}a}{\hbar}=\frac{2\times1.5\ \mathrm{eV}\times3.0\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}}{6.582\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{eV\,s}}=1.37\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m/s} $$

and the magnitude is $\abs{\bm{v}}=\sqrt2\times1.37\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m/s}=1.93\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m/s}$. At $\Gamma=(0,0)$, $\sin0=0$, so $\bm{v}=0$; at X$=(\pi/a,0)$, $\sin\pi=0$ and $\sin0=0$, so again $\bm{v}=0$ (these are stationary points where $\nabla_{\bm{k}}E=0$; $\Gamma$ is a minimum and X is a saddle point).

(3) At the $\Gamma$ point, $\partial^2E/\partial k_x^2=2\abs{\beta}a^2$, so $m^*=\hbar^2/(2\abs{\beta}a^2)$. Using $\hbar^2/(2m_{\mathrm e})=3.810\ \mathrm{eV\,\text{Å}^2}$, we obtain

$$ \frac{m^*}{m_{\mathrm e}}=\frac{3.810\ \mathrm{eV\,\text{Å}^2}}{1.5\ \mathrm{eV}\times(3.0\ \text{Å})^2}=\frac{3.810}{13.5}=0.282 $$

This is the result.

Exercise 42.2: Density of states at the bottom of a three-dimensional band

Solution

Near the bottom $\Gamma$, the energy can be expanded as $E-E_0=\abs{\beta}a^2k^2$ ($k=\abs{\bm{k}}$) (from the expansion of $-2\abs{\beta}(\cos k_xa+\cos k_ya+\cos k_za)$ with $\cos\theta\approx1-\theta^2/2$). Letting $\varepsilon=E-E_0$, the definition of the density of states (Eq. (42.21) of Chapter 42) reads, in three dimensions,

$$ D(E)=\left(\frac{a}{2\pi}\right)^3\int\delta\bigl(\varepsilon-\abs{\beta}a^2k^2\bigr)\,4\pi k^2\,\dd k $$

(in polar coordinates, $\dd^3k=4\pi k^2\dd k$). Regarding the argument of the delta function as a function of $k$ and dividing by the absolute value $2\abs{\beta}a^2k_\varepsilon$ of its derivative at the zero $k_\varepsilon=\sqrt{\varepsilon/\abs{\beta}}/a$, we obtain

$$ D=\frac{a^3}{8\pi^3}\cdot\frac{4\pi k_\varepsilon^2}{2\abs{\beta}a^2k_\varepsilon}=\frac{a\,k_\varepsilon}{4\pi^2\abs{\beta}}=\frac{1}{4\pi^2\abs{\beta}}\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon}{\abs{\beta}}}=\frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}{4\pi^2\abs{\beta}^{3/2}} $$

This is the density of states. At $\varepsilon=0.5\abs{\beta}$, $D=\dfrac{\sqrt{0.5}}{4\pi^2\abs{\beta}}=\dfrac{0.7071}{39.48\abs{\beta}}=\dfrac{0.0179}{\abs{\beta}}$. The difference from the numerically calculated value $0.0191/\abs{\beta}$ is about 7%; this is because at $\varepsilon=0.5\abs{\beta}$ the parabolic approximation (the expansion of $\cos$ up to second order) is already a little rough. The actual $E=-2\abs{\beta}\cos ka$ rises more gently than the parabola (the value of $k$ corresponding to $\varepsilon$ becomes larger), so $D$ is slightly larger than the approximation.

Exercise 42.3: Fermi surface of a half-filled three-dimensional lattice

Solution

(1) When $\alpha=0$ and $\beta=-0.5\ \mathrm{eV}$, the energies at $\Gamma$, X, M, and R are $6\beta$, $2\beta$, $-2\beta$, and $-6\beta$, that is, $-3.0$, $-1.0$, $+1.0$, and $+3.0\ \mathrm{eV}$.

(2) If the wavenumber is shifted by $\bm{Q}=(\pi/a,\pi/a,\pi/a)$, then $\cos(k_ja+\pi)=-\cos k_ja$, so $E(\bm{k}+\bm{Q})-\alpha=-\bigl(E(\bm{k})-\alpha\bigr)$. Therefore the states of energy $\alpha+\varepsilon$ and the states of energy $\alpha-\varepsilon$ are in one-to-one correspondence, so the number of states below $\alpha$ equals the number above, and both are $N^3$ (half of the band). With one electron per atom there are $N^3$ electrons, which is exactly half of the $2N^3$ states including spin, so filling the states from the bottom up gives $E_{\mathrm F}=\alpha$. The Fermi surface is $\cos k_xa+\cos k_ya+\cos k_za=0$.

(3) Set the energy on each path (Formula 42.2) equal to $0$.

  • $\Gamma\to\mathrm{X}$: $E=2\beta(\cos\kappa a+2)=-(\cos\kappa a+2)\ \mathrm{eV}$. Since $\cos\kappa a\ge-1$, $E\le-1\ \mathrm{eV}$, which never becomes $0$. The path does not cross the Fermi surface.
  • $\mathrm{X}\to\mathrm{M}$: $E=2\beta\cos\kappa a=0$ gives $\kappa a=\pi/2$, that is, $\bm{k}=(\pi/a,\ \pi/2a,\ 0)$.
  • $\mathrm{M}\to\Gamma$: $E=2\beta(2\cos\kappa a+1)=0$ gives $\cos\kappa a=-1/2$, $\kappa a=2\pi/3$, that is, $\bm{k}=(2\pi/3a,\ 2\pi/3a,\ 0)$.
  • $\Gamma\to\mathrm{R}$: $E=6\beta\cos\kappa a=0$ gives $\kappa a=\pi/2$, that is, $\bm{k}=(\pi/2a)(1,1,1)$.

The region containing $\Gamma$ ($E\lt\alpha$) is the occupied region filled with electrons, and the Fermi surface is the surface enclosing it. In the $\Gamma\to\mathrm{X}$ direction the occupied region extends completely up to the boundary (X, the center of a face of the Brillouin zone), and the X point lies inside the occupied region.

Exercise 42.4: The $p$ bands for $\beta_\sigma=3$, $\beta_\pi=1$

Solution

Substitute $\alpha=10$, $\beta_\sigma=3$, and $\beta_\pi=1$ into the three equations of Eq. (42.24) of Chapter 42. $E_{p_x}=10+6\cos k_xa-2\cos k_ya$, $E_{p_y}=10-2\cos k_xa+6\cos k_ya$, $E_{p_z}=10-2\cos k_xa-2\cos k_ya$.

  • $\Gamma$ ($\cos=1,1$): $E_{p_x}=14$, $E_{p_y}=14$, $E_{p_z}=6$. Sum $=34$.
  • X ($\cos k_xa=-1$, $\cos k_ya=1$): $E_{p_x}=10-6-2=2$, $E_{p_y}=10+2+6=18$, $E_{p_z}=10+2-2=10$. Sum $=30$.
  • M ($-1,-1$): $E_{p_x}=10-6+2=6$, $E_{p_y}=6$, $E_{p_z}=10+2+2=14$. Sum $=26$.

The sum changes with $k$: 34, 30, and 26. In general, $E_{p_x}+E_{p_y}+E_{p_z}=3\alpha+2(\beta_\sigma-2\beta_\pi)(\cos k_xa+\cos k_ya)=30+2(\cos k_xa+\cos k_ya)$, which gives $30+4=34$ at $\Gamma$, $30+0=30$ at X, and $30-4=26$ at M, in agreement. Only when $\beta_\sigma=2\beta_\pi$ is the sum constant at $3\alpha$. The splitting at $\Gamma$ is $E_{p_x}-E_{p_z}=14-6=8$, which agrees with $2(\beta_\sigma+\beta_\pi)=2\times4=8$ of Eq. (42.26).

Exercise 42.5: Why the $p_x$ band has its minimum at the X point

Solution

(1) We have $E_{p_x}-\alpha=2\beta_\sigma\cos k_xa-2\beta_\pi\cos k_ya$, and since $\beta_\sigma,\beta_\pi\gt0$, the first term takes its minimum $-2\beta_\sigma$ at $\cos k_xa=-1$, and the second term takes its minimum $-2\beta_\pi$ at $\cos k_ya=+1$. The two terms are functions of different variables, so they can be minimized simultaneously. The minimum value is $\alpha-2\beta_\sigma-2\beta_\pi$, and the wavenumber there is $k_xa=\pi$, $k_ya=0$, that is, the X point.

(2) At the X point the phase factor is $(-1)^{n-1}$, so the orientations of $p_x$ orbitals that are adjacent in the $x$ direction reverse alternately. With the neighbors in the $x$ direction the overlap is of $\sigma$ type, and the facing lobes have the same sign ($+$ with $+$, or $-$ with $-$), so the overlap is bonding; the matrix element $+\beta_\sigma$ is multiplied by the phase factor $-1$, giving two terms $-\beta_\sigma$ (from the two neighbors). For the neighbors in the $y$ direction, the phase factor is $+1$, so orbitals of the same orientation line up, and this is a bonding overlap of $\pi$ type in which lobes of the same sign sit next to each other side by side; the matrix element is $-\beta_\pi$, and there are two such terms. The total is $E=\alpha-2\beta_\sigma-2\beta_\pi$, which is bonding with all four neighbors.

(3) We have $E_{p_y}-\alpha=-2\beta_\pi\cos k_xa+2\beta_\sigma\cos k_ya$, which is minimal when $\cos k_xa=+1$ and $\cos k_ya=-1$, that is, at $\bm{k}=(0,\pi/a)$, the Y point, where it equals $\alpha-2\beta_\pi-2\beta_\sigma$. The path $\Gamma\to\mathrm{X}\to\mathrm{M}\to\Gamma$ does not pass through Y. On this path, $p_y$ has its maximum $\alpha+2\beta_\pi+2\beta_\sigma$ at X and becomes $\alpha-2\beta_\sigma+2\beta_\pi$ at M, so the lowest point on the path is M (for $\alpha=10$, $\beta_\sigma=2$, $\beta_\pi=1$, it is $4$ at Y and $8$ at M). X and Y are carried into each other by a 90-degree rotation ($x\to y$, $y\to-x$), and this rotation takes $p_x\to p_y$, so “the minimum of $p_x$ at the X point” and “the minimum of $p_y$ at the Y point” are equivalent.

Exercise 42.6: The gap of a lattice with two kinds of atoms in a checkerboard pattern

Solution

(1) In the checkerboard pattern, all the neighbors of an A lattice site (four of them, at $\pm a$ in the $x$ and $y$ directions) are B, and all the neighbors of a B site are A. The unit cell contains one A and one B, and the translation vectors are $(a,a)$ and $(a,-a)$. Taking the Bloch sums of A and B as the basis, the diagonal elements are $\alpha+\Delta$ and $\alpha-\Delta$, and the off-diagonal element is the sum of the phase factors to the four B neighbors as seen from A, $\beta\bigl(e^{ik_xa}+e^{-ik_xa}+e^{ik_ya}+e^{-ik_ya}\bigr)=2\beta(\cos k_xa+\cos k_ya)$ (real):

$$ H(\bm{k})=\begin{bmatrix}\alpha+\Delta&2\beta(\cos k_xa+\cos k_ya)\\ 2\beta(\cos k_xa+\cos k_ya)&\alpha-\Delta\end{bmatrix} $$

From $(\alpha-E)^2-\Delta^2-4\beta^2(\cos k_xa+\cos k_ya)^2=0$, the eigenvalues are $E=\alpha\pm\sqrt{\Delta^2+4\beta^2(\cos k_xa+\cos k_ya)^2}$ (since the unit cell has doubled, $\bm{k}$ moves within the reduced Brillouin zone $\abs{k_x}+\abs{k_y}\le\pi/a$).
