Chapter 48: d–d Transitions and Color — Ruby and Emerald, and Ligand Field Theory

Exercise 48.1: Colors of the hydrated ion and the ammonia complex of $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ ($d^9$)

Solution

(a) The wavelength is $\lambda=10^7/12\,500=800$ nm (the boundary with the near-infrared). The energy is $12\,500\times1.23984\times10^{-4}=1.55$ eV. The absorption band is broad and, centered at 800 nm, absorbs the whole of the visible red ($605$–$700$ nm). In Table 48.1, the complementary color of red absorption is blue-green. After red to orange has been absorbed, blue-green to blue to green remains, so the aqueous solution looks pale blue (light blue).

(b) $d^9$ is the “one-hole” configuration obtained by removing one electron from the closed-shell $d^{10}$. From the ground state ${}^2E_g$, in which the hole is in $e_g$, the only state that can be excited without changing the spin is ${}^2T_{2g}$, in which the hole has moved to $t_{2g}$. Therefore only one spin-allowed d–d transition appears. The ground state ${}^2E_g$ is orbitally degenerate and is strongly distorted by the Jahn–Teller effect (an elongated octahedron). ${}^2T_{2g}$ also splits in the lower symmetry, and several transitions overlap to form a single broad band.

(c) About $600$ nm corresponds to a wavenumber of $10^7/600=16\,667\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$. This is $16\,667/12\,500=1.33$ times the $12\,500\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ of the hydrated ion. That is, $\Delta$ has increased (the center of the band has moved toward higher energy). This agrees with the fact that, in the spectrochemical series, $\mathrm{NH_3}$ gives a stronger ligand field than $\mathrm{H_2O}$ (it lies farther to the right). Because the absorption band has moved to orange–red ($600$ nm) and absorbs yellow to red broadly, the remaining blue to violet is emphasized, and the color becomes a deep blue-violet.

Exercise 48.2: $B$, $\nu_3$, and color of $[\mathrm{Cr(NH_3)_6}]^{3+}$

Solution

(a) $\Delta=\nu_1=21\,600$. Substitute $\nu_2=28\,500$ into the $d^3$ formula $B=\dfrac{(\nu_2-\Delta)(\nu_2-2\Delta)}{15\nu_2-27\Delta}$. The numerator is $(28\,500-21\,600)(28\,500-43\,200)=6\,900\times(-14\,700)=-1.0143\times10^8$, and the denominator is $15\times28\,500-27\times21\,600=427\,500-583\,200=-155\,700$. $B=1.0143\times10^8/155\,700=651\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$. $\beta=B/B_0=651/918=0.71$. (This is comparable to the $\beta$ of ruby, and the covalent character is somewhat stronger than for $\mathrm{H_2O}$, whose value is $0.78$.)

(b) From the sum formula $\nu_2+\nu_3=15B+3\Delta$, $\nu_3=15\times651.4+3\times21\,600-28\,500=9\,772+64\,800-28\,500=46\,072\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ (wavelength $217$ nm, far ultraviolet).

(c) $\nu_1=21\,600\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ corresponds to $463$ nm (blue), and in Table 48.1 the complementary color of blue is yellow. $\nu_2=28\,500\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ corresponds to $351$ nm, which lies in the ultraviolet and does not contribute to the color. Therefore the complex is predicted to absorb blue and appear yellow to orange-yellow. Indeed, the salts of $[\mathrm{Cr(NH_3)_6}]^{3+}$ are yellow.

Exercise 48.3: The difference in color between ruby and emerald

Solution

$\Delta$ and $B$. From $B=\dfrac{(\nu_2-\Delta)(\nu_2-2\Delta)}{15\nu_2-27\Delta}$, for ruby, $\Delta=18\,000$ and $\nu_2=24\,700$ give $B=\dfrac{6\,700\times(-11\,300)}{370\,500-486\,000}=655\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, $\Delta/B=27.5$. For emerald, $\Delta=16\,000$ and $\nu_2=23\,200$ give $B=\dfrac{7\,200\times(-8\,800)}{348\,000-432\,000}=754\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, $\Delta/B=21.2$. In emerald, $\Delta$ is about $11\%$ smaller ($16\,000/18\,000=0.889$).

Positions of the absorption bands. From $\lambda=10^7/\nu$, the two bands of ruby are $\nu_1$: $555.6$ nm (green, close to yellow-green) and $\nu_2$: $404.9$ nm (violet), and those of emerald are $\nu_1$: $625.0$ nm (orange to red) and $\nu_2$: $431.0$ nm (blue-violet). A decrease of $2\,000\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ in $\Delta$ moves $\nu_1$ by $69$ nm and $\nu_2$ by $26$ nm toward longer wavelengths (since the wavelength is the reciprocal of the wavenumber, the lower the energy, the larger the shift).

Transmission windows. In ruby, the green band ($555.6$ nm) absorbs green to yellow-green, and the violet band absorbs violet. Light passes through the small window of blue to blue-green between them and through the large window of red (wavelengths longer than $630$ nm), so red stands out. In emerald, red to orange ($625$ nm) and blue-violet ($431$ nm) are absorbed, and the window of blue-green to green between them (about $470$–$570$ nm) lets light through. The center of this window is in the green (near $520$ nm), to which the human eye is highly sensitive.

Tanabe–Sugano diagram. The positions $\nu_i/B$ of the $d^3$ absorption bands are functions of $\Delta/B$ only (Figure 48.4). $\nu_1/B=\Delta/B$, and $\nu_2/B$ is a curve that increases monotonically with $\Delta/B$. The weaker the ligand field (the smaller $\Delta/B$, toward the left of the figure), the closer the two bands lie to the low-energy side, that is, the longer-wavelength side. Merely by lowering $\Delta/B$ from $27.5$ to $21.2$, the bands shift greatly toward the red, and the position of the window moves from red to green. For this reason, even for the same $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$, a slight difference in the strength of the ligand field of the host crystal (bond length and covalent character) determines the color.

Exercise 48.4: Threshold of a three-level laser and the lifetime of ${}^2E$

Solution

(a) In a three-level system the lower level is the ground state, so the condition for population inversion is that the number density $N_2$ of ${}^2E$ be larger than the number density $n-N_2$ of the ground state (stimulated emission exceeds absorption). Here, as a rough estimate that ignores the degeneracies and the population of R$_2$, we take $N_2\gt n/2=8\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$ from $N_2\gt n-N_2$. (Taking into account the degeneracies of 4 and 2 and the occupation fraction $0.535$ of R$_1$, $0.535N_2/2\gt(n-N_2)/4$ gives $N_2\gt0.48\,n$, which is nearly the same.) The energy density stored at this point is $N_2\times1.786\ \mathrm{eV}\times1.602\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J/eV}=8\times10^{18}\times2.861\times10^{-19}=2.29\ \mathrm{J/cm^3}$.

(b) In a four-level system with $N_2=10^{-3}n=1.6\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$, the energy density is $1.6\times10^{16}\times2.861\times10^{-19}=4.6\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{J/cm^3}$, which is $1/500$ ($=2\times10^{-3}$) of that in (a). The reason the threshold of a three-level system is high is that more than half of the ions must be excited from the ground state.

(c) The $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$ ions in ${}^2E$ decay by spontaneous emission with lifetime $\tau$, so to maintain $N_2$ we must keep pumping at a power density of at least $N_2h\nu/\tau$. For $\tau=3$ ms this is $2.29/(3\times10^{-3})=7.6\times10^2\ \mathrm{W/cm^3}$. For $\tau=3\ \mu\mathrm{s}$ it is $2.29/(3\times10^{-6})=7.6\times10^5\ \mathrm{W/cm^3}$, which is $1\,000$ times larger. That is, the longer the lifetime (it is spin-forbidden, so spontaneous emission is slow), the less pump power is needed to maintain the population inversion. The lifetime of about $3$ ms of ${}^2E$ in ruby is well suited to storing energy in the excited state during a flash-lamp pulse (of the order of milliseconds).

Exercise 48.5: What breaks the Laporte rule, and why tetrahedral complexes are intensely colored

Solution

(a) Octahedron: (i) Vibrations of odd parity ($t_{1u}$, $t_{2u}$) momentarily break the inversion symmetry and mix $p$ and odd-parity components of the ligands into $d$ (vibronic coupling). (ii) The fact that the site in an actual crystal (the site of $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$ is $C_3$ in ruby and $D_3$ in emerald) lacks an inversion center, as well as the covalent character through the ligand orbitals, also supplies odd-parity components. Tetrahedron: the absence of an inversion center in itself removes the premise of the Laporte rule (inversion symmetry). However, since transitions between states built from d orbitals alone are forbidden by the parity of the atom ($\Delta l=0$), mixing with odd-parity p orbitals and the like is required.

(b) In a tetrahedron, the odd-order $k=3$ term $\hat{V}_3=\dfrac{20\sqrt3}{3}\Lambda\dfrac{xyz}{a^4}$ remains in the expansion of the point charges of the ligands (for the four vertices $a(\pm1,\pm1,\pm1)/\sqrt3$ ($s_1s_2s_3=+1$), $\sum_iP_3(u_i)=\tfrac{20\sqrt3}{3}n_xn_yn_z$). In an octahedron the pairs $\pm\bm{R}$ cancel and give 0. $xyz$ belongs to the totally symmetric representation $A_1$ in $T_d$ and has odd parity. It mixes $d$ orbitals ($d_{xy}$ and others, which belong to $T_2$) and $p$ orbitals ($p_z$ and others, which belong to $T_2$) (angular integral $\int n_z(n_xn_yn_z)(n_xn_y)\,\dd\Omega=4\pi/105\ne0$). If the coefficient $c$ of the admixture of the $p$ component is, say, $0.05$, the intensity imparted to d–d is that of an allowed transition ($f\sim0.1$–$1$) multiplied by $c^2=2.5\times10^{-3}$. In $T_d$, $\hat{\bm{r}}$ belongs to $T_2$, and ${}^4A_2\to{}^4T_1$ is allowed because $A_2\otimes T_2\otimes T_1\ni A_1$, whereas for ${}^4A_2\to{}^4T_2$ the corresponding product does not contain it and the transition is forbidden. In an octahedron there is no such permanent admixture, only the admixture that arises momentarily through vibrations, so the transitions are weak.

(c) Since $f\propto c^2$, $c_{\mathrm{T}}/c_{\mathrm{O}}=\sqrt{f_{\mathrm{T}}/f_{\mathrm{O}}}=\sqrt{75}=8.7$. That is, the coefficient of $d$–$p$ mixing in the tetrahedron is about nine times the effective mixing coefficient of the octahedron (due to vibronic coupling).

Exercise 48.6: $\pi$-donor and $\pi$-acceptor ligands

Solution

A $\pi$ bond mixes the $\pi$ orbitals of the ligands into the metal $t_{2g}$, which remained isolated in the $\sigma$ bonding. When two levels mix, the levels repel each other and move apart (second-order perturbation). In $\mathrm{Cl^-}$, the $\pi$ orbitals of the lone pairs are filled and lie lower than the metal $t_{2g}$. Therefore the metal $t_{2g}$ is pushed up (the antibonding $t_{2g}^*$). Since $e_g^*$ does not move, $\Delta_o=E(e_g^*)-E(t_{2g}^*)$ decreases. $\mathrm{CO}$ has empty $\pi^*$ orbitals, which lie higher than the metal $t_{2g}$. The metal $t_{2g}$ is pushed down (back-donation from the metal to the ligand), and $\Delta_o$ increases.

Numerical values. From the solution of the two-level problem, the shift of $t_{2g}$ is $s=-\dfrac{\delta}{2}+\dfrac12\sqrt{\delta^2+4V_\pi^2}$, and with $\delta=3.0$ eV and $V_\pi=1.0$ eV, $s=-1.5+\tfrac12\sqrt{9+4}=-1.5+1.8028=0.3028$ eV (the second-order perturbation approximation $V_\pi^2/\delta=0.333$ eV is about $10\%$ too large). $\pi$ donation ($t_{2g}$ goes up by $s$): $\Delta_o=2.0-0.303=1.697$ eV ($13\,689\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$). $\pi$ acceptance ($t_{2g}$ goes down by $s$): $\Delta_o=2.0+0.303=2.303$ eV ($18\,573\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$). The two values lie on either side of the $\sigma$-only value of $2.0$ eV ($16\,131\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$), each shifted by about $0.3$ eV.

Exercise 48.7: Accuracy of the approximation in the two-level model

Solution

The exact solution is $\Delta_o=-\dfrac{\delta}{2}+\dfrac12\sqrt{\delta^2+4V^2}=-3+\tfrac12\sqrt{36+36}=-3+4.2426=1.2426$ eV. The approximation is $V^2/\delta=9/6=1.5$ eV. The difference is $1.5-1.2426=0.257$ eV, which is $21\%$ too large relative to the exact solution. Since $V/\delta=0.5$, the condition of perturbation theory, $V\ll\delta$, is not satisfied.

Including the fourth-order term, $\Delta_o\simeq\dfrac{V^2}{\delta}-\dfrac{V^4}{\delta^3}=1.5-\dfrac{81}{216}=1.5-0.375=1.125$ eV, which is $-9.5\%$ relative to the exact solution. The accuracy improves (the difference is $0.117$ eV), but now it is an underestimate. This is due to the alternating-series nature of the expansion of $\sqrt{1+4u}$; for a large $u$ such as $u=V^2/\delta^2=0.25$, the convergence is slow.

Exercise 48.8: $[\mathrm{CoCl_4}]^{2-}$ and cobalt blue

Solution

(a) From $\Delta_t=\tfrac49\Delta_o$, $\Delta_o=\tfrac94\Delta_t=\tfrac94\times3\,000=6\,750\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ (a rough guide from the point-charge model with the same ligands and the same distance).

(b) Tetrahedral $d^7$ follows the same formula as octahedral $d^3$. $\nu_1=\Delta_t=3\,000\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ (wavelength $3\,333$ nm). The quantity under the root is $225\times710^2-18\times710\times3\,000+3\,000^2=1.1342\times10^8-3.834\times10^7+9\times10^6=8.408\times10^7$, and its square root is $9\,170$. The sum is $15B+3\Delta_t=10\,650+9\,000=19\,650$. Therefore $\nu_2=(19\,650-9\,170)/2=5\,240\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ ($1\,908$ nm), and $\nu_3=(19\,650+9\,170)/2=14\,410\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ ($694$ nm).

(c) $\nu_1$ and $\nu_2$ are in the infrared ($1\,908$ nm and $3\,333$ nm) and do not contribute to the color. The only one in the visible region (the red end) is $\nu_3$ ($694$ nm; the band is broad and in fact extends over $600$–$750$ nm), and it absorbs red to orange light. In Table 48.1, the complementary color of red is blue-green and that of orange is green-blue, so blue to blue-green remains, and the color is a deep blue (since the band is not a single narrow line but absorbs yellow to red together, the blueness looks strong). The reason $\nu_3$ comes to lie in the visible region (or at the edge of the near-infrared) is found in the limit $\Delta\to0$ of the formula. At $\Delta=0$, $\nu_3=15B$ (the separation between ${}^4P$ and ${}^4F$; here $15\times710=10\,650\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, $939$ nm), and while $\Delta$ is small it increases as $\nu_3\simeq15B+1.2\Delta$ (for $\Delta=3\,000$, $14\,250\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, close to the exact $14\,410$). That is, even for a tetrahedral complex with a weak ligand field, because ${}^4P$ already lies higher by $15B$ in the free ion, $\nu_3$ exceeds 10,000 $\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ and reaches into the visible region. In CoAl$_2$O$_4$, $\Delta_t$ is somewhat larger (about $4\,000\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$), and $\nu_3\approx15\,900\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ ($629$ nm).

← Back to Chapter 48, “d–d Transitions and Color — Ruby and Emerald, and Ligand Field Theory”

Chapter 49: The Time-Dependent Schrödinger Equation — Superposition of Stationary States and Waves in a Box

Exercise 49.1: Superposition of $\psi_1+\psi_3$

Solution

Since $\omega_n=E_n/\hbar=n^2\omega_1$, we have $\omega_{31}=\omega_3-\omega_1=9\omega_1-\omega_1=8\omega_1$. Since $\psi_1,\psi_3$ are real, the probability density takes the same form as in the quantum-beat formula of Chapter 49:

$$ \abs{\Psi}^2=\frac12\bigl(\psi_1^2+\psi_3^2\bigr)+\psi_1\psi_3\cos\omega_{31}t $$

This is the probability density.

(1) $\expval{x}=\displaystyle\int_0^Lx\abs{\Psi}^2\dd x=\frac12\Bigl(\frac{L}{2}+\frac{L}{2}\Bigr)+x_{13}\cos\omega_{31}t$, where $x_{13}=\displaystyle\int_0^Lx\,\psi_1\psi_3\dd x$ (for each $\psi_n$, $\int x\psi_n^2\dd x=L/2$). Since $\psi_n(L-x)=\sqrt{2/L}\sin\bigl(n\pi-\tfrac{n\pi x}{L}\bigr)=(-1)^{n+1}\psi_n(x)$, both $\psi_1$ and $\psi_3$ are symmetric about $x=L/2$, and so is $\psi_1\psi_3$. Substituting $u=L-x$, we obtain

$$ x_{13}=\int_0^L(L-u)\,\psi_1(u)\psi_3(u)\dd u=L\underbrace{\int_0^L\psi_1\psi_3\dd u}_{0\ (\text{orthogonality})}-x_{13}\qquad\therefore\ x_{13}=0 $$

Therefore $\expval{x}=\dfrac{L}{2}$, independent of time.

(2) Similarly, $\expval{x^2}=\dfrac12\bigl(\expval{x^2}_1+\expval{x^2}_3\bigr)+(x^2)_{13}\cos\omega_{31}t$, where $(x^2)_{13}=\displaystyle\int_0^Lx^2\psi_1\psi_3\dd x$. Using $\expval{x^2}_n=L^2\Bigl(\dfrac13-\dfrac{1}{2n^2\pi^2}\Bigr)$, we obtain

$$ \frac12\bigl(\expval{x^2}_1+\expval{x^2}_3\bigr)=L^2\left[\frac13-\frac12\Bigl(\frac{1}{2\pi^2}+\frac{1}{18\pi^2}\Bigr)\right]=L^2\left[\frac13-\frac{5}{18\pi^2}\right]=0.3052\,L^2 $$

(Here $\dfrac{1}{2\pi^2}+\dfrac{1}{18\pi^2}=\dfrac{9+1}{18\pi^2}=\dfrac{5}{9\pi^2}$.) For $(x^2)_{13}$, we use the product-to-sum formula $\psi_1\psi_3=\dfrac{2}{L}\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{L}\sin\dfrac{3\pi x}{L}=\dfrac1L\Bigl[\cos\dfrac{2\pi x}{L}-\cos\dfrac{4\pi x}{L}\Bigr]$ together with $\displaystyle\int_0^Lx^2\cos qx\dd x=\dfrac{2L}{q^2}$ for $q=\dfrac{2m\pi}{L}$ ($m$ a positive integer), which follows from integrating by parts twice and using $\sin qL=0$ and $\cos qL=1$. This gives

$$ (x^2)_{13}=\frac1L\left[\frac{2L}{(2\pi/L)^2}-\frac{2L}{(4\pi/L)^2}\right]=\frac1L\left[\frac{L^3}{2\pi^2}-\frac{L^3}{8\pi^2}\right]=\frac{3L^2}{8\pi^2}=0.0380\,L^2 $$

Hence

$$ \expval{x^2}(t)=L^2\left[\frac13-\frac{5}{18\pi^2}+\frac{3}{8\pi^2}\cos8\omega_1t\right] $$

which oscillates with period $T_{31}=\dfrac{2\pi}{8\omega_1}=\dfrac{\pi}{4\omega_1}$ ($=h/(E_3-E_1)$).

(3) For example, at $x=L/4$ we have $\psi_1^2=\dfrac2L\sin^2\dfrac\pi4=\dfrac1L$, $\psi_3^2=\dfrac2L\sin^2\dfrac{3\pi}{4}=\dfrac1L$, and $\psi_1\psi_3=\dfrac2L\sin\dfrac\pi4\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{4}=\dfrac1L$, so $\abs{\Psi(L/4,t)}^2=\dfrac1L\bigl(1+\cos\omega_{31}t\bigr)$, which oscillates between $0$ and $2/L$. The probability density changes with time, so this is a non-stationary state. The reason $\expval{x}$ does not move is that the probability density of this state keeps a left–right symmetric shape and “breathes” symmetrically.

Exercise 49.2: Revival and mirror image, and the “fractional revival” at $T_{\mathrm{rev}}/4$

Solution

We expand $f(x)=\Psi(x,0)=\sum_nc_n\psi_n(x)$. With $E_n=n^2E_1$ ($E_1=\pi^2\hbar^2/2mL^2$) and $\theta=E_1t/\hbar$, we have $\Psi(x,t)=\sum_nc_n\,e^{-in^2\theta}\psi_n(x)$. Also, $\psi_n(L-x)=\sqrt{2/L}\sin\bigl(n\pi-\tfrac{n\pi x}{L}\bigr)=(-1)^{n+1}\psi_n(x)$ (we used $\sin n\pi=0$ and $\cos n\pi=(-1)^n$).

(1) At the time $T_{\mathrm{rev}}=\dfrac{2\pi\hbar}{E_1}=\dfrac{4mL^2}{\pi\hbar}$ when $\theta=2\pi$, $e^{-2\pi in^2}=1$, so $\Psi(x,T_{\mathrm{rev}})=f(x)$. At $t=T_{\mathrm{rev}}/2$ ($\theta=\pi$), $e^{-i\pi n^2}=(-1)^{n^2}=(-1)^n$, and

$$ \Psi\Bigl(x,\frac{T_{\mathrm{rev}}}{2}\Bigr)=\sum_nc_n(-1)^n\psi_n(x),\qquad f(L-x)=\sum_nc_n(-1)^{n+1}\psi_n(x) $$

so the former is $-1$ times the latter: $\Psi\bigl(x,\tfrac{T_{\mathrm{rev}}}{2}\bigr)=-f(L-x)$.

(2) We split $f$ into a part symmetric about $x=L/2$ and a part antisymmetric about it: $f_{\mathrm S}=\tfrac12[f(x)+f(L-x)]$, $f_{\mathrm A}=\tfrac12[f(x)-f(L-x)]$. Since $\psi_n$ with odd $n$ is symmetric and $\psi_n$ with even $n$ is antisymmetric, $f_{\mathrm S}=\sum_{n\,\text{odd}}c_n\psi_n$ and $f_{\mathrm A}=\sum_{n\,\text{even}}c_n\psi_n$. The phase $e^{-in^2\pi/2}$ at $t=T_{\mathrm{rev}}/4$ ($\theta=\pi/2$) is $e^{-2\pi ij^2}=1$ for even $n=2j$, because $n^2=4j^2$, and $e^{-i\pi/2}e^{-4\pi ij'}=-i$ for odd $n$, because $n^2=1+8j'$ ($j'$ is an integer). Therefore,

$$ \Psi\Bigl(x,\frac{T_{\mathrm{rev}}}{4}\Bigr)=f_{\mathrm A}-i\,f_{\mathrm S}=\frac12\bigl[f(x)-f(L-x)\bigr]-\frac{i}{2}\bigl[f(x)+f(L-x)\bigr]=\frac{1-i}{2}f(x)-\frac{1+i}{2}f(L-x) $$

and the wave becomes a superposition of the original waveform and its mirror-image waveform (two copies).

(3) For $f=\dfrac{\psi_1+\psi_2}{\sqrt2}$, $f(L-x)=\dfrac{\psi_1-\psi_2}{\sqrt2}$, so the right-hand side of (2) is

$$ \frac{1}{2\sqrt2}\Bigl[(1-i)(\psi_1+\psi_2)-(1+i)(\psi_1-\psi_2)\Bigr]=\frac{1}{2\sqrt2}\Bigl[-2i\,\psi_1+2\,\psi_2\Bigr]=\frac{-i\psi_1+\psi_2}{\sqrt2} $$

On the other hand, by direct calculation, at $\theta=\pi/2$ we have $e^{-i\theta}=-i$ and $e^{-4i\theta}=e^{-2\pi i}=1$, so $\Psi=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\bigl[\psi_1e^{-i\pi/2}+\psi_2e^{-4i\pi/2}\bigr]=\dfrac{-i\psi_1+\psi_2}{\sqrt2}$, which agrees. In this case the probability density is $\abs{\Psi}^2=\dfrac12(\psi_1^2+\psi_2^2)$ (the interference term vanishes because $\mathrm{Re}(i\psi_1\psi_2/2)=0$), which equals the average of $\tfrac12(\psi_1^2+\psi_2^2)+\psi_1\psi_2$ (the density at $t=0$) and $\tfrac12(\psi_1^2+\psi_2^2)-\psi_1\psi_2$ (that of the mirror image).

Exercise 49.3: Generalization from width $L$ to $aL$

Solution

Since $\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{L}}\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{aL}}=\dfrac{2}{L\sqrt a}$, the expansion coefficient is

$$ A_n=\frac{2}{L\sqrt a}\int_0^L\sin\frac{\pi x}{L}\,\sin\frac{n\pi x}{aL}\dd x $$

(The initial state exists only in $0\le x\le L$, so the upper limit of the integral is $L$.)

(1) For $n=a$, $\displaystyle\int_0^L\sin^2\frac{\pi x}{L}\dd x=\frac L2$, so $A_a=\dfrac{2}{L\sqrt a}\cdot\dfrac L2=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt a}$ and $P_a=\dfrac1a$. (This is because the initial state is the part, in $0\le x\le L$, of the $n=a$ eigenfunction $\sqrt{2/aL}\sin(\pi x/L)$ of the new box, multiplied by $\sqrt a$. For $a=2$, it agrees with $P_2=\tfrac12$.)

(2) For $n\ne a$, we apply the product-to-sum formula $\sin\alpha\sin\beta=\tfrac12[\cos(\alpha-\beta)-\cos(\alpha+\beta)]$ with $\alpha-\beta=\bigl(1-\tfrac na\bigr)\tfrac{\pi x}{L}$ and $\alpha+\beta=\bigl(1+\tfrac na\bigr)\tfrac{\pi x}{L}$, and use $\displaystyle\int_0^L\cos qx\dd x=\dfrac{\sin qL}{q}$. Then

$$ A_n=\frac{1}{L\sqrt a}\left[\frac{L\,\sin\bigl((1-\frac na)\pi\bigr)}{(1-\frac na)\pi}-\frac{L\,\sin\bigl((1+\frac na)\pi\bigr)}{(1+\frac na)\pi}\right]=\frac{1}{\sqrt a\,\pi}\left[\frac{\sin\bigl((1-\frac na)\pi\bigr)}{1-\frac na}-\frac{\sin\bigl((1+\frac na)\pi\bigr)}{1+\frac na}\right] $$

For $a=3$, $\sin\bigl(\pi-\tfrac{n\pi}{3}\bigr)=\sin\tfrac{n\pi}{3}$, $\sin\bigl(\pi+\tfrac{n\pi}{3}\bigr)=-\sin\tfrac{n\pi}{3}$, and $1\mp\tfrac n3=\tfrac{3\mp n}{3}$, so

$$ A_n=\frac{\sin\frac{n\pi}{3}}{\sqrt3\,\pi}\left[\frac{3}{3-n}+\frac{3}{3+n}\right]=\frac{\sin\frac{n\pi}{3}}{\sqrt3\,\pi}\cdot\frac{18}{9-n^2}=\frac{6\sqrt3\,\sin\frac{n\pi}{3}}{\pi\,(9-n^2)}\qquad(n\ne3) $$

(Combining over a common denominator: $\dfrac{3}{3-n}+\dfrac{3}{3+n}=\dfrac{3(3+n)+3(3-n)}{9-n^2}=\dfrac{18}{9-n^2}$, and $\dfrac{18}{\sqrt3}=6\sqrt3$.) Also, $A_3=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$. The numerical values are $A_1=\dfrac{6\sqrt3\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}{8\pi}=\dfrac{9}{8\pi}=0.3581$, $A_2=\dfrac{6\sqrt3\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}{5\pi}=\dfrac{9}{5\pi}=0.5730$, and $A_4=\dfrac{6\sqrt3\cdot\bigl(-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\bigr)}{-7\pi}=\dfrac{9}{7\pi}=0.4093$ ($\sin\frac{4\pi}{3}=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$, $9-16=-7$). Including $A_3^2=\tfrac13$, it can be confirmed numerically that the sum of probabilities is $1$.

Exercise 49.4: Probability of ending up in $2s$ after the β decay of tritium

Solution

Setting $a_0=1$, we have $R_{10}^{(1)}=2e^{-r}$ and $R_{20}^{(2)}=2\cdot1^{3/2}\bigl(1-r\bigr)e^{-r}=2(1-r)e^{-r}$ (for $Z=2$, $Z/2=1$ and $Zr/2=r$). The normalization of $R_{20}^{(2)}$ is confirmed by $4\displaystyle\int_0^\infty r^2(1-r)^2e^{-2r}\dd r=4\Bigl[\tfrac{2}{8}-2\cdot\tfrac{6}{16}+\tfrac{24}{32}\Bigr]=1$. Since the angular part is the same $Y_0^0$, the overlap integral is

$$ \int_0^\infty r^2R_{20}^{(2)}R_{10}^{(1)}\dd r=4\int_0^\infty\bigl(r^2-r^3\bigr)e^{-2r}\dd r=4\left[\frac{2!}{2^3}-\frac{3!}{2^4}\right]=4\left[\frac14-\frac38\right]=-\frac12 $$

The probability is $\Bigl(-\dfrac12\Bigr)^2=\dfrac14=0.250$. For a $2p$ state, the angular part is $Y_1^m$, and $\displaystyle\int Y_0^{0*}Y_1^m\dd\Omega=0$ (orthogonality of spherical harmonics with different $l$), so the overlap integral is $0$ regardless of the radial part, and the probability is $0$.

Exercise 49.5: Probability of being in the left half during a quantum beat, and the probability current

Solution

(1) The probability density is $\abs{\Psi}^2=\tfrac12(\psi_1^2+\psi_2^2)+\psi_1\psi_2\cos\omega_{21}t$. Since $\psi_n^2$ is symmetric about $x=L/2$ and its integral over $[0,L]$ is $1$, $\displaystyle\int_0^{L/2}\psi_n^2\dd x=\tfrac12$. Using $\psi_1\psi_2=\dfrac1L\Bigl[\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{L}-\cos\dfrac{3\pi x}{L}\Bigr]$ (product-to-sum formula), the integral of the cross term is

$$ \int_0^{L/2}\psi_1\psi_2\dd x=\frac1L\left[\frac{L}{\pi}\sin\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{L}{3\pi}\sin\frac{3\pi}{2}\right]=\frac1\pi\left[1+\frac13\right]=\frac{4}{3\pi} $$

Therefore,

$$ P_{\mathrm{left}}(t)=\frac12\Bigl(\frac12+\frac12\Bigr)+\frac{4}{3\pi}\cos\omega_{21}t=\frac12+\frac{4}{3\pi}\cos\omega_{21}t\qquad\Bigl(\frac{4}{3\pi}=0.424\Bigr) $$

At $t=0$ it is $0.924$, biased toward the left half, and after half a period it becomes $0.076$.

(2) Since $\omega_{21}=\dfrac{3\pi^2\hbar}{2mL^2}$,

$$ \frac{\dd P_{\mathrm{left}}}{\dd t}=-\frac{4\omega_{21}}{3\pi}\sin\omega_{21}t=-\frac{4}{3\pi}\cdot\frac{3\pi^2\hbar}{2mL^2}\sin\omega_{21}t=-\frac{2\pi\hbar}{mL^2}\sin\omega_{21}t $$

On the other hand, we evaluate the probability current $j(x,t)=\dfrac{\hbar}{2m}\bigl(\psi_1'\psi_2-\psi_1\psi_2'\bigr)\sin\omega_{21}t$ at $x=L/2$. We have $\psi_1(L/2)=\sqrt{2/L}$, $\psi_1'(L/2)=\sqrt{2/L}\,\dfrac{\pi}{L}\cos\dfrac\pi2=0$, $\psi_2(L/2)=\sqrt{2/L}\sin\pi=0$, and $\psi_2'(L/2)=\sqrt{2/L}\,\dfrac{2\pi}{L}\cos\pi=-\sqrt{2/L}\,\dfrac{2\pi}{L}$, so $\psi_1'\psi_2-\psi_1\psi_2'=0+\dfrac2L\cdot\dfrac{2\pi}{L}=\dfrac{4\pi}{L^2}$ and $j(L/2,t)=\dfrac{2\pi\hbar}{mL^2}\sin\omega_{21}t$. At the wall $x=0$, $j(0,t)=0$ because $\psi_n(0)=0$. Integrating the continuity equation over $[0,L/2]$ gives $\dfrac{\dd P_{\mathrm{left}}}{\dd t}=-\bigl[j(L/2,t)-j(0,t)\bigr]=-j(L/2,t)$, which agrees with the $\dfrac{\dd P_{\mathrm{left}}}{\dd t}$ obtained from (1). The decrease of the probability in the left half equals the flow that leaves through the center to the right.

Exercise 49.6: Sending a free-electron wave packet as narrow as possible

Solution

(1) Squaring $\sigma(t)=\sigma_0\sqrt{1+\bigl(\tfrac{\hbar t}{2m\sigma_0^2}\bigr)^2}$ and setting $t=t_{\mathrm{f}}$, we obtain $\sigma(t_{\mathrm{f}})^2=\sigma_0^2\Bigl[1+\dfrac{\hbar^2t_{\mathrm{f}}^2}{4m^2\sigma_0^4}\Bigr]=\sigma_0^2+\Bigl(\dfrac{\hbar t_{\mathrm{f}}}{2m\sigma_0}\Bigr)^2$.

(2) Letting $b=\dfrac{\hbar t_{\mathrm{f}}}{2m}$, we have $\sigma(t_{\mathrm{f}})^2=\sigma_0^2+\dfrac{b^2}{\sigma_0^2}$. From the inequality between the arithmetic and geometric means, $x+y\ge2\sqrt{xy}$ ($x=\sigma_0^2$, $y=b^2/\sigma_0^2$), we get $\sigma(t_{\mathrm{f}})^2\ge2b$, and equality holds when $\sigma_0^2=b^2/\sigma_0^2$, that is, when $\sigma_0^2=b$. Therefore,

$$ \sigma_0^{\mathrm{opt}}=\sqrt{\frac{\hbar t_{\mathrm{f}}}{2m}},\qquad\sigma(t_{\mathrm{f}})_{\min}=\sqrt{2b}=\sqrt{\frac{\hbar t_{\mathrm{f}}}{m}} $$

(Here $\sigma(t_{\mathrm{f}})_{\min}=\sqrt2\,\sigma_0^{\mathrm{opt}}$.) Numerically, with $m=9.109\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$, $t_{\mathrm{f}}=10^{-9}\ \mathrm{s}$, and $\hbar=1.0546\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$, we have $\dfrac{\hbar t_{\mathrm{f}}}{m}=\dfrac{1.0546\times10^{-43}}{9.109\times10^{-31}}=1.158\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{m^2}$, $\sigma(t_{\mathrm{f}})_{\min}=3.40\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}=0.340\ \mathrm{\mu m}$, and $\sigma_0^{\mathrm{opt}}=\dfrac{0.340}{\sqrt2}=0.241\ \mathrm{\mu m}$.

(3) Letting $\sigma_0=r\sqrt b$, we have $\sigma(t_{\mathrm{f}})^2=b\bigl(r^2+r^{-2}\bigr)$. For $r=\tfrac12$ this gives $b(\tfrac14+4)=4.25\,b$, and for $r=2$ it gives $b(4+\tfrac14)=4.25\,b$. In both cases $\sigma(t_{\mathrm{f}})^2$ is $2.125$ times its minimum value $2b$; that is, the width is $\sqrt{2.125}=1.46$ times as large, namely $\sigma(t_{\mathrm{f}})=0.496\ \mathrm{\mu m}$. If the packet is squeezed too narrow at the start (a small position uncertainty means a large spread in momentum, so the packet spreads quickly), or if it is made too wide (the initial width itself remains), the final width is not minimal. The minimum occurs when the initial width and the contribution to the width from the spreading are equal (the standard quantum limit).

Exercise 49.7: Quantum beats and light emission — a box with $L=2\ \mathrm{nm}$

Solution

(1) $E_1=\dfrac{h^2}{8mL^2}$, so $E_1\propto L^{-2}$. Since $E_1=0.3760\ \mathrm{eV}$ for $L=1\ \mathrm{nm}$, for $L=2\ \mathrm{nm}$ we have $E_1=\dfrac{0.3760}{4}=0.0940\ \mathrm{eV}$. Since $E_2=4E_1$, $E_2-E_1=3E_1=0.2820\ \mathrm{eV}$.

(2) The period of the oscillation of the probability density is $T_{21}=\dfrac{h}{E_2-E_1}=\dfrac{4.1357\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{eV\,s}}{0.2820\ \mathrm{eV}}=1.467\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{s}=14.7\ \mathrm{fs}$, and the frequency is $\nu_{21}=\dfrac{1}{T_{21}}=6.82\times10^{13}\ \mathrm{Hz}=68.2\ \mathrm{THz}$. The wavelength of the light emitted by the oscillation of the charge distribution is $\lambda=\dfrac{hc}{E_2-E_1}=\dfrac{1239.84\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}}{0.2820\ \mathrm{eV}}=4.40\times10^3\ \mathrm{nm}=4.40\ \mathrm{\mu m}$ (mid-infrared). The wider the box, the smaller the level spacing ($\propto L^{-2}$) and the longer the wavelength: it is four times the $1.10\ \mathrm{\mu m}$ for $L=1\ \mathrm{nm}$.

Exercise 49.8: Suddenly pushing the box wall in to $L/2$

Solution

(1) We have $\chi_n\psi_1=\sqrt{\dfrac4L}\sqrt{\dfrac2L}\sin\dfrac{2n\pi x}{L}\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{L}=\dfrac{2\sqrt2}{L}\sin\dfrac{2n\pi x}{L}\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{L}$, and by the product-to-sum formula $\sin\dfrac{2n\pi x}{L}\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{L}=\dfrac12\Bigl[\cos\dfrac{(2n-1)\pi x}{L}-\cos\dfrac{(2n+1)\pi x}{L}\Bigr]$. Moreover, $\displaystyle\int_0^{L/2}\cos qx\dd x=\dfrac{\sin(qL/2)}{q}$, and for $q=\dfrac{(2n\mp1)\pi}{L}$ we have $\sin\dfrac{qL}{2}=\sin\dfrac{(2n\mp1)\pi}{2}$, so

$$ c_n=\frac{2\sqrt2}{L}\cdot\frac12\left[\frac{L}{(2n-1)\pi}\sin\frac{(2n-1)\pi}{2}-\frac{L}{(2n+1)\pi}\sin\frac{(2n+1)\pi}{2}\right]=\frac{\sqrt2}{\pi}\left[\frac{\sin\frac{(2n-1)\pi}{2}}{2n-1}-\frac{\sin\frac{(2n+1)\pi}{2}}{2n+1}\right] $$

Now $\sin\dfrac{(2n-1)\pi}{2}=\sin\bigl(n\pi-\tfrac\pi2\bigr)=-\cos n\pi=(-1)^{n+1}$ and $\sin\dfrac{(2n+1)\pi}{2}=\sin\bigl(n\pi+\tfrac\pi2\bigr)=\cos n\pi=(-1)^n$, so

$$ c_n=\frac{\sqrt2\,(-1)^{n+1}}{\pi}\left[\frac{1}{2n-1}+\frac{1}{2n+1}\right]=\frac{\sqrt2\,(-1)^{n+1}}{\pi}\cdot\frac{4n}{4n^2-1}=\frac{4\sqrt2\,(-1)^{n+1}\,n}{\pi\,(4n^2-1)} $$

(Putting over a common denominator: $\dfrac{1}{2n-1}+\dfrac{1}{2n+1}=\dfrac{(2n+1)+(2n-1)}{4n^2-1}=\dfrac{4n}{4n^2-1}$.) In particular, $c_1=\dfrac{4\sqrt2}{3\pi}=0.6002$, $c_2=-\dfrac{8\sqrt2}{15\pi}=-0.2401$, and $c_3=\dfrac{12\sqrt2}{35\pi}=0.1543$.

(2) Since $\{\chi_n\}$ is an orthonormal complete set on the interval $[0,L/2]$, Parseval's identity gives $\sum_n\abs{c_n}^2=\displaystyle\int_0^{L/2}\abs{\psi_1}^2\dd x$ ($c_n$ are the expansion coefficients, in terms of $\chi_n$, of the function $\psi_1$ restricted to $[0,L/2]$). Since $\abs{\psi_1}^2$ is symmetric about $x=L/2$ and its integral over $[0,L]$ is $1$, this integral is $\dfrac12$. That is, with probability $\tfrac12$ the particle is inside the new box, and the remaining $\tfrac12$ is in the region $L/2\lt x\le L$ into which the wall is pushed (this part collides with the wall). Under the condition that the particle is inside the new box, the probability of obtaining the $n=1$ energy is

$$ \frac{\abs{c_1}^2}{1/2}=2\cdot\frac{32}{9\pi^2}=\frac{64}{9\pi^2}=0.7205 $$

(for $n=2$ it is $2\abs{c_2}^2=\dfrac{256}{225\pi^2}=0.115$). Note also that $\psi_1(L/2)=\sqrt{2/L}\ne0$, so the restricted wave function does not vanish at the new wall $x=L/2$ but has a jump. Hence $\abs{c_n}^2\approx\dfrac{2}{\pi^2n^2}$ ($n\gg1$) decreases only slowly, $\sum_nn^2\abs{c_n}^2$ diverges, and the expectation value of the energy is infinite.

← Back to Chapter 49, “The Time-Dependent Schrödinger Equation — Superposition of Stationary States and Waves in a Box”

Chapter 50: The Time-Evolution Operator and the Three Pictures — Schrödinger, Heisenberg, and Interaction Pictures

Exercise 50.1: Unitarity and group properties

Solution

Let $\tau=t-t_0$ (real). We start from the power-series definition $\hat{U}_S=\sum_{n}\dfrac{1}{n!}\left(-\dfrac{i\tau}{\hbar}\right)^n\hat{H}^n$. From $(\hat{H}^n)^\dagger=(\hat{H}^\dagger)^n=\hat{H}^n$ and $(-i\tau/\hbar)^*=+i\tau/\hbar$, the Hermitian conjugate is $\hat{U}_S^\dagger=\sum_m\dfrac{1}{m!}\left(\dfrac{i\tau}{\hbar}\right)^m\hat{H}^m$.

Unitarity. Since the powers of $\hat{H}$ commute with one another, the product can be written by collecting the double sum according to $N=m+n$:

$$ \hat{U}_S^\dagger\hat{U}_S=\sum_{m,n}\frac{1}{m!\,n!}\left(\frac{i\tau}{\hbar}\right)^m\left(-\frac{i\tau}{\hbar}\right)^n\hat{H}^{m+n}=\sum_{N=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{N!}\left(\frac{i\tau}{\hbar}\right)^N\hat{H}^N\sum_{n=0}^{N}\binom{N}{n}(-1)^n $$

(here we used $\dfrac{N!}{m!\,n!}=\binom{N}{n}$ and $\left(-\dfrac{i\tau}{\hbar}\right)^n=\left(\dfrac{i\tau}{\hbar}\right)^n(-1)^n$). By the binomial theorem, $\sum_{n=0}^{N}\binom{N}{n}(-1)^n=(1-1)^N$ equals $1$ for $N=0$ and $0$ for $N\ge1$, so $\hat{U}_S^\dagger\hat{U}_S=\hat{1}$. The same calculation also shows $\hat{U}_S\hat{U}_S^\dagger=\hat{1}$, with the order reversed.

Group property. Let $\tau_2=t_2-t_1$ and $\tau_1=t_1-t_0$. Similarly to the above,

$$ \hat{U}_S(t_2,t_1)\hat{U}_S(t_1,t_0)=\sum_{m,n}\frac{1}{m!\,n!}\left(-\frac{i\tau_2}{\hbar}\right)^m\left(-\frac{i\tau_1}{\hbar}\right)^n\hat{H}^{m+n}=\sum_{N=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{N!}\left(-\frac{i}{\hbar}\right)^N\hat{H}^N\sum_{n=0}^{N}\binom{N}{n}\tau_2^{N-n}\tau_1^{n} $$

By the binomial theorem the inner sum becomes $(\tau_2+\tau_1)^N=(t_2-t_0)^N$, so the right-hand side is $\hat{U}_S(t_2,t_0)$.

The non-Hermitian case. For $\hat{H}_{\mathrm{eff}}=\hat{H}-i\hbar\Gamma/2$, since $\hat{1}$ commutes with $\hat{H}$, we have $e^{-i\hat{H}_{\mathrm{eff}}\tau/\hbar}=e^{-i\hat{H}\tau/\hbar}\,e^{-\Gamma\tau/2}$ ($\hat{H}$ is Hermitian). Taking the conjugate gives $e^{+i\hat{H}\tau/\hbar}e^{-\Gamma\tau/2}$ ($\Gamma$ is real), so

$$ \hat{U}_{\mathrm{eff}}^\dagger\hat{U}_{\mathrm{eff}}=e^{+i\hat{H}\tau/\hbar}e^{-i\hat{H}\tau/\hbar}\,e^{-\Gamma\tau}=e^{-\Gamma\tau}\,\hat{1} $$

Since the squared norm decreases as $e^{-\Gamma\tau}$, $1/\Gamma$ is the lifetime. That the operator is not unitary means that probability escapes to other states (photons, for example).

Exercise 50.2: Two derivations of $\hat{a}_H(t)=\hat{a}\,e^{-i\omega t}$

Solution

$\hat{H}=\hbar\omega(\hat{a}^\dagger\hat{a}+\tfrac12)$ and $\hat{n}=\hat{a}^\dagger\hat{a}$. From $\comm{\hat{a}}{\hat{a}^\dagger}=1$ we get $\comm{\hat{n}}{\hat{a}}=\comm{\hat{a}^\dagger}{\hat{a}}\hat{a}=-\hat{a}$ (by the Leibniz rule for the commutator of a product, $\comm{\hat{a}^\dagger\hat{a}}{\hat{a}}=\hat{a}^\dagger\comm{\hat{a}}{\hat{a}}+\comm{\hat{a}^\dagger}{\hat{a}}\hat{a}$). Therefore $\comm{\hat{H}}{\hat{a}}=\hbar\omega\comm{\hat{n}}{\hat{a}}=-\hbar\omega\,\hat{a}$.

(a) Solving the equation of motion. Since $\comm{\hat{H}}{\hat{a}_H}=\comm{\hat{H}}{\hat{a}}_H=-\hbar\omega\,\hat{a}_H$,

$$ \frac{\dd\hat{a}_H}{\dd t}=\frac{i}{\hbar}\comm{\hat{H}}{\hat{a}_H}=\frac{i}{\hbar}(-\hbar\omega)\hat{a}_H=-i\omega\,\hat{a}_H $$

Just as for ordinary numbers, the solution with the initial condition $\hat{a}_H(0)=\hat{a}$ is $\hat{a}_H(t)=\hat{a}\,e^{-i\omega t}$.

(b) Expanding the commutator. We have $\hat{a}_H(t)=\sum_{n}\dfrac{1}{n!}\left(\dfrac{it}{\hbar}\right)^n\underbrace{\comm{\hat{H}}{\cdots\comm{\hat{H}}{\hat{a}}}}_{n\text{-fold}}$, and by repeating $\comm{\hat{H}}{\hat{a}}=-\hbar\omega\hat{a}$, the $n$-fold commutator is $(-\hbar\omega)^n\hat{a}$. Hence

$$ \hat{a}_H(t)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\left(\frac{it}{\hbar}\right)^n(-\hbar\omega)^n\hat{a}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-i\omega t)^n}{n!}\hat{a}=e^{-i\omega t}\hat{a} $$

which agrees with (a).

$\hat{n}_H$ and $\hat{H}_H$. Taking the Hermitian conjugate gives $\hat{a}_H^\dagger=\hat{a}^\dagger e^{+i\omega t}$. By the theorem (preservation of products), $\hat{n}_H=\hat{a}_H^\dagger\hat{a}_H=\hat{a}^\dagger e^{i\omega t}\hat{a}\,e^{-i\omega t}=\hat{a}^\dagger\hat{a}=\hat{n}$ (the phases cancel). Therefore $\hat{H}_H=\hbar\omega(\hat{n}_H+\tfrac12)=\hat{H}$, and both $\hat{n}$ and $\hat{H}$ are conserved quantities (this can also be confirmed from $\comm{\hat{H}}{\hat{n}}=0$, which gives $\dd\hat{n}_H/\dd t=0$).

Exercise 50.3: Heisenberg equations of motion for a spin $\tfrac12$ in a uniform magnetic field

Solution

$\hat{H}=\omega_{\mathrm{L}}\hat{S}_z$. The commutation relations $\comm{\hat{S}_z}{\hat{S}_x}=i\hbar\hat{S}_y$, $\comm{\hat{S}_z}{\hat{S}_y}=-i\hbar\hat{S}_x$, and $\comm{\hat{S}_z}{\hat{S}_z}=0$ have the same form in the Heisenberg picture as well. From the equation of motion $\dfrac{\dd\hat{S}_{i,H}}{\dd t}=\dfrac{i}{\hbar}\comm{\hat{H}}{\hat{S}_{i,H}}$,

$$ \frac{\dd\hat{S}_{x}}{\dd t}=\frac{i\omega_{\mathrm{L}}}{\hbar}(i\hbar\hat{S}_y)=-\omega_{\mathrm{L}}\hat{S}_y,\qquad\frac{\dd\hat{S}_{y}}{\dd t}=\frac{i\omega_{\mathrm{L}}}{\hbar}(-i\hbar\hat{S}_x)=+\omega_{\mathrm{L}}\hat{S}_x,\qquad\frac{\dd\hat{S}_{z}}{\dd t}=0 $$

(here all operators are understood to be Heisenberg-picture operators). Differentiating the first equation once more and using the second gives $\dfrac{\dd^2\hat{S}_x}{\dd t^2}=-\omega_{\mathrm{L}}^2\hat{S}_x$, and with the initial conditions $\hat{S}_x(0)=\hat{S}_x$ and $\dot{\hat{S}}_x(0)=-\omega_{\mathrm{L}}\hat{S}_y$,

$$ \hat{S}_{x,H}(t)=\hat{S}_x\cos\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t-\hat{S}_y\sin\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t,\qquad\hat{S}_{y,H}(t)=\hat{S}_y\cos\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t+\hat{S}_x\sin\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t,\qquad\hat{S}_{z,H}(t)=\hat{S}_z $$

(one can check that $\hat{S}_y$ is also a solution of the same equation and satisfies $\dfrac{\dd\hat{S}_y}{\dd t}=\omega_{\mathrm{L}}\hat{S}_x$). The result has the form of the spin operators rotated about the $z$ axis through the angle $\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t$.

For the spin along $+x$, $\ket{\psi}=(\ket{\uparrow}+\ket{\downarrow})/\sqrt{2}$, we have $\langle\hat{S}_x\rangle=\hbar/2$, $\langle\hat{S}_y\rangle=0$, and $\langle\hat{S}_z\rangle=0$, so

$$ \langle\hat{S}_x\rangle(t)=\frac{\hbar}{2}\cos\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t,\qquad\langle\hat{S}_y\rangle(t)=\frac{\hbar}{2}\sin\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t $$

which agrees with the result obtained in the Schrödinger picture in Example 50.3.

Exercise 50.4: Operators in the interaction picture and the Bohr frequencies

Solution

(a) We differentiate $\hat{A}_I(t)=e^{i\hat{H}_0t/\hbar}\hat{A}e^{-i\hat{H}_0t/\hbar}$ using the product rule. From $\dfrac{\dd}{\dd t}e^{\pm i\hat{H}_0t/\hbar}=\pm\dfrac{i}{\hbar}\hat{H}_0e^{\pm i\hat{H}_0t/\hbar}$ ($\hat{H}_0$ is time-independent),

$$ \frac{\dd\hat{A}_I}{\dd t}=\frac{i}{\hbar}\hat{H}_0\,e^{i\hat{H}_0t/\hbar}\hat{A}e^{-i\hat{H}_0t/\hbar}-\frac{i}{\hbar}\,e^{i\hat{H}_0t/\hbar}\hat{A}e^{-i\hat{H}_0t/\hbar}\hat{H}_0=\frac{i}{\hbar}\comm{\hat{H}_0}{\hat{A}_I} $$

(in the second term we used the fact that $\hat{H}_0$ commutes with $e^{\pm i\hat{H}_0t/\hbar}$ to move $\hat{H}_0$ to the right end). We also used that $\hat{A}$ does not depend explicitly on time.

(b) $\hat{H}_0=\dfrac{\hbar\omega_0}{2}\sigma_z$. Let $\sigma_{x,I}(t)=x(t)\,\sigma_x+y(t)\,\sigma_y$ (the coefficients are real functions). From $\comm{\sigma_z}{\sigma_x}=2i\sigma_y$ and $\comm{\sigma_z}{\sigma_y}=-2i\sigma_x$ we get $\comm{\sigma_z}{x\sigma_x+y\sigma_y}=2ix\,\sigma_y-2iy\,\sigma_x$, and the equation of (a) becomes

$$ \dot{x}\,\sigma_x+\dot{y}\,\sigma_y=\frac{i\omega_0}{2}\left(2ix\,\sigma_y-2iy\,\sigma_x\right)=\omega_0y\,\sigma_x-\omega_0x\,\sigma_y $$

The solution of $\dot{x}=\omega_0y$, $\dot{y}=-\omega_0x$ with the initial conditions $x(0)=1$ and $y(0)=0$ is $x=\cos\omega_0t$, $y=-\sin\omega_0t$, and $\sigma_{x,I}(t)=\sigma_x\cos\omega_0t-\sigma_y\sin\omega_0t$.

The method of expansion: let $\hat{X}=i\hat{H}_0t/\hbar$. Then $\comm{\hat{H}_0}{\sigma_x}=\dfrac{\hbar\omega_0}{2}\,2i\sigma_y=i\hbar\omega_0\sigma_y$ and $\comm{\hat{H}_0}{\comm{\hat{H}_0}{\sigma_x}}=i\hbar\omega_0\cdot\dfrac{\hbar\omega_0}{2}(-2i\sigma_x)=\hbar^2\omega_0^2\sigma_x$. The even-order ($n=2k$) term is $\dfrac{1}{(2k)!}\left(\dfrac{it}{\hbar}\right)^{2k}(\hbar\omega_0)^{2k}\sigma_x=\dfrac{(-1)^k(\omega_0t)^{2k}}{(2k)!}\sigma_x$, and the odd-order ($n=2k+1$) term is $\dfrac{1}{(2k+1)!}\left(\dfrac{it}{\hbar}\right)^{2k+1}(\hbar\omega_0)^{2k}\,i\hbar\omega_0\sigma_y=\dfrac{(-1)^{k+1}(\omega_0t)^{2k+1}}{(2k+1)!}\sigma_y$ (using $i^{2k+2}=(-1)^{k+1}$). Summing them gives $\cos\omega_0t\,\sigma_x-\sin\omega_0t\,\sigma_y$, in agreement with the above.

(c) For $\sigma_+=\ket{\uparrow}\bra{\downarrow}=(\sigma_x+i\sigma_y)/2$, we have $\comm{\sigma_z}{\sigma_+}=\sigma_+-(-\sigma_+)=2\sigma_+$ ($\sigma_z\sigma_+=\sigma_+$, $\sigma_+\sigma_z=-\sigma_+$), so the equation of (a) is $\dfrac{\dd\sigma_{+,I}}{\dd t}=\dfrac{i\omega_0}{2}\cdot2\sigma_{+,I}=i\omega_0\sigma_{+,I}$, and $\sigma_{+,I}(t)=\sigma_+\,e^{i\omega_0t}$. By Hermitian conjugation, $\sigma_{-,I}=\sigma_-\,e^{-i\omega_0t}$. This agrees with the formula for the matrix elements ($\mel{\uparrow}{\sigma_{+,I}}{\downarrow}=e^{i\omega_{\uparrow\downarrow}t}\mel{\uparrow}{\sigma_+}{\downarrow}$, $\omega_{\uparrow\downarrow}=(E_\uparrow-E_\downarrow)/\hbar=\omega_0$). Also, from $\sigma_x=\sigma_++\sigma_-$ we obtain $\sigma_{x,I}=\sigma_+e^{i\omega_0t}+\sigma_-e^{-i\omega_0t}=\sigma_x\cos\omega_0t-\sigma_y\sin\omega_0t$, which is consistent with (b) (this can be checked by substituting $\sigma_\pm=(\sigma_x\pm i\sigma_y)/2$).

Exercise 50.5: The third-order Dyson term and $1/3!$

Solution

(a) According to the ordering of the three times, a point $(t_1,t_2,t_3)$ of the cube $[t_0,t]^3$ belongs to one of the following $3!=6$ regions (the boundaries where equality holds have volume $0$ and do not contribute to the integral): $t_1\gt t_2\gt t_3$, $t_1\gt t_3\gt t_2$, $t_2\gt t_1\gt t_3$, $t_2\gt t_3\gt t_1$, $t_3\gt t_1\gt t_2$, $t_3\gt t_2\gt t_1$. In every region the time-ordered product is the product with “later times to the left”; for example, for $t_3\gt t_1\gt t_2$ we have $T[\hat{H}(t_1)\hat{H}(t_2)\hat{H}(t_3)]=\hat{H}(t_3)\hat{H}(t_1)\hat{H}(t_2)$. In this region, if we rename the integration variables as $t_3\to t_1'$, $t_1\to t_2'$, $t_2\to t_3'$, the region becomes $t_1'\gt t_2'\gt t_3'$ and the integrand becomes $\hat{H}(t_1')\hat{H}(t_2')\hat{H}(t_3')$, which is the same as the third-order term $J=\displaystyle\int_{t_0}^{t}\!\dd t_1\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\!\dd t_2\int_{t_0}^{t_2}\!\dd t_3\,\hat{H}(t_1)\hat{H}(t_2)\hat{H}(t_3)$ in the exercise. The other five regions are similar, so the integrals over the six regions are all equal to $J$, and the following relations

$$ \int_{t_0}^{t}\!\dd t_1\int_{t_0}^{t}\!\dd t_2\int_{t_0}^{t}\!\dd t_3\,T\bigl[\hat{H}(t_1)\hat{H}(t_2)\hat{H}(t_3)\bigr]=6J,\qquad J=\frac{1}{3!}\int_{t_0}^{t}\!\!\int_{t_0}^{t}\!\!\int_{t_0}^{t}T[\cdots] $$

hold.

(b) If $\hat{H}_{1I}=\hat{V}$ (time-independent), $T$ is unnecessary, and the $n$th-order term is $\hat{V}^n$ multiplied by the volume of the ordered region $t\ge t_1\ge\cdots\ge t_n\ge t_0$. This volume is $1/n!$ times the volume $(t-t_0)^n$ of the cube (the same argument as in (a): the cube divides into $n!$ congruent regions), so it equals $(t-t_0)^n/n!$. Therefore,

$$ \hat{U}(t,t_0)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(-\frac{i}{\hbar}\right)^n\hat{V}^n\frac{(t-t_0)^n}{n!}=\exp\left[-\frac{i}{\hbar}\hat{V}(t-t_0)\right] $$

In the case $\hat{H}_0=0$, $\hat{H}=\hat{V}$, this agrees with $\hat{U}_S=e^{-i\hat{H}(t-t_0)/\hbar}$.

Exercise 50.6: A particle in a uniform force field

Solution

$\hat{H}=\hat{p}^2/2m-F\hat{x}$. From $\comm{\hat{p}^2}{\hat{x}}=-2i\hbar\hat{p}$ we get $\comm{\hat{H}}{\hat{x}}=-\dfrac{i\hbar}{m}\hat{p}$, and from $\comm{-F\hat{x}}{\hat{p}}=-F\,i\hbar$ we get $\comm{\hat{H}}{\hat{p}}=-i\hbar F$ ($\hat{p}^2$ commutes with $\hat{p}$). The Heisenberg equations are

$$ \frac{\dd\hat{p}_H}{\dd t}=\frac{i}{\hbar}(-i\hbar F)=F,\qquad\frac{\dd\hat{x}_H}{\dd t}=\frac{i}{\hbar}\left(-\frac{i\hbar}{m}\hat{p}_H\right)=\frac{\hat{p}_H}{m} $$

Integrating the first equation gives $\hat{p}_H(t)=\hat{p}+Ft$; putting this into the second and integrating, we obtain

$$ \hat{x}_H(t)=\hat{x}+\frac{\hat{p}}{m}t+\frac{F}{2m}t^2,\qquad\hat{p}_H(t)=\hat{p}+Ft $$

This has the same form as the solution $x=x_0+p_0t/m+Ft^2/2m$, $p=p_0+Ft$ of Newton's equations of motion $\dot{p}=F$, $\dot{x}=p/m$ (only the initial values have become operators).

The variance of the position is determined by the deviation from the average, $\delta\hat{x}_H=\hat{x}_H-\langle\hat{x}_H\rangle$. Since $\langle\hat{x}_H\rangle=\langle\hat{x}\rangle+\langle\hat{p}\rangle t/m+Ft^2/2m$, the plain-number term $Ft^2/2m$ cancels in the subtraction, and $\delta\hat{x}_H=\delta\hat{x}+\delta\hat{p}\,t/m$. This is the same as for a free particle, so $\sigma_x^2(t)=\sigma_x^2+\dfrac{2C}{m}t+\dfrac{\sigma_p^2}{m^2}t^2$, which does not depend on $F$. A uniform force only moves the center of the wave packet and does not change its shape.

Exercise 50.7: Larmor precession and the equality in the Mandelstam–Tamm relation

Solution

$\hat{H}=\dfrac{\hbar\omega_{\mathrm{L}}}{2}\sigma_z$ and $\hat{H}^2=\left(\dfrac{\hbar\omega_{\mathrm{L}}}{2}\right)^2$, so $(\Delta E)^2=\left(\dfrac{\hbar\omega_{\mathrm{L}}}{2}\right)^2\left(1-\langle\sigma_z\rangle^2\right)$.

Along $+x$: Since $\langle\sigma_z\rangle=0$, $\Delta E=\hbar\omega_{\mathrm{L}}/2$. Take $\hat{A}=\hat{S}_x$; then $\langle\hat{S}_x\rangle=\dfrac{\hbar}{2}\cos\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t$ (Exercise 50.3). Since $\hat{S}_x^2=\hbar^2/4$, we have $(\Delta S_x)^2=\dfrac{\hbar^2}{4}-\langle\hat{S}_x\rangle^2=\dfrac{\hbar^2}{4}\sin^2\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t$ and $\Delta S_x=\dfrac{\hbar}{2}\abs{\sin\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t}$. On the other hand, $\left|\dfrac{\dd\langle\hat{S}_x\rangle}{\dd t}\right|=\dfrac{\hbar\omega_{\mathrm{L}}}{2}\abs{\sin\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t}$, so

$$ \Delta t_{S_x}=\frac{\Delta S_x}{\abs{\dd\langle\hat{S}_x\rangle/\dd t}}=\frac{1}{\omega_{\mathrm{L}}},\qquad\Delta E\,\Delta t_{S_x}=\frac{\hbar\omega_{\mathrm{L}}}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{\omega_{\mathrm{L}}}=\frac{\hbar}{2} $$

Thus the equality holds at any time.

General angle $\theta$: For $\ket{\psi}=\cos\dfrac{\theta}{2}\ket{\uparrow}+\sin\dfrac{\theta}{2}\ket{\downarrow}$, $\langle\sigma_z\rangle=\cos\theta$, so $\Delta E=\dfrac{\hbar\omega_{\mathrm{L}}}{2}\sin\theta$. The components of the time-evolved state are $\cos\frac{\theta}{2}e^{-i\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t/2}$ and $\sin\frac{\theta}{2}e^{i\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t/2}$, and $\langle\hat{S}_x\rangle=\dfrac{\hbar}{2}\sin\theta\cos\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t$ ($\langle\sigma_x\rangle=2\mathrm{Re}(a^*b)$). Hence $(\Delta S_x)^2=\dfrac{\hbar^2}{4}\left(1-\sin^2\theta\cos^2\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t\right)$ and $\left|\dfrac{\dd\langle\hat{S}_x\rangle}{\dd t}\right|=\dfrac{\hbar\omega_{\mathrm{L}}}{2}\sin\theta\abs{\sin\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t}$, and therefore we obtain

$$ \Delta E\,\Delta t_{S_x}=\frac{\hbar\omega_{\mathrm{L}}}{2}\sin\theta\cdot\frac{(\hbar/2)\sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta\cos^2\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t}}{(\hbar\omega_{\mathrm{L}}/2)\sin\theta\abs{\sin\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t}}=\frac{\hbar}{2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta\cos^2\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t}}{\abs{\sin\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t}} $$

Since $1-\sin^2\theta\cos^2\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t-\sin^2\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t=\cos^2\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t\,(1-\sin^2\theta)=\cos^2\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t\cos^2\theta\ge0$, the quantity inside the square root is at least $\sin^2\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t$, which confirms $\Delta E\,\Delta t_{S_x}\ge\hbar/2$. The equality holds when $\cos\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t\cos\theta=0$, that is, for $\theta=\pi/2$ (the spin lies in the $xy$ plane; this is the case above) or when $\cos\omega_{\mathrm{L}}t=0$ (only at that instant). For $\theta\to0$ (the direction of the magnetic field, a stationary state), $\Delta E\to0$ and $\Delta t_{S_x}\to\infty$, and the expectation value $\langle\hat{S}_x\rangle=0$ does not change.

Exercise 50.8: The difference between the $T$-exponential and the simple exponential

Solution

(a) $\hat{H}_1(t)=\dfrac{\hbar\Omega}{2}(\sigma_x\cos\omega t+\sigma_y\sin\omega t)$. The commutator of $\sigma_x$ with itself and that of $\sigma_y$ with itself are $0$, and $\comm{\sigma_x}{\sigma_y}=2i\sigma_z=-\comm{\sigma_y}{\sigma_x}$, so

$$ \comm{\hat{H}_1(t)}{\hat{H}_1(t')}=\left(\frac{\hbar\Omega}{2}\right)^2\bigl[\cos\omega t\sin\omega t'\,\comm{\sigma_x}{\sigma_y}+\sin\omega t\cos\omega t'\,\comm{\sigma_y}{\sigma_x}\bigr]=\left(\frac{\hbar\Omega}{2}\right)^2\,2i\sigma_z\sin\omega(t'-t) $$

that is, $\dfrac{i\hbar^2\Omega^2}{2}\sin\omega(t'-t)\,\sigma_z$ (using $\cos\omega t\sin\omega t'-\sin\omega t\cos\omega t'=\sin\omega(t'-t)$). For $t\ne t'$ it is not $0$.

(b) The difference is $\dfrac12\left(-\dfrac{i}{\hbar}\right)^2\displaystyle\int_0^{t}\!\dd t_1\int_0^{t_1}\!\dd t_2\,\comm{\hat{H}_1(t_1)}{\hat{H}_1(t_2)}$, and by (a), $\comm{\hat{H}_1(t_1)}{\hat{H}_1(t_2)}=\dfrac{i\hbar^2\Omega^2}{2}\sin\omega(t_2-t_1)\sigma_z$, so

$$ -\frac{1}{2\hbar^2}\cdot\frac{i\hbar^2\Omega^2}{2}\sigma_z\int_0^{t}\!\dd t_1\int_0^{t_1}\!\dd t_2\,\sin\omega(t_2-t_1)=-\frac{i\Omega^2}{4}\sigma_z\int_0^{t}\!\dd t_1\left[-\frac{1-\cos\omega t_1}{\omega}\right] $$

Here the inner integral is $\displaystyle\int_0^{t_1}\sin\omega(t_2-t_1)\dd t_2=\left[-\dfrac{\cos\omega(t_2-t_1)}{\omega}\right]_0^{t_1}=-\dfrac{1}{\omega}+\dfrac{\cos\omega t_1}{\omega}$. The outer integral is $\displaystyle\int_0^{t}(1-\cos\omega t_1)\dd t_1=t-\dfrac{\sin\omega t}{\omega}$. Hence the difference is given by

$$ +\frac{i\Omega^2}{4\omega}\left(t-\frac{\sin\omega t}{\omega}\right)\sigma_z $$

This is the difference.

(c) For $t=20\pi/\omega$ (10 periods), $\sin\omega t=0$ and the coefficient is $\dfrac{\Omega^2t}{4\omega}=\dfrac{(0.1)^2\times20\pi}{4}=0.157$ (radians). The difference $i\,0.157\,\sigma_z$ corresponds to a phase rotation $e^{i\varphi\sigma_z}$ ($\varphi=0.157\ \mathrm{rad}=9.0^{\circ}$), which in terms of the spin direction is a rotation by $2\varphi=0.314\ \mathrm{rad}=18^{\circ}$ about the $z$ axis. In the exponential with $T$ removed, $\sin(\omega t/2)=\sin10\pi=0$ at $t=20\pi/\omega$, so $\hat{U}=\hat{1}$ and this rotation is overlooked. In the exact solution (the solution of Example 50.13), $W=\sqrt{\Omega^2+\omega^2}=1.005\,\omega$, and the phase of $\hat{U}_{\uparrow\uparrow}$ is $0.156\ \mathrm{rad}$, which agrees well with the estimate $0.157$ above (the probability of moving to $\ket{\downarrow}$ at this time is $(\Omega/W)^2\sin^2(Wt/2)=2.4\times10^{-4}$, which is very small). Even if the rotating field is weak, the phase shift accumulates in proportion to time.

Chapter 51: Time-Dependent Perturbation Theory and Fermi's Golden Rule — Transition Probabilities, Rabi Oscillations, and the Adiabatic Approximation

Exercise 51.1: Scattering of free electrons by a $\delta$-function impurity

Solution

(1) By the property of the $\delta$ function, $\int g(\bm{r})\delta(\bm{r})\dd^3r=g(0)$, the factor $e^{-i\bm{k}'\cdot\bm{r}}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{r}}$ equals $1$ at $\bm{r}=0$, so

$$ V_{\bm{k}'\bm{k}}=\int\frac{e^{-i\bm{k}'\cdot\bm{r}}}{L^{3/2}}\,v_0\,\delta(\bm{r})\,\frac{e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{r}}}{L^{3/2}}\dd^3r=\frac{v_0}{L^3},\qquad\abs{V_{\bm{k}'\bm{k}}}^2=\frac{v_0^2}{L^6} $$

These are constants independent of $\bm{k},\bm{k}'$, so electrons are scattered with equal probability in every direction.

(2) In box normalization, the allowed wavenumbers are $\bm{k}=\frac{2\pi}{L}(n_x,n_y,n_z)$, so the number of states in $\dd^3k'$ is $L^3\dd^3k'/(2\pi)^3$. In a spherical shell of radius $k'$ and thickness $\dd k'$ it is $\dfrac{L^3}{(2\pi)^3}4\pi k'^2\dd k'$, and since $\dd E'=\hbar^2k'\dd k'/m_{\mathrm e}$ follows from $E'=\hbar^2k'^2/2m_{\mathrm e}$, the density of states is

$$ g(E)=\frac{L^3}{2\pi^2}k^2\cdot\frac{m_{\mathrm e}}{\hbar^2k}=\frac{L^3m_{\mathrm e}k}{2\pi^2\hbar^2} $$

(The orientation of the spin does not change, so the spin degrees of freedom are not included.) Substituting into Fermi's golden rule for a constant perturbation, $w=\dfrac{2\pi}{\hbar}\abs{V_{\bm{k}'\bm{k}}}^2g(E)$, we obtain

$$ w=\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}\cdot\frac{v_0^2}{L^6}\cdot\frac{L^3m_{\mathrm e}k}{2\pi^2\hbar^2}=\frac{m_{\mathrm e}k\,v_0^2}{\pi\hbar^3L^3} $$

Dimension check: $[m_{\mathrm e}kv_0^2/(\hbar^3L^3)]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\cdot J^2m^6/(J^3s^3\cdot m^3)}=\mathrm{kg\,m^2/(J\,s^3)}=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ ($\mathrm{J}=\mathrm{kg\,m^2s^{-2}}$).

(3) If there are $N=n_{\mathrm{imp}}L^3$ impurities at random positions, the interference terms average out, and the scattering rate is $N$ times that for a single impurity:

$$ \frac{1}{\tau}=Nw=\frac{n_{\mathrm{imp}}\,m_{\mathrm e}k\,v_0^2}{\pi\hbar^3} $$

(The volume $L^3$ of the box drops out.) Numerical values: for $E=0.05\ \mathrm{eV}=8.011\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{J}$, we have $k=\dfrac{\sqrt{2m_{\mathrm e}E}}{\hbar}=\dfrac{\sqrt{2\times9.1094\times10^{-31}\times8.011\times10^{-21}}}{1.05457\times10^{-34}}=1.146\times10^9\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$. Since $v_0=1.0\ \mathrm{eV\,nm^3}=1.6022\times10^{-19}\times10^{-27}=1.6022\times10^{-46}\ \mathrm{J\,m^3}$,

$$ \frac{1}{\tau}=\frac{1.0\times10^{24}\times9.1094\times10^{-31}\times1.146\times10^9\times(1.6022\times10^{-46})^2}{\pi\times(1.05457\times10^{-34})^3}=7.3\times10^{12}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} $$

and hence $\tau=1.4\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{s}=0.14\ \mathrm{ps}$. (If we regard this $\tau$ as the time that impedes the motion of the electron, the Drude formula gives a mobility of about $\mu=e_0\tau/m_{\mathrm e}=2.4\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^2/(V\,s)}=2.4\times10^2\ \mathrm{cm^2/(V\,s)}$.)

(4) The speed of the electron is $v_{\mathrm e}=\hbar k/m_{\mathrm e}=1.33\times10^5\ \mathrm{m/s}$. For the scattering cross section of a single impurity, the scattering rate is the volume $v_{\mathrm e}\sigma$ “swept” by the electron per unit time multiplied by the impurity density $n_{\mathrm{imp}}$, so $\dfrac1\tau=n_{\mathrm{imp}}v_{\mathrm e}\sigma$; that is,

$$ \sigma=\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{imp}}v_{\mathrm e}\tau}=\frac{m_{\mathrm e}kv_0^2}{\pi\hbar^3}\cdot\frac{m_{\mathrm e}}{\hbar k}=\frac{m_{\mathrm e}^2v_0^2}{\pi\hbar^4}=5.5\times10^{-17}\ \mathrm{m^2}\ (=55\ \mathrm{nm^2}) $$

On the other hand, in the Born approximation the differential cross section of a $\delta$-function potential is independent of direction, $\dfrac{\dd\sigma}{\dd\Omega}=\Bigl(\dfrac{m_{\mathrm e}v_0}{2\pi\hbar^2}\Bigr)^2$, and integrating over the total solid angle $4\pi$ gives $4\pi\cdot\dfrac{m_{\mathrm e}^2v_0^2}{4\pi^2\hbar^4}=\dfrac{m_{\mathrm e}^2v_0^2}{\pi\hbar^4}$, which agrees with the result of Fermi's golden rule. Fermi's golden rule is the same as the Born approximation.

Exercise 51.2: Second-order perturbation and two-photon absorption

Solution

(1) Writing $\hat{H}_1$ as $V_{ni}(t'')=V_{ni}e^{-i\omega t''}+(V^\dagger)_{ni}e^{i\omega t''}$, the second-order transition amplitude is

$$ c_f^{(2)}(t)=\Bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}\Bigr)^2\sum_n\int_0^t\dd t'\,V_{fn}(t')e^{i\omega_{fn}t'}\int_0^{t'}\dd t''\,V_{ni}(t'')e^{i\omega_{ni}t''} $$

For the process in which the energy $2\hbar\omega$ is absorbed ($E_f=E_i+2\hbar\omega$), we take the $e^{-i\omega t}$ term from both $V$ factors. The inner integral is

$$ \int_0^{t'}e^{i(\omega_{ni}-\omega)t''}\dd t''=\frac{e^{i(\omega_{ni}-\omega)t'}-1}{i(\omega_{ni}-\omega)} $$

Substituting this into the outer integral, the integrand is $V_{fn}V_{ni}\dfrac{e^{i(\omega_{fn}-\omega)t'}\bigl[e^{i(\omega_{ni}-\omega)t'}-1\bigr]}{i(\omega_{ni}-\omega)}$, and since $\omega_{fn}+\omega_{ni}=\omega_{fi}$, the first term is $e^{i(\omega_{fi}-2\omega)t'}$ and the second term is $-e^{i(\omega_{fn}-\omega)t'}$. If $\omega_{fn}-\omega\ne0$ (the intermediate state is not resonant), the second term does not grow with $t$ when integrated, and can be neglected. The first term is, for $\Delta=\omega_{fi}-2\omega\approx0$, a resonant term that grows with $t$, and its integral is

$$ \int_0^te^{i\Delta t'}\dd t'=\frac{e^{i\Delta t}-1}{i\Delta} $$

Therefore,

$$ c_f^{(2)}\simeq(-1)\cdot\sum_n\frac{V_{fn}V_{ni}}{\hbar^2\,i(\omega_{ni}-\omega)}\cdot\frac{e^{i\Delta t}-1}{i\Delta}=\frac{1}{\hbar^2}\sum_n\frac{V_{fn}V_{ni}}{\omega_{ni}-\omega}\cdot\frac{e^{i\Delta t}-1}{\Delta} $$

(Since $(-i)^2=-1$ and $\dfrac{1}{i\cdot i}=-1$, the sign becomes $+$.) Using $\hbar(\omega_{ni}-\omega)=E_n-E_i-\hbar\omega$ and defining $M_{fi}\equiv\displaystyle\sum_n\dfrac{V_{fn}V_{ni}}{E_i+\hbar\omega-E_n}$, we obtain

$$ c_f^{(2)}\simeq-\frac{M_{fi}}{\hbar}\,\frac{e^{i\Delta t}-1}{\Delta},\qquad\Delta=\omega_{fi}-2\omega $$

This has the same form as the first-order resonant term $-\dfrac{V_{fi}}{\hbar}\dfrac{e^{i\Delta t}-1}{\Delta}$ after the replacements $V_{fi}\to M_{fi}$ and $\omega\to2\omega$. By the same argument as in Section 51.2 ($\sin^2\to2\pi t\delta$, summation over the final states), we obtain

$$ w=\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}\abs{M_{fi}}^2\,\delta(E_f-E_i-2\hbar\omega)=\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}\left|\sum_n\frac{V_{fn}V_{ni}}{E_i+\hbar\omega-E_n}\right|^2\delta(E_f-E_i-2\hbar\omega) $$

This is the result.

(2) The denominator $E_i+\hbar\omega-E_n$ is the mismatch between the energy $E_i+\hbar\omega$ of the state that has absorbed one photon and the energy $E_n$ of the intermediate state $\ket{n}$. This intermediate state is a virtual state that does not satisfy energy conservation, and an intermediate state with a smaller mismatch contributes more. Since the strength of the external field is $\hat{V}\propto E_0$, we have $M_{fi}\propto E_0^2$ and $w\propto\abs{M_{fi}}^2\propto E_0^4\propto I^2$. The rate of two-photon absorption is proportional to the square of the intensity of the light, and it can be observed only with intense laser light. When the denominator is close to $0$ ($E_n\approx E_i+\hbar\omega$), $\ket{n}$ resonates as a real level, and the absorption becomes sequential, one photon at a time (the expression then diverges, and the width due to the lifetime of the state must be taken into account).

(Numerical example: for the three levels $E_i=0$, $E_n=1$, $E_f=1.8$, with $\hbar\omega=0.9$ ($\hbar=1$), $V_{ni}=0.012$, and $V_{fn}=0.010$, we have $M_{fi}=\dfrac{0.010\times0.012}{0.9-1}=-1.2\times10^{-3}$. For these three levels, integrating the simultaneous equations for $c_i,c_n,c_f$ up to $t=60$ with a high-order Runge–Kutta method (relative tolerance $10^{-10}$) and reading off $\abs{c_f}^2$ gives $P_f(t=60)=4.9\times10^{-3}$, which agrees with $\abs{M_{fi}}^2t^2=5.2\times10^{-3}$ to within a difference of about 5%. The difference is due to higher-order effects such as the light shifts of the levels.)

Exercise 51.3: Width of the Rabi resonance curve and the Fourier limit of a $\pi$ pulse

Solution

(1) $P_{\max}=\dfrac{\Omega^2}{\Omega^2+\Delta\omega^2}=\dfrac12$ holds when $\Delta\omega^2=\Omega^2$, that is, $\Delta\omega=\pm\Omega$, so the full width at half maximum is $2\Omega$ (the width grows as the external field is strengthened; this is power broadening).

(2) For $\Omega t=\pi$, letting $r=\Delta\omega/\Omega$, we have $\Omega_{\mathrm R}t/2=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{1+r^2}$, so $P_2(r)=\dfrac{\sin^2\bigl(\frac\pi2\sqrt{1+r^2}\bigr)}{1+r^2}$. Solving $P_2=\frac12$ numerically (by bisection) gives $r_{1/2}=0.7987$ (for $r=0.7987$, we have $\sqrt{1+r^2}=1.2798$, $\dfrac\pi2\sqrt{1+r^2}=2.0103$, $\sin^2(2.0103)=0.8189$, and $0.8189/1.6379=0.5000$). The full width at half maximum is $\Delta\omega_{\mathrm{FWHM}}=2r_{1/2}\Omega=1.597\,\Omega=1.597\,\dfrac{\pi}{t}$. Written in terms of the frequency $\nu=\omega/2\pi$,

$$ \Delta\nu_{\mathrm{FWHM}}=\frac{1.597\,\pi}{2\pi\,t}=\frac{0.799}{t} $$

The Fourier limit of a rectangular pulse, that is, the full width at half maximum for a weak pulse ($\Omega t\ll1$), for which $P\propto\sin^2(\Delta\omega\,t/2)/(\Delta\omega/2)^2$, follows from $u=1.3916$, the solution of $\dfrac{\sin^2u}{u^2}=\dfrac12$: $\Delta\omega_{\mathrm{FWHM}}=4u/t=5.566/t$ and $\Delta\nu=0.886/t$. The value $0.799/t$ for the $\pi$ pulse is about $10\%$ narrower than this (because of saturation), but of the same order, and the shorter the pulse, the greater the width. For a weak pulse, the Rabi formula agrees with the perturbation-theory expression (for example, for $\Omega=0.05$, $t=1$, $\Delta\omega=0$, the Rabi formula gives $6.2487\times10^{-4}$, and the perturbative $\dfrac{\Omega^2t^2}{4}\mathrm{sinc}^2\dfrac{\Delta\omega\,t}{2}$ gives $6.2500\times10^{-4}$).

(3) It suffices that the full width at half maximum satisfy $\Delta\nu\lt1\ \mathrm{MHz}$, so a $\pi$ pulse requires $t\gt\dfrac{0.799}{1\ \mathrm{MHz}}=0.80\ \mu\mathrm{s}$, and a weak pulse requires $t\gt\dfrac{0.886}{1\ \mathrm{MHz}}=0.89\ \mu\mathrm{s}$. The Rabi frequency is then $\Omega=\pi/t\approx4\times10^6\ \mathrm{rad/s}$ ($\Omega/2\pi=0.6\ \mathrm{MHz}$). When the pulse is short, a broad spectrum is excited simultaneously.

Exercise 51.4: Ramsey interference and the atomic clock

Solution

(1) The equation for the Bloch vector is $\dot{\bm{s}}=\bm{W}\times\bm{s}$, $\bm{W}=(\Omega,0,-\Delta\omega)$. During a pulse, $\Omega\gg\abs{\Delta\omega}$, so we regard $\bm{W}\approx(\Omega,0,0)$.

  1. Starting from the south pole $(0,0,-1)$, the vector rotates about the $x$ axis by $\Omega t=\pi/2$. Since $\dot{\bm{s}}=(\Omega,0,0)\times(0,0,-1)=(0,\Omega,0)$, it moves in the $+y$ direction and reaches $\bm{s}=(0,1,0)$.
  2. Free time $\tau$ ($\Omega=0$): $\bm{W}=(0,0,-\Delta\omega)$. Substituting $\bm{s}=(0,1,0)$ into $\dot{\bm{s}}=\bm{W}\times\bm{s}$ gives $\dot{\bm{s}}=(0,0,-\Delta\omega)\times(0,1,0)=(\Delta\omega,0,0)$, so the $x$ component increases in the positive direction. For a rotation about the $z$ axis, this gives $\bm{s}(\tau)=(\sin\Delta\omega\tau,\ \cos\Delta\omega\tau,\ 0)$.
  3. The second $\pi/2$ pulse is a rotation by $+90^\circ$ about the $x$ axis; from $\dot{\bm{s}}=(\Omega,0,0)\times\bm{s}=(0,-\Omega s_z,\Omega s_y)$, the $y$ component moves into the $z$ component, and the $z$ component moves into the $-y$ component. That is, $(x,y,z)\to(x,-z,y)$. Therefore $\bm{s}=(\sin\Delta\omega\tau,\ 0,\ \cos\Delta\omega\tau)$.

The probability of being in the upper level is $P_2=\dfrac{1+s_z}{2}=\dfrac{1+\cos\Delta\omega\tau}{2}$. (If the pulse has a finite length $t_{\mathrm p}=\pi/2\Omega$, the positions of the fringes shift slightly because of the detuning during the pulse. Multiplying the three rotation matrices for the pulse (a rotation about $\bm{W}=(\Omega,0,-\Delta\omega)$, which includes the detuning $\Delta\omega$), the free time, and the pulse, and computing $P_2$ for $\Omega=10^4$, $\Delta\omega=1.3$, $\tau=1$, we obtain $0.63362$, compared with $0.63375$ from the formula; the two agree well if the pulse is sufficiently short. If the pulse is made longer, with $\Omega=100$, the value drops to $0.621$.)

(2) $P_2=\cos^2\dfrac{\Delta\omega\tau}{2}$ equals $\frac12$ at $\Delta\omega\tau=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so the full width at half maximum of the central fringe is $\Delta\omega_{\mathrm{FWHM}}=\dfrac{\pi}{\tau}$, and in terms of frequency $\Delta\nu_{\mathrm{FWHM}}=\dfrac{1}{2\tau}$. The longer the free time, the narrower the fringes, and the width does not depend on the length of the pulse itself (power broadening).

(3) For $\tau=1\ \mathrm{s}$, we have $\Delta\nu_{\mathrm{FWHM}}=0.5\ \mathrm{Hz}$, and $Q=\dfrac{\nu_0}{\Delta\nu_{\mathrm{FWHM}}}=\dfrac{9.19\times10^9\ \mathrm{Hz}}{0.5\ \mathrm{Hz}}=1.8\times10^{10}$. If the center of the resonance is determined to $10^{-3}$ of the fringe width ($0.5\ \mathrm{Hz}$), an accuracy of $0.5\ \mathrm{Hz}\times10^{-3}/(9.19\times10^9\ \mathrm{Hz})\approx5\times10^{-14}$ is obtained (about $5\times10^{-13}$ if it is $10^{-2}$ of the fringe width). This is the reason why atomic clocks have high accuracy.

Exercise 51.5: Checking the Landau–Zener formula numerically

Solution

(1) We divide time as $t_j=-T+(j+\tfrac12)\Delta t$, regard $\hat{H}(t_j)$ as constant in each interval, and update the state as $\ket{\psi}\to e^{-i\hat{H}(t_j)\Delta t}\ket{\psi}$ (as long as $\hat{H}$ changes slowly, the error is of order $\Delta t^2$). The eigenvalues of $\hat{H}(t)$ are $\pm\varepsilon(t)$ with $\varepsilon(t)=\sqrt{(vt/2)^2+V^2}$, and since $\hat{H}^2=\varepsilon(t)^2\cdot1$, we have $e^{-i\hat{H}\Delta t}=\cos(\varepsilon(t)\Delta t)-i\dfrac{\hat{H}}{\varepsilon(t)}\sin(\varepsilon(t)\Delta t)$. The initial state is the lower eigenstate of $\hat{H}$ at $t=-T$, and the measurement is the projection onto the upper eigenstate of $\hat{H}$ at $t=+T$. The program looks like this:

import numpy as np
def lz(V, v, T, dt):
    H = lambda t: np.array([[v*t/2, V], [V, -v*t/2]], complex)
    w, U = np.linalg.eigh(H(-T)); psi = U[:, 0].astype(complex)   # lower adiabatic state
    for j in range(int(round(2*T/dt))):
        t = -T + (j + 0.5)*dt
        eps = np.sqrt((v*t/2)**2 + V**2)            # the eigenvalues of H(t) are ±eps
        psi = (np.cos(eps*dt)*np.eye(2) - 1j*np.sin(eps*dt)/eps*H(t)) @ psi
    w2, U2 = np.linalg.eigh(H(T))
    return abs(np.vdot(U2[:, 1], psi))**2          # probability of being in the upper adiabatic state

print(lz(0.3, 1.0, 60, 0.005), np.exp(-2*np.pi*0.3**2/1.0))

For $V=0.3$, $v=1$, $T=60$, $\Delta t=0.005$, the result is $0.56808$, which agrees to five digits with the formula $P_{\mathrm{dia}}=\exp(-2\pi\times0.09/1)=0.56808$ (the result is also $0.56808$ for $T=200$).

(2) For $v=0.3$ the exponent is $\dfrac{2\pi\times0.09}{0.3}=1.885$, and $P_{\mathrm{dia}}=e^{-1.885}=0.1518$. The numerical calculation also gives $0.15185$ ($T=60$) and $0.15184$ ($T=200$), in agreement. The slower the passage, the more adiabatic the process becomes ($P_{\mathrm{dia}}$ becomes smaller).

(3) If we use the occupation probability $\abs{c_1}^2$ of a diabatic state (the basis of the diagonal elements of $\hat{H}$), then for finite $T$ the adiabatic states at $t=\pm T$ do not coincide exactly with the diabatic states, and the state contains a mixture of adiabatic states (oscillating cross terms). The difference in angle between the adiabatic and diabatic states is of order $\sim V/(vT/2)$; it goes to 0 as $T$ is increased, but only slowly (accompanied by oscillations that decrease as $1/T$ with increasing $T$). Indeed, if we start from the diabatic state $\ket{1}$ and measure $\abs{c_1}^2$ for $v=1$, $V=0.3$, we obtain $0.596$ for $T=20$, $0.554$ for $T=40$, $0.574$ for $T=100$, and $0.566$ for $T=200$; it converges slowly while oscillating around $0.568$. If we start and measure in the basis of adiabatic states, the numerical error is small regardless of $T$, and, as in (1) above, an accurate value is obtained for finite $T$.

Exercise 51.6: Changing the direction of the magnetic field applied to a spin 1/2 — sudden versus adiabatic

Solution

(1) When the direction of the magnetic field is suddenly rotated by $\alpha$, the state does not change (sudden approximation). The overlap of the spin $+$ states for two directions that differ by $\alpha$ is the overlap of two points separated by the angle $\alpha$ on the Bloch sphere, $\abs{\braket{\bm{n}',+}{\bm{n},+}}^2=\cos^2\dfrac\alpha2$ (for example, for $\bm{n}=(0,0,1)$ and $\bm{n}'=(\sin\alpha,0,\cos\alpha)$, we have $\ket{\bm{n},+}=(1,0)^{\mathsf T}$ and $\ket{\bm{n}',+}=(\cos\frac\alpha2,\sin\frac\alpha2)^{\mathsf T}$). Therefore, with respect to the new field direction, the probability of $+$ is $\cos^2\dfrac\alpha2$, the probability of $-$ is $\sin^2\dfrac\alpha2$, and the expectation value of the energy is

$$ \expval{E}=\frac{\hbar\omega_{\mathrm B}}{2}\Bigl(\cos^2\frac\alpha2-\sin^2\frac\alpha2\Bigr)=\frac{\hbar\omega_{\mathrm B}}{2}\cos\alpha $$

For $\alpha=90^\circ$, the two probabilities are $\frac12$ each and $\expval{E}=0$; for $\alpha=180^\circ$, the state becomes the $-$ state and $\expval{E}=-\hbar\omega_{\mathrm B}/2$. In contrast, in the adiabatic case, where the field is rotated sufficiently slowly, the state remains $+$ and $\expval{E}=+\hbar\omega_{\mathrm B}/2$.

(2) We have $\hat{H}(t)=\dfrac{\hbar\omega_{\mathrm B}}{2}\bigl(\sin\omega_{\mathrm{rot}}t\,\sigma_x+\cos\omega_{\mathrm{rot}}t\,\sigma_z\bigr)=U(t)\,\dfrac{\hbar\omega_{\mathrm B}}{2}\sigma_z\,U(t)^\dagger$ with $U=e^{-i\omega_{\mathrm{rot}}t\sigma_y/2}$ (rotating $\sigma_z$ about the $y$ axis by the angle $\omega_{\mathrm{rot}}t$ gives $\cos\omega_{\mathrm{rot}}t\,\sigma_z+\sin\omega_{\mathrm{rot}}t\,\sigma_x$). Expressing the state as $\ket{\phi}=U^\dagger\ket{\psi}$, we have $i\hbar\partial_t\ket{\phi}=\bigl(U^\dagger\hat{H}U-i\hbar U^\dagger\dot{U}\bigr)\ket{\phi}$, and since $-i\hbar U^\dagger\dot{U}=-i\hbar\cdot\bigl(-\tfrac{i\omega_{\mathrm{rot}}}{2}\sigma_y\bigr)=-\dfrac{\hbar\omega_{\mathrm{rot}}}{2}\sigma_y$, we obtain

$$ i\hbar\,\partial_t\ket{\phi}=\frac{\hbar}{2}\bigl(\omega_{\mathrm B}\sigma_z-\omega_{\mathrm{rot}}\sigma_y\bigr)\ket{\phi} $$

This is a time-independent Hamiltonian. The state that is in $+$ with respect to the direction of rotation is $\ket{\phi(0)}=(1,0)^{\mathsf T}$ ($\sigma_z=+1$), and the probability of being in $-$ is $\abs{\braket{-z}{\phi}}^2$. This has the same form as the Rabi problem: the Bloch vector rotates about the rotation-axis vector $\bm{W}'=(0,-\omega_{\mathrm{rot}},\omega_{\mathrm B})$. Let $\chi$ be the angle between $\bm{s}(0)=+\hat{z}$ and $\bm{W}'$. Then $\sin\chi=\omega_{\mathrm{rot}}/\sqrt{\omega_{\mathrm{rot}}^2+\omega_{\mathrm B}^2}$, and since $\bm{s}$ moves on a cone of half apex angle $\chi$, the minimum value of $s_z$ is $\cos2\chi$, and the maximum value of the probability of $-$ is $\dfrac{1-\cos2\chi}{2}=\sin^2\chi$. That is,

$$ P_{\mathrm{flip}}^{\max}=\frac{\omega_{\mathrm{rot}}^2}{\omega_{\mathrm{rot}}^2+\omega_{\mathrm B}^2}\qquad\Bigl(P_{\mathrm{flip}}(t)=\frac{\omega_{\mathrm{rot}}^2}{\omega_{\mathrm{rot}}^2+\omega_{\mathrm B}^2}\sin^2\frac{\sqrt{\omega_{\mathrm{rot}}^2+\omega_{\mathrm B}^2}\,t}{2}\Bigr) $$

(This is the Rabi formula with $\Omega\to\omega_{\mathrm{rot}}$ and $\Delta\omega\to\omega_{\mathrm B}$.) For $\omega_{\mathrm{rot}}\ll\omega_{\mathrm B}$, $P_{\mathrm{flip}}^{\max}\approx(\omega_{\mathrm{rot}}/\omega_{\mathrm B})^2\ll1$ and the process is adiabatic; for $\omega_{\mathrm{rot}}\gg\omega_{\mathrm B}$, the state does not move (sudden approximation) and is left behind by the amount of the rotation, $\omega_{\mathrm{rot}}t=\alpha$. (Check: keeping the Hamiltonian $\hat{H}(t)$ of the rotating magnetic field as it is, we integrate the Schrödinger equation by a high-order Runge–Kutta method and read off the maximum value of the probability of the “opposite-direction” component of the instantaneous eigenstate; for $\omega_{\mathrm{rot}}/\omega_{\mathrm B}=0.1,\ 0.3,\ 1$ we obtain $0.00990,\ 0.0826,\ 0.5000$, in agreement with the formula.)

(3) We read the condition in the problem statement as keeping the probability of finding the spin in the opposite direction at or below $10^{-6}$ at every moment during the rotation. Therefore, we impose the condition on the maximum value, $P_{\mathrm{flip}}^{\max}\lt10^{-6}$. (If only the final time mattered, then for $\omega_{\mathrm{rot}}=\omega_{\mathrm B}/\sqrt3$ and $t=\sqrt3\pi/\omega_{\mathrm B}=87\ \mathrm{ns}$, we would have $P_{\mathrm{flip}}=0$ at the instant when the rotation by $\pi$ has just been completed, but along the way $P_{\mathrm{flip}}$ reaches $\tfrac14$. Such a way of rotating is not what “rotating adiabatically” means here.) Since $P_{\mathrm{flip}}^{\max}\lt10^{-6}$, we need $\omega_{\mathrm{rot}}\lt\omega_{\mathrm B}\times10^{-3}=2\pi\times10^7\times10^{-3}=6.3\times10^4\ \mathrm{rad/s}$. The time required to rotate by $180^\circ$ ($=\pi$) is $t=\pi/\omega_{\mathrm{rot}}\gt\dfrac{\pi}{6.3\times10^4\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}}=5.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{s}=50\ \mu\mathrm{s}$.

Exercise 51.7: STM scanning tunneling spectroscopy — when the sample's density of states has a peak

Solution

(1) At absolute zero, when the density of states of the tip and the matrix element are constant, $I=C\displaystyle\int_0^{e_0V_{\mathrm b}}\rho_{\mathrm s}(\varepsilon)\dd\varepsilon$ ($C=4\pi e_0\abs{M}^2\rho_{\mathrm t}/\hbar$). Differentiating with respect to $V_{\mathrm b}$ gives the value at the upper limit of the integral:

$$ \frac{\dd I}{\dd V_{\mathrm b}}=C\,e_0\,\rho_{\mathrm s}(e_0V_{\mathrm b})=Ce_0\Bigl[\rho_0+\rho_{\mathrm p}\frac{(\Gamma/2)^2}{(e_0V_{\mathrm b}-\varepsilon_{\mathrm p})^2+(\Gamma/2)^2}\Bigr] $$

The maximum (height $\rho_0+\rho_{\mathrm p}$) occurs at $e_0V_{\mathrm b}=\varepsilon_{\mathrm p}$; it is a Lorentzian peak sitting on top of the background $\rho_0$, and its full width at half maximum is $\Gamma/e_0$ in terms of the bias $V_{\mathrm b}$ and $\Gamma$ in terms of energy (an empty state with $\varepsilon_{\mathrm p}\gt0$ is observed at positive bias, and an occupied state with $\varepsilon_{\mathrm p}\lt0$ is observed at negative bias (the direction in which electrons flow from the sample to the tip)).

(2) Using $\displaystyle\int_0^{e_0V_{\mathrm b}}\dfrac{(\Gamma/2)^2}{(\varepsilon-\varepsilon_{\mathrm p})^2+(\Gamma/2)^2}\dd\varepsilon=\dfrac\Gamma2\Bigl[\arctan\dfrac{2(\varepsilon-\varepsilon_{\mathrm p})}{\Gamma}\Bigr]_0^{e_0V_{\mathrm b}}$, we obtain

$$ I(V_{\mathrm b})=C\Bigl[\rho_0\,e_0V_{\mathrm b}+\rho_{\mathrm p}\frac\Gamma2\Bigl(\arctan\frac{2(e_0V_{\mathrm b}-\varepsilon_{\mathrm p})}{\Gamma}+\arctan\frac{2\varepsilon_{\mathrm p}}{\Gamma}\Bigr)\Bigr] $$

(we used $\arctan(-x)=-\arctan x$). Around the point where $e_0V_{\mathrm b}$ passes through $\varepsilon_{\mathrm p}$, the current increases stepwise, by $C\rho_{\mathrm p}\dfrac\Gamma2\pi$ in total ($\arctan$ changes from $-\pi/2$ to $+\pi/2$). The background slope $C\rho_0e_0$ is superimposed on top of this.

(3) The function $-\partial f/\partial\varepsilon=\dfrac{1}{4k_{\mathrm B}T}\cosh^{-2}\dfrac{\varepsilon}{2k_{\mathrm B}T}$ falls to half its maximum value when $\cosh^2\dfrac{\varepsilon}{2k_{\mathrm B}T}=2$, that is, when $\dfrac{\varepsilon}{2k_{\mathrm B}T}=\mathrm{arccosh}\sqrt2=0.8814$; thus $\varepsilon=\pm1.763\,k_{\mathrm B}T$, and the full width at half maximum is

$$ \Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{FWHM}}=3.525\,k_{\mathrm B}T $$

Numerically, $k_{\mathrm B}T$ is $0.362\ \mathrm{meV}$ at $T=4.2\ \mathrm{K}$, $6.64\ \mathrm{meV}$ at $77\ \mathrm{K}$, and $25.9\ \mathrm{meV}$ at $300\ \mathrm{K}$, so $3.525\,k_{\mathrm B}T$ is $1.28\ \mathrm{meV}$, $23.4\ \mathrm{meV}$, and $91\ \mathrm{meV}$, respectively. The spectrum at finite temperature is $\rho_{\mathrm s}$ convolved with a thermal spread of this width. A peak with $\Gamma=5\ \mathrm{meV}$ can be resolved at $4.2\ \mathrm{K}$ (thermal spread $1.3\ \mathrm{meV}$), but at $77\ \mathrm{K}$ ($23\ \mathrm{meV}$) it is buried in the thermal spread, and at $300\ \mathrm{K}$ it is completely invisible. This is the reason why probing narrow electronic states by STM requires cooling to liquid helium temperature ($4.2\ \mathrm{K}$) or below.

Exercise 51.8: Derivation of the Bloch–Siegert shift (Advanced)

Solution

Let $a=\bar{a}+\delta a$ and $b=\bar{b}+\delta b$. Here $\bar{a},\bar{b}$ are the parts that change slowly on the time scale $1/\Omega$, and $\delta a,\delta b$ are small parts that oscillate rapidly as $e^{\pm2i\omega t}$. Extracting only the rapidly oscillating part of the equation $i\dot{a}=-\dfrac{\Delta\omega}{2}a+\dfrac\Omega2b+\dfrac\Omega2e^{2i\omega t}b$, we get $i\,\delta\dot{a}\simeq\dfrac\Omega2e^{2i\omega t}\bar{b}$ (the other terms on the right-hand side contain $\delta a,\delta b$ and are smaller still). Setting $\delta a=Ae^{2i\omega t}$, we have $i\cdot2i\omega A=-2\omega A=\dfrac\Omega2\bar{b}$, hence $A=-\dfrac{\Omega}{4\omega}\bar{b}$. Similarly, from $i\dot{b}=\dfrac{\Delta\omega}{2}b+\dfrac\Omega2a+\dfrac\Omega2e^{-2i\omega t}a$ we get $i\,\delta\dot{b}\simeq\dfrac\Omega2e^{-2i\omega t}\bar{a}$, and setting $\delta b=Be^{-2i\omega t}$ gives $i\cdot(-2i\omega)B=2\omega B=\dfrac\Omega2\bar{a}$, hence $B=\dfrac{\Omega}{4\omega}\bar{a}$. Therefore

$$ \delta a=-\frac{\Omega}{4\omega}\,e^{2i\omega t}\,\bar{b},\qquad\delta b=+\frac{\Omega}{4\omega}\,e^{-2i\omega t}\,\bar{a} $$

Next, we write the equations for the slowly changing parts. The products of the rapidly oscillating coefficients $\frac\Omega2e^{\pm2i\omega t}$ on the right-hand sides of the original equations and the rapid parts $\delta a,\delta b$ found above leave a nonzero time average:

$$ i\dot{\bar{a}}=-\frac{\Delta\omega}{2}\bar{a}+\frac\Omega2\bar{b}+\Bigl\langle\frac\Omega2e^{2i\omega t}\,\delta b\Bigr\rangle=-\frac{\Delta\omega}{2}\bar{a}+\frac\Omega2\bar{b}+\frac\Omega2\cdot\frac{\Omega}{4\omega}\,\bar{a}=-\frac12\Bigl(\Delta\omega-\frac{\Omega^2}{4\omega}\Bigr)\bar{a}+\frac\Omega2\bar{b} $$ $$ i\dot{\bar{b}}=\frac{\Delta\omega}{2}\bar{b}+\frac\Omega2\bar{a}+\Bigl\langle\frac\Omega2e^{-2i\omega t}\,\delta a\Bigr\rangle=\frac{\Delta\omega}{2}\bar{b}+\frac\Omega2\bar{a}+\frac\Omega2\cdot\Bigl(-\frac{\Omega}{4\omega}\Bigr)\bar{b}=\frac12\Bigl(\Delta\omega-\frac{\Omega^2}{4\omega}\Bigr)\bar{b}+\frac\Omega2\bar{a} $$

These are the equations of the rotating-wave approximation, with the detuning $\Delta\omega$ replaced by the effective detuning

$$ \Delta\omega_{\mathrm{eff}}=\Delta\omega-\frac{\Omega^2}{4\omega} $$

Therefore, the resonance ($\Delta\omega_{\mathrm{eff}}=0$) occurs at $\omega-\omega_0=\dfrac{\Omega^2}{4\omega}\approx\dfrac{\Omega^2}{4\omega_0}$. That is, the resonance is shifted from $\omega_0$ to a higher frequency by $\delta\omega=\Omega^2/4\omega_0$ (the Bloch–Siegert shift).

(Numerical example: for $\Omega/\omega_0=0.1$, we integrate the original two-level equations over one period $2\pi/\omega$ by the Runge–Kutta method to build the time-evolution matrix; the frequency at which the splitting of the Floquet quasienergies obtained from its eigenvalues is minimal is $\omega=1.00249\,\omega_0$, while the formula gives $1.0025\,\omega_0$. Also, at $\omega=0.95\,\omega_0$ the splitting is $0.11291\,\omega_0$, while the formula $\sqrt{\Omega^2+\Delta\omega_{\mathrm{eff}}^2}=0.11301\,\omega_0$ agrees with it far better than the rotating-wave approximation without the correction, $\sqrt{\Omega^2+\Delta\omega^2}=0.11180\,\omega_0$, does.)
