Chapter 52: Absorption and Emission of Light — Electric Dipole Approximation, Selection Rules, Einstein Coefficients, Lifetimes, and Linewidths

Exercise 52.1: With circularly polarized light, only the transition from hydrogen $1s$ to $2p_{+1}$ occurs

Solution

(1) The angular parts are $Y_0^0=1/\sqrt{4\pi}$ (independent of $\varphi$), $Y_1^{\pm1}=\mp\sqrt{3/8\pi}\,\sin\theta\,e^{\pm i\varphi}$, and $Y_1^0=\sqrt{3/4\pi}\cos\theta$. The angular integral is the product of a $\varphi$ integral and a $\theta$ integral. Multiplying $Y_1^{m'*}\propto e^{-im'\varphi}$ by $\sin\theta\,e^{i\varphi}$, the $\varphi$ integral is

$$ \int_0^{2\pi}e^{-im'\varphi}\,e^{i\varphi}\dd\varphi=\int_0^{2\pi}e^{i(1-m')\varphi}\dd\varphi=2\pi\,\delta_{m',1} $$

For $m'=0$ we have $\int_0^{2\pi}e^{i\varphi}\dd\varphi=0$, and for $m'=-1$ we have $\int_0^{2\pi}e^{2i\varphi}\dd\varphi=0$, so both are $0$. The only case that is not $0$ is $m'=+1$.

(2) We carry the calculation through to the $\theta$ integral for $m'=+1$. Since $Y_1^{1*}=-\sqrt{3/8\pi}\,\sin\theta\,e^{-i\varphi}$,

$$ \int Y_1^{1*}\,\sin\theta\,e^{i\varphi}\,Y_0^0\dd\Omega=-\sqrt{\frac{3}{8\pi}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}}\cdot2\pi\int_0^\pi\sin^3\theta\dd\theta=-\frac{\sqrt3}{4\sqrt2\,\pi}\cdot2\pi\cdot\frac43=-\frac{2\sqrt3}{3\sqrt2}=-\sqrt{\frac23} $$

(here $\sqrt{8\pi}\sqrt{4\pi}=4\sqrt2\,\pi$ and $\int_0^\pi\sin^3\theta\dd\theta=4/3$). The operator carries a factor $1/\sqrt2$, so $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\left(-\sqrt{\dfrac23}\right)=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$, and its magnitude equals the $z$-component integral $\displaystyle\int Y_1^{0*}\cos\theta\,Y_0^0\dd\Omega=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$. Because $1s$ is spherically symmetric, all the directions $x,y,z$ are equivalent, and the intensity of the transition up to $2p_0$ with $\pi$ polarization is the same as that of the transition up to $2p_{+1}$ with $\sigma^+$ (since the radial integral $1.290\,a_0$ is common to both, $\abs{\mel{2p_{+1}}{(x+iy)/\sqrt2}{1s}}=0.7449\,a_0$).

(3) Since $x=r\sin\theta\cos\varphi=\tfrac12r\sin\theta\,(e^{i\varphi}+e^{-i\varphi})$, the $e^{i\varphi}$ term causes the transition to $m'=+1$ and the $e^{-i\varphi}$ term causes the transition to $m'=-1$. The angular integral is $\tfrac12\times(-\sqrt{2/3})=-\sqrt6/6$ for $\mel{2p_{+1}}{\sin\theta\cos\varphi}{1s}$ and $+\sqrt6/6$ for $\mel{2p_{-1}}{\sin\theta\cos\varphi}{1s}$ (the sign is opposite because $Y_1^{-1}=+\sqrt{3/8\pi}\sin\theta e^{-i\varphi}$). Light linearly polarized along the $x$ direction raises the atom to both $2p_{+1}$ and $2p_{-1}$ with equal probability ($1/6$ each, $1/3$ in total, the same as for the $z$ direction), and what is actually excited is the superposition of the two, $(Y_1^{-1}-Y_1^{1})/\sqrt2=\sqrt{3/4\pi}\sin\theta\cos\varphi$, that is, the real orbital $2p_x$.

Exercise 52.2: Allowed transitions in hydrogen, and the lifetime of $3d\to2p$

Solution

Allowed transitions. Among electric dipole transitions, only those with $\Delta l=\pm1$ are allowed. The transitions $3d\to2p$ ($2\to1$), $3p\to2s$ ($1\to0$), and $3s\to2p$ ($0\to1$) are allowed. The transitions $3d\to1s$ ($2\to0$, $\Delta l=2$) and $3d\to2s$ ($2\to0$) are forbidden (the parity is the same, even to even).

Spontaneous emission rate of $3d\to2p$. We have $\hbar\omega=13.606\times\left(\tfrac14-\tfrac19\right)=1.890\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $\omega=1.890\times1.602\times10^{-19}/1.0546\times10^{-34}=2.871\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ ($656\ \mathrm{nm}$). From $R_{21}=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt6}re^{-r/2}$ and $R_{32}=\dfrac{4}{81\sqrt{30}}r^2e^{-r/3}$, the radial integral is

$$ \int_0^\infty R_{21}\,r\,R_{32}\,r^2\dd r=\frac{4}{2\sqrt6\cdot81\sqrt{30}}\int_0^\infty r^6e^{-5r/6}\dd r=1.840\times10^{-3}\times720\left(\frac65\right)^7=1.840\times10^{-3}\times2579.9=4.748\ (a_0\text{ units}) $$

The angular part is the sum of the squared matrix elements from the upper state $3d_0$ ($l=2$, $m=0$) to the three $2p$ states. The $Y_1^0$ component of $\cos\theta\,Y_2^0$ is $\sqrt{\dfrac{l^2-m^2}{(2l-1)(2l+1)}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{4}{15}}$ (the $z$ component, $m'=0$), and the magnitude of the coefficient of the $Y_1^{\pm1}$ component of $\sin\theta\,e^{\pm i\varphi}\,Y_2^0$ is $\sqrt{\dfrac{2\cdot1}{3\cdot5}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{15}}$ (the $x\pm iy$ components). From $x=\tfrac12[(x+iy)+(x-iy)]$ and $y=\tfrac1{2i}[(x+iy)-(x-iy)]$, the sum of the squares of the $x,y$ components is $\left(\tfrac14+\tfrac14\right)\tfrac{2}{15}=\tfrac1{15}$ for $m'=+1$, and the same $\tfrac{1}{15}$ for $m'=-1$. The total is $\dfrac{4}{15}+\dfrac1{15}+\dfrac1{15}=\dfrac25$. Therefore the sum of $\abs{\bm{d}}^2$ from $3d_0$ to all the $2p$ states is

$$ \sum_f\abs{\bm{d}_{fi}}^2=e_0^2\cdot\frac25\cdot4.748^2\,a_0^2=e_0^2\times9.017\,a_0^2=e_0^2\times2.525\times10^{-20}\ \mathrm{m^2} $$

The spontaneous emission rate (summed over the final states) is

$$ A=\frac{\omega^3\sum_f\abs{\bm{d}_{fi}}^2}{3\pi\varepsilon_0\hbar c^3}=\frac{(2.871\times10^{15})^3\times2.567\times10^{-38}\times2.525\times10^{-20}}{2.371\times10^{-19}}=\frac{1.534\times10^{-11}}{2.371\times10^{-19}}=6.47\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} $$

and the lifetime is $\tau=1/A=15.5\ \mathrm{ns}$.

Comparison with $2p\to1s$. We have $A(3d\to2p)/A(2p\to1s)=6.47\times10^{7}/6.27\times10^{8}=0.103$. The ratio of $\omega^3$ is $(1.890/10.204)^3=6.35\times10^{-3}$ ($1/157$), the ratio of $\abs{\bm{d}}^2$ is $9.017/0.5549=16.2$ (compared with the $0.5549\,a_0^2$ of $2p_0\to1s$), and the product is $0.103$. What mainly determines the ratio is $\omega^3$ (about $1/160$), and the difference in the transition dipoles (about 16 times) compensates for part of it.

Exercise 52.3: The selection rule $\Delta n=\pm1$ for the harmonic oscillator

Solution

Acting with $\hat{x}=\sqrt{\hbar/2m\omega}\,(\hat{a}+\hat{a}^\dagger)$ on the state $\ket{n}$ gives $\hat{x}\ket{n}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\hbar}{2m\omega}}\left(\sqrt{n}\ket{n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\ket{n+1}\right)$. Multiplying this from the left by $\bra{n'}$ and using the orthogonality $\braket{n'}{n}=\delta_{n'n}$, we obtain

$$ \mel{n'}{\hat{x}}{n}=\sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2m\omega}}\left(\sqrt{n}\,\delta_{n',n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\,\delta_{n',n+1}\right) $$

Except for $n'=n\pm1$ the Kronecker delta is $0$, so the matrix element is $0$. Therefore the electric dipole selection rule is $\Delta n=\pm1$. The values are $\mel{n+1}{\hat{x}}{n}=\sqrt{(n+1)\hbar/2m\omega}$ and $\mel{n-1}{\hat{x}}{n}=\sqrt{n\hbar/2m\omega}$.

Since $\abs{\mel{1}{\hat{x}}{0}}^2=\dfrac{\hbar}{2m\omega}\cdot1$ and $\abs{\mel{2}{\hat{x}}{1}}^2=\dfrac{\hbar}{2m\omega}\cdot2$, the ratio is $1:2$. That is, the probability (per molecule) that a molecule in the excited state $n=1$ absorbs and goes up to $n=2$ is twice the probability that a molecule in the ground state absorbs and goes up to $n=1$. However, at room temperature the fraction of molecules in $n=1$ is only $e^{-\hbar\omega/k_{\mathrm B}T}$ (small for molecular vibrations), so the observed intensity of the $1\to2$ transition (the hot band) is, overall, much weaker than that of $0\to1$. In the harmonic approximation both absorptions occur at the same frequency $\omega$, but in a real molecule, because of anharmonicity, the $1\to2$ transition is shifted slightly to the low-wavenumber side.

Exercise 52.4: A two-level system with degeneracy — the excited state cannot be fully populated even in strong light

Solution

(1) In the stationary state $\dd N_2/\dd t=0$, so $N_2(A_{21}+B_{21}u)=B_{12}uN_1$. Hence

$$ \frac{N_2}{N_1}=\frac{B_{12}u}{A_{21}+B_{21}u}=\frac{g_2}{g_1}\,\frac{B_{21}u}{A_{21}+B_{21}u}=\frac{g_2}{g_1}\,\frac{1}{1+A_{21}/(B_{21}u)} $$

(we used $B_{12}=(g_2/g_1)B_{21}$).

(2) As $u\to\infty$, $A_{21}/(B_{21}u)\to0$, so $N_2/N_1\to g_2/g_1$, and the fraction in the upper level is $\dfrac{N_2}{N_1+N_2}\to\dfrac{g_2}{g_1+g_2}$. For $g_1=g_2$, $N_2/N_1\to1$ and the fraction is $1/2$. For the Na D$_2$ line, $g_1=2$ and $g_2=4$, so $N_2/N_1\to2$ and the fraction is $4/6=2/3$. (For reference: for the hydrogen $1s$–$2p$ pair, ignoring spin, $g_2/g_1=3$ and the fraction is $3/4$.)

(3) The net rate of absorption is $B_{12}N_1-B_{21}N_2=B_{21}\left(\dfrac{g_2}{g_1}N_1-N_2\right)=B_{21}g_2\left(\dfrac{N_1}{g_1}-\dfrac{N_2}{g_2}\right)$. The condition for this to be negative (stimulated emission wins over absorption, and the light is amplified) is that the occupation number per state satisfy $\dfrac{N_2}{g_2}\gt\dfrac{N_1}{g_1}$ (population inversion). The result of (1) shows that, no matter how much the intensity of the light is increased, $\dfrac{N_2}{g_2}\le\dfrac{N_1}{g_1}$ (with equality for $u\to\infty$). That is, even if a two-level system is excited only by light resonant with its transition, a population inversion cannot be produced (it goes only as far as transparency). This is the reason why a laser needs a three-level or four-level system (Chapter 53). Furthermore, the condition for $N_2\gt N_1$ follows from the result of (1), $\dfrac{N_2}{N_1}=\dfrac{g_2}{g_1}\dfrac{1}{1+A_{21}/(B_{21}u)}\gt1$: it is that $g_2\gt g_1$ and, in addition, $1+\dfrac{A_{21}}{B_{21}u}\lt\dfrac{g_2}{g_1}$, that is, $u\gt\dfrac{A_{21}}{B_{21}\,(g_2/g_1-1)}$. For example, for the Na D$_2$ line ($g_2/g_1=2$), $N_2\gt N_1$ can occur if $u\gt A_{21}/B_{21}$. However, $N_2/g_2\le N_1/g_1$ still holds, and this is not a population inversion (the net rate of absorption remains positive).

Exercise 52.5: Equivalence of the length and velocity forms — $\mel{2p_0}{\hat{p}_z}{1s}$ in hydrogen

Solution

(1) Since $V$ is a function of position only, $\comm{\hat{\bm{r}}}{V}=0$. Since $\comm{\hat{x}}{\hat{p}_x^2}=\hat{p}_x\comm{\hat{x}}{\hat{p}_x}+\comm{\hat{x}}{\hat{p}_x}\hat{p}_x=2i\hbar\hat{p}_x$, we have $\comm{\hat{\bm{r}}}{\hat{H}_0}=\dfrac{1}{2m_{\mathrm e}}\comm{\hat{\bm{r}}}{\hat{\bm{p}}^2}=\dfrac{i\hbar}{m_{\mathrm e}}\hat{\bm{p}}$. Sandwiching between the eigenstates $\ket{i},\ket{f}$, the left-hand side is $\mel{f}{\hat{\bm{r}}\hat{H}_0-\hat{H}_0\hat{\bm{r}}}{i}=(E_i-E_f)\bm{r}_{fi}=-\hbar\omega_{fi}\bm{r}_{fi}$, and the right-hand side is $\dfrac{i\hbar}{m_{\mathrm e}}\bm{p}_{fi}$. This gives $\bm{p}_{fi}=\dfrac{m_{\mathrm e}}{i\hbar}(-\hbar\omega_{fi})\bm{r}_{fi}=im_{\mathrm e}\omega_{fi}\bm{r}_{fi}$ (note that $-1/i=i$).

(2) In atomic units ($m_{\mathrm e}=\hbar=a_0=1$), $\omega_{fi}=\tfrac38$ ($\hbar\omega=\tfrac38E_{\mathrm h}$, where $E_{\mathrm h}=\hbar^2/m_{\mathrm e}a_0^2$ is 1). Since $z_{fi}=0.7449$, $\abs{\mel{2p_0}{\hat{p}_z}{1s}}=m_{\mathrm e}\omega_{fi}\abs{z_{fi}}=\tfrac38\times0.7449=0.2794$ (in units of $\hbar/a_0$; exactly $16\sqrt2/81$). In SI units this is $0.2794\times1.0546\times10^{-34}/5.292\times10^{-11}=5.567\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$.

(3) Since $\omega_{fi}=1.5503\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $A_0=E_0/\omega_{fi}=868.0/1.5503\times10^{16}=5.599\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{V\,s/m}$. In the velocity gauge,

$$ \abs{V_{fi}}=\frac{e_0A_0}{2m_{\mathrm e}}\abs{p_{fi}}=\frac{1.602\times10^{-19}\times5.599\times10^{-14}}{2\times9.109\times10^{-31}}\times5.567\times10^{-25}=4.924\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m/s}\times5.567\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}=2.741\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{J} $$

In the length gauge, $\abs{V_{fi}}=\dfrac{E_0}{2}\abs{d_{fi}}=\dfrac{868.0}{2}\times6.316\times10^{-30}=2.741\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{J}$, and the two agree (this corresponds to $0.017\ \mathrm{\mu eV}$).

Exercise 52.6: Doppler width — the Lyman $\alpha$ line of hydrogen

Solution

We have $\nu_0=c/\lambda=2.998\times10^{8}/(121.567\times10^{-9})=2.466\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $mc^2=1.6735\times10^{-27}\times(2.998\times10^{8})^2=1.504\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{J}$.

(1) $T=300\ \mathrm{K}$: $k_{\mathrm B}T=4.142\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{J}$, the quantity under the square root is $\dfrac{8\times4.142\times10^{-21}\times0.6931}{1.504\times10^{-10}}=1.527\times10^{-10}$, and its square root is $1.236\times10^{-5}$. Then $\Delta\nu_{\mathrm D}=2.466\times10^{15}\times1.236\times10^{-5}=3.05\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{Hz}=30.5\ \mathrm{GHz}$. This is 305 times the natural linewidth of $99.8\ \mathrm{MHz}$ ($30.5\ \mathrm{GHz}/99.8\ \mathrm{MHz}=305$).

(2) $T=10^4\ \mathrm{K}$: since $\Delta\nu_{\mathrm D}\propto\sqrt{T}$, we have $30.5\times\sqrt{10^4/300}=30.5\times5.774=176\ \mathrm{GHz}$. This is about $1.8\times10^{3}$ times the natural linewidth.

(3) $\Delta\nu_{\mathrm D}=\nu_0\sqrt{8k_{\mathrm B}T\ln2/mc^2}$ is proportional to $m^{-1/2}$ (the heavier the atom, the slower its thermal motion and the narrower the width). Compared with the $1.32\ \mathrm{GHz}$ of Na ($589\ \mathrm{nm}$, $300\ \mathrm{K}$), the $30.5\ \mathrm{GHz}$ of hydrogen is $23$ times wider. This is because (i) the mass is $22.99/1.008=22.8$ times lighter ($\sqrt{22.8}=4.8$ times), and (ii) the frequency $\nu_0$ is $2.466\times10^{15}/5.09\times10^{14}=4.8$ times higher (the width is proportional to $\nu_0$); together they give $4.8\times4.8\approx23$ times.

Exercise 52.7: Properties of the Lorentzian — the peak value and the area within the FWHM

Solution

(1) Let $x=\omega-\omega_0$ and $a=A/2$. Then $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{\dd x}{x^2+a^2}=\frac1a\left[\arctan\frac xa\right]_{-\infty}^{\infty}=\frac1a\left(\frac\pi2+\frac\pi2\right)=\frac{\pi}{a}=\frac{2\pi}{A}$. Therefore $\displaystyle\int L\dd\omega=\frac{A}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{2\pi}{A}=1$, so it is normalized. The peak value is $L(\omega_0)=\dfrac{A}{2\pi}\cdot\dfrac{1}{(A/2)^2}=\dfrac{2}{\pi A}=\dfrac{0.637}{A}$.

(2) The fraction of the area in the range $\omega_0\pm X$ is $\displaystyle\int_{-X}^{X}L\dd\omega=\frac{A}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{2}{A}\cdot2\arctan\frac{2X}{A}=\frac{2}{\pi}\arctan\frac{2X}{A}$. Within the full width at half maximum (FWHM, $X=A/2$) it is $\dfrac2\pi\arctan1=\dfrac2\pi\cdot\dfrac\pi4=\dfrac12$; that is, exactly half of the area lies inside. For $X=5A$ (five times the FWHM) it is $\dfrac2\pi\arctan10=0.9365$, so $6.3\%$ lies outside it.

(3) For a Gaussian function with the same FWHM $A$ and with area $1$, the fraction inside the FWHM is $\mathrm{erf}(\sqrt{\ln2})=0.761$ ($76\%$), which is more concentrated at the center than the $50\%$ of the Lorentzian. The area outside $\omega_0\pm5A$ is at most $10^{-30}$ for the Gaussian (effectively $0$), whereas for the Lorentzian it is as much as $6.3\%$. This is because the tail of the Lorentzian decreases only as $1/(\omega-\omega_0)^2$, whereas the Gaussian decreases rapidly as $\exp(-(\omega-\omega_0)^2/2\sigma^2)$. Also, for the same area and the same FWHM, the peak value of the Lorentzian ($2/\pi A=0.637/A$) is $0.68$ times that of the Gaussian ($2\sqrt{\ln2/\pi}/A=0.939/A$); it is lower and has broader tails.

Exercise 52.8: Linewidth of the ruby R lines — natural width and observed width

Solution

(1) $A=1/\tau=1/(3\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s})=333\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The natural linewidth is, in energy, $\Delta E=\hbar A=1.0546\times10^{-34}\times333=3.5\times10^{-32}\ \mathrm{J}=2.2\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{eV}$, and in frequency, $\Delta\nu=A/2\pi=53\ \mathrm{Hz}$. The frequency of the light is $c/694.3\ \mathrm{nm}=4.32\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$, so the relative width is $53/4.32\times10^{14}=1.2\times10^{-13}$.

(2) $10\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}=10\times29.98\ \mathrm{GHz}=3.0\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ (in energy, $1.24\ \mathrm{meV}$), which is $3.0\times10^{11}/53=5.7\times10^{9}$ times the natural linewidth. The observed width is about 10 orders of magnitude larger than the natural linewidth.

(3) The natural linewidth is effectively invisible in experiments. There are two kinds of causes of broadening. The main cause of homogeneous broadening is dephasing ($1/T_2^*$) due to the interaction with phonons: as the temperature falls, the number of phonons decreases and the dephasing becomes slower ($T_2^*$ becomes longer), so the linewidth decreases along with the temperature. Ideally, as $T\to0$, the system approaches the condition $T_2=2T_1$, and the linewidth can reach the natural linewidth. The cause of inhomogeneous broadening is that, because of defects and strain in the crystal, fluctuations in the impurity concentration, and so on, the local crystal field differs slightly from one $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$ ion to another (the center frequency of the emission is shifted from one $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$ ion to another); this does not depend on temperature. When the temperature is lowered, the homogeneous broadening becomes smaller and only the inhomogeneous broadening remains, so the linewidth approaches a certain constant value (the width of the inhomogeneous broadening). To investigate the homogeneous width, methods that are not affected by the inhomogeneous broadening (fluorescence line narrowing and spectral hole burning) are used.

← Back to Chapter 52, “Absorption and Emission of Light — Electric Dipole Approximation, Selection Rules, Einstein Coefficients, Lifetimes, and Linewidths”

Chapter 53: Stimulated Emission and Lasers, and the Optical Absorption Spectra of Materials

Exercise 53.1: Population-inversion condition for a four-level system

Solution

Rate equations. Let $S_{32}$ be the relaxation rate from level 3 to level 2. In the steady state (time derivative equal to 0), for level 3 we have $\dd N_3/\dd t=WN_0-S_{32}N_3=0$, so $N_3=(W/S_{32})N_0$, which is almost 0 if $S_{32}\gg W$ (atoms do not accumulate in level 3). Level 2 is a balance between the inflow from level 3, $S_{32}N_3=WN_0$, and the loss by decay, $A_{21}N_2$:

$$ \diff{N_2}{t}=WN_0-A_{21}N_2=0\ \Longrightarrow\ N_2=\frac{W}{A_{21}}N_0=x\,N_0\qquad\left(x=\frac{W}{A_{21}}\right) $$

Level 1 is a balance between the inflow from level 2, $A_{21}N_2$, and the loss by relaxation to the ground state, $S_{10}N_1$:

$$ \diff{N_1}{t}=A_{21}N_2-S_{10}N_1=0\ \Longrightarrow\ N_1=\frac{A_{21}}{S_{10}}N_2=r\,N_2\qquad\left(r=\frac{A_{21}}{S_{10}}\right) $$

The total number of atoms is $N=N_0+N_1+N_2=N_0(1+x+rx)$, so $N_0=N/[1+x(1+r)]$, $N_2=xN/[1+x(1+r)]$, $N_1=rxN/[1+x(1+r)]$, and

$$ \frac{N_2-N_1}{N}=\frac{x(1-r)}{1+x(1+r)}\ \xrightarrow{\ r\to0\ }\ \frac{x}{1+x} $$

is obtained. Condition for population inversion. For $x\gt0$, $N_2-N_1\gt0$ is equivalent to $1-r\gt0$, that is, $r=A_{21}/S_{10}\lt1$. In other words, if the relaxation rate of the lower level, $S_{10}$, is larger than the decay rate of the upper level, $A_{21}$, a population inversion is formed no matter how small the pump is. This is the difference from the three-level system, which requires more than half of the atoms to be excited ($x\gt1$). Concretely, the excitation rate that reaches the required degree of inversion $\Delta N_{\mathrm{th}}/N=0.0132$ (Example 53.3) is $x=0.0134$ for $r=0$ and $x=0.0149$ for $r=0.1$.

Thermal excitation. When level 1 lies $0.25\ \mathrm{eV}$ above the ground state, the ratio of the occupation numbers in thermal equilibrium is given by the Boltzmann factor, $N_1/N_0=e^{-0.25/0.02585}=e^{-9.67}=6.3\times10^{-5}$. This is the fraction of atoms that are already in level 1 even without the pump, and it is much smaller than the $x\sim10^{-2}$ needed for the threshold. There is no concern that atoms accumulate in the lower level through thermal excitation and hinder the inversion.

Exercise 53.2: Molar absorption coefficient and transmittance

Solution

(a) $A=\varepsilon c_{\mathrm M}\ell=5\times0.10\times1=0.50$. $T=10^{-A}=10^{-0.50}=0.316$ ($31.6\,\%$).

(b) Since the optical path length is 10 times as long, the absorbance is also 10 times as large, $A=5.0$. $T=10^{-5.0}=1.0\times10^{-5}$ ($0.001\,\%$). Almost no light is transmitted.

(c) $\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}=\ln10\cdot\varepsilon c_{\mathrm M}=2.303\times5\times0.10=1.15\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$. (The absorption length is $1/1.15=0.87\ \mathrm{cm}$. $T=e^{-\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}\ell}=e^{-1.15}=0.316$, which agrees with (a).)

(d) $A=2400\times1.0\times10^{-4}\times1=0.24$. $T=10^{-0.24}=0.575$ ($57.5\,\%$). At a concentration $1/1000$ of that of the $0.10\ \mathrm{mol/L}$ $\mathrm{Ti}$ complex ($A=0.50$), $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}$ has an absorbance nearly half that of the complex. This reflects the difference in intensity between a charge-transfer transition and a $d$–$d$ transition (the ratio of the values of $\varepsilon$ is $480$).

Exercise 53.3: Reading the gap from a Tauc plot

Solution

(a) Multiplying both sides of $\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}=K\sqrt{\hbar\omega-E_{\mathrm g}}/\hbar\omega$ by $\hbar\omega$ and squaring, we obtain $(\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}\hbar\omega)^2=K^2(\hbar\omega-E_{\mathrm g})=K^2\hbar\omega-K^2E_{\mathrm g}$, which is a linear function of $\hbar\omega$. Since the slope is $K^2$ and the intercept is $-K^2E_{\mathrm g}$, the point where $(\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}\hbar\omega)^2=0$ (the intersection with the horizontal axis) gives $E_{\mathrm g}=-(\text{intercept})/(\text{slope})$.

(b) The values of $(\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}\hbar\omega)^2\ [10^9\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}\,eV^2}]$ at $\hbar\omega=2.50$, $2.55$, $2.60$, $2.65$, $2.70\ \mathrm{eV}$ are $(1.41\times10^4\times2.50)^2=1.243$, $(1.80\times10^4\times2.55)^2=2.107$, $(2.12\times10^4\times2.60)^2=3.038$, $(2.40\times10^4\times2.65)^2=4.045$, and $(2.65\times10^4\times2.70)^2=5.119$, respectively. These lie almost on a straight line against $\hbar\omega$. The least-squares line has slope $1.94\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}\,eV}$ and intercept $-4.73\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}\,eV^2}$, which gives $E_{\mathrm g}=4.73\times10^{10}/1.94\times10^{10}=2.44\ \mathrm{eV}$ (joining just the two end points also gives $2.44\ \mathrm{eV}$). From the slope, $K=\sqrt{1.94\times10^{10}}=1.39\times10^5\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}\,eV^{1/2}}$. The wavelength is $1239.84/2.44=508\ \mathrm{nm}$ (green). Light with wavelengths shorter than this (blue and violet) is absorbed by interband transitions, so this semiconductor transmits the remaining yellow, orange, and red light and appears yellow (for the same reason that CdS ($E_{\mathrm g}=2.4\ \mathrm{eV}$) is yellow).

When $\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}^2$ is used. The values of $\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}^2\ [10^8\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}}]$ are $1.988$, $3.240$, $4.494$, $5.760$, $7.023$, and the least-squares line (slope $2.52\times10^9\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}\,eV^{-1}}$, intercept $-6.10\times10^9\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}}$) gives $E_{\mathrm g}=6.10/2.52=2.42\ \mathrm{eV}$. This is $0.02\ \mathrm{eV}$ smaller than the value $2.44\ \mathrm{eV}$ read from $(\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}\hbar\omega)^2$. The reason is that the factor $1/(\hbar\omega)^2$ remains in $\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}^2=K^2(\hbar\omega-E_{\mathrm g})/(\hbar\omega)^2$, and even in this range ($2.50$–$2.70\ \mathrm{eV}$) $1/(\hbar\omega)^2$ changes by about $14\,\%$, so $\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}^2$ is not exactly a straight line, and the intercept obtained by extrapolating a straight line is shifted. The plot of $(\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}\hbar\omega)^2$, which starts from the form of the equation in Formula 53.3, $\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}\hbar\omega\propto\sqrt{\hbar\omega-E_{\mathrm g}}$, is the reading that is consistent with the theory. (In experiments, the factor $1/\hbar\omega$ is sometimes ignored and the analysis is done with $\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}^2$; the difference is of the order of $0.01$–$0.02\ \mathrm{eV}$.)

Exercise 53.4: Origin of the exponent 2 for indirect transitions

Solution

(a) Letting $E_{\mathrm e}=E\sin^2\theta$, the range $E_{\mathrm e}:0\to E$ corresponds to $\theta:0\to\pi/2$. Since $\dd E_{\mathrm e}=2E\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\dd\theta$, $\sqrt{E_{\mathrm e}}=\sqrt{E}\sin\theta$, and $\sqrt{E-E_{\mathrm e}}=\sqrt{E}\cos\theta$, the integrand is $\sqrt{E}\sin\theta\cdot\sqrt{E}\cos\theta\cdot2E\sin\theta\cos\theta=2E^2\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta$. Integrating $\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta=\tfrac14\sin^22\theta=\tfrac18(1-\cos4\theta)$ from $0$ to $\pi/2$ gives $\tfrac18\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{16}$, so

$$ \int_0^E\sqrt{E_{\mathrm e}}\sqrt{E-E_{\mathrm e}}\,\dd E_{\mathrm e}=2E^2\cdot\frac{\pi}{16}=\frac{\pi}{8}E^2 $$

is obtained.

(b) In a direct transition, the photon does not change $\bm{k}$, so the electron and the hole have the same $\bm{k}$, and the number of states for which the sum of the kinetic energies, $\hbar^2k^2/2\mu$, is at most $E$ is the volume of a sphere in three-dimensional wavenumber space, $\propto k^3\propto E^{3/2}$. The number of states per unit energy width is obtained by differentiating this with respect to $E$, which gives $\sqrt{E}$. In an indirect transition, a phonon makes up the difference in wavenumber, so the wavenumber of the electron and that of the hole can be chosen independently. The wavenumber space doubles in dimension, from three dimensions to three dimensions $\times$ three dimensions = six dimensions, and the number of states for which the sum of the kinetic energies is at most $E$ is proportional to the volume of a six-dimensional sphere, $\propto k^6\propto E^3$. Differentiating this gives $E^2$. This is the same as the fact that the convolution integral found in (a) is proportional to $E^2$.

(c) When the excess energies measured from the respective thresholds are equal, the intensity of the absorption process is proportional to $n$ and that of the emission process to $n+1$, so the ratio is $n/(n+1)=e^{-\hbar\Omega/k_{\mathrm B}T}$ (from $n=1/(e^{x}-1)$ and $x=\hbar\Omega/k_{\mathrm B}T$, $n/(n+1)=1/e^{x}$). Since $\hbar\Omega/k_{\mathrm B}T=0.058/0.02585=2.24$, $e^{-2.24}=0.106$. We have $n=1/(e^{2.24}-1)=0.119$ and $n+1=1.119$, and $0.119/1.119=0.106$ agrees with this. At $300\ \mathrm{K}$, the process that emits a phonon is about nine times stronger than the process that absorbs one (this holds when they are compared at the same energy above the respective thresholds. When they are compared at the same photon energy $\hbar\omega$, the ratio is not this value, because the expression in the brackets of the absorption-coefficient formula for indirect transitions in Chapter 53, Section 53.4.4, is different, being $\hbar\omega-E_{\mathrm g}\pm\hbar\Omega$). For a phonon of about $18\ \mathrm{meV}$ ($n=0.99$), the ratio is $0.50$, and absorption and emission are of the same order. At low temperatures $n\to0$, and the absorption process vanishes.

Exercise 53.5: Force constant of CO and the isotope shift

Solution

(a) $\omega=2\pi c\tilde\nu=2\pi\times2.998\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm/s}\times2143\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}=4.037\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Since $\mu=6.856\ \mathrm{u}=6.856\times1.6605\times10^{-27}=1.1385\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{kg}$, we have $k_0=\mu\omega^2=1.1385\times10^{-26}\times(4.037\times10^{14})^2=1.1385\times10^{-26}\times1.630\times10^{29}=1.86\times10^3\ \mathrm{N/m}$ ($1855\ \mathrm{N/m}$). (If we use the wavenumber of the harmonic oscillator, $\omega_{\mathrm e}=2170\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, we obtain $1902\ \mathrm{N/m}$; because of the anharmonicity, the observed wavenumber of the fundamental is about $1.2\,\%$ lower, which makes the spring constant appear about $2.5\,\%$ smaller.)

(b) The reduced mass of ${}^{13}\mathrm{C}{}^{16}\mathrm{O}$ is $\mu'=\dfrac{13.0034\times15.9949}{13.0034+15.9949}=7.172\ \mathrm{u}$. Since isotopic substitution does not change the spring constant (the potential created by the electrons), $\tilde\nu\propto\omega=\sqrt{k_0/\mu}\propto\mu^{-1/2}$. Therefore $\tilde\nu'=2143\times\sqrt{6.856/7.172}=2143\times0.9777=2095\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$. This agrees with the measured value of about $2096\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ to within a difference of about $1\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ ($0.04\,\%$). This difference arises because the anharmonic correction also changes with the isotope. Indeed, if we multiply the harmonic wavenumber $\omega_{\mathrm e}$ by $\mu^{-1/2}$ ($2169.81\times0.9777=2121.4$), multiply the anharmonicity constant $\omega_{\mathrm e}x_{\mathrm e}$ by $\mu^{-1}$ ($13.29\times0.9559=12.70$), and take the fundamental to be $\omega_{\mathrm e}-2\omega_{\mathrm e}x_{\mathrm e}=2121.4-25.4=2096.0\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, we obtain almost perfect agreement with the measured value.

Exercise 53.6: Wavelength design of a semiconductor laser

Solution

(a) $\lambda\,[\mathrm{nm}]=1239.84/E\,[\mathrm{eV}]$. For GaAs, $1239.84/1.42=873\ \mathrm{nm}$ (near-infrared), with photon energy $1.42\ \mathrm{eV}$. For InGaN, $1239.84/3.0=413\ \mathrm{nm}$ (blue-violet), with photon energy $3.0\ \mathrm{eV}$. (b) From $\lambda=1550\ \mathrm{nm}$, $E_{\mathrm g}=1239.84/1550=0.800\ \mathrm{eV}$. (For $1.31\ \mu\mathrm{m}$ it is $0.946\ \mathrm{eV}$.) (c) The photon energy at $780\ \mathrm{nm}$ is $1239.84/780=1.590\ \mathrm{eV}$. Setting this equal to $E_{\mathrm g}(x)=1.424+1.247x$, we obtain $x=(1.590-1.424)/1.247=0.133$. The active layer is about $\mathrm{Al}_{0.13}\mathrm{Ga}_{0.87}\mathrm{As}$ (since $x\lt0.45$, the gap is direct); adding 13% Al to GaAs and widening the gap by $0.17\ \mathrm{eV}$ shortens the wavelength from $873\ \mathrm{nm}$ to $780\ \mathrm{nm}$.

Exercise 53.7: Oscillator strength and the spontaneous-emission lifetime

Solution

(a) From $d=e_0r$, $\abs{d_{12}}^2=e_0^2\abs{r}^2$. From $f=2m_{\mathrm e}\omega\abs{r}^2/(3\hbar)$, $\abs{r}^2=3\hbar f/(2m_{\mathrm e}\omega)$, so

$$ A_{21}=\frac{\omega^3e_0^2}{3\pi\varepsilon_0\hbar c^3}\cdot\frac{3\hbar f}{2m_{\mathrm e}\omega}=\frac{e_0^2\omega^2}{2\pi\varepsilon_0m_{\mathrm e}c^3}\,f $$

is obtained (the $\hbar$ and the 3 cancel). (b) For $\hbar\omega=2.5\ \mathrm{eV}$, $\omega=2.5\times1.602\times10^{-19}/1.0546\times10^{-34}=3.798\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The coefficient is $\dfrac{e_0^2\omega^2}{2\pi\varepsilon_0m_{\mathrm e}c^3}=\dfrac{(1.602\times10^{-19})^2\times(3.798\times10^{15})^2}{2\pi\times8.854\times10^{-12}\times9.109\times10^{-31}\times(2.998\times10^8)^3}=2.71\times10^8\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, so for $f=10^{-4}$, $A_{21}=2.7\times10^4\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and the lifetime is $\tau=1/A_{21}=37\ \mu\mathrm{s}$. For $f=1$, $A_{21}=2.7\times10^8\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $\tau=3.7\ \mathrm{ns}$, so the lifetimes of an allowed transition and a $d$–$d$ transition ($f\sim10^{-4}$) differ by four orders of magnitude. (c) For $\hbar\omega=10.204\ \mathrm{eV}$, $\omega=1.550\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and the coefficient is $(10.204/2.5)^2=16.66$ times that of (b), that is, $4.52\times10^9\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$. $A_{21}=\dfrac13\times4.52\times10^9\times0.4162=6.27\times10^8\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and the lifetime is $1/A_{21}=1.60\ \mathrm{ns}$, which agrees with the value for the $2p\to1s$ transition of hydrogen obtained from the Einstein coefficients in the previous chapter.

Exercise 53.8: Oscillator strength of the harmonic oscillator and the sum rule

Solution

Since $\mel{n+1}{\hat{x}}{n}^2=(n+1)\hbar/2\mu\omega$ and $\omega_{n+1,n}=+\omega$, we have

$$ f_{n+1,n}=\frac{2\mu\omega}{\hbar}\cdot\frac{(n+1)\hbar}{2\mu\omega}=n+1 $$

Similarly, since $\mel{n-1}{\hat{x}}{n}^2=n\hbar/2\mu\omega$ and $\omega_{n-1,n}=-\omega$ (a downward transition), we have

$$ f_{n-1,n}=\frac{2\mu(-\omega)}{\hbar}\cdot\frac{n\hbar}{2\mu\omega}=-n $$

which is negative. The matrix elements to all other $n'$ vanish, so the sum is $\sum_{n'}f_{n'n}=(n+1)+(-n)=1$, which equals 1 for every $n$ (the sum rule). The fact that $f_{n-1,n}\lt0$ corresponds to stimulated emission “canceling” absorption (in Section 53.1, the difference between absorption $\propto N_1$ and stimulated emission $\propto N_2$ determined the increase or decrease of the light).

Let $P_n$ be the probability of being in the $n$th level at temperature $T$. The total intensity of light absorption (upward) is $\sum_nP_n(n+1)$, and the total intensity of stimulated emission (downward) is $\sum_nP_nn$, so the net absorption is $\sum_nP_n[(n+1)-n]=\sum_nP_n=1$. Absorption becomes stronger the more highly the level from which the transition starts is thermally excited ($\propto n+1$), but stimulated emission also becomes stronger by the same amount ($\propto n$), so the intensity of the net absorption does not depend on $T$ and is the same as at $T=0$ ($P_0=1$, $f=1$). This happens because the lines of all the transitions $n\to n\pm1$ of the harmonic oscillator coincide at the same frequency $\omega$. In real molecules, anharmonicity shifts the position of the $n\to n+1$ line with $n$, and the lines of the transitions starting from levels with $n\ge1$ (hot bands) appear slightly on the low-wavenumber side of the fundamental.

← Back to Chapter 53, “Stimulated Emission and Lasers, and the Optical Absorption Spectra of Materials”

Chapter 54: Linear Response and an Introduction to the Kubo Formula — Response Functions, Causality, Kramers–Kronig Relations, and the Complex Permittivity

Exercise 54.1: Derivation of the Lehmann representation and the high-frequency limit

Solution

(1) The time representation in Chapter 54, Section 54.3 is $\chi_{AB}(t)=\dfrac{i}{\hbar}\theta(t)\displaystyle\sum_n\Bigl[A_{0n}B_{n0}\,e^{-i\omega_{n0}t}-B_{0n}A_{n0}\,e^{+i\omega_{n0}t}\Bigr]$. We multiply by $e^{i(\omega+i\eta)t}$ and integrate from $t=0$ to $\infty$. Thanks to $\theta(t)$, the lower limit is $0$. The first term is $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty e^{i(\omega-\omega_{n0}+i\eta)t}\dd t$ and the second term is $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty e^{i(\omega+\omega_{n0}+i\eta)t}\dd t$, and for a complex number $z$ with $\mathrm{Im}\,z\gt0$ we have $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty e^{izt}\dd t=\Bigl[\dfrac{e^{izt}}{iz}\Bigr]_0^\infty=\dfrac{i}{z}$ (at the upper limit, $\abs{e^{izt}}=e^{-\mathrm{Im}\,z\,t}\to0$). The imaginary part of $z=\omega\mp\omega_{n0}+i\eta$ is $\eta\gt0$, so this formula can be used:

$$ \chi_{AB}(\omega)=\frac{i}{\hbar}\sum_n\Bigl[A_{0n}B_{n0}\frac{i}{\omega-\omega_{n0}+i\eta}-B_{0n}A_{n0}\frac{i}{\omega+\omega_{n0}+i\eta}\Bigr] =\frac1\hbar\sum_n\Bigl[\frac{A_{0n}B_{n0}}{\omega_{n0}-\omega-i\eta}+\frac{B_{0n}A_{n0}}{\omega_{n0}+\omega+i\eta}\Bigr] $$

(Since $i\cdot i=-1$, the first term becomes $-\dfrac{1}{\omega-\omega_{n0}+i\eta}=\dfrac{1}{\omega_{n0}-\omega-i\eta}$.) This is the Lehmann representation.

(2) Setting $\hat{B}=\hat{A}$, we have $A_{0n}A_{n0}=\abs{A_{0n}}^2$ (Hermiticity), and $\chi_{AA}=\dfrac1\hbar\sum_n\abs{A_{0n}}^2\Bigl[\dfrac{1}{\omega_{n0}-\omega}+\dfrac{1}{\omega_{n0}+\omega}\Bigr]=\dfrac{2}{\hbar}\sum_n\dfrac{\omega_{n0}\abs{A_{0n}}^2}{\omega_{n0}^2-\omega^2}$ ($\eta\to0$). For $\omega\gg\omega_{n0}$ the denominator approaches $-\omega^2$, so $\chi_{AA}\to-\dfrac{2}{\hbar\omega^2}\displaystyle\sum_n\omega_{n0}\abs{A_{0n}}^2$.

(3) Take $\hat{A}=\hat{x}$. From the TRK sum rule $\displaystyle\sum_n\dfrac{2m\omega_{n0}}{\hbar}\abs{x_{n0}}^2=1$ we obtain $\displaystyle\sum_n\omega_{n0}\abs{x_{0n}}^2=\dfrac{\hbar}{2m}$. Therefore $\chi_{xx}\to-\dfrac{2}{\hbar\omega^2}\cdot\dfrac{\hbar}{2m}=-\dfrac{1}{m\omega^2}$. This agrees with the response function for the displacement $x=-F/(m\omega^2)$ ($m(-\omega^2)x=F$) of a free particle $m\ddot{x}=F$ subjected to $F=F_\omega e^{-i\omega t}$. When the vibration is fast, the particle responds as a free particle, regardless of the details of the binding.

Exercise 54.2: Derivation of the $f$ sum rule and its check for the harmonic oscillator

Solution

(1) Since $V(\hat{x})$ commutes with $\hat{x}$, $\comm{\hat{H}_0}{\hat{x}}=\dfrac{1}{2m}\comm{\hat{p}^2}{\hat{x}}=\dfrac{1}{2m}\bigl(\hat{p}\comm{\hat{p}}{\hat{x}}+\comm{\hat{p}}{\hat{x}}\hat{p}\bigr)=\dfrac{1}{2m}\bigl(-2i\hbar\hat{p}\bigr)=-\dfrac{i\hbar}{m}\hat{p}$. The commutator of $\hat{x}$ with this is $\comm{\hat{x}}{-\dfrac{i\hbar}{m}\hat{p}}=-\dfrac{i\hbar}{m}\cdot i\hbar=\dfrac{\hbar^2}{m}$.

On the other hand, sandwiching $\comm{\hat{x}}{\comm{\hat{H}_0}{\hat{x}}}=2\hat{x}\hat{H}_0\hat{x}-\hat{x}^2\hat{H}_0-\hat{H}_0\hat{x}^2$ in the ground state $\ket{0}$, we have $\bra{0}\hat{x}^2\hat{H}_0\ket{0}=\bra{0}\hat{H}_0\hat{x}^2\ket{0}=E_0\bra{0}\hat{x}^2\ket{0}$ because $\hat{H}_0\ket{0}=E_0\ket{0}$. Inserting the complete set $\sum_n\ket{n}\bra{n}=\hat{1}$, we get $\bra{0}\hat{x}\hat{H}_0\hat{x}\ket{0}=\sum_nE_n\abs{x_{n0}}^2$ and $\bra{0}\hat{x}^2\ket{0}=\sum_n\abs{x_{n0}}^2$, so

$$ \bra{0}\comm{\hat{x}}{\comm{\hat{H}_0}{\hat{x}}}\ket{0}=2\sum_n(E_n-E_0)\abs{x_{n0}}^2=\frac{\hbar^2}{m} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad\sum_n\frac{2m(E_n-E_0)}{\hbar^2}\abs{x_{n0}}^2=\sum_nf_{n0}=1 $$

holds (here $f_{n0}=2m\omega_{n0}\abs{x_{n0}}^2/\hbar$ and $\hbar\omega_{n0}=E_n-E_0$).

(2) In terms of the creation and annihilation operators, $\hat{x}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\hbar}{2m\omega_0}}(\hat{a}+\hat{a}^\dagger)$. Acting on the ground state $\ket{0}$, we have $\hat{a}\ket{0}=0$ and $\hat{a}^\dagger\ket{0}=\ket{1}$, so $\hat{x}\ket{0}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\hbar}{2m\omega_0}}\ket{1}$; hence $x_{10}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\hbar}{2m\omega_0}}$ and $x_{n0}=0$ ($n\ge2$). Since $\omega_{10}=\omega_0$, we get $f_{10}=\dfrac{2m\omega_0}{\hbar}\cdot\dfrac{\hbar}{2m\omega_0}=1$ and $f_{n0}=0$ ($n\ge2$). The sum is $1$, and the sum rule holds. For the harmonic oscillator, the entire intensity is concentrated in the single line of the fundamental vibration (that of one classical oscillator with natural angular frequency $\omega_0$).

Exercise 54.3: Derivation of the Kramers–Kronig relations and a check with an exponentially decaying response

Solution

(0) In the complex $\omega'$ plane, consider the closed integration contour $C$ that runs along the real axis from $-R$ to $R$ (detouring around the point $\omega$ along a small semicircle of radius $\delta$) and returns through the upper half-plane along a large semicircle of radius $R$. In the upper half-plane $\chi(\omega')$ is analytic, and it tends to $0$ as $\abs{\omega'}\to\infty$.

When the small semicircle is on the upper side. The point $\omega$ lies outside $C$, and $\dfrac{\chi(\omega')}{\omega'-\omega}$ is analytic inside $C$, so by Cauchy's integral theorem $\displaystyle\oint_C\dfrac{\chi(\omega')}{\omega'-\omega}\dd\omega'=0$. We split the contour integral into three parts. Large semicircle: for $\omega'=Re^{i\varphi}$ ($0\le\varphi\le\pi$), $\abs{\dd\omega'}=R\,\dd\varphi$ and $\abs{\omega'-\omega}\ge R-\abs{\omega}$, so $\Bigl|\displaystyle\int\Bigr|\le\pi\,\dfrac{R}{R-\abs{\omega}}\max_{\abs{\omega'}=R}\abs{\chi}\to0$ ($R\to\infty$). Small semicircle: setting $\omega'=\omega+\delta e^{i\varphi}$, we have $\dd\omega'=i\delta e^{i\varphi}\dd\varphi$ and $\omega'-\omega=\delta e^{i\varphi}$, and when going around the upper side of the point $\omega$, $\varphi$ moves from $\pi$ to $0$ (clockwise). Then $\displaystyle\int_\pi^0\chi(\omega+\delta e^{i\varphi})\,i\,\dd\varphi\to i\chi(\omega)\,(0-\pi)=-i\pi\chi(\omega)$ ($\delta\to0$; $\chi$ is continuous at $\omega$). Real axis: the limit $\delta\to0$, $R\to\infty$ is the principal-value integral $\mathrm{P}\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\dfrac{\chi(\omega')}{\omega'-\omega}\dd\omega'$. Since the sum of the three is $0$, $\mathrm{P}\displaystyle\int\dfrac{\chi(\omega')}{\omega'-\omega}\dd\omega'-i\pi\chi(\omega)=0$, that is, $\chi(\omega)=\dfrac{1}{i\pi}\mathrm{P}\displaystyle\int\dfrac{\chi(\omega')}{\omega'-\omega}\dd\omega'$.

When the small semicircle is on the lower side. If we move the small semicircle $\omega'=\omega+\delta e^{i\varphi}$ with $\varphi$ going from $\pi$ to $2\pi$ (counterclockwise around the lower side of the point $\omega$), the point $\omega$ falls inside $C$. By Cauchy's integral formula, $\displaystyle\oint_C\dfrac{\chi(\omega')}{\omega'-\omega}\dd\omega'=2\pi i\,\chi(\omega)$. The contribution of the large semicircle is again $0$. For the small semicircle, $\displaystyle\int_\pi^{2\pi}\chi\,i\,\dd\varphi\to i\pi\chi(\omega)$. Hence $\mathrm{P}\displaystyle\int\dfrac{\chi(\omega')}{\omega'-\omega}\dd\omega'+i\pi\chi(\omega)=2\pi i\,\chi(\omega)$, which gives $\mathrm{P}\displaystyle\int\dfrac{\chi(\omega')}{\omega'-\omega}\dd\omega'=i\pi\chi(\omega)$. We obtain the same equation as in the upper case. (Between the upper case and the lower case, both the contribution of the small semicircle ($-i\pi\chi$ and $+i\pi\chi$) and the value of the contour integral ($0$ and $2\pi i\chi$) differ, but after transposing terms the same equation results.)

(1) $\chi(\omega)=\displaystyle\int_0^\infty e^{-\Gamma t}e^{i\omega t}\dd t=\Bigl[\dfrac{e^{(-\Gamma+i\omega)t}}{-\Gamma+i\omega}\Bigr]_0^\infty=\dfrac{1}{\Gamma-i\omega}=\dfrac{i}{\omega+i\Gamma}$. Multiplying by the complex conjugate of the denominator, $\Gamma+i\omega$, we obtain $\chi(\omega)=\dfrac{\Gamma+i\omega}{\omega^2+\Gamma^2}$, so $\mathrm{Re}\,\chi=\dfrac{\Gamma}{\omega^2+\Gamma^2}$ and $\mathrm{Im}\,\chi=\dfrac{\omega}{\omega^2+\Gamma^2}$.

(2) The pole is at $\omega=-i\Gamma$, whose imaginary part is negative; that is, it lies in the lower half-plane. Consider the integrand $g(\omega')=\dfrac{i}{(\omega'+i\Gamma)(\omega'-\omega)}$ of the right-hand side of the complex form, $\dfrac{1}{i\pi}\mathrm{P}\displaystyle\int\dfrac{\chi(\omega')}{\omega'-\omega}\dd\omega'$. On the large semicircle in the upper half-plane, $\abs{g}\sim1/R^2$, so the contribution of the semicircle is $0$ as $R\to\infty$. There is no pole inside the upper half-plane (the pole at $-i\Gamma$ is in the lower half-plane, and $\omega$ is on the real axis). If we avoid the pole $\omega'=\omega$ on the real axis by a small semicircle on the upper side, the principal-value integral is $\mathrm{P}\displaystyle\int g\,\dd\omega'=i\pi\,\mathrm{Res}_{\omega'=\omega}g$ (a pole on the real axis counts as half a residue, corresponding to the contribution $-i\pi\chi$ of the small semicircle in Figure 54.6). The residue is $\mathrm{Res}_{\omega'=\omega}g=\dfrac{i}{\omega+i\Gamma}$, so $\mathrm{P}\displaystyle\int g\,\dd\omega'=i\pi\cdot\dfrac{i}{\omega+i\Gamma}=-\dfrac{\pi}{\omega+i\Gamma}$. Hence the right-hand side is $\dfrac{1}{i\pi}\cdot\Bigl(-\dfrac{\pi}{\omega+i\Gamma}\Bigr)=-\dfrac{1}{i(\omega+i\Gamma)}=\dfrac{i}{\omega+i\Gamma}=\chi(\omega)$, which agrees with the left-hand side.

(3) At $\omega=\Gamma$, decompose $\dfrac{1}{\pi}\mathrm{P}\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\dfrac{\omega'}{(\omega'^2+\Gamma^2)(\omega'-\Gamma)}\dd\omega'$ into partial fractions: $\dfrac{\omega'}{(\omega'^2+\Gamma^2)(\omega'-\Gamma)}=\dfrac{1}{2\Gamma}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\omega'-\Gamma}+\dfrac{-\omega'/(2\Gamma)+1/2}{\omega'^2+\Gamma^2}$ (this can be checked by putting the right-hand side over a common denominator and comparing coefficients: the numerator is $\tfrac{1}{2\Gamma}(\omega'^2+\Gamma^2)+\bigl(-\tfrac{\omega'}{2\Gamma}+\tfrac12\bigr)(\omega'-\Gamma)=\omega'$). The principal-value integral of the first term over a symmetric interval is $\ln\bigl|\tfrac{R-\Gamma}{R+\Gamma}\bigr|\to0$. In the second term, the odd-function part $-\dfrac{\omega'}{2\Gamma(\omega'^2+\Gamma^2)}$ gives $0$ in a symmetric integral, and the remainder is $\dfrac12\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^\infty\dfrac{\dd\omega'}{\omega'^2+\Gamma^2}=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{\Gamma}$. Hence $\dfrac1\pi\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2\Gamma}=\dfrac{1}{2\Gamma}$, which agrees with $\mathrm{Re}\,\chi(\Gamma)=\dfrac{\Gamma}{2\Gamma^2}=\dfrac{1}{2\Gamma}$ (numerical integration at $\Gamma=0.7$ also gives $0.714$).

Exercise 54.4: Static response of a two-level system with a permanent dipole

Solution

(1) We have $\hat{H}=\hat{H}_0-F\hat{B}=\Bigl(\dfrac{\hbar\omega_0}{2}-Fc\Bigr)\sigma_z-Fb\,\sigma_x$, and letting $a=\hbar\omega_0/2$, the eigenvalues are $\pm\sqrt{(a-Fc)^2+F^2b^2}$; the ground state is the negative one: $E_0(F)=-\sqrt{(a-Fc)^2+F^2b^2}$. For small $F$, $\sqrt{(a-Fc)^2+F^2b^2}=(a-Fc)\sqrt{1+\dfrac{F^2b^2}{(a-Fc)^2}}=(a-Fc)+\dfrac{F^2b^2}{2(a-Fc)}+\cdots=a-Fc+\dfrac{F^2b^2}{2a}+O(F^3)$, so

$$ E_0(F)=-\frac{\hbar\omega_0}{2}+Fc-\frac{F^2b^2}{\hbar\omega_0}+O(F^3) $$

holds. (2) Here $E_0=-\hbar\omega_0/2$. The ground state is the state $\ket{\downarrow}$ with $\sigma_z=-1$, and $B_{00}=\mel{\downarrow}{(b\sigma_x+c\sigma_z)}{\downarrow}=-c$, so $-FB_{00}=+Fc$ (the first-order term, due to the permanent dipole). The matrix element with the excited state $\ket{\uparrow}$ is $B_{10}=\mel{\uparrow}{b\sigma_x}{\downarrow}=b$, and $E_1-E_0=\hbar\omega_0$, so $\chi_{BB}(0)=\dfrac{2\abs{B_{10}}^2}{E_1-E_0}=\dfrac{2b^2}{\hbar\omega_0}$, and $-\tfrac12\chi_{BB}(0)F^2=-\dfrac{F^2b^2}{\hbar\omega_0}$ agrees with the second-order term. (3) For $b=0.6$, $c=0.3$, $\hbar\omega_0=1$, $F=0.1$: the exact value is $E_0=-\sqrt{(0.5-0.03)^2+0.0036}=-\sqrt{0.2245}=-0.47381$. To second order: $-0.5+0.03-0.0036=-0.4736$. The difference is $-2.1\times10^{-4}$ ($0.045\ \%$), which corresponds to the nonlinear terms of third order and higher.

Exercise 54.5: From the complex permittivity to the refractive index, extinction coefficient, and absorption coefficient

Solution

(1) From the real and imaginary parts of $N^2=(n+i\kappa)^2=n^2-\kappa^2+2in\kappa=\varepsilon_1+i\varepsilon_2$ we get $n^2-\kappa^2=\varepsilon_1$ and $2n\kappa=\varepsilon_2$. Taking the sum and the difference of $\abs{\varepsilon}=\sqrt{(n^2-\kappa^2)^2+4n^2\kappa^2}=n^2+\kappa^2$ and $\varepsilon_1=n^2-\kappa^2$, we obtain $n^2=\dfrac{\abs{\varepsilon}+\varepsilon_1}{2}$ and $\kappa^2=\dfrac{\abs{\varepsilon}-\varepsilon_1}{2}$. Therefore $n=\sqrt{(\abs{\varepsilon}+\varepsilon_1)/2}$ and $\kappa=\sqrt{(\abs{\varepsilon}-\varepsilon_1)/2}$ ($n,\kappa\gt0$).

(2) $\abs{\varepsilon}=\sqrt{3.0^2+0.5^2}=\sqrt{9.25}=3.0414$. Then $n=\sqrt{(3.0414+3.0)/2}=\sqrt{3.0207}=1.738$ and $\kappa=\sqrt{(3.0414-3.0)/2}=\sqrt{0.02069}=0.1438$ (check: $2n\kappa=0.500$, $n^2-\kappa^2=3.000$). The absorption coefficient is $\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}=\dfrac{4\pi\kappa}{\lambda_0}=\dfrac{4\pi\times0.1438}{600\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{cm}}=\dfrac{1.808}{6.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{cm}}=3.01\times10^4\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$. The distance over which the intensity of light falls to $1/e$ is $1/\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}=3.3\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{cm}=0.33\ \mu\mathrm{m}$ ($330\ \mathrm{nm}$). The reflection coefficient is $R=\dfrac{(n-1)^2+\kappa^2}{(n+1)^2+\kappa^2}=\dfrac{0.5447+0.0207}{7.4966+0.0207}=\dfrac{0.5654}{7.5173}=0.0752$ (about $7.5\ \%$).

Exercise 54.6: Plasma edge of the Drude model — sodium

Solution

(1) $\omega_{\mathrm p}^2=\dfrac{n_{\mathrm e}e_0^2}{\varepsilon_0m_{\mathrm e}}=\dfrac{2.65\times10^{28}\times(1.602\times10^{-19})^2}{8.854\times10^{-12}\times9.109\times10^{-31}}=\dfrac{6.80\times10^{-10}}{8.065\times10^{-42}}=8.43\times10^{31}\ \mathrm{s^{-2}}$, so $\omega_{\mathrm p}=9.18\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$. $\hbar\omega_{\mathrm p}=1.0546\times10^{-34}\times9.18\times10^{15}/1.602\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{eV}=6.04\ \mathrm{eV}$. The vacuum wavelength is $\lambda_{\mathrm p}=2\pi c/\omega_{\mathrm p}=\dfrac{1239.84\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}}{6.04\ \mathrm{eV}}=205\ \mathrm{nm}$ (ultraviolet).

(2) In the limit $\gamma\to0$, $\varepsilon_1=1-(\omega_{\mathrm p}/\omega)^2=1-\dfrac{(6.04)^2}{(\hbar\omega)^2}$ ($(6.04)^2=36.5$). For $\hbar\omega=2\ \mathrm{eV}$: $\varepsilon_1=1-36.5/4=-8.1\lt0$. $N=\sqrt{\varepsilon}$ is purely imaginary ($n\simeq0$, $\kappa=\sqrt{8.1}=2.85$), so the electromagnetic wave cannot enter the interior and is almost completely reflected (metallic luster). For $\hbar\omega=8\ \mathrm{eV}$: $\varepsilon_1=1-36.5/64=0.43\gt0$, $n=\sqrt{0.43}=0.66$, and $\kappa\simeq0$, so the metal becomes transparent (the phenomenon in which alkali metals become transparent in the ultraviolet). The boundary is at $\hbar\omega_{\mathrm p}=6.04\ \mathrm{eV}$ (wavelength $205\ \mathrm{nm}$).

(3) From $\varepsilon_1=1-\dfrac{\omega_{\mathrm p}^2}{\omega^2+\gamma^2}=0$ we get $\omega^2+\gamma^2=\omega_{\mathrm p}^2$, so $\omega=\sqrt{\omega_{\mathrm p}^2-\gamma^2}$. If $\gamma\ll\omega_{\mathrm p}$, this is approximately $\omega_{\mathrm p}$.

Exercise 54.7: Conversion to the sign convention of AD 08 ($\hat{H}_{\mathrm{ext}}=+f\hat{B}$)

Solution

(1) The commutator of the harmonic oscillator at different times is $\comm{\hat{x}_H(t)}{\hat{x}_H(0)}=-\dfrac{i\hbar}{m\omega_0}\sin\omega_0t$ (Chapter 50; the commutator is a number that contains no operators, that is, a c-number). $\chi^{\mathrm R}_{xx}(t)=-\dfrac{i}{\hbar}\theta(t)\Bigl(-\dfrac{i\hbar}{m\omega_0}\sin\omega_0t\Bigr)=\dfrac{i\cdot i}{m\omega_0}\theta(t)\sin\omega_0t=-\theta(t)\dfrac{\sin\omega_0t}{m\omega_0}$ ($-i\times(-i)=i^2=-1$). Comparing with this book's $\chi_{xx}(t)=+\theta(t)\dfrac{\sin\omega_0t}{m\omega_0}$, we have $\chi^{\mathrm R}_{xx}=-\chi_{xx}$. The same holds after the Fourier transform: $\chi^{\mathrm R}_{xx}(\omega)=-\dfrac{1}{m(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)}$. This corresponds to $f=-F$: $\hat{H}_{\mathrm{ext}}=+f\hat{x}=-F\hat{x}$, and from the same physical response $\delta\langle\hat{x}\rangle=\chi F=\chi^{\mathrm R}f=\chi^{\mathrm R}(-F)$ we get $\chi^{\mathrm R}=-\chi$.

(2) The ground-state energy under the external field $+f\hat{B}$ is, in second-order perturbation theory, $E_0(f)=E_0+fB_{00}-f^2\displaystyle\sum_{n\ne0}\dfrac{\abs{B_{n0}}^2}{E_n-E_0}+\cdots$. Differentiating this twice with respect to $f$ gives $\dfrac{\partial^2E_0}{\partial f^2}=-2\displaystyle\sum_n\dfrac{\abs{B_{n0}}^2}{E_n-E_0}$. On the other hand, this book's static susceptibility is $\chi_{BB}(0)=2\displaystyle\sum_n\dfrac{\abs{B_{n0}}^2}{E_n-E_0}\gt0$, and $\chi^{\mathrm R}_{BB}(0)=-\chi_{BB}(0)=-2\displaystyle\sum_n\dfrac{\abs{B_{n0}}^2}{E_n-E_0}\lt0$. Therefore $\chi^{\mathrm R}_{BB}(0)=\dfrac{\partial^2E_0}{\partial f^2}\lt0$ (the ground-state energy is lowered in proportion to the square of the external field $f$, so the curvature is negative). Since $F=-f$ ($\partial^2/\partial F^2=\partial^2/\partial f^2$), this result differs from this book's $\chi_{BB}(0)=-\dfrac{\partial^2E_0}{\partial F^2}\gt0$ only in how the sign is assigned, and both express the same bending of the energy. (For example, for the two-level system (Example 54.4), $\chi^{\mathrm R}_{xx}(0)=-\dfrac{2d^2}{\hbar\omega_{10}}$.)

Exercise 54.8: Numerical evaluation of the oscillator strengths and the sum rule for the infinite well

Solution

(1) For $L=1$, numerical integration of $x_{n1}=2\displaystyle\int_0^1x\sin(n\pi x)\sin(\pi x)\dd x$ gives $-0.180127$ for $n=2$ and $-0.0144101$ for $n=4$. Substituting $n=2$ into the formula $-\dfrac{8n}{\pi^2(n^2-1)^2}$ gives $-\dfrac{16}{9\pi^2}=-0.180127$, and for $n=4$ it gives $-\dfrac{32}{225\pi^2}=-0.0144101$, which agree.

(2) The sum over the even $n=2,4,\dots,20$, obtained by adding $f_{21}=0.960675$, $f_{41}=0.030742$, $f_{61}=0.005445$, $f_{81}=0.001660$, $f_{10,1}=0.000668$, $\dots$, is $0.999883$, and the difference is $1-0.999883=1.166\times10^{-4}$. For the tail, approximating the sum over $n=22,24,\dots$ (spacing $2$) by an integral, $\displaystyle\sum_{n=22,24,\dots}\dfrac{64}{\pi^2n^4}\simeq\dfrac12\int_{21}^\infty\dfrac{64}{\pi^2n^4}\dd n=\dfrac{32}{\pi^2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{3\cdot21^3}=\dfrac{32}{9.8696\times27\,783}=1.167\times10^{-4}$. This agrees well with the actual difference $1.166\times10^{-4}$.

(3) With an effective mass $m^*$, $E_n-E_1=(n^2-1)\dfrac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2m^*L^2}$, and from $x_{n1}^2=\dfrac{64n^2L^2}{\pi^4(n^2-1)^4}$ we get $f^*_{n1}=\dfrac{2m^*}{\hbar^2}(E_n-E_1)x_{n1}^2=\dfrac{2m^*}{\hbar^2}\cdot(n^2-1)\dfrac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2m^*L^2}\cdot\dfrac{64n^2L^2}{\pi^4(n^2-1)^4}=\dfrac{64n^2}{\pi^2(n^2-1)^3}$, in which both $m^*$ and $L$ cancel. Therefore, even if the effective mass is used, the values of the oscillator strengths and the sum rule $\sum_nf^*_{n1}=1$ are the same.

← Back to Chapter 54, “Linear Response and an Introduction to the Kubo Formula — Response Functions, Causality, Kramers–Kronig Relations, and the Complex Permittivity”

Chapter 55: Propagators and an Introduction to Green's Functions — Retarded Green's Function, Local Density of States, and Lifetimes

Exercise 55.1: Deriving the free-particle $K$ from the momentum representation

Solution

The momentum-space wave function is $\phi(p)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\hbar}}\displaystyle\int\delta(x-x')\,e^{-ipx/\hbar}\dd x=\dfrac{e^{-ipx'/\hbar}}{\sqrt{2\pi\hbar}}$. The momentum eigenstates are eigenstates of the free-particle $\hat{H}=\hat{p}^2/2m$ with eigenvalue $E_p=p^2/2m$, so the time evolution merely multiplies each $p$ component by a phase: $\phi(p,t)=\phi(p)\,e^{-ip^2t/2m\hbar}$. Returning to the position representation ($\psi(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\hbar}}\int\phi(p)e^{ipx/\hbar}\dd p$), we obtain

$$ \Psi(x,t)=\frac{1}{2\pi\hbar}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\exp\left[\frac{ip(x-x')}{\hbar}-\frac{ip^2t}{2m\hbar}\right]\dd p $$

Since the initial state is a $\delta$ function, this is by definition $\Psi(x,t)=K(x,t;x',0)$, that is, the free-particle propagator written as an integral over the momentum $p$. We carry out the integral. Let $R=x-x'$ and complete the square of the exponent in $p$: $-\dfrac{it}{2m\hbar}p^2+\dfrac{iR}{\hbar}p=-\dfrac{it}{2m\hbar}\Bigl(p-\dfrac{mR}{t}\Bigr)^2+\dfrac{imR^2}{2\hbar t}$ (this can be checked by expanding the right-hand side). Letting $a=\dfrac{it}{2m\hbar}$, we use the Gaussian integral $\int e^{-a(p-p_0)^2}\dd p=\sqrt{\pi/a}$ in the limit $\mathrm{Re}\,a\to+0$ (this corresponds to $t\to t-i0$); from $a=\dfrac{t}{2m\hbar}e^{i\pi/2}$ we get $\sqrt{\pi/a}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2\pi m\hbar}{t}}\,e^{-i\pi/4}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2\pi m\hbar}{it}}$. Therefore

$$ K(x,t;x',0)=\frac{1}{2\pi\hbar}\sqrt{\frac{2\pi m\hbar}{it}}\;e^{imR^2/2\hbar t}=\sqrt{\frac{m}{2\pi i\hbar t}}\;\exp\left[\frac{im(x-x')^2}{2\hbar t}\right] $$

(Here $\frac{1}{2\pi\hbar}\sqrt{\frac{2\pi m\hbar}{it}}=\sqrt{\frac{2\pi m\hbar}{4\pi^2\hbar^2\,it}}=\sqrt{\frac{m}{2\pi i\hbar t}}$.)

For an electron ($m=9.109\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$) at $t=1.0\ \mathrm{fs}=1.0\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{s}$, $\abs{K}^2=\dfrac{m}{2\pi\hbar t}=\dfrac{9.109\times10^{-31}}{2\pi\times1.0546\times10^{-34}\times1.0\times10^{-15}}=1.375\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{m^{-2}}$, so $\abs{K}=1.17\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}=1.17\ \mathrm{nm^{-1}}$ (the dimension is the reciprocal of a length). This magnitude is independent of the position $x$.

Exercise 55.2: Green's function of a free particle in three dimensions

Solution

Let $R=\abs{\bm{r}-\bm{r}'}$, $\bm{p}=\hbar\bm{q}$, and $k=\sqrt{2mE}/\hbar$. Since $E-\dfrac{p^2}{2m}=\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2m}(k^2-q^2)$ and $\dd^3p/(2\pi\hbar)^3=\dd^3q/(2\pi)^3$,

$$ G=\frac{2m}{\hbar^2}\int\frac{\dd^3q}{(2\pi)^3}\frac{e^{i\bm{q}\cdot(\bm{r}-\bm{r}')}}{k^2-q^2+i\eta} $$

In spherical coordinates with $\bm{r}-\bm{r}'$ as the polar axis, the angular integral is $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}2\pi\sin\theta\,e^{iqR\cos\theta}\dd\theta=2\pi\dfrac{2\sin qR}{qR}$, so $\displaystyle\int\dd^3q\,e^{i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{R}}f(q)=\dfrac{4\pi}{R}\int_0^\infty q\sin(qR)f(q)\dd q$. Therefore,

$$ G=\frac{2m}{\hbar^2}\cdot\frac{1}{8\pi^3}\cdot\frac{4\pi}{R}\int_0^\infty\frac{q\sin qR}{k_+^2-q^2}\dd q=\frac{m}{2\pi^2\hbar^2R}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{q\sin qR}{k_+^2-q^2}\dd q $$

(we used the fact that the integrand is an even function of $q$ to change the range of integration to $-\infty\sim\infty$; $k_+=k+i\eta'$). Writing $\sin qR=(e^{iqR}-e^{-iqR})/2i$ and letting $J=\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{q\,e^{iqR}}{k_+^2-q^2}\dd q$, the $e^{-iqR}$ term becomes $-J$ upon the replacement $q\to-q$, so the integral is $\dfrac{J-(-J)}{2i}=\dfrac{J}{i}$. For $J$, we close the integration contour in the upper half-plane ($e^{iqR}$ is small in the upper half-plane). The pole in the upper half-plane is $q=k_+$, and since $k_+^2-q^2=-(q-k_+)(q+k_+)$, the residue is $-\dfrac{k_+e^{ik_+R}}{2k_+}=-\dfrac{e^{ik_+R}}{2}$, and $J=2\pi i\cdot\Bigl(-\dfrac{e^{ikR}}{2}\Bigr)=-i\pi\,e^{ikR}$. Hence $J/i=-\pi e^{ikR}$, and we obtain

$$ G(\bm{r},\bm{r}';E)=\frac{m}{2\pi^2\hbar^2R}\bigl(-\pi e^{ikR}\bigr)=-\frac{m}{2\pi\hbar^2}\,\frac{e^{ikR}}{R} $$

For the local density of states, since the imaginary part of $\dfrac{e^{ikR}}{R}=\dfrac1R+ik+\mathrm{O}(R)$ as $R\to0$ is $k$, we have $\mathrm{Im}\,G(\bm{r},\bm{r};E)=-\dfrac{mk}{2\pi\hbar^2}$, and $g=-\dfrac1\pi\mathrm{Im}\,G=\dfrac{mk}{2\pi^2\hbar^2}$ (the divergence $1/R$ in the real part does not affect the imaginary part). This is equal to $\dfrac{1}{4\pi^2}\Bigl(\dfrac{2m}{\hbar^2}\Bigr)^{3/2}\sqrt{E}$, the density of states of free electrons per unit volume, not including spin. For example, for an electron with $E=1\ \mathrm{eV}$, $k=5.12\ \mathrm{nm^{-1}}$ and $g=3.41\ \mathrm{eV^{-1}nm^{-3}}$.

Exercise 55.3: Green's function and local density of states of a heteronuclear diatomic molecule

Solution

(1) $E+i\eta-\hat{H}=\begin{pmatrix}E-\varepsilon_1&t\\t&E-\varepsilon_2\end{pmatrix}$ (below, $E$ means $E+i\eta$), and the determinant is $D=(E-\varepsilon_1)(E-\varepsilon_2)-t^2$, so the inverse matrix is $\dfrac{1}{D}\begin{pmatrix}E-\varepsilon_2&-t\\-t&E-\varepsilon_1\end{pmatrix}$. That is, $G_{11}=\dfrac{E-\varepsilon_2}{D}$, $G_{22}=\dfrac{E-\varepsilon_1}{D}$, and $G_{12}=G_{21}=\dfrac{-t}{D}$. The poles, from $D=0$, are $E_\pm=\dfrac{\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2}{2}\pm\sqrt{\Bigl(\dfrac{\varepsilon_2-\varepsilon_1}{2}\Bigr)^2+t^2}$, and since $\sqrt{1.0^2+1.5^2}=\sqrt{3.25}=1.803\ \mathrm{eV}$, we have $E_-=1.0-1.803=-0.803\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $E_+=1.0+1.803=2.803\ \mathrm{eV}$ (the eigenvalues of $\hat{H}$).

(2) Decomposing $G_{11}=\dfrac{E-\varepsilon_2}{(E-E_-)(E-E_+)}$ into partial fractions, we get $G_{11}=\dfrac{P_-}{E-E_-}+\dfrac{P_+}{E-E_+}$ with $P_\pm=\dfrac{E_\pm-\varepsilon_2}{E_\pm-E_\mp}$. Since $E_--E_+=-3.606$, $P_-=\dfrac{-0.803-2.0}{-3.606}=\dfrac{-2.803}{-3.606}=0.777$ and $P_+=\dfrac{2.803-2.0}{3.606}=0.223$, and the sum is $1$. The LDOS of atom 1 is $g_1(E)=0.777\,\delta(E-E_-)+0.223\,\delta(E-E_+)$ (Lorentzian if $\eta$ is finite), and the lower-energy level $E_-$ contains the orbital of atom 1 (which lies lower in energy) to the extent of $78\ \%$ (a polar bond). In general, letting $\varepsilon_{21}=\varepsilon_2-\varepsilon_1$, we have $P_\mp=\tfrac12\Bigl(1\pm\dfrac{\varepsilon_{21}/2}{\sqrt{(\varepsilon_{21}/2)^2+t^2}}\Bigr)$ ($P_\pm$ is the area of the peak at the position $E_\pm$).

(3) $G_{11}=\dfrac{E-\varepsilon_2}{(E-\varepsilon_1)(E-\varepsilon_2)-t^2}=\dfrac{1}{E-\varepsilon_1-\dfrac{t^2}{E-\varepsilon_2}}$ (we divided the numerator and the denominator by $E-\varepsilon_2$). This has the form of the formula $G_{ii}=\dfrac{1}{E-E_i-\Sigma(E)}$, $\Sigma=\sum_c\dfrac{\abs{V_{ci}}^2}{E-\varepsilon_c}$ for the coupling between the level $\ket{1}$ and a “continuum” (here a single level $\varepsilon_c=\varepsilon_2$, with coupling $V=-t$), and the self-energy is $\Sigma(E)=\dfrac{t^2}{E-\varepsilon_2}$. Its value at $E=\varepsilon_1$ is $\Sigma(\varepsilon_1)=-\dfrac{t^2}{\varepsilon_2-\varepsilon_1}=-1.125\ \mathrm{eV}$, which is the energy shift of level 1 due to second-order perturbation. The exact shift is $E_--\varepsilon_1=-0.803\ \mathrm{eV}$; since $t=1.5\ \mathrm{eV}$ is large, comparable to the level splitting $2.0\ \mathrm{eV}$, the difference from the second-order value is large (if the $E$ in the denominator of $\Sigma$ is replaced by $E_-$, the solution of $E=\varepsilon_1+\Sigma(E)$ becomes the exact $E_-$).

(4) Setting $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_2=0$, the result of (1) gives $D=E^2-t^2$, $G_{11}=\dfrac{E}{E^2-t^2}$, and $G_{12}=\dfrac{-t}{E^2-t^2}$, which agree with $G_{11}=\dfrac{E}{E^2-t^2}$ and $G_{12}=-\dfrac{t}{E^2-t^2}$ of Example 55.12. We write the Dyson equation $\hat{G}=\hat{G}_0+\hat{G}_0\hat{V}\hat{G}$ in components. Since $\hat{G}_0=\dfrac1E\hat{1}$ and $\hat{V}=-t\sigma_x$ ($V_{12}=V_{21}=-t$, and the diagonal elements are $0$), we have $G_{11}=G_{0,11}+G_{0,11}V_{12}G_{21}=\dfrac1E-\dfrac{t}{E}G_{21}$ and $G_{21}=G_{0,22}V_{21}G_{11}=-\dfrac{t}{E}G_{11}$. Substituting the latter into the former gives $G_{11}=\dfrac1E+\dfrac{t^2}{E^2}G_{11}$, that is, $G_{11}\Bigl(1-\dfrac{t^2}{E^2}\Bigr)=\dfrac1E$, from which $G_{11}=\dfrac{1}{E}\cdot\dfrac{E^2}{E^2-t^2}=\dfrac{E}{E^2-t^2}$, in agreement with the exact result. Also $G_{21}=-\dfrac{t}{E}G_{11}=-\dfrac{t}{E^2-t^2}$, which is equal to $G_{12}$. The Dyson equation has thus summed up at once, in the form of the sum of a geometric series, the Born series of Example 55.12 (only the even orders of $\hat{V}$).

Exercise 55.4: Sum rule and moments of the spectral function

Solution

(1) Since $g_i(E)=\mel{i}{\delta(E-\hat{H})}{i}=\sum_n\abs{\braket{i}{n}}^2\delta(E-E_n)$, integrating over $E$ gives $\sum_n\abs{\braket{i}{n}}^2=\sum_n\braket{i}{n}\braket{n}{i}=\braket{i}{i}=1$ (completeness $\sum_n\ket{n}\bra{n}=\hat{1}$).

(2) We have $\int E\,g_i\dd E=\sum_nE_n\abs{\braket{i}{n}}^2=\mel{i}{\hat{H}}{i}=H_{ii}$ ($\sum_nE_n\ket{n}\bra{n}=\hat{H}$). Similarly, $\int E^2g_i\dd E=\sum_nE_n^2\abs{\braket{i}{n}}^2=\mel{i}{\hat{H}^2}{i}$, and inserting the completeness relation of the basis states $\ket{j}$ gives $\mel{i}{\hat{H}^2}{i}=\sum_j\mel{i}{\hat{H}}{j}\mel{j}{\hat{H}}{i}=\sum_j\abs{H_{ij}}^2$.

(3) An atom at the end of the chain has one neighbor and $H_{12}=-t$, so $\sum_j\abs{H_{1j}}^2=t^2$. An interior atom has two neighbors, so the sum is $2t^2$. Let us also check this with the LDOS formula. For the end atom, putting $E=2t\sin\varphi$, we get $\int_{-2t}^{2t}E^2\dfrac{\sqrt{4t^2-E^2}}{2\pi t^2}\dd E=\dfrac{1}{2\pi t^2}\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}4t^2\sin^2\varphi\cdot2t\cos\varphi\cdot2t\cos\varphi\,\dd\varphi=\dfrac{8t^2}{\pi}\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\sin^2\varphi\cos^2\varphi\,\dd\varphi=\dfrac{8t^2}{\pi}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{8}=t^2$ (here $\sin^2\varphi\cos^2\varphi=\tfrac14\sin^22\varphi$, and $\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\tfrac14\sin^22\varphi\,\dd\varphi=\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac{\pi}{2}=\tfrac{\pi}{8}$). For an interior atom, $\int_{-2t}^{2t}\dfrac{E^2\,\dd E}{\pi\sqrt{4t^2-E^2}}=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}4t^2\sin^2\varphi\,\dd\varphi=\dfrac{4t^2}{\pi}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}=2t^2$ (with $\dd E=2t\cos\varphi\,\dd\varphi$ and $\sqrt{4t^2-E^2}=2t\cos\varphi$). Both agree with the general theory above. The second moment determines the width of the LDOS (the standard deviations are $\sqrt{t^2}=t$ and $\sqrt2\,t$): the more neighboring atoms there are, the broader the LDOS.

Exercise 55.5: The Dyson equation and the $T$-matrix

Solution

(1) Let $A=\hat{G}_0^{-1}=E-\hat{H}_0+i\eta$ and $B=\hat{G}^{-1}=E-\hat{H}_0-\hat{V}+i\eta$. Then $B-A=-\hat{V}$. Substituting into the identity $A^{-1}-B^{-1}=A^{-1}(B-A)B^{-1}$ (expanding the right-hand side gives $A^{-1}BB^{-1}-A^{-1}AB^{-1}=A^{-1}-B^{-1}$), we obtain $\hat{G}_0-\hat{G}=\hat{G}_0(-\hat{V})\hat{G}$, that is, $\hat{G}=\hat{G}_0+\hat{G}_0\hat{V}\hat{G}$.

(2) For $\hat{T}=\hat{V}+\hat{V}\hat{G}_0\hat{T}$, assume $\hat{G}=\hat{G}_0+\hat{G}_0\hat{T}\hat{G}_0$ and substitute it for $\hat{G}$ on the right-hand side of the equation in (1). This gives $\hat{G}_0+\hat{G}_0\hat{V}\bigl(\hat{G}_0+\hat{G}_0\hat{T}\hat{G}_0\bigr)=\hat{G}_0+\hat{G}_0\bigl(\hat{V}+\hat{V}\hat{G}_0\hat{T}\bigr)\hat{G}_0=\hat{G}_0+\hat{G}_0\hat{T}\hat{G}_0$, which agrees with the assumption. Directly: inserting $\hat{T}=\hat{V}+\hat{V}\hat{G}_0\hat{V}+\hat{V}\hat{G}_0\hat{V}\hat{G}_0\hat{V}+\cdots$ (obtained by repeatedly substituting $\hat{T}=\hat{V}+\hat{V}\hat{G}_0\hat{T}$ into itself) into $\hat{G}_0+\hat{G}_0\hat{T}\hat{G}_0$ gives $\hat{G}_0+\hat{G}_0\hat{V}\hat{G}_0+\hat{G}_0\hat{V}\hat{G}_0\hat{V}\hat{G}_0+\cdots$, which coincides with the Born series.

(3) For $\hat{H}_0=\mathrm{diag}(E_1,E_2)$ and $\hat{V}=v\sigma_x$, the $(1,1)$ element of the inverse matrix of $E-\hat{H}_0-\hat{V}=\begin{pmatrix}E-E_1&-v\\-v&E-E_2\end{pmatrix}$ is $G_{11}=\dfrac{E-E_2}{(E-E_1)(E-E_2)-v^2}=\dfrac{1}{E-E_1}\cdot\dfrac{1}{1-\dfrac{v^2}{(E-E_1)(E-E_2)}}=\dfrac{1}{E-E_1}+\dfrac{v^2}{(E-E_1)^2(E-E_2)}+\dfrac{v^4}{(E-E_1)^3(E-E_2)^2}+\cdots$ (a geometric series). On the other hand, the $(1,1)$ element of the Born series is $0$ at odd orders because $\hat{V}$ is off-diagonal; the zeroth order is $G_{0,11}=\dfrac{1}{E-E_1}$ and the second order is $G_{0,11}vG_{0,22}vG_{0,11}=\dfrac{v^2}{(E-E_1)^2(E-E_2)}$. The two agree through second order, and they differ starting at $v^4$. The series converges when $\abs{v^2/[(E-E_1)(E-E_2)]}\lt1$.

Exercise 55.6: The Fetter–Walecka $iG$ and the retarded Green's function

Solution

(1) We have $\hat{\psi}(\bm{x},t)=\sum_n\psi_n(\bm{x})\hat{c}_ne^{-i\varepsilon_nt/\hbar}$, and $\hat{c}_n\ket{0}=0$ for the vacuum $\ket{0}$. For $t\gt t'$, the time-ordered product is just $\hat{\psi}(\bm{x},t)\hat{\psi}^\dagger(\bm{x}',t')$, and since $\bra{0}\hat{c}_n\hat{c}_m^\dagger\ket{0}=\bra{0}\bigl(\delta_{nm}-\hat{c}_m^\dagger\hat{c}_n\bigr)\ket{0}=\delta_{nm}$ (the second term is $0$ because $\hat{c}_n\ket{0}=0$), we get $\bra{0}\hat{\psi}(\bm{x},t)\hat{\psi}^\dagger(\bm{x}',t')\ket{0}=\sum_n\psi_n(\bm{x})\psi_n^*(\bm{x}')e^{-i\varepsilon_n(t-t')/\hbar}=K(\bm{x},t;\bm{x}',t')$. For $t\lt t'$, the time-ordered product for fermions is $-\hat{\psi}^\dagger(\bm{x}',t')\hat{\psi}(\bm{x},t)$, which is $0$ because $\hat{\psi}(\bm{x},t)\ket{0}=0$. Therefore, $G^{\mathrm T}=-\dfrac{i}{\hbar}\theta(t-t')K(\bm{x},t;\bm{x}',t')=K^{\mathrm R}(\bm{x},t;\bm{x}',t')$ (for $\hbar=1$, this is the same as reading Fetter–Walecka's $iG=\langle T[\hat{\psi}\hat{\psi}^\dagger]\rangle$ as $G=-i\langle\cdots\rangle$).

(2) From Example 55.17 in Chapter 55, $G^{\mathrm T}(k,E)=\dfrac{1-n_k}{E-\varepsilon_k+i\eta}+\dfrac{n_k}{E-\varepsilon_k-i\eta}$ and $G^{\mathrm R}(k,E)=\dfrac{1}{E-\varepsilon_k+i\eta}$. For the difference, using $\dfrac{1-n_k}{E-\varepsilon_k+i\eta}-\dfrac{1}{E-\varepsilon_k+i\eta}=-\dfrac{n_k}{E-\varepsilon_k+i\eta}$, we get $G^{\mathrm T}-G^{\mathrm R}=n_k\Bigl[\dfrac{1}{E-\varepsilon_k-i\eta}-\dfrac{1}{E-\varepsilon_k+i\eta}\Bigr]=n_k\cdot\dfrac{2i\eta}{(E-\varepsilon_k)^2+\eta^2}\to2\pi i\,n_k\,\delta(E-\varepsilon_k)$ (over a common denominator, the numerator is $(E-\varepsilon_k+i\eta)-(E-\varepsilon_k-i\eta)=2i\eta$; and $\dfrac{\eta}{x^2+\eta^2}\to\pi\delta(x)$). In the time domain as well, $G^{\mathrm T}-G^{\mathrm R}$ is, for $t\gt0$, $-\tfrac{i}{\hbar}(1-n_k)e^{-i\varepsilon_kt/\hbar}+\tfrac{i}{\hbar}e^{-i\varepsilon_kt/\hbar}=\tfrac{i}{\hbar}n_ke^{-i\varepsilon_kt/\hbar}$, and for $t\lt0$, $+\tfrac{i}{\hbar}n_ke^{-i\varepsilon_kt/\hbar}$, so it has the same form $\tfrac{i}{\hbar}n_ke^{-i\varepsilon_kt/\hbar}$ at all times; its Fourier transform (with $\int e^{iEt/\hbar}e^{-i\varepsilon_kt/\hbar}\dd t=2\pi\hbar\,\delta(E-\varepsilon_k)$) is $\tfrac{i}{\hbar}n_k\cdot2\pi\hbar\,\delta(E-\varepsilon_k)=2\pi in_k\delta(E-\varepsilon_k)$, in agreement with the above. The difference between the time-ordered and retarded types lies only in the time-independent part of the occupied orbitals.

Exercise 55.7: A decaying level in the time domain and the Lorentzian form

Solution

We have $G_{ii}(E)=\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\dd t\,e^{iEt/\hbar}K^{\mathrm R}_{ii}(t)=-\dfrac{i}{\hbar}\int_0^\infty e^{i(E-E_i+i\Gamma/2)t/\hbar}\dd t$ (since $e^{-\Gamma t/2\hbar}$ is already a decay factor, the convergence factor $\eta$ may be taken to be $\eta\to0$). With $a=E-E_i+i\Gamma/2$ (its imaginary part is positive), $\int_0^\infty e^{iat/\hbar}\dd t=\dfrac{i\hbar}{a}$, so $G_{ii}=-\dfrac{i}{\hbar}\cdot\dfrac{i\hbar}{a}=\dfrac{1}{E-E_i+i\Gamma/2}$. From $\dfrac{1}{E-E_i+i\Gamma/2}=\dfrac{E-E_i-i\Gamma/2}{(E-E_i)^2+(\Gamma/2)^2}$, the imaginary part is $-\dfrac{\Gamma/2}{(E-E_i)^2+(\Gamma/2)^2}$, and $A_i(E)=-\dfrac1\pi\mathrm{Im}\,G_{ii}=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\dfrac{\Gamma/2}{(E-E_i)^2+(\Gamma/2)^2}$. The value at the peak, $E=E_i$, is $\dfrac{1}{\pi}\cdot\dfrac{2}{\Gamma}$; it drops to half of that when $(E-E_i)^2=(\Gamma/2)^2$, that is, $E-E_i=\pm\Gamma/2$, so the full width at half maximum is $\Gamma$. For the area, with $\gamma=\Gamma/2$ and $x=E-E_i$, we get $\dfrac{1}{\pi}\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\dfrac{\gamma\,\dd x}{x^2+\gamma^2}=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\bigl[\arctan\tfrac{x}{\gamma}\bigr]_{-\infty}^{\infty}=1$.

For $\Gamma=1.0\ \mathrm{meV}$, the lifetime is $\tau=\dfrac{\hbar}{\Gamma}=\dfrac{658.2\ \mathrm{meV\,fs}}{1.0\ \mathrm{meV}}=658\ \mathrm{fs}$, and the peak height is $A_i(E_i)=\dfrac{2}{\pi\Gamma}=\dfrac{2}{\pi\times1.0\ \mathrm{meV}}=0.637\ \mathrm{meV^{-1}}$. The narrower the width, the longer the lifetime and the higher the peak (the area is constant).

Exercise 55.8: Poles of a two-level system coupled to a decaying level (complex $E$ plane)

Solution

(1) From the eigenvalue equation $\det(\lambda-H_{\mathrm{eff}})=(\lambda+i\Gamma/2)\lambda-V^2=0$ of the effective Hamiltonian $H_{\mathrm{eff}}=\begin{pmatrix}-i\Gamma/2&V\\V&0\end{pmatrix}$, we obtain $\lambda^2+\dfrac{i\Gamma}{2}\lambda-V^2=0$. By the quadratic formula, $\lambda=\dfrac{-i\Gamma/2\pm\sqrt{(i\Gamma/2)^2+4V^2}}{2}=-\dfrac{i\Gamma}{4}\pm\sqrt{V^2-\dfrac{\Gamma^2}{16}}$ (here $(i\Gamma/2)^2=-\Gamma^2/4$, and $\sqrt{4V^2-\Gamma^2/4}/2=\sqrt{V^2-\Gamma^2/16}$). The sum of the two poles is $-i\Gamma/2$ (the trace of the matrix), which is constant.

(2) For $\Gamma=10\ \mathrm{meV}$, $\Gamma/4=2.5\ \mathrm{meV}$ and $\Gamma^2/16=6.25\ \mathrm{meV^2}$.
$V=1.0\ \mathrm{meV}$: $V^2-\Gamma^2/16=1-6.25=-5.25$ and $\sqrt{\ }=2.291\,i$, so $\lambda=-2.5\,i\pm2.291\,i$, that is, $\lambda=-0.209\,i$ and $-4.791\,i$ meV, both on the imaginary axis. The widths (full width at half maximum $-2\,\mathrm{Im}\,\lambda$) are $0.417\ \mathrm{meV}$ and $9.58\ \mathrm{meV}$, and the lifetimes are $\hbar/0.417\ \mathrm{meV}=1.58\ \mathrm{ps}$ and $68.7\ \mathrm{fs}$. When the level $\ket{2}$ (which does not decay by itself) is weakly coupled to the strongly decaying level $\ket{1}$, $\ket{1}$ escapes into the continuum too quickly, so there is little chance of hopping over to $\ket{2}$, and the width of $\ket{2}$ is about $4V^2/\Gamma=0.40\ \mathrm{meV}$, smaller than $\Gamma$ by $1$ or more orders of magnitude (through weak mixing with a strongly decaying level, it “borrows” width). The width of $\ket{1}$ is smaller by that amount, about $\Gamma-4V^2/\Gamma=9.6\ \mathrm{meV}$.
$V=2.5\ \mathrm{meV}$ ($=\Gamma/4$): the discriminant is $0$, and the two poles coincide at $\lambda=-2.5\,i\ \mathrm{meV}$ (degenerate; this point is an exceptional point, where the eigenvectors also coincide).
$V=4.0\ \mathrm{meV}$: $V^2-\Gamma^2/16=16-6.25=9.75$ and $\sqrt{\ }=3.122$, so $\lambda=\pm3.122-2.5\,i\ \mathrm{meV}$. The two poles separate, with real parts $\pm3.12\ \mathrm{meV}$ (level splitting $6.24\ \mathrm{meV}$) and the same imaginary part $-2.5\ \mathrm{meV}$ (width $\Gamma/2=5\ \mathrm{meV}$, lifetime $132\ \mathrm{fs}$): the two levels split because of the coupling, and they have the same lifetime (they share the decay equally).

Therefore, for $V\lt\Gamma/4$ the two poles separate up and down on the imaginary axis (overdamped; the motion does not oscillate), and for $V\gt\Gamma/4$ the real parts separate (the motion oscillates). $V=\Gamma/4$ is the boundary. This has the same structure as the overdamping ($\gamma^2\gt4m^2\omega_0^2$), critical damping, and underdamping of the classical damped oscillator (AD 03, Chapter 7, Section 7.3).
