Chapter 65: Toward Quantum Field Theory and Elementary Particle Physics — A World Where Particle Number Changes, an Introduction to QED, and Dirac Electrons in Solids

Exercise 65.1: Electron–positron pair with momentum $0.5\,m_{\mathrm e}c$

Solution

The pair state $\hat{b}_{\bm{p}\uparrow}^\dagger\hat{d}_{-\bm{p}\downarrow}^\dagger\ket{0}$ contains one electron with momentum $\bm{p}$ and one positron with momentum $-\bm{p}$. We use $\hat{H}=\sum E_p(\hat{b}^\dagger\hat{b}+\hat{d}^\dagger\hat{d})$, $\hat{\bm{P}}=\sum\bm{p}(\hat{b}^\dagger\hat{b}+\hat{d}^\dagger\hat{d})$, and $\hat{Q}=q\sum(\hat{b}^\dagger\hat{b}-\hat{d}^\dagger\hat{d})$ from Theorem 65.2 of Chapter 65 (only two modes are occupied).

For $p=0.5\,m_{\mathrm e}c$, $E_p=\sqrt{1+0.5^2}\,m_{\mathrm e}c^2=1.11803\,m_{\mathrm e}c^2=1.11803\times0.510999\ \mathrm{MeV}=0.57131\ \mathrm{MeV}$. Therefore

$$ E=E_p+E_{-p}=2E_p=1.1426\ \mathrm{MeV},\qquad\bm{P}=\bm{p}+(-\bm{p})=0,\qquad Q=q(1-1)=0. $$

This exceeds the threshold $2m_{\mathrm e}c^2=1.0220\ \mathrm{MeV}$ by $0.1206\ \mathrm{MeV}$, and this difference is the sum of the kinetic energies of the electron and the positron, $2(E_p-m_{\mathrm e}c^2)=0.1206\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

In the decay into two photons (energies $\hbar\omega_1,\hbar\omega_2$, momenta $\hbar\bm{k}_1,\hbar\bm{k}_2$), conservation of energy $\hbar\omega_1+\hbar\omega_2=E$ and conservation of momentum $\hbar\bm{k}_1+\hbar\bm{k}_2=\bm{P}=0$ hold. From the latter, $\bm{k}_2=-\bm{k}_1$, and since the photon energy is $\hbar\omega=\hbar c\abs{\bm{k}}$, $\omega_1=\omega_2$. Hence each photon has energy $E/2=E_p=0.5713\ \mathrm{MeV}$, and the two photons travel in exactly opposite directions (since $\bm{P}=0$, the laboratory frame is also the center-of-mass frame). This energy is of the same order as the rest energy of the electron, $0.511\ \mathrm{MeV}$, and in the limit $p\to0$ the pair becomes two photons of $0.511\ \mathrm{MeV}$ each (the gamma rays of pair annihilation).

Exercise 65.2: Properties of the Yukawa potential

Solution

(1) Differentiating $F=\dfrac{e^{-mr}}{4\pi r}$ with respect to $r$ gives $\dfrac{\dd F}{\dd r}=-\dfrac{(1+mr)\,e^{-mr}}{4\pi r^2}$ (product rule: $\dfrac{\dd}{\dd r}\dfrac{e^{-mr}}{r}=\dfrac{-m\,e^{-mr}\,r-e^{-mr}}{r^2}$). Therefore $r^2\dfrac{\dd F}{\dd r}=-\dfrac{(1+mr)\,e^{-mr}}{4\pi}$. Differentiating this once more,

$$ \frac{\dd}{\dd r}\Bigl(r^2\frac{\dd F}{\dd r}\Bigr)=-\frac{1}{4\pi}\Bigl[m\,e^{-mr}-m(1+mr)e^{-mr}\Bigr]=\frac{m^2r\,e^{-mr}}{4\pi}. $$

Dividing by $r^2$ gives $\nabla^2F=\dfrac{m^2e^{-mr}}{4\pi r}=m^2F$. That is, $(\nabla^2-m^2)F=0$ for $r\gt0$.

(2) Integrate $\nabla^2F$ over the volume of a sphere $S_\varepsilon$ of radius $\varepsilon$ and use Gauss's theorem:

$$ \int_{r\lt\varepsilon}\nabla^2F\,\dd^3r=\oint_{r=\varepsilon}\nabla F\cdot\dd\bm{S}=4\pi\varepsilon^2\frac{\dd F}{\dd r}\Big|_{r=\varepsilon}=-(1+m\varepsilon)\,e^{-m\varepsilon}\ \xrightarrow{\ \varepsilon\to0\ }\ -1. $$

On the other hand, $\int_{r\lt\varepsilon}m^2F\,\dd^3r=m^2\int_0^\varepsilon\dfrac{e^{-mr}}{4\pi r}4\pi r^2\dd r\to0$ ($\varepsilon\to0$). Therefore, for a small sphere containing the origin, $\int(\nabla^2-m^2)F\,\dd^3r\to-1$, and away from the origin the integrand is $0$ by (1), so $(\nabla^2-m^2)F=-\delta^3(\bm{r})$, that is, $(-\nabla^2+m^2)F=\delta^3(\bm{r})$ holds. Taking the Fourier transform of both sides gives $(k^2+m^2)\tilde{F}(\bm{k})=1$, so $\tilde{F}=1/(k^2+m^2)$, which agrees with the result of the integral in the main text, $F(r)=\int\frac{\dd^3k}{(2\pi)^3}\frac{e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{r}}}{k^2+m^2}$.

(3) The range is $\hbar c/(mc^2)$. For $\rho$: $\dfrac{197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}}{775.26\ \mathrm{MeV}}=0.2545\ \mathrm{fm}$. For $\omega$: $\dfrac{197.327}{782.66}=0.2521\ \mathrm{fm}$. The simultaneous exchange of two $\pi$'s corresponds to exchanging a system of mass $2\times139.57\ \mathrm{MeV}=279.14\ \mathrm{MeV}$, which gives $\dfrac{197.327}{279.14}=0.7069\ \mathrm{fm}$, exactly half the range of a single $\pi$, $1.414\ \mathrm{fm}$. The heavier the particle, the shorter the range: the exchange of $\rho$ and $\omega$ contributes to the short-range force between nucleons, and the exchange of $\pi$ to the long-range force.

Exercise 65.3: Wavelength shift in Compton scattering and the limit of the Thomson approximation

Solution

(1) The wavelength of the incident light is $\lambda=\dfrac{hc}{E}=\dfrac{1239.84\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}}{17440\ \mathrm{eV}}=0.071092\ \mathrm{nm}=71.092\ \mathrm{pm}$. At $\theta=180^\circ$ (backward scattering), $1-\cos\theta=2$, so $\lambda'-\lambda=2\lambda_{\mathrm C}=2\times2.4263\ \mathrm{pm}=4.853\ \mathrm{pm}$ and $\lambda'=75.944\ \mathrm{pm}$. The energy of the scattered photon is $\dfrac{1239.84\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}}{0.075944\ \mathrm{nm}}=16.326\ \mathrm{keV}$. By conservation of energy, the recoil kinetic energy received by the electron is $17.44-16.326=1.114\ \mathrm{keV}$.

(2) The wavelength of a $100\ \mathrm{keV}$ photon is $\lambda=\dfrac{1239.84\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}}{10^5\ \mathrm{eV}}=12.398\ \mathrm{pm}$. At $\theta=90^\circ$, $\lambda'-\lambda=\lambda_{\mathrm C}=2.426\ \mathrm{pm}$ and $\lambda'=14.825\ \mathrm{pm}$. The relative shift is $2.426/12.398=19.6\ \%$. The energy of the scattered photon is $1239.84/0.014825=83.63\ \mathrm{keV}$, and the recoil energy is $16.4\ \mathrm{keV}$. From Table 65.4, the total cross section is $0.741$ times the Thomson value ($26\ \%$ smaller).

The condition for the Thomson formula to be a good approximation is $\hbar\omega\ll m_{\mathrm e}c^2$, that is, that the recoil the photon gives to the electron is small ($\varepsilon=\hbar\omega/m_{\mathrm e}c^2\ll1$). As a rule of thumb, the deviation of the cross section is about $2\varepsilon$, so it is about $4\ \%$ at $10\ \mathrm{keV}$ ($\varepsilon=0.02$) and about $0.8\ \%$ at $2\ \mathrm{keV}$. The other condition is that the electron can be regarded as free ($\hbar\omega$ is sufficiently larger than the binding energy of the electron); when treating elastic scattering by bound electrons, as in X-ray diffraction, the Thomson formula is used multiplied by the atomic scattering factor.

Exercise 65.4: Scattering and attenuation of X-rays by an aluminum plate

Solution

(1) The number of electrons per $1\ \mathrm{g}$ of Al is $N_{\mathrm A}Z/A=6.0221\times10^{23}\times0.4818=2.901\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{g^{-1}}$. With $\sigma_{\mathrm T}=6.652\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{cm^2}$, the mass attenuation coefficient for Thomson scattering is

$$ \frac{\mu_{\mathrm T}}{\rho}=\frac{N_{\mathrm A}Z}{A}\,\sigma_{\mathrm T}=2.901\times10^{23}\times6.652\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{cm^2/g}=0.1930\ \mathrm{cm^2/g} $$

Multiplying by the density $2.70\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$ gives $\mu_{\mathrm T}=0.1930\times2.70=0.5211\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$. For a thickness $x=1\ \mathrm{mm}=0.1\ \mathrm{cm}$, $\mu_{\mathrm T}x=0.05211$, and $I/I_0=e^{-0.05211}=0.9492$. The fraction attenuated (upper bound) is $1-0.9492=0.051$, that is, about $5\ \%$.

(2) $\varepsilon=\hbar\omega/m_{\mathrm e}c^2=30/510.999=0.0587$. The expansion gives $\sigma_{\mathrm{KN}}/\sigma_{\mathrm T}\approx1-2\varepsilon+\tfrac{26}{5}\varepsilon^2=1-0.1174+0.0179=0.9005$ (evaluating the Klein–Nishina total cross-section formula directly gives $0.898$). The corrected value is $\mu/\rho=0.1930\times0.898=0.1733\ \mathrm{cm^2/g}$, $\mu=0.1733\times2.70=0.4679\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, and $\mu x=0.04679$, so the fraction attenuated is $1-e^{-0.04679}=0.0457$, about $4.6\ \%$. This is about $10\ \%$ ($1-0.898$) smaller than the Thomson value.

(3) Using the actual total mass attenuation coefficient $1.1\ \mathrm{cm^2/g}$ (from published data on X-ray absorption coefficients), $\mu=1.1\times2.70=2.97\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, $\mu x=0.297$, and $I/I_0=e^{-0.297}=0.743$. The fraction attenuated is $26\ \%$, about $5$ times the estimates in (1) and (2) (about $5\ \%$). The contribution of scattering by free electrons (Klein–Nishina) is $0.1733/1.1\approx16\ \%$, only about $1/6$ of the total attenuation. Most of the remainder is photoelectric absorption by the core electrons of the atoms. Photoelectric absorption increases steeply with atomic number (roughly in proportion to $Z^4$–$Z^5$) and decreases steeply as the photon energy rises (roughly as $E^{-3}$). Therefore the values of $\mu_{\mathrm T}$ and of Klein–Nishina are estimates of the attenuation due to “scattering by free electrons alone,” and the main cause of the attenuation of X-rays near $30\ \mathrm{keV}$ in Al is photoelectric absorption, not scattering. At higher energies of several tens of $\mathrm{keV}$ or more, and in light materials such as carbon and water, the contribution of scattering (Compton scattering) gradually becomes larger (Example 65.6).

Exercise 65.5: The $N=0$ Landau level of graphene

Solution

(1) $\hat{a}=(\hat{\pi}_x-i\hat{\pi}_y)/\sqrt{2\hbar e_0B}$ and $\hat{a}^\dagger=(\hat{\pi}_x+i\hat{\pi}_y)/\sqrt{2\hbar e_0B}$ ($\hat{\pi}_x,\hat{\pi}_y$ are Hermitian). The commutator is

$$ \comm{\hat{a}}{\hat{a}^\dagger}=\frac{1}{2\hbar e_0B}\Bigl(i\comm{\hat{\pi}_x}{\hat{\pi}_y}-i\comm{\hat{\pi}_y}{\hat{\pi}_x}\Bigr)=\frac{2i\comm{\hat{\pi}_x}{\hat{\pi}_y}}{2\hbar e_0B}=\frac{2i\,(-i\hbar e_0B)}{2\hbar e_0B}=1 $$

(here $\comm{\hat{\pi}_x}{\hat{\pi}_x}=0$, and $\comm{\hat{\pi}_x-i\hat{\pi}_y}{\hat{\pi}_x+i\hat{\pi}_y}=i\comm{\hat{\pi}_x}{\hat{\pi}_y}-i\comm{\hat{\pi}_y}{\hat{\pi}_x}$). The Hamiltonian, from $\sigma_x\hat{\pi}_x+\sigma_y\hat{\pi}_y=\begin{pmatrix}0&\hat{\pi}_x-i\hat{\pi}_y\\\hat{\pi}_x+i\hat{\pi}_y&0\end{pmatrix}$, is

$$ \hat{H}=v_{\mathrm F}\sqrt{2\hbar e_0B}\begin{pmatrix}0&\hat{a}\\\hat{a}^\dagger&0\end{pmatrix}. $$

(2) $E=0$: from $\hat{H}\begin{pmatrix}\psi_A\\\psi_B\end{pmatrix}=v_{\mathrm F}\sqrt{2\hbar e_0B}\begin{pmatrix}\hat{a}\psi_B\\\hat{a}^\dagger\psi_A\end{pmatrix}=0$ we get $\hat{a}\psi_B=0$ and $\hat{a}^\dagger\psi_A=0$. The solution of $\hat{a}\psi_B=0$ is the ground state of the harmonic oscillator, $\psi_B=\ket{0}$ (the lowest state of the Landau orbit). There is no state that becomes $0$ when $\hat{a}^\dagger$ acts on it ($\hat{a}^\dagger\ket{n}=\sqrt{n+1}\ket{n+1}\ne0$, and $\norm{\hat{a}^\dagger\psi}^2=\bra{\psi}\hat{a}\hat{a}^\dagger\ket{\psi}=\norm{\hat{a}\psi}^2+\norm{\psi}^2\gt0$), so $\psi_A=0$. Therefore the zero mode is $(\psi_A,\psi_B)=(0,\ket{0})$, which has, of the two components, only the one on sublattice B.

$N\ge1$: Let $\psi=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\bigl(\ket{N-1},\ \pm\ket{N}\bigr)^{\mathsf T}$. Then from $\hat{a}\ket{N}=\sqrt{N}\ket{N-1}$ and $\hat{a}^\dagger\ket{N-1}=\sqrt{N}\ket{N}$ we get $\hat{H}\psi=\pm v_{\mathrm F}\sqrt{2\hbar e_0BN}\,\psi$. That is, it is an eigenstate with $E_N=\pm v_{\mathrm F}\sqrt{2\hbar e_0BN}$.

(3) $E_1=v_{\mathrm F}\sqrt{2\hbar e_0B}=36.28\sqrt{B[\mathrm{T}]}\ \mathrm{meV}$ ($v_{\mathrm F}=1.0\times10^6\ \mathrm{m/s}$): this is $36.3\ \mathrm{meV}$ at $B=1\ \mathrm{T}$, $81.1\ \mathrm{meV}$ at $5\ \mathrm{T}$, and $114.7\ \mathrm{meV}$ at $10\ \mathrm{T}$. To convert to temperature, divide by $k_{\mathrm B}=0.08617\ \mathrm{meV/K}$, which gives $421\ \mathrm{K}$, $941\ \mathrm{K}$, and $1331\ \mathrm{K}$, respectively.

Exercise 65.6: Dirac points of the honeycomb lattice and the two valleys

Solution

(1) From $\bm{a}_1=\bm{\delta}_1-\bm{\delta}_2$ and $\bm{a}_2=\bm{\delta}_1-\bm{\delta}_3$ we get $\bm{\delta}_2=\bm{\delta}_1-\bm{a}_1$ and $\bm{\delta}_3=\bm{\delta}_1-\bm{a}_2$. Hence

$$ f(\bm{k})=e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{\delta}_1}+e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{\delta}_1}e^{-i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{a}_1}+e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{\delta}_1}e^{-i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{a}_2}=e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{\delta}_1}\bigl(1+z_1+z_2\bigr),\quad z_j=e^{-i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{a}_j}. $$

Since $\abs{z_1}=\abs{z_2}=1$, $f=0$ means that the sum of the three numbers $1,z_1,z_2$ of magnitude 1 in the complex plane is $0$. Three vectors of equal magnitude sum to zero only when they make angles of $120^\circ$ ($2\pi/3$) with one another (that is, when they form an equilateral triangle), so $(z_1,z_2)=(\omega,\omega^2)$ or $(\omega^2,\omega)$ ($\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$). This means $\bm{k}\cdot\bm{a}_1=-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ and $\bm{k}\cdot\bm{a}_2=+\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ (this corresponds to K, which can be checked from $\bm{K}=(4\pi/3a,0)$ and $\bm{a}_{1,2}=a(\mp\tfrac12,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2})$, giving $\bm{K}\cdot\bm{a}_1=-2\pi/3$ and $\bm{K}\cdot\bm{a}_2=2\pi/3$), or the pair with the opposite signs (K$'=-$K), in either case holding up to integer multiples of $2\pi$. From these two conditions, $\bm{k}$ is determined, apart from differences by reciprocal lattice vectors, to just two points, K and K$'$.

(2) From the expansion in the main text (Chapter 42, Section 42.8), $f(\bm{K}+\bm{q})\approx\dfrac{3a_{\mathrm{cc}}}{2}(-q_x+iq_y)$. Using $f(-\bm{k})=\sum e^{-i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{\delta}_j}=f^*(\bm{k})$, we have $f(\bm{K}'+\bm{q})=f(-\bm{K}+\bm{q})=f(-(\bm{K}-\bm{q}))=f^*(\bm{K}-\bm{q})$. Since $f(\bm{K}-\bm{q})\approx\dfrac{3a_{\mathrm{cc}}}{2}(q_x-iq_y)$, taking the complex conjugate gives

$$ f(\bm{K}'+\bm{q})\approx\frac{3a_{\mathrm{cc}}}{2}(q_x+iq_y). $$

The Hamiltonian is $H_{\mathrm K'}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-tf\\-tf^*&0\end{pmatrix}=-\hbar v_{\mathrm F}\begin{pmatrix}0&q_x+iq_y\\q_x-iq_y&0\end{pmatrix}=-\hbar v_{\mathrm F}\,(\sigma_xq_x-\sigma_yq_y)$ (since the $(1,2)$ component of $\sigma_y$ is $-i$, the $(1,2)$ component of $-\sigma_yq_y$ is $+iq_y$).

For the eigenstates, let $\bm{q}=q(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$, set the upper component to $1$, and denote the lower component by $u$. Then from $-\hbar v_{\mathrm F}q\,e^{i\theta}u=s\hbar v_{\mathrm F}q$ we get $u=-s\,e^{-i\theta}$. The expectation value of the pseudospin is $\langle\bm{\sigma}\rangle=\bigl(\operatorname{Re}u,\ \operatorname{Im}u\bigr)=s\,(-\cos\theta,\ \sin\theta)$, which is the form of $s\,(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ at K reflected by $x\to-x$. When the angle $\theta$ of the direction of $\bm{q}$ increases counterclockwise, the angle of the pseudospin direction turns as $\theta$ (counterclockwise) at K, and as $\pi-\theta$ (clockwise) at K$'$. That is, the helicity (the sense of winding) of the pseudospin is opposite at K and K$'$ (the winding numbers are $+1$ and $-1$). Together with the real spin, this gives a fourfold degeneracy, and the valley degree of freedom becomes the source of the valley-dependent differences in properties that appear when spatial inversion symmetry is broken (for example, on h-BN).

Exercise 65.7: Klein tunneling — massless and massive

Solution

(1) In the massless case, as in the derivation in the main text, a wave traveling to the right always has $\sigma_x=+1$ (spinor $(1,1)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2$), and a wave traveling to the left always has $\sigma_x=-1$ ($(1,-1)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2$). The continuity conditions for the incident wave $(1,1)^{\mathsf T}e^{ik_1x}$, the reflected wave $r\,(1,-1)^{\mathsf T}e^{-ik_1x}$, and the transmitted wave $t\,(1,1)^{\mathsf T}e^{ik_2x}$ (for $x\gt0$, $E-V_0=-0.15\ \mathrm{eV}\lt0$, so this is a valence-band state with $k_2\lt0$, but its group velocity points to the right) are $1+r=t$ for the upper component and $1-r=t$ for the lower component. Hence $r=0$, $t=1$, $T=1$. The reason is that the pseudospin of the transmitted wave points in the same direction as that of the incident wave ($\sigma_x=+1$) and is orthogonal to the pseudospin of the reflected wave ($\sigma_x=-1$), so no reflection occurs unless the potential $V(x)$ flips the pseudospin. The result does not depend on the value of $V_0$, either.

(2) Let $\Delta=0.1\ \mathrm{eV}$, and write $\hbar v_{\mathrm F}k\to k$ in units of energy. The eigenvector $(u_1,u_2)$ of $H=k\sigma_x+\Delta\sigma_z+V$ satisfies, from the first row $(\Delta-\varepsilon)u_1+k\,u_2=0$, $u_2=(\varepsilon-\Delta)u_1/k$, and, from the second row $k\,u_1-(\Delta+\varepsilon)u_2=0$, $u_2=k\,u_1/(\varepsilon+\Delta)$ (the two agree because $\varepsilon^2-\Delta^2=k^2$). The dispersion is $\varepsilon^2=k^2+\Delta^2$. The sign of the group velocity is the sign of $\partial\varepsilon/\partial k=k/\varepsilon$. The current is $j=v_{\mathrm F}\,\psi^\dagger\sigma_x\psi=2v_{\mathrm F}\operatorname{Re}(\psi_1^*\psi_2)$.

Region 1 ($\varepsilon=0.15$): $k_1=\sqrt{0.15^2-0.1^2}=0.11180$, the incident wave is $(1,\ k_1/(\varepsilon+\Delta))=(1,\ 0.4472)$, and the reflected wave ($k\to-k_1$) is $(1,\ -0.4472)$. Region 2 ($\varepsilon=E-V_0=-0.15$): $k_2=\pm0.11180$, and the sign for which the group velocity points to the right ($k_2/\varepsilon\gt0$) is $k_2=-0.11180$. The transmitted wave is $(1,\ k_2/(\varepsilon+\Delta))=(1,\ -0.1118/(-0.05))=(1,\ 2.2361)$. From the matching condition $(1,0.4472)+r(1,-0.4472)=t(1,2.2361)$ we obtain

$$ 1+r=t,\qquad0.4472\,(1-r)=2.2361\,t\ \Longrightarrow\ 0.4472-0.4472r=2.2361+2.2361r\ \Longrightarrow\ r=-0.6667,\quad t=0.3333. $$

The currents are $j_{\mathrm{in}}=2\times0.4472=0.8944$ and $j_{\mathrm t}=\abs{t}^2\times2\times2.2361=0.1111\times4.4721=0.4969$, so $T=j_{\mathrm t}/j_{\mathrm{in}}=0.5556=5/9$, $R=\abs{r}^2=0.4444=4/9$, and $T+R=1$, which means that the current is conserved. We check this against the result for the step in Chapter 64: $p=\sqrt{E^2-\Delta^2}=0.1118$; in the Klein region, $p'=-\sqrt{(E-V_0)^2-\Delta^2}=-0.1118$ (the branch whose group velocity points to the right), $\kappa=\dfrac{p'}{p}\dfrac{E+\Delta}{E-V_0+\Delta}=(-1)\dfrac{0.25}{-0.05}=5$, $T=\dfrac{4\kappa}{(1+\kappa)^2}=\dfrac{20}{36}=\dfrac59$, and $R=\Bigl(\dfrac{1-\kappa}{1+\kappa}\Bigr)^2=\dfrac49$, which agree. For $\Delta\to0$, $\kappa\to1$ and $T\to1$, which returns us to (1).

(3) For $V_0=0.20\ \mathrm{eV}$, in $x\gt0$ we have $\varepsilon=E-V_0=-0.05\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $\abs{\varepsilon}\lt\Delta=0.1\ \mathrm{eV}$, which is an energy inside the gap. Since $k^2=\varepsilon^2-\Delta^2=0.0025-0.01=-0.0075\lt0$, the wavenumber is purely imaginary, $k=\pm i\kappa'$, with $\kappa'=\sqrt{0.0075}=0.0866\ \mathrm{eV}$ (in energy units). The only waves are those that decay as $e^{-\kappa'x/\hbar v_{\mathrm F}}$ (evanescent waves), and there is no wave that carries current to $x\to\infty$, so the transmission coefficient is $T=0$ and $R=1$ (total internal reflection). The decay length is $\hbar v_{\mathrm F}/\kappa'=0.658\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}/0.0866\ \mathrm{eV}=7.6\ \mathrm{nm}$. For a barrier of finite width $d$, just as in the case of the Schrödinger equation, a tunneling current as small as about $e^{-2d/7.6\ \mathrm{nm}}$ flows. We see that when there is a mass, a gap opens, and perfect transmission is lost even at normal incidence.

Exercise 65.8: What happens if the statistics are mixed up

Solution

(1) In the course of the derivation, from the expansion of the Dirac field we obtained $\hat{H}=\sum_{\bm{p},s}E_p\bigl(\hat{b}_{\bm{p}s}^\dagger\hat{b}_{\bm{p}s}-\hat{d}_{\bm{p}s}\hat{d}_{\bm{p}s}^\dagger\bigr)$. If $\hat{d}$ is a boson ($\hat{d}\hat{d}^\dagger=\hat{d}^\dagger\hat{d}+1$), then

$$ \hat{H}=\sum_{\bm{p},s}E_p\bigl(\hat{b}^\dagger\hat{b}-\hat{d}^\dagger\hat{d}\bigr)-\sum_{\bm{p},s}E_p. $$

and the sign of $\hat{d}^\dagger\hat{d}$ remains negative. For the state $(\hat{d}_{\bm{p}\uparrow}^\dagger)^n\ket{0}$ we have $\hat{d}^\dagger\hat{d}=n$ (the occupation number of a boson can take the values $n=0,1,2,\dots$), so the energy relative to the vacuum is $-nE_p$, which becomes arbitrarily low as $n\to\infty$. The energy has no lower bound, and no ground state exists. (The charge also becomes $\hat{Q}=q\sum(\hat{b}^\dagger\hat{b}+\hat{d}\hat{d}^\dagger)=q\sum(\hat{b}^\dagger\hat{b}+\hat{d}^\dagger\hat{d})+\text{constant}$, so a quantum of $\hat{d}$ carries a charge of the same sign as the electron and does not play the role of an antiparticle.) In Fermi statistics, $\hat{d}^\dagger\hat{d}=0,1$, and from $\hat{d}\hat{d}^\dagger=1-\hat{d}^\dagger\hat{d}$ we get $+E_p\hat{d}^\dagger\hat{d}$, so $\hat{H}\ge$ constant is preserved.

(2) Consider the antiparticle operator $\hat{\bar{a}}$ of the Klein–Gordon field (a boson in Definition 65.1). For the Klein–Gordon field, $\hat{H}=\sum\omega_k(\hat{a}^\dagger\hat{a}+\hat{\bar{a}}\hat{\bar{a}}^\dagger)$ (an equation in the middle of the derivation of Theorem 65.1 in Chapter 65). If $\hat{\bar{a}}$ is a fermion ($\hat{\bar{a}}\hat{\bar{a}}^\dagger=1-\hat{\bar{a}}^\dagger\hat{\bar{a}}$), then

$$ \hat{H}=\sum_{\bm{k}}\omega_k\bigl(\hat{a}^\dagger\hat{a}-\hat{\bar{a}}^\dagger\hat{\bar{a}}\bigr)+\sum_{\bm{k}}\omega_k $$

holds. The energy of the vacuum (all $\hat{\bar{a}}$ modes empty) is $E_0=\sum\omega_k$; in the state in which all $\hat{\bar{a}}$ modes are occupied ($\hat{\bar{a}}^\dagger\hat{\bar{a}}=1$), the energy is $\sum\omega_k(1-1)=0$, so $E-E_0=-\sum_{\bm{k}}\omega_k\lt0$. Even a single quantum $\hat{\bar{a}}_{\bm{k}}^\dagger\ket{0}$ has $E-E_0=-\omega_k$, which is lower than the vacuum. If there is no upper bound on the magnitude of the momentum, the number of modes can be increased without limit, so the energy has no lower bound, and the vacuum ceases to be the state of lowest energy. With Bose statistics (commutation relations), $\hat{\bar{a}}\hat{\bar{a}}^\dagger=\hat{\bar{a}}^\dagger\hat{\bar{a}}+1$, so that $\hat{H}\ge$ constant holds.

From the above, we see that imposing commutation relations (Bose statistics) on the spin-0 field and anticommutation relations (Fermi statistics) on the spin-$\tfrac12$ field is the condition for the energy to be bounded from below (a heuristic reason for the relation between spin and statistics).
